Really fascinating game.  Still obviously rough around the edges, especially as the difficulty ramps WAY up in the campaign very fast - I might say frustratingly fast.  A bit more "Clicky" than I normally prefer but a very interesting alternative the the usual RTS fare and a lovely visual presentation.  A lot of potential, assuming it keeps getting developed.
A few things I hope will play out as development goes along:
1) A gentler ramping up of difficulty.  The first two planets are challenging for a newcomer, but easily beaten.  The third one is suddenly far more difficult.  I find this just a bit too punishing - a smoother curve is needed.
2) Something to automate repairs.  Having to manually send out one drone at a time while you're being harried to death is a bit much in my opinion.  Interesting idea but I'm not sure it scans, because there aren't really any "lulls" in combat to support a manual repair mechanic.
3) Menu transitions in the game are too long.  Just getting out of the game when you're done takes thirty seconds or so, which doesn't seem like a lot until you wait through it.
And one suggestion:
Multiple star systems.  This would make a very interesting basis for an extended, or even a procedural campaign mechanic, and would help keep the game fresh.  And after all there are a lot of elements in the Periodic Table.
In spite of my quibbles it's a game that shows a great deal of interest and promise and I am looking forward to seeing it take shape.  Definitely worth its buy-in cost, even taking all the above into account.

Estranged Act I is a Half Life 2 modification released onto steam on January 16, 2014. It was released to good reviews from consumers and large reviewers alike, and is even getting a sequel developed right now. I believe that this is the best HL2 mod out, at least on Steam. This review will contain spoilers for the game, so leave now if you haven't played the game yet.
Story:
One of Estranged's weaker points is it's story, along with it's length. You play as a fisherman that has crashed his boat onto a seemingly deserted island, which turns out to not be the case. There are plenty of people on the island, especially in the sewers and the large Arque Corperation building. Your first encounter will be with Johnathan Daryl, a survivor that came here with his family for a nice vacation. Sadly, you can't find his wife or kids in the game. Presumably, they were killed by the zombies. The zombies don't serve much purpose to the story, they're mostly just used as an excuse to have the island empty and have easy kill fodder. Then you make your way through the island, through the sewers, and through the Arque Corperation building to find a rouge scientist who will help get a message out. But Arque is blocking the signal, so you're set to shut it down, but not before you narowly escape being captured by some Arque goons. After one last shoot out, you find yourself at an abandoned shack. The floor falls under you into a cave, and... the game ends. This is one of the worst cliffhangers I've ever seen in any game or form of media. It's up there with HL2 Episode 2 for me. The game is also very short, my first playthrough took me about an hour, while subsequent ones for achievements took me about 40 - 50 minutes. Still pretty good for an independent mod.
Presentation:
For the Source Engine, this game actually looks really good. It uses lots of assets from the HL2 games, but they're implemented so seemlessly, you won't notice most of them. The music's alright, thought the last shootout music goes way past when it should be over. The game even comes with optional settings that make the game look better, like ambient occlusion, or ssao. The depth of field leaves something to be desired, but it's really good for a mod and for the source engine.
Gameplay:
The gameplay here is your standard FPS/survival horror deal. Just like the Half Life games, the game is very linear, and there's nothing wrong with that for the genre. I like how you can only have one weapon at a time, the flashlight system is good, it's just too bad it doesn't get used a lot. Yes, for a "horror" game, there are barely any dark areas that require a flashlight. I could barely call this game a horror game. There really aren't any jumpscares, besides the first zombie encounter, although I could barely call it a jump scare. It's about as scary as a Half Life game, maybe as scary as Ravenholm in HL2 at certain points. The gameplay still works for what it's worth.
Estranged Act I is the best HL2 mod on Steam that I have played. Yes, I have played Minerva: Metastasis, and I didn't like at much as everyone else. My favorite part of the game would have to be coming upon the train and riding it to the station. It's fun, it's frantic when the zombies appear, and it perfectly sums up this mod. Traditional fun with some tension here and there. Also IT'S FREE. Get it.

Estranged: Act I is a solo only Half-Life 2 mod with a focus on story, shooting, and unique design features.
Gunplay was fun, with far less of the standard "bullet-sponginess" of the base Half-Life 2 that we're used to (Eg, 1 bullet from the pistol to an enemy's head will kill them), but at the same time, isn't some kind of hardcore game either. A nice mix between both, I'd say. The weapons felt a tad recycled from base Half-Life 2. Eg, the pistol has a unique model, but uses the default pistol animations. The enemies on the other hand, felt distinct enough to be unique to Estranged.
The real advantage of this mod (besides being 100% free) is the unique features. Such as using a FULLY interactive desktop terminal, and having to physically (by your own movement) tip over a chair you're strapped to. Basically, this game will keep you interested until completion, and is decent fun.
All-in-all, a good Half-Life 2 mod. Especially good if you're looking for a good break-away from whatever else you're busy with, as its totally free.

The Dawn of War 40k series of RTS games have always included hundreds of units battling it out in a variety of settings and environments. Now, DOWII offers a more squad-focused style of gameplay, with the single player campaign never allowing more than a dozen or so units to be controlled. While singleplayer is interesting, cinematics are rare and explanation of events can be crude.
The Good
Graphics. A huge leap from the 1st generation of DOW games. Smoke, gunfire, enviroment, explosions, look good for an RTS.
Cover. More complex (and realistic) means a more strategic use of units is required.
Campaign. Although not always straight forward, you have more control over the choices avaliable, i.e, where, when you deploy.
The Bad
Scale. DOW games have always been of huuuuge scale. Going to squad sized armies is dissapointing.
Storyline. Not always clear why you are fighting in a region.
Repetitive. Combat is almost the same everytime.
Pace. Much slower
Score: 6.5/10

This game is godly. Go play it, no matter how good you are at bullet hell.
PROS:
- It's very approachable. If you were a complete newbie to the bullet hell genre, you would still be able to blaze through the game on Novice Mode, with unlimited continues, while if you were a shmup killing machine, you would still have lots of fun playing for score on Arcade Mode.

- It's very well-designed. Everything from enemy placement, to enemy amount, was carefully and cleverly adjusted, so that you can feel like you're actually creating completely new strategies, while in reality, the developers expected your every move.
- Clever, well hidden safespots.
- An actual FAIR AND DODGEABLE TLB. I KNOW RIGHT?!
CONS:
- Some stages can be a stray bullet hell. You honestly have no idea how many times I died, just because I didn't notice that one small bullet that wasn't deleted in time.
- Sometimes, my homing shots just wouldn't lock on, for some reason.
- Stage 3 is way harder than Stage 4. (Goddamn enemies with hitboxes.)
No, seriously, go play this game.

Awesome game. It's a big step away from the original Dawn of War. Gone is the base building and resource collecting. DoW II's gameplay sees you dropping in a set number of squads to take on the mission. In this is respect, it mirrors the tabletop game a lot more than the original.
The game is a joy to watch, with everything rendered very nicely. Gameplay is a little awkward at first, as the player will need to take advantage of each unit's inventory and special abilities in order to win. This means a fair bit of fast clicking, but you get used to it. Anyone who mastered Starcraft or Warcraft will find this a walk in the park, as you've only got four units to worry about.
The fact that you can only bring in four squads means that tactics really are important. I've found this game has a lot of tactical depth, and most situations have multiple solutions. If you like games that really make you think and plan ahead, then you'll thoroughly enjoy this.

Alright, let's get this out of the way. Eve is not a perfect MMO.
But it tries, and if you put the time in, you'll find that it comes fairly close.
I have played a lot, a LOT, of Eve. I first subscribed in 2008 after having heard the same stories that you have if you're sitting here trying to decide whether or not to install it. And even having played it for nine goddamn years, I learn new things pretty regularly. This is not a simple game. It's complex in infuriating ways. Until you get the hang of it, the UI is going to get in the way. Although CCP has attempted to improve the new player experience, the underlaying mechanics of how anything works are often frustratingly arcane or counterintuitive. All the cool ships are locked away behind months of skill training. The ♥♥♥♥ing scrollwheel zoom is backwards.
But Eve sucks you in. Yeah, the community is smaller than WoW, for instance, but they're active and they're passionate. You'll make friends and enemies. There are people sitting on my standings list that I've had a grudge against for years, and it works because that's the time scale that you start to think on when you're playing Eve.
I guess there are free-to-play accounts now, and if you want to give Eve a shot it'll be no skin off your nose. But if you do, and I hope you do, take my advice and be social. This isn't a game to play alone.

The Bug Butcher is another balloon popper game, similar to games like Pang Adventure. The only difference is that instead of balloons, you have bugs. The objective is to kill all the bugs in a given level by a specified time limit. You use a machine gun called Ol'Reliable and as you kill bugs, the game will drop boxes that contain weapons such as the rocket launcher, laser beam, lightning gun and gatling gun. The game loop is as follows, play 5 levels of the same floor, go to the elevator and move to the next floor. Rinse and repeat. There are only 5 levels and the only differences between them is the artwork. You will get the same level with only walls blocking you.
Gameplay-wise, it's best to use a controller. Basically, you only need to move left and right, shoot upwards and use your special power. That's it. The special powers come in Boot Juice (where you shoot faster and become invincible), Freeze Grenade (where everything freezes), Homing Missiles (a whole bunch of missiles fly out from out from you).
Conclusion, this isn't really recommendable. The developers, Awfully Nice Studios, made only 5 levels and repeated them over and over again. I was hoping that there was going to be more, like another zone but no. Their entire scheme seems to be to entice players with good marketing and screw the content. Thus, I cannot in good faith recommend this game to anyone. They draw mechas and alien mouths but that's it. They are just drawings and not a tangible boss to fight against.
Note : Awfully Nice Studios is a 2 man team located in Kustein, Austria.
1. Simple Controls
Move left and right and shoot. How much more complexity is there? You don't even need to roll, jump or slide.
2. Faster Pace Relative to Other Balloon Poppers
It's definitely more interesting compared to the slow pace of other balloon poppers.
3. The Forge Hammer
That is the only stage that I felt was different as you had to avoid the hammer crushing you. All the other stages were just the different coloured backgrounds. Even the mouth spitter didn't count.
1. Only 5 Levels
Seriously? That's it? For such simple gameplay, I was expecting at least 20 different levels. You drew big mechs in the background but it never came to pass.
2. Short Game
It's over in 2 hours. 1 hour if you play easy mode.
3. Really Few Mechanically Different Enemies
Most of the enemies just bounce around like balls hitting the walls. You've only got a few interesting models like the lightning bug, scientist eater and big bouncing boss.
4. No Online Multiplayer
It's local co-op max. For a game like this, it would be a simple addition for direct hosting.
5. Repeating the Same Level
This is one of the worst sins. If all you do for every level is change the artwork in the background, at the very least, you could have updated the background each time you play another stage. To play the same level 5 times over is just bad design. A simple additional effect would have made it so much better. E.g. Alarms could go off in stage 2, mechanical arms could go haywire.
6. False Advertising
What is the deal with the mecha? I feel extremely disappointed with this one. You drew it, put it in the ad but it played no part except as a background.

As a casual wrestling gamer I honestly haven't noticed that much of a change from the previous game to this one, yeah sure the roster has been updated and there are a couple of more noticeable features that the previous release didn't have, however if you're asking me whether you can justify almost 80 Australian dollars on this game I honestly don't know if I could give you a definitive yes.
Career mode still feels like a bit of an endless grind, they certainly made improvements from the previous game in relation to the career mode but it still nowhere near as good as you find in other sports games such is NBA 2K17 and now FIFA 17.
Customisation wise I actually feel like they've gone backwards, when creating a custom superstar you can no longer select from premade faces, it's now entirely up to you to supply any kind of individuality to your CAW, the pre-selected attire is still restrictive to say the least, the one thing I will give about the player customisation is the hair you can assign to your custom superstar finally looks halfway to being realistic but is still nowhere near acceptable for a 5 star game.
From a mechanics point of view the game still feels laggy, it still tends to glitch out especially when playing a game involving more than two Superstars, the Royal Rumble mode is near unplayable especially when the ring is filling up.
DLC wise I think they have done the best they could, the NXT addition was a nice improvement to the game, many people wanted Shinsuke Nakamura added to the game and we finally got it.
Overall I would give this game a 7 out of 10, the argument could be made that it's better and more enjoyable than WWE 2K16 and the new features would to some people merit spending the money to upgrade to the new version, however I still believe that it is nowhere near as good as the old SmackDown vs Raw games used to be.
Overall improvements have been made but there is still a very long way to go to call this the best wrestling game ever made, it's in the top 10 but it's probably not in the top 5.

Overall the game aged remarkably well and left me quite stunned as to how modern-games have regressed in terms of making games. To start off I will say there are elements in the game that are rather old-fashioned in comparison to how games have progressed, for example the developers took an extreme use of the ctrl key that is normally used for crouching (or walking depending on the person). So that being said the combat, menus, lockpicking, and nearly every action you can think of is bound to the ctrl key which takes time to get used to.
The story of the game was all that a generic story tells and nothing more. I wouldn't expect for people to play this game and be stunned as to the twists that the story told, everything comes at face value in the game, and it's meant to be taken more light-heartedly than other RPGs of it's kind as told by the dialogue and various cutscenes.
The combat is relatively interesting and I was reminded of the style of combat that Witcher (CDProjekt RED) decided to use as well. So much so that I even thought perhaps it was the same developers working on the games. I can't say for sure but it is mighty suspicious knowing that Gothic 1 was distributed by CD Projekt a subsidary of CD Projekt RED. It's mainly odd that no one mentions the connection that Gothic 1 had rhythmic styled fighting where you press the directional movement (with ctrl) in accordance to how your character holds the sword. At any rate I can help but feel that Witcher was inspired by Gothic possibly through the connection mentioned above or simply because it was quite popular for it's time, your choice.
I'll go ahead and say there wasn't anything sound-wise in the game to make me hate having to hear the same song over and over again. But I also won't say I heard anything too spectacular aside from the one german band that wandered it's way into Chapter 2 of the story in Old Town.
Now for some odd faults I found with the game. I'll say previous to this that there was an unofficial patch I found out about after finishing the game with a vanilla playthrough. This could be a fix to all the problems I'm going to mention, but I feel I should say some of them anyways.
-Ladders are completely broken in certain areas which can leave players stuck
-Enemies can completely dodge attacks infinitely until you block and allow them to attempt a shot at the hero
-Enemies grouping give an unfair experience due to you being unable to attack anything but the single target you lock on to while they can mindlessly swing at you
-Getting hit causes the hero to get 'stunned' See: Enemies grouping^ to understand why this sucks so horribly
-Any and all animations are not invincible animations and while I can understand why this is placed in certain areas, the final boss desperately should have had some sort of invincibility frames when doing actions
-Mud
-Humans are completely annoying to kill which leads back to invincibility animations as you have to stop attacking them when they fall to the ground, and THEN press ctrl+up to finish them off otherwise they'll infinitely stand back up
-Mud again because he got me stuck in the bed when he tried to dialogue with me as I tried to sleep and was forced to reload a save quite a ways back
-other odd glitches and whatnot such as clipping through the floor and just dying or sliding off areas that didn't appear to be unsafe leading to untimely deaths
Overall despite the glaring flaws towards the end of the game (at least to me), the first half of the game was amazingly fun.
The main reason I disliked the last half of the game is because it felt like it was working backwards while trying to progress, for example I had someone working on giving me a piece of armor while I had already gotten the end-game armor. And he still hadn't finished the armor that was weaker than the one I'd gotten. It just felt like I was constantly dealing with stuff like this. Another instance was when I was a high-ranking member of the city and was told that I couldn't buy armor since I was a stranger.
To me this is something easily worth checking out and be sure to look for the unofficial patch, perhaps it'll make the game even better for you than I since I had encountered so many bugs.
Also there are tons of bugs with simply STARTING the game
Here's a quick troubleshoot list before I found an end-all solution for my problem
If you get an error when you try starting the game, i.e. you can launch the game but then you get an error when you load or start a new game.
-Disable Steam Community
If that doesn't work
-Run Gothic as an Administrator
The final one
-Disable sound in the .ini Gothic file or in the settings menu
This doesn't have to be the background music, but it does take away all dialogue/sound effects for the rest of the game including cutscenes. But doing this fixed the game entirely for me and I no longer had any start-up issues.
Again patch may or may not fix this.

TL;DR: I really liked this game. Even if you don't like "walking simulators" you might like this game since it has a good story.
Everything in the game has meaning; every word, every image. Remember in English class when your teacher tried to get you to look for the meaning in a story and you didn't get it? Well, this game is filled with hidden meanings. Being able to actually walk around in a world and experience it rather than read about it makes it so much easier to see the hidden meanings. While the game points out what you need to interact with to continue the story, it doesn't point out anything else.
If you're a cryer, you're going to cry at some point in the game. If you're not a cryer, you're going to hold back tears at some point. That doesn't mean this is a story where the writer was thinking how they can make the story as sad as possible. We learn about each family member and experience what it was like to be them. Even though each of these experiences is short, it makes each story feel tragic rather than just a random senseless death.
The lighting sets the mood as we enter and explore through the house. The house feels like it's been lived in with the living areas filled with books, family pictures, and other various things. You can imagine what each family member was like, looking through the things they left behind when they died.
Despite the tragedies that have afflicted the Finches, this is a very enjoyable game.

Probably the best western game on Steam right now. You play as a gunslinger who is hunting down his family's killer. You gather clues about your culprit's identity through a bunch of different (side-)quests. The murderer is different every playthrough, which makes this game highly replayable.
What makes this game unique is its surprisingly large open world, along with its interesting mechanics. You can pull your gun on anyone, including important NPCs, and this sometimes leads to unique dialogue. Everyone can die, too.
The combat-system is surprisingly intuitive, if a bit simple. You can carry up to three hats. These hats protect you from gunshots. If you get hit, you lose one. If you get hit when your hat-stash is depleted, it's game over, and you'll have to restart from the last checkpoint.
All in all, I highly recommend this game. It's worth it at full price, and a must-buy when it's on sale.

Because it was very misleading.
I never got into EVE as I wasn't interested in paying for yet another online game, so, when I saw an official advertisment stating "Play EVE for free" I said it's worth giving it a go.
The games systems are quite alright, plenty of choice for ships, weapons, mods, playstyle, you get my point.
BUT
The game is NOT free. Not more than World of Warcraft is.
If WOW would state it's a "free game" everyone would respond: Bull$%*#. Even though, you can play wow up to lvl 20 and enjoy EVERY aspect of the game up to that point.
Why is this relevant?
Because EVE states that it's free in order for you to give it a try, but after you get past the "tutorial" /hand-holding little part at the start of the game, you see a lot of premium status barriers.

To all those saying this version doesn't have good graphics and the hd patch is the same they are completely wrong. I have both versions and this one has far superior graphics.
What the unofficial hd patch does is blow the map portion up to 1920x1080 so it fills your screen. It doesn't increase the resolution of any of the assets, and probably most irritating to me, it doesn't rescale the UI to match the larger resolution. So yeah, you see a huge area of map all shrunk down, but all the icons and creatures and towns are tiny! I actually had to downsize my res to like 1400 something just so I could read the text without squinting.
The HD remake here on steam is a ton better. It displays in 1920x1080 but it keeps the correct scaling of UI and creatures. And they look really nice, they have been touched up for this edition.
So all these people complaining about price, really you get what you pay for sometimes, or wait for a sale. I got my copy of a humble bundle. Although I do understand missing the expansions, that could be a deal breaker. But just want to put to rest the idea that the hd patch is equal to this remake- it's not at all. This version is comfortable to play and definitely doesn't feel like a 15 year old game.

WWE 2k17 fixes a lot of my gripes about previous editions. They stepped it up on graphics and people look way more realistic this year than ever. Face scanning is actually done correctly in this game allowing the community to do amazing things. They took the restrictive editing of imported superstars from last year in MyCareer as you can change everything about downloaded content. The matches are more exciting and not a drag. I recall last year having to completely destroy your opponent no matter who it is to win. This year it actually matters who you face. I've had matches with Sin Cara that last about 5 mins and matches against Seth Rollins that take 10-15 mins where we actually pushed each other to the limit. The MyCareer isn't as grindy as previous years which I like a lot more. VC is more easily obtained and you aren't grinding for 100 hours to get your character to a decent level.
Tutorials in this game are a hit or miss, there are some things that are well explained and others that aren't explained at all. Leaving to a lot of confusion sometimes. Nothing that will ruin the experience for you but it can be slightly annoying. The game currently crashes sometimes during loading transitions which is a big part of the game. I assume it will be fixed but it has been an issue for almost 2 days now. I also wish they allowed you to skip the intro to the show every week. Not only is it super repetitive but it is also glitched to where the logo on the titantron constantly loops, creating an annoying sound. The Characters voiceover is questionable. I don't know if it's glitched or if they are supposed to not have dialouge in promo's and such. They did last year so it only makes sense that they would right?
Overall WWE 2k17 is a great experience that will leave you wanting to play and is definitely a step forward for the franchise. It's a little buggy and they could have made better choices here and there but it's worth a look at.

A decent Arcade style Shoot em up, its got good music, good sound, good 2D graphics. You get 4 kinds of ships, one is unlockable, all ships only differ in shot width and movement speed. Basically this is some nice old fashioned arcade action. You fill your gauge up and get breaker and double breaker modes, doubling then trippling your fire power.
When you activate that breaker mode, you unload on your enemies, they start exploding, the screen starts shaking, god damn it's a good feeling. You also have this other weapon, basically a missle system. You hold the button down, enemies around you get marked, then when you release the button, missiles get fired at them; while you hold this button down, you move a bit slower.
Why do I not recomend this game though? Because of 2 flaws:
1.) Your ship moves way too freaken fast, every ship has two speeds, fast as♥♥♥♥♥♥ and too fast. As you need to dodge a lot of bullets in this game, many of which slow moving, that means you need to move through some pretty tight spaces. Try doing that at top speed, you can't be precise enough to survive. The slowest speed your ship goes, is just too fast.
2.) The slow down button is also an attack button. So when you hold down the missle button, you move slow, but when you release it to fire the missiles, you suddenly go super sonic speed. And since your holding then releasing the button often, you basically shift from moving ultra fast, to just fast. Try dodge bullets while doing this! In the later levels, there are some things that you need to kill as fast as possible, while dodging bullets. So that means holding and releasing the missle button, which makes to shift speeds. It is agonizing.
Aside from that the game is just very generic, theres nothing really new in terms of weapons or level design. Despite that, it could still be fun if not for the above problems.
I must say I do enjoy the game up to the end of level 2, but level 3 and beyond it becomes purely anoying.

Now let me tell you about my little experience with the saintly clover. For the keen eye Cave's two color shot and speeds with score system and hyper mode (aka Break Mode) , some layer locking and secondary shot slowdown, AND even Cho Ren Sha's "trinity" Power-up all says you're in for a good time. Mind you though, the above is just an over time sentement. This is a key modern arcade shooter for the budding pilot and 'core grazer' alike.

Early Access Watcher Public Service Announcement
Game: Fapic
Version: Initial Release
Gameplay Footage:
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Where do I ever begin with this one? Fapic is a project that starts off in a side view room and drops you into the sixth dimension. You meet a guy outside a portal then drop down onto a barren landscape that randomly pops in enemies and has a bizarre music loop that repeats segments randomly. Textures overlap in some areas while the obvious layout lines crossover and lead to areas missing textures. The guy you meet also discusses a few points, but his volume adjustment is set low enough to barely be audible. There is no tutorial or any options menu to speak of outside the Unity pre-start up for windowed/resolution. There is a input selection along side the pre-start up, but my changes didn’t seem to save properly.
The only good thing I could say about this title: sprinting is on by default. Given the barren terrain, running is about all you can do. Turning causes the character to stagger a second, walking animates a single step then stops, and jumping sends you about twenty feet into the air with a chance of screwing up the camera. It looks awkward no matter what you do, thanks to the worst camera positioning I have ever seen. It can randomly change from looking behind Mark with the focal point on his lower back to the camera panning out so Mark is running at the left side of the screen. This alone made playing the project intolerable.
Combat is probably the worst offender in this maelstrom. Enemies spawn upon reaching certain areas and follow you until they are able to melee you. If you run far enough away, they will disengage or you can just roll out of the way to avoid undetectable attack animation. I have yet to kill a single enemy using the standard laser that causes a reflex mechanic, but doesn’t seem to cause any damage. The only enemy types I have seen are some green guys, a blue hulk and a suited individual that looks similar to Slenderman if he had definition added to his face. Regardless of how long I kept the stream on them, they would persist and eventually cause the game over screen to appear.
The game over screen has some interesting glitches, ranging from continual firing, health bar manipulation and automatic cancellation to the menu screen. I also discovered saving did nothing and loading just returns you to the default starting point. Hitting quit will do the same, as well as lock up the game, or not work at all. I was forced to restart my pc in these situations since it would lock up the screen and prevent access to the task manager. The game crashes on exiting from the menu anyway, so I wasn’t surprised by most of these issues.
I spent more time on this then I really needed. I have seen some messes on Early Access, but they at least felt playable. This was just infuriating to maneuver and left me utterly baffled. I cannot recommend this project. I will end it with that before I find myself questioning the lack of curation with Steam Direct.

Bombing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s is a pretty funny game. It definitely shines in the multiplayer department, but the solo play is decent as well, albeit pretty hard and sometimes frustrating.
The game reminds me a lot of the good old bomberman, that I used to play good 20 years ago. You drop bombs left and right, and try to demolish all other creatures on screen, while trying not to blow yourself up - easier said than done! You place the bomb exactly where you stand, so it's pretty easy to trap yourself. The bombs don't really indicate, when they are gonna explode, so you have to rely on your inner timer about that. I think in the original bomberman the bombs were changing colors or blinking to help you see, when things are gonna go boom - this could definitely be a positive change for Bombing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
The game has quite a few upgrades for your character, or for your bombs - some are mutually exclusive - for example you can't have piercing bombs and bombs with a timer at the same time. Once you start getting a lot of upgrades, downgrades will start to appear to make stuff more interesting. I have not seen an upgrade time out on the screen, but they do get destroyed by bombs or creatures walking over them. The upgrade drop is random and can be somewhat frustrating, if you keep getting not the ones you "need"/ want, in order to achieve 3 stars for the level.
The controls are ok, it would be a plus if I get to rebind them. You can use either a keyboard, keyboard + mouse or a gamepad. My universal gamepad was working just fine, so I used that.
There are quite a few different enemies to blow up and the bosses in adventure mode are pretty challenging as well. The music is solid and I even found it pretty good at times - it's electronic spinoff of classical pieces. The voice acting is pretty witty and well done.
I would like to praise the multiplayer connection options - you can pick from LAN / WAN and even direct IP - always nice to see! Since I think multiplayer is the game's strong suit, I would love to see a 2- and / or 4-pack bundles available for purchase.

This game is not for the faint hearted. It is very slow paced with a significant learning cliff, the developers have lessened the difficulty of getting into this game with the excellent tutorials and learning features introduced into the game over the years.
But the depth of knowledge you learn as you play makes this game very interesting to those who want more than a point and shoot experience. Yes, it is a “spreadsheet” game, but only through the detailed stats of ships and equipment you use and trade. Similar in aspects to comparing weapons and armor in say Skyrim but with so much more depth. And then having a player driven market very much like the X Universe in complexity.
I have been playing this game over 10 years on and off, my oldest character is from 5th May 2007. I have amassed 100 million skill points and I am still unable to flying or do a lot of aspects in the game. I can say mining is very relaxing and profitable venture, if you’re looking at doing industry and crafting this would be the best place to start in eve.
Combat in EVE is very tactical under the hood and dependent of your ability with your skills and equipment. Best place to start with PvP is to do missions to learn the mechanics and train the skills before advancing onto PvP in low security space or null security space.
Then you have all the aspects of the game which take parts of both above main areas, wormholes are very rewarding with valuable loot and ore’s but comes with a lot of risk. Exploration can also yield relic and data sites which drop rewards to aid in crafting and industry. Null security space and low security space offer different experiences of PvP with varying rewards (the best DED sites, abundant ores, C6 wormholes) and difficulty set by the other players (i.e. are your neighbours friendly? Is your corporation/alliance stable and capable?). With all of the above sellable for profit ;)
The greatest reward in any situation in EVE is the experience and interaction with the other players, forming corporations (guilds) to achieve goals from Merc’s for hire to Manufacturing. But also, when facing individual situations through playing the game, the brutal experience of finding a gate camp or getting caught in a wormhole and killed. Or helping another player in need. Whichever side you happen to be on; in EVE, like many MMO's, the experience is made from the other players you meet and is the core “mechanic” of this game.

Westerado: Double Barrelled looks, at first glance, like a cheapie indie game. The graphics are extremely primitive and blocky, and the game itself is extremely simple.
And yet, when you play it, you realize that some real love went into making it. Unfortunately, while this game has some real charm in its Western theming, and it certainly is clever in some ways, by the end of it I was left feeling as if it never really delivered.
But I’m getting ahead of myself.
Westerado is a pretty simple game – you move around in a top-down 2D fashion, you can talk to people and interact with (a very small number of objects) with A, you pull out your gun with the right shoulder button, you♥♥♥♥♥♥your gun and shoot it with right trigger (and you must♥♥♥♥♥♥your gun before firing it), and you reload with the left shoulder button. That’s it.
Where the game is interesting is that it is a mystery game – the central driving theme of the game is that your family was murdered and you, the Gunslinger, are going out into the desert to the nearby towns to collect clues. You’re given one random clue by your dying brother at the start of the game, and you must collect additional clues by talking to people – and, mostly, by completing various tasks on their behalf. The Native Americans want you to drive off the farmers and help them kill the soldiers and take over the nearby town. The Sheriff is depressed and needs to get back in the saddle, and his cowardice leaves you responsible for looking after the local people. The local railroad has had its tracks blocked off by some bandits, who are being paid off by the Banker, who in turn is in debt to the Oil Baron…
There’s a bunch of pretty standard Western tropes at play here, and the game plays with them, simultaneously poking fun at the tropes while simultaneously mostly playing them straight. For instance, your health is represented by hats, and when you get shot, your hat gets shot off – at which point you put on another hat. If you are shot when you are hatless, you die. You can buy new hats at the hatteries, which are definitely not at all suggestive of brothels, and you can also get hats by shooting them off the heads of enemies.
And yet, the game is often pretty serious – people can and do die, and you can even kill off main characters (or get them killed off when they follow you around on quests). Moreover, it is a revenge plot, as you try to track down your family’s murderer, and it plays that revenge plot quite straight – the murderer really is a terrible person, and when you gun them down at the end, your own homicidal tendencies are put under close examination.
The game has a lot of quests, and these quests, though short, are how you get most of your clues. Helping out various people with various deeds – some moral, some evil, some gray – helps you accumulate clues, and completing entire questlines with people will often reshape the world in some way.
The intent of the game’s multiple endings is to make these plots matter – if you follow a plot through to the end, the ending of the game will reveal that your family’s murder is related in some way to what you did during the game.
It also makes the game replayable – if you only complete enough quests to get enough clues to find the (randomized in appearance) murderer, who poses as one of the townsfolk in the towns, you can then play the game through again, do a different questline, and then track down the murderer again and get a different ending.
However, you can do a great deal of the content in a single playthrough, and this at times makes the game exhibit some odd bugs, such as the oil baron getting to take over a lot of land despite the fact that I never helped him, or a character making reference to some event they couldn’t have seen because they weren’t around at that location to observe it. This was kind of disappointing, and drew me out of the world in my first playthrough.
My other problem with this game is that, in the end, while the game’s simplicity is a virtue, it also didn’t really give the game much in the way of variety – ultimately, you just use your gun to shoot bad guys, and talk to people. The bad guys are all pretty samey in the end, with limited variety, and you have seen all that the game has to offer within the first hour or so of gameplay. And while the game itself is pretty short – and indeed, there’s an achievement for beating it within an hour, something which is eminently doable – after I beat it for the first time I wasn’t left feeling like I really needed or wanted to do so again.
This isn’t a terrible game, but it isn’t a very meaty one. If you appreciate very short games, and are willing to go after the murderer fairly swiftly, I suspect this may be okay for you; if you try to play this like a RPG where you try and complete all the sidequests before beating the final boss, I suspect you’re going to feel a bit disappointed.

If you can look past some rough edges and old-fashioned design, considering the game's age, you'll find a rather simple and charming game. Gothic 1 starts off with you being thrown into a prison colony and you'll have to decide which of the three factions causes suits you the best.
The game is fully voiced with some pretty goofy voice-acting quality at times.
The interface can be rather cumbersome but you can definitely get used to it. What might stick in your craw are the controls; movement often feels clumsy; combat is stiff but does require a bit of skill to time your attacking and blocking correctly. Get the rhythm right and you can take on some really tough customers and walk away with a kickass new weapon and a bunch of money.
If you're willing to put up with Gothic 1's quirks then you will be pleased as peach when you move on to Gothic II, which follows up the story immediately; it's also an excellent upgrade in all technical aspects. Better progression, bigger map, higher stakes, vastly better interface and control..
Certainly something to look forward to.

This game is fantastic. Absolutely fantastic. Despite its simple graphics, the game is visually stunning, with some backdrops looking intensely gorgeous. The dialogue is well written, the game mechanics are fascinating, and the story is simple, yet satisfying.
It's a simple revenge story, but with a hint of mystery thrown in. I won't spoil the ending, as you need to play it to fully understand this, but once it's finally over, it's overwhelmingly satisfying.
The freeroam aspect of this game is also great - you can kill pretty much whoever you want (with very few exceptions), do whatever you want, help whoever you want, fight whoever you want, and you can even play card games in one of the two saloons.
This game is also full of references and easter eggs, as well as another hidden little story about a certain group of bandits that doesn't affect the story, but adds another layer of depth to this game.
There are very few problems, but I guess I should mention them. The combat system can be a little annoying to new players, and it can sometimes seem a little unfair. However, once you've mastered the gunfighting system, it's pretty straightforward - draw weapon,♥♥♥♥♥♥weapon, shoot weapon, reload - and it does add a little more accuracy to this game (which to be fair isn't very outlandish to begin with).
Do I recommend this game? Yes. This game is absolutely fantastic, and definitely deserves to be played.

This might be my first review because this game is so dang fun, I thought it deserved one.
This game is very fun.  I got it on sale from the Humble Bundle Store, and it was a great decision, but I'd gladly pay the full $10.

You play the game as a freelance stealth agent.  You can take jobs from various client who want you to infiltrate buildings and steal/manipulate information.  To do this, you rewire buildings' electrical systems, avoid guards, sneak around in the dark, and hack computer systems.  Each mission is a puzzle that can be solved in a number of different ways.

As you complete missions, you earn cash.  You can purchase new devices that let you take on other missions or help you complete missions easier.
Also, the music in this game is outstanding.  You get to listen to cool jazz (a la Miles Davis) while infiltrating competing businesses that have hired you against each other.  It gives the game a cool noir atmosphere.
The graphics are not the point of the game.  They communicate what you need to know in a slick and stylized manner.  They're perfect for what they're intended to do.

Last thing, I'm only an hour in, but I'm loving the plot/writing.  I usually do not care AT ALL about that sort of thing, but it adds to the experience as a whole and is very enjoyable.

Ah, the Bug Butcher, it quickly made its way into my favorites. Why? Because it is simple and addictive little game. Older players will find the mechanics similar to the ‘Pang’ game of many, many years ago.
The premise is simple, there are creatures bouncing around and you shoot them, however when they are hit, they will split up into smaller aliens, until they are to small to further split up and only then truly die. In the very early levels this is pretty easy, but as you can imagine, more enemies will be on the playing field in later levels and things get hectic pretty fast.
It’s better then Pang in many ways. First, the enemies have attacks, which the balloons in Pang never had. That is OK because you have so many power-ups available and between levels you can upgrade your weapons, speed, armor, etc.
Secondly, The crispy hand-drawn 2D graphics are full of colors and charm, excellent animations which go hand-in-hand with excellent sound effects. The weapons all have a satisfying sound as well as the splattering-splut sound when killing aliens. Characters speak goobly gook between eachother, not sure if that was really needed, but it doesn’t take away any of the fun.
On top of the excellent single player game, you can also play this with a buddy, turn up the hectic dial to 11!
Highly recommended if you’re looking for a no-nonsense, simple, straight forward, shoot’em’up.

The first episode of the previous season did not leave a good first impression, and when the first episode of this one goes free you can see the improvements they made.
I recommend this because it’s more of the same from season 1 – but with all of the improvements in story and characterization that was apparent into the latter episodes of the first season.  Episode 1, so far, feels like a HUGE step in the right direction: an epic, self-contained single story that opens up a larger arc.
I’ll be looking forward to checking out the rest of the season!

I blew a hole in a wall with a sticky grenade, grappling hooked through it, then slashed a guy with my energy sword before touching the ground. Soon after, I narrowly escaped a horde of zombies on my hoverbike before accidentally running it off a cliff. Later, I pulled a guy out of a helicopter using my newly-grown zombie tentacles and ate him.
That was my first hour playing this game, so yeah, I would say I got my $2 worth almost immediately.
This game looks silly, and it definitely is. But the gameplay is solid, with lots of variation and fun to be had. Gunplay is very similar to the original Halo, with community maps and gamemodes that exceed the scope of any FPS I've played before. The simple, 90's era graphics might be a turn off for some, but they really allow the gameplay to flourish in ways big studio FPS games rarely do. Maps can be massive in scale, vertically and horizontally. The community created maps range from entirely original, unique concepts, to faithful recreations of classic FPS maps (the other day I was playing CTF on Halo's Blood Gulch and Zombie mode on Goldeneye's Complex). The rudimentary graphics also mean the game runs as smooth as butter, with no latency or framerate issues to speak of.
In short, this game is immediately fun, excellently conceived and executed, and is a great value at only $2. Recommended ad infinitum.

What is HoMM?
Some people might have never even heard of this game, and most of the reviews I've seen are just pointing out the differences and not explaining what the actual game is.
Heroes of Might and Magic III is a turn-based Fantasy strategy game. You play a faction of your choice (Or depending on the scenario a specific one) based on many different mythological fantasies.
First up is the Castle. These are the humans of the game, based on high-fantasy humanity, Griffins, Pikemen, Swordsman, Knights, etc. Fairly basic, not too much fantasy there, but still a fun game.
Fortress: This is a Swamp-based faction, such as Lizard men, Dragonfly, Gorgon and even Hydra. Most of these creatures all follow that theme.
Dungeon: Pretty much what it says on the box. Beholders, Minotaur, Black Dragon, Beholders, Naga, the things you can expect in a higher-fantasy underground based faction.
Rampart: The true 'high fantasy' faction, in my eyes. Dwarves, Elves, Unicorn, Centaur. These are the woodland creatures which are staple in nearly all high fantasy settings.
Tower: This is the 'magical' faction, so to speak. Magi, Animated Golem, Gargoyles and Genie are the sort of units you'll expect from here.
Necropolis: Much like the dungeon, it's self explanatory. Skeletons, Undead, Lich, Vampires, etc. The darkest of the factions focused on the risen dead.
The game is played on an 'overhead map' where you control a hero with a certain set of movement, exploring the map and fighting monsters. Capturing things like Gold Mines and Crystal mines will generate those resources each turn (very valuable). The aim of the game is to simply beat your enemy in most scenarios. Although there are some specific campaign levels and scenarios where you have to achieve a certain objective, such as Kill X, take Y or find Z.
Upon engaging an enemy you effectively zoom into a turn-based battlefield where your units are on one side and the enemy's are on the other. It's your job to command your troops (Each has specific health, attack, etc) and simply kill all the enemy (Unless they retreat)
Each type of unit will stack into one group unless you split them and choose otherwise. (For example you can have a near unlimited amount of units in a single stack as long as they are the same troop, EG. 14 Swordsman)
The way you recruit units is by going into your cities and Purchasing the required buildings. You may only build one a turn so you should think things through before you buy them. For example, the game revolves around a weekly/monthly system, where each turn is one day. At the start of the week you can buy a fresh set of recruited troops. So it's often best on the later days of the week to either buy a building that unlocks new troops, or purchase something that increases the amount of men you generate per week, such as the Griffon Bastion in the Castle faction (Generates extra griffon a week).
In conclusion it's a fairly decent game, It has it's problems now as it also had it's problems then, is it worth the full price they're asking? No, not in my opinion. But if you can grab it on offer? Yeah, I'd say it's worth it. Even more so if you use Steam as your sole games platform. As stated at the top at the time of writing this review you can pick it, and many many more Might and Magic games up on the Humble Bundle.

When the granddaughter of a scientist who can create a drug that will give the terrorist organization known as the Bloody Scorpion Group control over super-soldiers is kidnapped they call in the Shock Troopers.
Eight members head off to take out the BSG either as "Lonely Wolf" operatives (all three lives are one character, like a normal game) or as a three-person team (when you lose one life, one of your other chosen team members steps in, or you can swap them in at will). You'll fight your way through jungle, mountain, or valley terrain to reach BSG HQ.
Depending on the route you choose the scenery, as well as the types of soldiers and weaponry you face, will be somewhat specific to each of these terrains. Each of these routes consists of six stages you have to battle through to win the game, and halfway through you are given the option to switch routes for the rest of the way.
Your default gun is a standard machine gun that has infinite ammo, but you can pick up special weapons and get a temporary boost in your destructive power, at least until your ammo runs out.
These weapon pickups include the Heavy Machine Gun, Vulcan, Flamethrower, 3-Way & Tank Buster. There is also the weapon pickup simply titled Bomb.
Each of the eight characters in this game has a unique secondary weapon of the explosive variety (grenades, napalm, rocket launcher, etc.), by grabbing a Bomb pickup you'll add one additional weapon to this inventory.
A more rare but equally as important pickup are the various health pickups available in this game. They come in various forms, such as a first aid kit, a can of some sort of drink, a bunch of bananas, a side of meat, etc.
Another rare pickup is the S pickup, which stands for speed. When you grab it your character will be temporarily granted with a massive boost in foot speed.
The final item you'll come across in Shock Troopers are various coloured diamonds, which sometimes appear on their own but usually appear after you kill an enemy in close range combat (hand to hand, without your weapon).
The blue diamond gives you bonus points, the yellow diamond grants you temporary invincibility, and the red diamond destroys every enemy currently on the game screen.

One of my biggest gripes with the open world genre as of recent is how the main quest always seems to conflict with the idea of "do whatever you want, go wherever you want" that these games intend to transmit. "The world is under threat by an evil force and I am the only one who has the mcguffin to stop it, but im going to help this man find his goat first"
There always seems to exist a clash between the optional content and the main quest of these games, where the urgency of  the main storyline is brought to a hault so the player can do some side missions that in no way influence the outcome of the plot. This is not the always the case, but I do see some struggle in making a worthwhile and compelling story intertwined with sidequests, and even big games like Witcher 3 suffer from it, having a Hero's Journey narrative as the main quest when the optional content is so much more entertaining and interesting, and so removed from what you expect of the main storyline.
This isnt an easy thing to do, I can think of Morrowind and New Vegas as games that manage those aspects very well.
Well, I can now add Westerado to those games that balance the main quest with the optional ones.
In Westerado, your family is killed by a criminal, and your objetive is to find out who this guys is so you can kill him. Thats it. Simplistic I know, but it works wonders for how the game's quests revolve around that main goal.
You see, everytime you do a favor for someone in this world, they will give you a clue about how the bad guy looks, narrowing it down a-la Guess Who? boardgame.
This criminal is of course randomized, so the nature of the game is about replaying it so you can see the different outcomes of every storyline, because you essencially create it using the template the game provides you as a canvas.
Its such a simple thing, but it makes every single quest mean something to the main plot and giving you the choice of how you want to build that main plot since every quest can factor to the end goal.
Quests even intertwine with others, creating some surprising domino effects that increase the game's replayabilty.
The game also has an hilarious mechanic where you can pull out your revolver mid conversation with NPCs and just shoot them if you are sick of hearing them. You can literally kill everyone and still reach the ending and in fact, the game lets you accuse anyone you find on the street from the get-go and you could actually find the criminal just by mere coincidence doing that.
These simple yet inventive design choices for the game provide some quite hilarious and movie inspired scenes where you are pulling your gun at everyone, making false accusations and creating a quick bloodbath.
Now, im aware that this alone isnt gonna get Westerado all the awards for best storytelling or whatever, but I wish other games would be this creative about how they implement their narratives on games and I think this game is a great source of inspiration for it.
I really appreciate when games manage to merge gameplay and story in a meaningful way to the point you cant distinguish them, and I think you wont waste your time on this underappreciated gem.
As for the rest, you can already see it has very charming pixel art and cool Western aestethic, and the game doesnt shy away from showing from what movies it takes inspiration from. Good soundtrack and a great sense of humor.
This isnt a very long game so take that into consideration going into it, its all about replaying it .

I am old. My first PC game purchase ever was Heroes of Might and Magic III. A Windows 95 CD-Rom with an instruction book on real paper and my PC was not even met the requirements. It was an amazing experience. Little figures on a map searching for treasures and fighting monsters was something I only knew from table top games and now happened live on my 14" CRT screen.
A whole world opened for me and since then I was really addicted to the Fantasy Turn Based Strategy genre.
Later played the Warlords series, the Age of Wonders series and the Disciples series.
Almost 20 years later I still have Homm3 installed on my PC and now and then I even met people with the same experience from this game and we play hotseat together a whole night.
I still own the original homm3 box, the Shadows of Magic boxed edition, the Collector's edition and the GOG version and when I don't have one available when I'm somewhere else I pirate it for a moment. I guess that's legal because I own the game in four different versions.

Actual Review:
Westerado's a game where you go around shooting bandits and finding clues as to who slapped your ranch, mother, and brother with fire and bullets. Everything about the murderer is random; from his look, to his allegiances, hell, he can even be your pops. Now that's freaky.
The game world isn't too big, but it's fun to explore and filled with personality. However, the game can be incredibly short, especially when one character gives you a metric ♥♥♥♥ ton of clues in one go. This is one game I wouldn't mind having some padding, frankly. Hell, each time I've played the game I've killed the murderer before I even bought a second revolver! Shame.
Since I wrote this review, I've unlocked the other two characters. Hero is totally standard. He starts off with 3 hats and a revolver, and can take 4 hits before death with full hats. Brother is different; he starts with a revolver AND dual revolvers (which I didn't even realize until I tried to buy the dual revolvers from the general store, that was embarassing) and he can't wear hats. He's basically the "What you thought this game was going to be when you bought it" character. Sister and Indian are basically different looking Hero-s with different weapons (Sister has a shotgun and revolver, Indian has like a tomahawk or something).
The combat is...unusual. You and enemies can only fire horizontally; no diagonals or verticals here. I can understand why they wouldn't let you shoot diagonally, but I feel like if they let you shoot vertically it could make the combat even better; then again, the final boss basically hinges on the fact that you can only shoot horizontally, so...yeah. The AI is decent enough, but it's really easy to trick them by camping near a transition...zone...thing...and killing them all there. I used this tactic a lot against groups simply because I found it amusing how they couldn't follow me out of their area. But if you actually fight in the zone the combat is much more tense and entertaining.
Also, if you kill enough bandits, those that are still alive will become absolutely terrified of you and won't shoot unless you do. It's a beautiful thing :,)
Oh, also, all the controls are on the keyboard.
tl;dr: westerado is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing and if you like twinstick shooters and rpgs you should totally play it

Alright, so this my first time reviewing a game on Steam, and I felt I had to do it because this game is really awesome. It's huge in every sense of the word - long, hard (that's what she said :P) and has a level of freedom you wouldn't expect from a game more than ten years old. You can do pretty much everything you want - sleep, grill meat, forge weapons, make potions, skin animals and take their teeth  and even smoke pot and sell it for profit - and go anywhere you want in the game's world without a quest asking you to go there.
The sun rises and sets, NPC sleep, wake up, work, gather to talk with each other, etc. etc.
Being a RPG, the development of the character is always important in such a genre, and Gothic really shines in that department. You start as a poor weakling who gets beaten up by everyone and hardly can kick  harmless little creatures called meatbugs. Then, as you complete quests and defeat enemies, you gain XP which can be converted in strength, dexterity and mana points. You go all the way to a badass warrior, a lethal ranger or a supreme mage - you chose how you want to play it.
As for the bad parts, I just can think of one: the game is VERY buggy, and that can totally ruin your game experience if you don't know how to avoid it.
A few important considerations about the game if you want to play and enjoy it:
- Steam doesn't provide a game manual for Gothic, and that truly sucks.  If there are some games which you can start playing without reading the manual first - most modern games carry in-game tutorials - this is NOT one of them. The controls are a bit akward and if you don't read about them first I guarantee you won't be able to play the game at all. Just visit the Steam community page and you'll easily find a link to download the official manual in PDF.
- You can and you SHOULD run the game on Windows 7. My desktop computer is a Pentium IV with Windows XP, and I thought It would be better choice for this game to avoid system compatibility issues. Well, that was a mistake. The game kept crashing anywhere between 5 and 30 minutes of gameplay, especially when facing multiple foes, not to mention some inventory items didn't even show the picture. I googled it and updated all my Nvidia and sound card drivers, but the problems aforementioned remained unchanged. I was very close to quit playing the game at all, but I thought what the heck, let me try it on my laptop which runs on W 7. It got A LOT better. It only crashed about 10% of the time (ah ah), especially during the first visit to the Sleeper's temple (be sure to save a lot there) and the inventory issue got fixed. I don't know about Vista or 8, but the game seems to like Windows 7. Oh, and make sure to disable Steam interface during gameplay, or the game might not start at all.
- The game allows you to save whenever you want, so make sure you take advantage of it. I suggest this not for cheating purposes, but to avoid losing your game progress due to a crash or even worse, some bug where a gate doesn't open when it was supposed to or you end up killing NPCs vital to the plot who shouldn't be allowed to die at that point of the game.
- Get a walkthrough. I suggest the one by JemyM, which you can easily find online. Again, I recommend it not for cheating (you can even skip the walkthrough part per se) but for the unvaluable information it contains regarding gameplay and common bugs and how to avoid them.
- Go to a place like
and download the map pictures. Trust me, you will need them.
- If you're more into action games, maybe this game is not for you. Through most part of the game (especially the first chapters), you keep running from place to place around the colony, doing chores for other people, looking for objects, etc. Sure, later you'll feel like an invencible killing machine - it felt VERY rewarding going back to the Old Camp and slaughtering all those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who mugged me in the beginning :P - but it takes a while to get there. Play this game for the RPG experience and the story, and you will enjoy it.

Here I am, once again reviewing Minecraft: Story Mode. When I first heard they were making season 2, I honestly, didn't know whether or not I would still be interested in the series. After playing the season premiere, I can say I am pleasantly surprised. Though I liked the first season a lot, I can say that this season is more well-designed. I'll review each episode individually.
Episode 1: Hero In Residence
Release Date: July 11, 2017
So, here we are. Season 2 of this series. This is perhaps Telltale's most divisive game, with many people being big fans of it and many who think it's a pointless cash grab. I am more in the middle, as I used to love the series but over time stated to lose interest. I think it was due to the series starting to lose focus after episode 4, with many episodes not adding much to the overall story and relying too much on fan service (Case in point, the YouTubers in episode 6). But now, the series is back to being a more interconnected narrative, rather than individual storylines. The story starts fresh, with a few references to season 1, but other than that it's all brand new. The main cast has been swapped around, with a few main characters sticking around, but most have changed. I can say that the series feels very different. Most characters have new designs, and Olivia even has a new voice actor. However, I still loved being able to return to this series.
One of the more prominent changes is how much more interactive the game is. Most of the episode involves freely roaming around and interacting with things you find. There are sidequest-like interactions with certain characters as well, which is pretty interesting. The story also branches a lot more than the first season. The combat has also been revamped, and instead of just being bare bones like the first season, it's very intuitive. There's dodging and a stamina meter, which actually reminded me a lot of Dark Souls.
The music is also spectacular. The soundtrack of this series has been one of my personal favourite things about it. I don't have much to say about that, but it's got some great tunes.
I won't spoil the story, but it's a lot more well-written then the first season. The characters are pretty likeable and there are some pretty charming moments. The story is interesting and I'm curious to see what will happen next. Overall, it was a great introduction to the series, and I hope that the full season will be as good as this. This could turn out much more well-received than the first season was. I give it an 8/10.

-WWE 2k16 improved and fixed.
-Full 21:9 ultrawide support unlike 2k16. Some menus and loading screens are 16:9 but even entrances are 21:9 which is great.
- Major con : Many classic WWE superstars can't be unlocked unless you buy a dlc. But the roster in the game is big enough that I think it's fine, but I won't be paying for the dlcs. The game has Bret Hart, Macho Man, Earthquake, Ultimate warrior, Ted Dibiase, Vader, Diesel, Scot Hall, Andre and so many other classic wresters too but a few that are missing are : Hulk Hogan, Kurt Angle, and another major newtimer : Batista. While Batista can be downloaded from Custom Creations, some of the others are blocked behind dlcs which is a shame.
-Triple Threat match type greatly improved by having a "rollout system" whereby the injured guy rolls out of the ring, and if needed, can get back in when he's up, at a cost, or stay outside longer so he'll receieve a buff. This makes the matches more interesting and more real WWE like (well WWE isn't exactly real, but you know what I mean.)
-Steel Cage match vs AI is still boring and broken when playing Coop vs AI when we can let one enemy AI to get out and we can 2v1 the other guy until he's flat and we both can exit the cage simultaneously.
-Crowd looks more packed and somewhat believable and less cringeworthy than 2k16.
-Be warned though, there is no Hall of Fame like game mode like 2k16 where you got to play as Stone Cold and got to relive his real matches with cinematic real life footage. But there is a Wrestler creation section of course and that has a story mode. Basically this is a big drawback for those interested in playing more story related content.
-There is a WWE Universe mode, which I don't know if it was present in previous WWEs, but here you get to make custom alliances, rivalries and even have run in interferences during / before / after matches, which adds to more wwe realism. You can simulate or play the matches that you like and this is sort of like a never ending story mode. There are promos to make any wrestler a Face or Heel too.
-Heard online multiplayer has flaws, but I haven't tried it nor want to play it online. Great for couch coop with friends. Also other reviews here say the game crashes a lot, but hasn't occured to me even once yet maybe because my pc is good. i7 4790k @4 ghz, 16gb ram and gtx 970.
-Overall, if you own 2k16 this doesn't change too much, with less story related content, but packs a bunch of improvements and extra features in the details that 2k16 lacks. So for those looking for local coop, this should be great, especially if you own an ultrawide monitor.

Before Aeria took over, this game was owned by ijji. It was honestly a really great game back then. Weapons were permanent, they would have occasional events, and there were little to no hackers at all in the game. This game was skill based, similar to counter strike, but the graphics were better in my opinion. Plus, it was really fun to mess around in the game. One thing you can do in this game is hold a grenade, and once someone kills you, the grenade drops and sets off. Me and a friend would do that during a demolition game (pretty much counter strike's search and destroy). It was great times back then.
After Aeria took over, this game started to get worse and worse. There were more hackers. Weapons suddenly changed from permanent to having expiration dates. I still played when Aeria took over, but it was so hard for me to love something that changed so drastically.
I do not recommend this game. Not at all. Not while this game is run by Aeria. This company ruined something that was once wonderful. Do not play any games published by aeria. This company doesn't deserved to be supported.

Pros:
1) The game runs great. Very smooth graphics running UHD off an NVidia 970.
2) The sound and feel is well done. It feels like you are taking hits, and giving them. Very tactile.
3) Its quite immersive and fun to play.
4) Play customization is on point. Crisp designs and some interesting combinations can be achieved. Very customizable look and feel, overall.
Cons:
1) Way too many load screens and the break up of the recorded WWE stock video get old quick.
2) The controls using an XBOX One controller are at times nimble, and other times non responsive. Click on the controller appears to have lag input at moments. For example, you have to click to release a pin, but sometimes i press before the wheel goes into green, and the game shows me selecting after passing the green butter zone. Other times, during the defensive return sessions (press right trigger by default), the indicator only lasts a second and even if you press, it either doesnt register in the game, or it registers as too late. Very frustrating in general and easily aids in the CPU winning matches.
3) The game appears to have some kind of bug in the Tag Team mode. If you tag out, you will be unable to easily tag in. Again, on the controller, the Right Button doubles as your entrance into the ring and as the tag button. So when you are outside the ring, you wont get a tag. Ever. You will either enter the ring for no reason, or you will drop to the floor beside the ring. I find myself wandering over to the CPUs partner and roughing him up while my CPU partner does the work inside the ring.
bottom line - I recommend this game but understand the controller drawbacks. It kind of brings back a feeling of nostalgia, for me, playing Wrestlemania and a like in my youth. It does get frustrating when the interrupt abilities are lagging to your response, because often times it means game over and you lose.

You wander through the house, searching for answers of some kind about each of the untimely deaths of the Finch family. And as you live each character's last days or hours or moments you realize that their lives - who they were and what they loved and all their aspirations - were significantly more important than how those lives ended. There is no good game about loss without love and these developers certainly knew what they were doing.
I loved how the gameplay mechanics were done. The use of a controller was recommended but I don't have one and for the most part I didn't have too many issues. Assumably the controller made the mini-stories (the main interactive part of the game) easier to control. But I managed. And having each individual story catered to it's specific character added so much to the stories. You can really tell how much care these guys put into this game.
I only honestly had a few problems with the game and I'm attributing them to my "gaming" laptop, which is a cheaper than average HP with run-of-the-mill operating system and graphics.  But I had to carefully choose which graphics got bumped up to medium while the rest were set at low. And boy, oh boy did my computer hate Lewis' story. Which gameplay-wise was just brilliant in concept. The cleverest one in the game, in my opinion.
My only other complaint is that I wish it was longer? It took me about three hours to beat the game and  I would love to explore for hours more. Or honestly be able to free roam after completion. I'll probably just replay it again though, I know there's definitely things I missed or didn't understand the significance of the first time around.

Borderlands is a great game, especially for those who love to loot in video games.  It's incredibly rewarding to know that you eventually become almost immortal if you keep investing time and effort into the game. While I still like Borderlands 2 better, mostly because the gameplay was touched up and improved a lot, the first entry to the series is just as good and worthy of a playthrough if you haven't gotten to it yet.
Borderlands is always better with at least one buddy, but even as a solo experience, it's a good time shooting up enemies and doing side quests. The game isn't very frustrating either, which surprises even me because of how intense the action can get. If you're dying a lot, it's because you're tackling an objective that'll get easier once you level up some more, nothing more than that. The graphics have a sort of cel-shaded style to them, and while yes, this game is pretty old now, thanks to the graphical style, it manages not to look all that dated, which is impressive. I think everyone will play this game at least twice because playing as a different character adds a new element to the experience and allows you to play with different tactics. Brick is an up close and personal kind of character, but Mordecai is more of hands off kind of character that focuses more on sniping.
So less than 10 dollars for a game jam-packed with fun content and all DLC's is an absolute bargain.
