Westerado: Double Barreled may not be the prettiest game around with its blocky pixel art, but what it lacks in the visuals department is made up with its gameplay and humor. It captures the feel of a good ol’ fashioned Wild West revenge flick while having a good, and sometimes really weird, sense of humor.
The fact that you can pull out your gun on anyone during any point in a conversation should tell you quite a bit about the tone of the game. The metaphor for physical intimacy also deserves a nod. You’ll run into weirdos, bandits, hat makers, bandits, people that can use your help, and more bandits. On your quest for revenge you can change the fate of some characters if you follow through on their questlines or just murder them in cold blood.
All of the above means that there are different outcomes and methods to solving the same quest. For example, there’s a group of bandits blocking the railway with their shenanigans. You could murder them all, turn them into the sheriff’s deputies through a series of complicated steps, or even scare them away with a certain NPC. If you’re looking for an uncomplicated experience, murder tends to be a viable method of solving things, but know that it doesn’t have to be the only way. Making good dialogue choices might also accomplish the same task. Let’s not forget, you’re actively collecting clues to have a more complete picture of who the murderer is and the identity changes with every new game. Completing quests for NPCs rewards you with a single clue. You can also find the murderer by accident which I was able to do once. Let’s just say I forgot how to holster my pistol correctly.
Discovery is a big part of the game and the multiple endings add to that feeling. The kind of person you are is reflected in the ending and can be affected by siding yourself with important quest givers. If you’re achievement hunter, Westerado might have an even greater appeal to you since they generally have you going after different outcomes or scenarios that you might not have thought were possible. You can also have fun just by finishing the game a couple of times.
The gameplay is simple, responsive, and satisfying. You can shoot left or right and can move up or down. You have to pull back the hammer before you can fire and each round must be manually reloaded. This leads to some tense moments as you have to balance when to reload versus shooting back. Revolvers aren’t the only weapons, but they’re what I prefer. You can buy a shotgun, a rifle, or another revolver for some dual-wielding action.
Another great thing about the combat for Westerado is that enemies can harm each other. Maybe you don’t have a great window for reloading and there are enemies on both sides. Some nimble footwork can have enemies shooting at each other while you dance around. Most of the time, it happens accidentally, but doing it deliberately is also fun. Keep in mind that friendlies can unintentionally do the same thing to you and vice versa. Your lives are represented by the number of hats you have. You can have up to three hats to absorb shots; a man with no hat has a very short life expectancy.
There are only a couple negative criticisms I can make. Sometimes alternate solutions to quests are just really complicated, even if you bust out a guide. If you mess up, you’ll need to start a new game. The fact that playthroughs can become very short once your familiarity with the game increases does soften the blow. The other aspect of the game I didn’t like were the really blocky characters. The environments looked fairly okay with the pixel art, but the people were just giant pixels to me. A few more details wouldn’t have hurt.
Other than those two things, I think Westerado is worth your time, especially if you’re a fan of the wild west setting. The fun gameplay, the silly things you can do, and the varied outcomes make this game pretty fun. Man, ah love my revolver.

, for all its quirks. That is, you're more interested in an interactive story where your choices are mostly reflected in dialogue, rather than changing major plot points. Where the outcome is largely the same but the details along the way become your own - a customized telling, so to speak. If that style isn't your thing, then this won't be either.
This might well be the most successful transition of another intellectual property to Telltale game I've played. The Borderlands series seems at first like a really odd choice for a story-based game, given it has always been about shooting guns and then looting better guns. But beneath the violence and over-the-top style of humour, the games have always had heart.
So it's in this bizarre setting that two non-action heroes can really shine. The game's world is utterly insane, but everyone knows it and they just try to roll with it.
Sure, it's a horrible death world where masked psychopaths regularly have murder for breakfast, but it's still a world where people have family, friends, and dreams. It's cartoonish but never consequence-free, and though death is practically the wallpaper, it's still something to be afraid of and sometimes mourned.
The writing is enjoyable and mostly maintains a good balance between silliness and seriousness. Moments of drama are interrupted by someone's awkward phrasing, or a surprisingly easy solution to the problem. Characters maybe are a little too self-aware, frequently commenting on their own actions even as they do them, but there are
that hit the mark along with oodles of physical humour. I laughed out loud more than once.
. Instead of the usual set of grizzled mercenaries spouting one-liners, the dual protagonists are a corporate jerk and a devious con-woman. You alternate between controlling each of them, and their adversarial relationship turned begrudging respect is consistently fun to play around with. They're not action heroes, but you're frequently plunged into situations the heroes of the main games would have shrugged off with barely a sweat, and so you're left to see how normal people would deal with it.
There are plenty of gems in the supporting cast as well. Some faces are familiar, but for the most part it doesn't rely too heavily on returning characters. They're mostly cameos, temporary allies, or even opposition along the way, but they're never the main focus. The cast is brought to life by
by some of the best talents in the business, though the typically clunky facial animation can take away from that a little.
Also of note, as ever with the series, the creators have
, making for some awesome musical action sequences to introduce the episodes. I have at this point frequently had to admit I found certain bands I like through the Borderlands games.
There was just a whole lot I liked about this particular story. From its pacing, to its characters, to its consistent tone. I would say there are a few narrative missteps that I won't get into here, but my final feelings are thoroughly positive.

Overall, if you enjoy the setting, and want to know what comes next, this is a great way to enjoy the universe from another perspective and in another style.

This might be one of the best shoot 'em up games out there.
I didn't expect having as much fun with this as I did, but something about it seems to hit exactly the right spots in this genre!
It's basically Pang. Although I didn't know about Pang, I had played a rip-off game from Miniclip many years ago called Bubble Trouble.
Basically, you can only shoot up, and large enemies split into smaller enemies.
Pang didn't have a gun, but a hook that would disappear once it hit an enemy or the ceiling, and enemies would die even by hitting the hook's "trail". In this sense, The Bug Catcher is more traditional, i.e. you have an actual gun that functions like one - although you can only shoot vertically.
The core gameplay is just really fun! But I would also say that the developers structured the game very nicely.
The core gameplay is basically predicting the enemies' arc movements to avoid them, while clearing the screen. This requires quite a lot of focus, but it's very satisfying.
I'm focusing on the single-player missions. There is also an Endless both, both for single player and for co-op. (I actually didn't enjoy co-op very much. But I usually don't anyway? I like to concentrate on the game I'm playing and that doesn't work very well with other people, but maybe that's just me...)
The levels are a mixture of reflex and memorization, if you're going for all the objectives.
Each level has 3 stars for score, and an additional objective to hit a X-combo. Your combo meter is incremented every time you kill an enemy, but it's reset when you don't kill any enemy for 4-6 seconds.
I think this is the part that made the game so enjoyable for me. Because in every level, you're trying to figure out the order in which to kill the enemies so that you don't lose your combo, and maximizing your score as a result. A higher combo gives you a higher score, exponentially (it seemed).
There are 5 areas. They play similarly, but each one has a different environmental hazard. One has a hammer that comes down in the center of the room, from time to time, another has breakable (and respawnable) platforms at some height, etc.
Each area has 6 levels, the 6th being a special elevator level that introduces some tougher enemies - minibosses, if you will - that will appear later in the game.
So, 30 levels in total, which took me maybe 7-7.5 hours to master. All objectives on every level. I often get frustrated when going for these "perfect" scores in most game, but not on this one. The whole time, I was focused enough and enjoying myself the whole time. That very rarely happens.
So yeah, I don't know exactly why, but this game is really, really, good. The modes designed seem to bring the best out of the core gameplay.
There are also temporary guns and powerups, which are good to give some variety to repeated retries. Temporary invincibility, freeze enemies, etc. The weapons are usually better screen clearers than your basic weapon.
You upgrade all of this, although the upgrade system is fairly shallow.
Not much weapon or power-up variety, but I honestly think it doesn't need it. The core game is that satisfying that it doesn't need much dressing up.
Not as descriptive as most of my reviews, I guess. But I don't think there's much to describe, here. The game isn't very original - mostly a derivative of Pang with some modern aspects. Yet, it works. Really well!
So yeah, definitely give it a go if the game seems up your alley. Won't change your world, but you'll probably have a great time, knowing what game to expect!

I went into this game vaguely aware of the Borderlands series, knowing that it was Space Western Shenanigans and thus was interested in the premise at the very least. FPS games aren't usually my thing unless I'm super interested in the worldbuilding, so hey, a Telltale game should be enough for me to find out if I want to put in the time on the actual games, right?
The answer is yes, totally right. I finished this game a complete and absolute fan of Pandora, that narcissistic psychopath Handsome Jack, the humor and the lore and how freaking odd the entire thing is. Every single last character was actualized and weren't cardboard cut-outs. The plot didn't make me roll my eyes once-- which is a big deal for me, I roll my eyes a lot at the really obvious plot devices like I'm some kind of narrative elitist or something, you'd think this was an issue here. The witty writing forced me to laugh multiple times-- also a Big Deal, please note the use of proper capitalization and give it the proper gravitas.
And the music? The music is fantastic. One of the better soundtracks I've ever heard, so whoever chose the tracks to use, kudos to that guy, cos that guy knows what's what.
Tales from the Borderlands is ultimately a Telltale game, so yeah, it's interactive fiction with good voice work and some prompts to push the buttons. But if you're like me and want to know if Borderlands is something you want to dump hours of your life into, it's an excellent introduction and you'll definitely come out the other side either totally repulsed or absolutely enraptured.
I'm one of the enraptured ones, so leave me alone, I've got some Vault Hunting to go do.

When I saw what rating this game has, I was stunned.  I've played through from start to finish three times and am now starting my fourth.  There's an incredible amount of replayability with NG+, all of the radnet challenges and tonnes of collectibles.
I found the combat to be very impactful and the unlocks are quite well paced.  Loads of skins and bonus toys (cheats, basically) are around for those who have beaten the game.  There are (what feels like) hours of backstory cutscenes done with real people in a weird ultra edited kind of style that are a blast to watch, too.
My complaints would be that James Heller and Alex Mercer are both a bit bland and the story from the direct perspective of the player has a way to go to be truly immersive and believable (the backstory scenes tell the story very well, but these are optional and a lot is left out during the main course of the game).  The combat is what completely makes up for it, for me.  In fact, the Prototype games are side-by-side my favourite games of all time.

I waited a few days to write this review as I needed some time to digest it. Hmm, first and foremost, I think that if you hate "walking sims" on sight, well, there is nothing to see here, move along.
Ok for those who stuck around, this is perhaps my favourite so far. That's probably a little unfair to previous entries, as it isn't that they were bad, it's more that as a narrative experience these things keep evolving.
The games tale is about a young woman revisiting her ancesteral home and, via various means, reliving the last moments of past family members. Don't let it being a game about recurring death put you off though, despite being a bit dark, it is by no means bleak. A lot of these stories play out so wonderfully that it's the life behind it that matters. We know the death is inevitable, but most of the time, the game gives enough of a framework of the life that even though you know death is coming, you are still engaged.
For me, the key thing that kept me going was the unique way each story was presented, in that the way it was told matched the personality and identity of the character was so well reflected in the way it was presented,  the medium really did become the message. I wish I could explain more clearly what I mean here but to do so would border on spoilers. Ugh, that's so vague and a terrible review of the plot. I hope that if you play it you'll forgive me once you see what I mean.
The graphics are good, though there are some fuzzy textures here and there, the whole thing really looks great and the art design nails the feel of an oddly designed house surrounded by barely touched forest. Despite how eccentric the achitecture of the house is, the place feels lived in. It reminds me of Gone Home in this regard and Ive read others comment in the forums about the same vibe. Absurd as the house is, it feels genuinely lived in.
Sound and music are also excellent. The music features a recurring melancholy theme that helps link everything together and the ambient sound really helps you feel like you are in an old abandoned house. Not only did the house feel real visually, but I felt like I was hearing it creak and groan around me. The voice work is excellent all round, which is essential given the emotional beats the story is going for. The characters were really bought to life by the voice actors. The voice actor for young Molly, the first story you encounter, really managed to emtionally match the things I was feeling as a player as I went through her story. Everyother story is equally on par.
As I said at the start, if you aren't on board for the "walking sim" style of game, this isn't going to convince you. For anyone else, this is a great itteration that actually does a lot to show how much can be accomplished with this kind of interactive art. The type of story telling on display here, in a lot of ways, only has the impact it has because you are playing it and therfore become part of it.
If any of this has you at all intruiged, give it a shot.
Cons: Price.
Look, I have been kind of effusive in this review but the fact that it costs $20 for a 2 hour experience can't be ignored. Value is subjective of course, and I don't regret paying full price for this. That said I can see where people would. Despite saying I thought $20 was worth it, that was for me. For you it might not be. If price is an issue, if any of this sounded like something you would enjoy, whack it on your wish list and wait for a sale.
Score: 8/10
Closure:
A delight from an artistic and storytelling perspective. These type of games seem to be buliding on each other and I can't wait to see where they go next. While the gameplay itself is not huge, the way it presents narrative by making you feel part of said narrative touches you deeper than just sitting as a passive observer of say a movie or tv series. I felt Edith's story and I cried for her and the Finches in the closing credits. If art is meant to move you, then we should not dismiss "walking sims"

Absolutely wonderful. You play a girl in search of her family's past, by visiting the "storyline" of each family member.
Pros:
1. Beautifully rendered environments, with amazing attention to detail where even "inconsequential" background items add depth to the narrative.
2. Great music.
3. Believable, natural voice acting.
4. Innovative, fresh gameplay elements I have not seen in any game; these elements are not simply included for novelty sake but actually admirably fit into the particular story being told.
Cons (relative ones):
1. Story is extremely interesting but also ambiguous in interpretation. As is often the case with these walking simulator games, there is a philosophical or psychologic element to the story and it is uncertain how much should be taken at face value. One may argue that there is no satisfactory ending and no "ah ha" moment, but I do not think this detracts from the overall experience.
2. Controls are clunky and slow. You can only walk and turn with the speed of a turtle swimming in molasses. This I can see helps with the storytelling, as there are events and spoken speech which occur in concert with the walking, and running will now allow them to be correctly paced. Nonetheless I hoped some bits would have moved faster.
3. Short gameplay time with virtually no replay value. I finished in about two hours, and I see from the other reviews most other players averaged roughly the same, depending on whether one is an achievement completionist or not. Whether this is worth the $20 price tag is subjective, but I believe for something so unique and polished it is a definite yes. It is, essentially, an interactive movie, for about the same time investment and cost (at least in Australia).
In summary, What Remains of Edith Finch is an almost-perfect combination of story, gameplay, music and voice acting. For players who enjoy a moving, original story, told through some quite innovative mechanics, this is one not to be missed.

Full disclosure: I love Shock Troopers. I mean, I REALLY love Shock Troopers. It's one of my favorite games ever made. I spent countless hours playing it in the arcades in the late 90's, then playing it through emulators, then playing it on a Neo-Geo MVS cabinet that I bought later. A great level of difficulty balance with a brilliant control scheme, multiple paths through the game for replayibility, and one of the most amazing jungle/drum 'n bass soundtracks I've ever heard in a video game. But I'm talking about the Neo-Geo version of Shock Troopers. This port that you can buy on Steam? Terrible.
Let's start with the most glaring problem, the problem that smacked my ears immediately and made them cry out in agony - the sound emulation. I don't know what happened, I don't know how anyone could find this acceptable, but the sound in this game is so many levels of wrong. Every track in the game sounds chopped up, playing completely out of tune. I don't know how anyone could think this is what the game really sounds like. And no, this is not a problem with my computer, and I have since confirmed that it happens for other people too.
There are frame drops, too. Visually the game is almost never running at 60 fps, you can see little stutters here and there - it's most obvious on the character select screen if you watch the scrolling background. I'm unsure if changing the visual options (what little options there are) have any impact on this.
Even better, this game has input lag. Yes, even when playing offline. There's additional frames of delay that you would not get if you were playing on the original hardware, or even a competent emulator like MAME. Considering this is an action-packed game and being able to time rolling through bullets is pretty important, any additional input delay is a huge no-no. Not like it matters when you can just play the game through on infinite credits though, right?!
There are 4 difficulty levels to choose from - Easy, Normal, Hard, and Insane. Normally higher difficulties make you take more damage, but in this port? I have tested and absolutely nothing is different on each difficulty level. Whoops.
To its credit, the game does have functional leaderboards, and they haven't been hit by bugged out scores like what happened with Twinkle Star Sprites. Too bad it allows scores that used multiple continues, but to be fair this is a fault of the original game too.
There is online play, but at the time of writing this review I have not tested it with another player. Let's just say that I do have high expectations of it, especially after reading about desyncs and sound breaks. I can only imagine the netcode makes the input delay even worse.
Bottom line - Shock Troopers is still one of the best arcade games that many people don't know about. If you can look past the sound being garbage (which is inexcusable because this game's soundtrack needs to be enjoyed to its fullest), some extra input lag, and frame drops here and there.... well, you still have a fairly playable port, kind of. But there is no excuse for these problems, after the game's been ported to at least 4 other consoles, and none of those prior ports had anywhere near the same level of problems. I highly recommend the PS3 version if you want to properly enjoy this game on a console. Do *NOT* support DotEmu and these terrible ports, there is no reason we should have to stand for this garbage.

There are some people who wish videogames dealt with complex themes like war and terrorism with just an ounce of seriousness. I’m not one of them. Games like
epitomize what it means to be a digital soldier to me. You can expect violence at its most glorious, getting points for making others suffer, and then flexing, laughing, and maybe even doing a sexy pose when it’s all over. This Neo Geo game makes war seem pretty dang fantastic.
Videogame plots exist to give the most paper-thin reasoning behind why you should kill everyone. Some guy points you in the general direction of the bad guys, hands you the biggest gun and sends you on your merry way. To be more specific: The Bloody Scorpions are a terrorist organization, and they have captured a neurologist and his grand-daughter, in the hopes that they’ll create a drug that mutates regular people into invincible super-soldiers. In Operation “Delta Storm”, the eight members of Vulcan Team must make their way to the enemy base, and destroy everything. You didn’t really need to know all that did you? Just pick a route, go through seven stages, and... destroy everything.
The game gives you the option to go it alone like a wolf or as a three member team… like a pack of wolves. Either way you have one life* to work with, and each life is backed by a health bar that can take between 8 and 12 hits. Each of the eight playable characters has their own speed, defense, weapon and bomb ratings. To be honest, I’m an incredibly shallow person, so my team consists of the three ladies of Shock Troopers:
If you’ve ever played a
game then you’ll find that Bloody Scorpions make for quite the familiar antagonists. They stick to wearing ski-masks and somehow become endearing through their antics and well-animated deaths. It’s one thing just to take a few bullets and slump to the ground but these guys go the extra mile by losing arms, taking bullets in the knee-caps, exploding, and doing everything in their power to make their deaths satisfying to you, the player. They also commandeer vehicles and weapon emplacements, which also tend to explode when you put enough bullets into them. These guys also do what they can to defend themselves, using guns, knives, and whatever they happen to be lugging around. Still when just one of your soldiers is billed as a one-man (or woman) army you’re pretty much expected to mow them down singlehandedly. At the end of each stage you can expect a boss-fight. The generals of the Bloody Scorpions tend to get the nicest vehicles and after so many stages will take the fight to you on foot.
Running riot on this battlefield is as simple as turning one’s palm. Shock Troopers works in a manner similar to the classic Capcom title
. By tapping the fire button you can move and fire in any direction, while holding the button allows you to strafe. The dodge-roll is an amazing technique since you’re completely invulnerable for a brief moment. Just be sure not to dodge-roll into danger. As with similar games the enemy loves to leave random weapons lying around for you to take advantage of. These guns have limited ammo and run the gamut of spreadshots, heavy machine guns, rocket launchers, and what looks like the freaking Cobra gun from
.
Unique to this game is the mechanics of the close-range attack. This is performed by getting close and attacking, if you kill an enemy with this move they will drop bonus point items or power-ups. It’s somehow more rewarding to be able to look into the enemies’ eyes while you take their life away. More likely however it’s because getting the close-range kills is much more difficult. If you mess up you’re going to eat a bullet. This technique is difficult to master but can be very rewarding, especially because a boss taken out with a punch can drop an incredibly useful medkit.
As far as concerns the game itself, Shock Troopers is one of the better overhead run’n’guns I’ve played. It is a bit on the easy side if you play it safe — even in just a couple hours of play I’ve already come somewhat close to beating the game without continuing. Still, if you think about it, I have a ways to go. I’ve come nowhere close to beating the game without taking damage. Aside from the challenge ahead, the game also offers multiple paths, five other playable characters and cooperative play. All in all, I highly recommend that you check this game out.
*This version of
is version A. There's a second version (known as B) that makes the player-character take more damage, but they have three lives to work with. This adds a strategic element to the team-mode, since each member has a separate life-meter. The Playstation Network edition (available on PS3) is version B. In my opinion, B is the way to go, but it's not available on Steam. Hopefully Dotemu looks into this omission, along with the online/sound issues that tend to crop up in these SNK releases.

Welcome to the Robot Maid Review of... SHOCK TROOPERS.
This is an arcade masterpiece from the 90s. A game I played in my childhood and burned more quarters than I care to admit.
SHOCK TROOPERS puts you in the shoes of one (or three) of a multinational team of absolute badasses who are fighting some very generic bad guys (called the Blood Scorpions) in three different mission paths. Of course, you won't get an amazing story here, nor will you see much of it as this is formerly an arcade game and quite a quarter eater at it.
The game handles just as well as it did almost 20 years ago and is just as fun as a result. As a top down view, 8 direction shooter, it's a very simple game from simpler times. There honestly isn't much to say about the game aside from it's very simple and very fun as a result.
8 dollars for this game is practically a steal. If you're not versed in these games, you can easily spend twice as much on this quarter eater in an arcade.
On top of that, it's a great game to run solo, couch co-op. or online co-op. Which means you can bring a friend along to your destructive shenanigans against the Blood Scorpions.
All in all, SHOCK TROOPERS is a refreshing blast from the past in an era where creativity seems to be either stunted or moving incredibly fast.
After beating the game, you can also ask yourself why a group called the "Bloody Scorpions" is led by a man that looks like a lion.
This has been a Robot Maid Review. Thank you for reading.

The Bug Butcher has the essence of a pang game at it's core yet it manages to still break away and create a modern take on the 2d shooting genre.
Music, sounds, animation are all of high quality. Story is pretty non existent. I didn't experience any issues or crashes. Some of the menu screens were a bit tedious to navigate around, but that's about the only annoying thing I came across. Controls are very tight (even on keyboard). You can rebind all the keys if required.
Gameplay is pretty simple. You're able to only move left and right on the screen and only shoot up. Bugs come out in swarms and you need to break them down to destroy them. i.e kill a large bug and it breaks into 2 medium bugs, shoot them and they each break into 2 small bugs etfc Allowing you to finally kill the small bugs to clear the screen. Naturally if you shoot anything that moves the entire screen fills up with bugs making it hard to move/attack. As the levels pile on you'll get a pretty good variety of environmental obstacles and enemies with their own individual movement patterns and shooting rhythms, health stats etc.
There is a fairly large amount of weapons that randomly appear in game to utilise (including different power ups as well - like freezing enemies for a few seconds etc). The game also puts in a combo system to help create higher scores and forcing you to make a kill every few seconds to keep the combo alive. It works really well for the most part as you start to learn how to juggle the kills in a certain way for better effect. Most of the time the screen will be filled up with plenty of enemies and it's beautiful chaos. There is a pretty great feeling when you pull off a large amount of kills in a couple of seconds with a combination of skill and pure luck.
In standard mode there are 30 levels in total. Doesn't sound like much but they are all pretty replayable if you are trying to 100% the game. The last level will give you a good run for your money as it forces you to juggle just about every weapon and skill in a well timed run. There is an additional co-op mode and another single player endless horde mode. All levels have global scores to see where you rank in the world. General game time to complete story mode would probably be under 4 hours (based on average difficulty), to 100% the game it took me about 5-6hrs. All achievements popped without any issues. While it would be nice to see additional levels, I've read the game hasn't sold well enough to break even/justify further development work. I feel there is easily enough content to justify the current asking price as it's quality over quantity (and it's under $10).
If you are purely in it for single player story mode and are not worried about achievements/co-op I'd probably recommend waiting for a sale. If you like to try 100% the game or have a buddy to play with then I'd recommend giving it a go. It's a fair price and It runs really well. There is no long loading times. The level of polish is impressive for an indie game, get on it! Way better than any other pang game on steam.

Reading through all the Gothic reviews I noticed barely anyone has something negative to say about the game, so yeah... I'm afraid this is going to be the most negative review on gothic and some people are probably gonna hate me for it, and if you disagree with my review feel free to hit the dislike button but please read the entire review first.
First of all I did really enjoy the game, and I do concider myself a Gothic fan, I'm definitly not the biggest Gothic fan but I do think that the Gothic trilogy is the best RPG franchise ever. This game is without a doubt really great. the controlls are a bit akward but you can get used to it. the storyline is pretty danm good. you take the role of the nameless hero who is send to the prison colony with a letter for the magicians of the circle of fire. the colony is surrounded by a magic barrier, you can get in the colony but you cannot get out of it alive, so your goal is to escape the colony. I won't tell anymore than that about the story because I donnot want to spoil anything for those who still want to play it. besides the main story there are a lot of interesting side quests and there are a lot of interesting memorable characters.
the leveling system is a bit different from other RPG's like The Elder Scrolls. every time you level up you get 10 learning points/skill points which you can spend to improve your skills or learn new skills and you have to find a teacher to teach you instead of let's say increase your fighting skill by fighting hoards of enemies. I really love the leveling system for multiple reasons, it's something refreshing because you donnot see that in any other game and it gives you the option to train skills you're not using much at that moment because your skills with let's say two handed weapons isn't good enough yet to handle strong opponents. there's quite a lot of variety in skills and it will be difficult selecting the skills that work best for you, like should you train hunting skills so you could obtain trophies from dead animals, or alchemy to create your own potions or should you just train your fighting skills/strength/dex and so on, every skill is usefull in it's own way.
the world is also interesting. there are three camps, the old camp which was the first camp, the new camp which consists of people who disagreed with the old camp and there's the sect camp which consists of people who pray to the sleeper, a giant beast who will free them from the prison colony once it wakes up according to their "religion". besides the 3 camps there are a lot of different sites you can visit, and what i really like about gothic is taht some areas are filled with creatures you donnot want to meet if you're a low level which makes it even more rewarding if you're finally strong enough to search for loot in that area.
If you're a new player the combat system will be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ well the controlls in general will probably be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥but it won't take long before you master it. Let me start with some technical tips in order to fully enjoy this old gem.
If you should encounter problems with starting the game I recommend you to visit
, or search the game hub. I'm sure you will quickly find a solution for your problem. Furthermore, I recommend you to take a look at the widescreen patch and the FPS fix.
It's a really well made (controls need getting used to it though) roleplaying game, where roleplaying is defined by actually playing a role, making decisions with eminent influence on the game's world and story, befriending and antagonizing with several NPCs and interacting with many little things, even if it is just to sit down on a bench, rather than having tons of loot and a skilltree.
However, the lack of a skilltree doesn't mean that there is no character development. In fact, it will feel far more present than you are used to it by most of the games. Right at the beginning of the game you will discover a strict hierarchy in the game's world with you starting at the very bottom. Many players abandon this game, because the protagonist is so extremely weak in the beginning, but if you accept this fact and slowly but steady climb up the hierarchy you will encounter moments, which are extremely rewarding and make you realize that you made significant progress with your character. For example getting your first real armor.
The game offers you to join one of three factions, which provides quite a different gameplay, depending on your choice. This also guarantees at least a second playthrough, if not even a third one.
The world itself is lovely designed, surely the graphics are pretty much outdated by now, but just the arrangement of all the objects and the overall design is amazing. It's still one of my favourite worlds I would like to visit in real life.
I know it can be quite rough to dive into an older game, if you have never taken a look at it before, but in this case it definitely deserves a chance and even a second one. Once you've overcome the quirky controls and prefer games, which aren't casualized you will love this game.

Quite pretty and atmospheric, Estranged: Act I is a short, more adventure than horror, experience. Since the combat is kept rudimentary and feels a little wonky, it is best to approach it as an exploratory story game with a pinch of puzzling.
Estranged does a pretty good job on "show, don't tell" storytelling. The few NPCs don't bother too much explaining the player what exactly happened. That works well in order to keep the events of the past deliberately vague. Even though it is quite foreseeable, the lack of clear explanations engages the player in speculations. The story itself seems to be rather generic, however the abrupt ending left me wanting to continue.
Although there are a lot of open areas to explore, the level design is very linear and focused. Cleverly placed blocks navigate the player through the level while still retaining a realistic world. Except for the apparently blatant disobedience of the people on the island regarding storage of goods, nothing feels out of place.
Surprisingly good voice acting, ambient sound and eerie music add to the impression of a carefully crafted game. With the most important criterion, the atmosphere, being on point, Estranged is worth a try.

Looking at What Remains of Edith Finch you get a walking simulator, of a girl returning to her family home in search of answers. The story is rather deep in a philosophical kinda way but it's easy to get stuck on the big looming question of  WHY everything is happening. I'd say don't go into it looking to get an answer to that because that is not the main focus of the story.
Delivery wise, it's neat and innovative style of changing the gameplay aspects as you're introduced to the stories of deceased family members is something to continually anticipate as you play this game. Besides the basic waking an interacting with objects, the game also changes to things like first person platforming or to a 3D isometric adventure. These are nice additions but it's clear early on that they're not well-flushed out enough to sustain the game on their own. Utimately they're there to push the narrative.
Presentation wise, it's really good. Alot of polish in the texture quality, almost excellent draw distance and plenty of detail in the environment for you to look at. Better yet is the amount of detail and craftsmanship that goes into the FInch home (where you'll spend most of your time) and how that translates to information on the deceased Finches. Background music is great too, plenty of ambient tunes for you to hear to set the mood for each new scene. Voice acting is mostly great. Ironically I found the one for the child star to be the most average of the bunch but the more prominent roles do well to immerse you into the world.
It's a good game. I don't think there's enough here to change anyone's mind about buying a walking sim at full price, especially at a pricey 20 dollars, but that's fine. From the perspective of the niche market that this game targets, I would say it's worth it,

At first What Remains of Edith Finch looks like a game that's clinging a little too closely to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and there are definitely similarities and probably inspirations there, but as a whole Edith Finch does a good job of taking that formula and using it to do something different. It uses different mechanics in creative ways to make each of the Finch family's stories feel interesting and unique, in ways that are better to see for yourself than read about in a review. It does have the same problem than Ethan Carter had in that it's fairly short, possibly even shorter than Ethan Carter (it took me about 2 hours to finish, vs Ethan Carter's 3), but if you're the kind of person who enjoyed Ethan Carter and appreciate quality over quantity (and you probably are, if you enjoyed Ethan Carter) then What Remains of Edith Finch is a great game in the same vein.
It's also worth noting that while the store page says a controller is strongly recommended, I actually liked the mouse and keyboard controls, and never had any problem playing the game with them aside from sometimes having to use the movement keys to open doors when I didn't have enough mouse space on my desk to make the full movement (most of the interactions are done by moving the mouse/joystick to move things instead of just pressing a button).

Finch Manor looks and feels like an actual, honest-to-god home, with some elements of the Winchester House or Hearst Castle. So far as tone goes, imagine
mixed with a healthy spoonful of
and you might not be too far off. Or perhaps its the other way around. You'll explore the family curse, as told through the experiences of the protagonist's various deceased relatives, stretching back to her great grandmother.
This is what impressed me the most about it, really. The game guides you gently, making it clear where to proceed
shunting you along like you're on a conveyor belt. Sure, it's only two to three hours long, but that's a perfect length for it. It sits down, tells you a quirky story in a nifty way, then leaves you to your business before it overstays its welcome.
It's weird to say this in reference to a "walking simulator", but the gameplay is actually
. The experimental control schemes and presentation methods for the various side stories are intuitive, interesting, and varied in ways I certainly didn't expect going in.
Overall a fascinating, short game that is as impressive from an artistic standpoint as it is a technical one. There are a lot of lessons here that other developers should be taking notes on, certainly. If you like story-driven content with immense polish, you could do a helluva lot worse than
.

Also, there are slots for extra save games available in the game's settings, but you can't access them when starting a new game - all it does is overwrite the first slot. I just found this out when my daughter tried it out and it wiped out my save - next epsiode will have her choices only, unless I play it again and push my options back through.
A little more polishing before release would've been a good idea. I hear tell of some large DirectX problem, but I was spared this so can't comment on that aspect of it.
So far the story is interesting, but with the semi-crotchety controls and incomplete save settings, I can only give this a rating of 7/10. That may change in future if they address these issues.
Recommended, but only if you can get it on sale like i did. Don't pay full price for something that isn't complete.
Update: July 13, 2017: I've also just discovered the options to import your choices from the first game are very limited: it won't allow me to choose which save slot I want to use from Season One and is defaulting to slot 4 from that game for no apparent reason. It's not even the most recently used slot. Again, this seems liek soem of the more mundane file management portions of the game were completely forgotten to get it out on time.

Dawn of War II reminds me of something of a hybrid between the addictive, yet brainless Facebook Zynga games (Farmvile, etc) and Company of Heroes. The missions are /mostly/ banal, "kill or destroy objective X and survive" types that almost feel like MMO quests, yet the character upgrade system and decent story line compel long game sessions. Multiplayer is solid, if not a one-for-one copy of the Company of Heroes, excepting the fun yet underpopulated "Last Stand" co-op survival mode. Be weary of the "expansions", except for multiplayer. If you want multiplayer only, skip this and straight for Retribution, which features (almost) ALL units while forging the asinine Games for Windows Live side-program that is built in to DoWII and Chaos Rising.
I should also add that the gameplay style is a MASSIVE departure from the earlyer DoW games, which were traditional RTS games. DoWII is much more of an RPG game than RTS, and has more in common with KOTR and Baldur's Gate than DoW1 or Company of Heroes. If you want an RTS experience, look elsewhere (except multiplayer, which as I said earlier, DoW is just a Warhammer 40k version of Company of Heroes - great but not groundbreaking). If you want a decent, perhaps solid RPG experience with acceptable RTS elements, this is a great choice.

Eve is what you make of it.
If you want to fill your screen up top to bottom with spreadsheets and never take your eyes off the marketplace then by all means go ahead, that is a perfectly valid way to play the game.
If you want to chill out, enjoy the game, and have an immersive experience with a subtle UI yep, you can do that too.
Yes, there are a lot of ways for other players to screw you in the game. You can be ganked, scammed, and griefed. At any point you can have everything in your ship destroyed and stolen but this stuff is easily mitigated and/or completely avoidable by common sense and preparation. It also makes the game incredibly fun. My favorite moment was from early on exploring a wormhole with 100 million ISK of loot in the cargo hold of my Heron that barely cost 1 mil when a Stratios jumps in and starts locking me up. Luckily I came into the wormhole prepared for when something like that happens. If you are under-prepared and complacent in this game just know that you WILL lose everything and probably come here to write a negative review.
Two more points to make:
The gameplay itself is deceivingly deep. At first glance you click a button, your guns turn on, the bad guys die. As you play more you will realize flying effectively is highly dependant on a player's ability. It's easy to write the game off as un-fun because of this initial impression so you have to give it a chance. Given equal ships and skills the better player will win every time.

The real strength of the VN isn't the framing or setting but seeing empathy, depravity, and forgiveness woven together to weave a compelling romance-based narrative.
Certain romance-centered cliches are played completely straight, don't expect subversion here. I can't say it's a perfect VN, some parts do tonally shift rather quickly, jumping from melancholy to comedy characteristic of Japanese VNs rather quickly but it's overall balanced pretty well. The . Certain plot twists sometimes feel haphazardly used relative to the rest of the narrative and so there is a sense of needless convolution to confuse the reader rather than genuine feeling of deception based on the narrative structure.  The settings aren't historically accurate and the modern tone of the narrative introduces anachronisms and cultural sensibilities that simply were not present in the depicted eras.
Regardless, its strengths in delivering its pathos overcomes its narrative faults.

This is my absolute favorite VN of all time in all aspects (at least until Hanada Keika writes another)--there's an immense amount of love and care taken into the writing as well as the translation. For the content being as mature and dark as it is (sexual abuse, gender identity, gray morality, and divine justice [and unconditional romantic love, which is easy to ♥♥♥♥ up]), it's sensitive and empathetic. This review will not be analyzing if the game is good or bad. It will simply analyze if the mod is worth it's 5 dollar price tag it carries with it. If you are looking for the former I'll give you the short version; its good.
But that is not the purpose of the review. Instead this will help you decide if you want to whip out 5 bucks to play the game.
Aperture Tag is a well polished, fun, intuitive, and interesting modification with a extremely linear plot. It focuses around a new device simular to what TWTM did (but this time it's good) known as the Aperture Handheld Paint Gun or just Paint Gun for short. This paint gun, instead of firing off blue and orange portals will fire off blue and orange gel.
Now with that in mind it may seem as if it will be more of an action mod, but this is not at all the case. The puzzles are extremely well made in introducing ideas to the game as well as being carefully planned out so they take brains instead of ninja skills (although ninja skills are sometimes needed). All in all the puzzle design is great and also very visually cleansing as well. Nothing looks ugly or plays ugly through the entirety of the mod.
This mod is at it's best when you are testing in regular puzzles but it also does a good job with exploration elements. No exploring lasts for too long and the tasks that must be done never seem tedious or boring.
Howver there is also an attemped 'action' sequence that is not so good and this is for four reasons.
-The pacing of the section which gives you around a minute to navigate a course is god-awful.
-The ugly text that shows up on the screen trying to give a feeling of tension is just well ugly and distracting.
-You can entirely skip the section by clicking a button which destroys the concept of actually having to go through the course to escape.
-Instead of the action scence being an amazing ending it is more of an anti-climactic section of the game as there isnt much of a big boom for completing the task.
This action sequence can be forgiven however due to the beatiful landscapes shown when navigating through tubes to get from place to place. The capturing beaty and awe in the maps shows just how much effort was put into the mod.
Now here comes the big handicap, and that is the story. As I briefly mentioned the plot is extremely linear and in turn seems pointless and boring. The ending is practically a direct copy of the Portal 1 scene before the final fight and the characters are pretty lifeless and badly voice acted. All in alll the story did not do me much good and story is one of the most important elements of the game. This story was dull, uninspired, and way too linear. Both endings are unsatisfying as well.
The performance is very well. There are no sudden stutters or drops in FPS and the games graphics are great.
However this game is not worth the price. There are much better mods that are entirely free. I reccomend getting it on sale.

It's been described as Red Dead Redemption in 2D. And while I haven't played RDR (being a PC gamer) from what I know of Rockstar's open-world Western outing, it seems like an uncannily accurate comparison.
Westerado has simple mechanics: it's 2D, top-down, side-scrolling, and has just a few different weapons - but it's how it uses those mechanics that makes the game really shine. From the outset you can explore the open world as you wish, talking to anyone, killing anyone (if that's the way you like your Westerns), taking names and taking hats. The protagonist's accent is captured surprisingly well for text-based dialogue, and it adds that little extra charm to the game.
There are warring factions in the West: the army, the Indians, the townsfolk, the oil tycoon. You can side with anyone and reap the consequences, or remain a lone gunman on his quest for vengeance.
The music provides a huge part of the Western feel too, though it does eventually get a bit repetitive.
There's also a good number of easter eggs and pop culture references, and the writing is just all-around light-humoured and entertaining to read.
A typical game from start to finish can last anywhere from 30 minutes to 10 hours or so depending on how thorough you are. This is a game designed for replayability: there are lots of things you can't do in a single playthrough due to the nature of choice and consequence.
In summary, a charming Western game that gives you a great amount of freedom to play as you like.

Ignore the naysayers. As someone who plays his PC games on a 40" screen, this HD version was necessary and greatly appreciated.
Heroes III is one of my favourite games of all time, and easily my favourite strategy game. I've been playing it since I was 6 or 7 and never really stopped but in recent years, along with upgrading to bigger and higher reslolution screens, the games visuals increasingly looked pixellated and basically pretty damn ugly.
I tried the unofficial HD mod but all that really did was increase the interface size and did very little for the actual textures themselves. Now with this HD version, the game looks beautiful and so it's as good as it's ever been.
Are there flaws? Well yes. It doesn't include the expansions, the battles are still in 4:3 ratio (with borders) and a few of the repainted models look a bit derpy (I'm looking at you wood elves). But truly, this is a small price to pay for an old  game to look absolutely stunning. This breathes life in one of the best turn-based strategy games ever made.
However I would appreciate it if Ubisoft added the expansions as DLC. And because of the price point I can see why people would rather just stick to the original version which you can get on GOG for a small fraction of the price of this HD version. My advice to you is to look at your monitor size. If it's 1080p and bigger than, say, 24", then I recommend getting the HD version all day. Either way you can't really go wrong. Heroes III is still Heroes III.

Westerado Double Barreled is a wonderful little game where you play as a poncho-clad gunslinger, wandering around a nice western landscape, while you try to find the man that killed your family. A single play through won't last you long (about 3 hours), but randomized murderers, multiple characters, and various secrets can provide a good amount of replayability. The gameplay itself is also quite good. The gunfights are quite fun, and can even be a bit tactical, at time. However, the conversation system and how you can interact with NPCs are the most interesting parts. In any conversation you can whip out your gun, with varying degrees of success, and you can just shoot everybody, if you want to. Overall, Westerado is a great game, that's totally worth your money.

With every year, 2K have got lazier and lazier, and they've finally tapped out with no subtlety.
- Showcase is gone, with nothing replacing it.
We all thought about the great ideas they could do for the next few Showcases, and this year would've been a good one for a Women's or 4 Horsewomen Showcase, and their reaction was to just remove the main mode of the recent series entirely. I'm gobsmacked.
Note that last year they did an Austin Showcase, which a lot of was just a copy/paste of a previous game's Attitude Era Showcase. This year they couldn't even be bothered to have one at all.
Though they're releasing a Hall of Fame DLC in the near future, so look forward to just a handful of random matches that weren't even all that important to their career and a whopping 30 minutes of Showcase gameplay.
- But Career and Universe haven't been improved, and actually are still exactly the same, broken, and boring as ♥♥♥♥
What they've been doing with all this free time they have by just not bothering with Showcase I don't know, because the other two main modes are exactly the same. Career still has you slogging away beating the same jobbers 100 times and delivering awful gibberish 'promos' inbetween, Universe is similarly just random matches.
To top it off, your created guy in Career can't use most moves because you have to 'buy' them with imaginary currency you have to grind. Imagine yourself with a Lionsault and a certain DDT? Then you have to slog a no doubt riveting bunch of matches against Bo Dallas on Main Event first to buy them.
- Promos are the only new feature, and they're broken too. Everyone has split-personality.
You can now deliver promos if you feel like. You could do this in the last game, and this time it's similar, but now it's in Universe too, but without the voice acting. So you have the same generic promo text being 'said' by anyone from Undertaker to Bayley. But the conversation choices are obscure.
- WWE 2k17 presents: a promo between anti-establishment champion Dean Ambrose and corporate heel Kevin Owens
I was crazy Dean delivering a promo, and Owens came down to talk some smack for our feud. Kevin had a go at Dean for being part of the Authority. (What?) So I had a go at him for being part of the Authority. (What?) I was face, but was apparently delivering a heel promo. (What?) Kevin was heel, but was apparently delivering a face promo. (What?) We traded generic insults. Dean said Kevin is too mentally unwell to challenge him and he has to see a psychiatrist and calm down before getting a match with him. (WHAT?)
DEAN 'LUNATIC FRINGE' AMBROSE SAID THIS. Dean Ambrose told someone else they were too crazy so they didn't deserve a title chance!
I, Dean, 'won' the promo battle for some unknown reason.
Hooray?
- Conclusion
And that's it. That's all there is in the game. It's only for exhibition matches really.
In short: 2K16 was exactly the same game as 2K15 but with slick animation and flow into other moves and a much-needed reversal system. 2k17 is exactly the same as 2K16 but with the entire main game mode taken out.
I fear for the franchise's future. Very sad.
UPDATE: There's even a bit of commentary in the HoF DLC (yet to be released on PC) where King MESSES HIS LINES and rereads them. TWICE. IN THE GAME! Evidently 2K don't give a crap about their professionalism and standards any more. They actually have my sympathy; I pity them. Good luck in their future endeavours.

A point and click game based of a shooter franchise, what could go wrong? In this case, nothing, in fact it turned out better than everyone expected. A story in the Borderlands setting, matching the tone and expanding on the lore, this game is one that stands out for many, even those who aren't big fans of the point&click. A narrative like the one in Tales from the Borderlands is not one you could find in most games. It dares to be original, it dares to be humorous no matter what and it dares to change to a darker tone in key moments. Sometimes you'll laugh, sometimes you'll stare, most times you'll be relaxed. This game consists of 5 entertaining episodes, which tell a story in a fair pace.
Looking at the game-play mechanics, it follows the TellTale formula: lines of dialogue with limited time to choose, walking, pointing&clicking and the QTE's. Doesn't sound like anything special, but it's in those moments you realize how charming the game is. QTE's consist of awesome and often times humorous moments, dialogue choices are comprehensive and they can even extend to being choices of how you approach things, which garner different reaction for the rest of the game.
I'd like to say graphics are ageless due to their art-style, but while characters scale nicely with the resolution, there are some low texture environments, however their blended well with the rest(most of the time it's either rocky grounds or a wall with high quality posters). There are plenty of breathtaking views on the way, but personally I was too focused on the story to take my time. There are options to click for better views on certain things, which also come with one liners from the current protagonist.
Where the game truly shines is the story. 4 and a half of the episodes are narrated by the protagonists, which sometimes can lead to hyperbolous situations, quickly interrupted however. There are two protagonist, Rhys "The Salary Man" and Fiona "The Con Artist". The former works on Hyperion, dreaming day and night about owning the place and the latter is pulling a big score. The build up is quick, as halfway through the first episode, they cross paths and so does the story begin.  Having certain characters from past video games with the same old Borderlands end game of hunting for a vault and a narrative that was seriously worked on to not be serious, you have yourself a fine taste comedy that's blended in with a survival motif, obvious character development, that all leads to the sensation of completing a game you've enjoyed. The cast of characters is pretty extensive, from the young and "cutely" innocent to killers that looks like their inside rot is growing to the outside, just like you'd expect in Borderlands.  In direct proportionality with the character development, the tone gets darker, reaching the pinnacle in the last episode, where even the intro is different. However, in the second half, they get back to a more lighter tone since the gang is back together, however it's not the comedy it was before, as they face the grand threat, which as a substitute for the funny lines it had motivational ones and awesome moments, balancing the first half in order to maintain the more light-heartet tone of the series.  I won't give spoilers, but here are a few lines from the end which best describe the narrative:
Those lines are on point. Don't judge the writing though, it's just a casual moment.
One thing to add is that you don't need to have played any of the previous Borderlands games. While I imagine old fans would have their thrills seeing some of the NPCs and Vault Hunters in the story, new comers will have the right introductions to said characters, if not better ones.
If you want to have a good time, find out how loud you can laugh and expand your list of fictional characters you'll never forget, you can pick this game up. Full price, on sale that's up to you really. It's worth both and note, there won't be any future seasons, but it might be the game you'll replay once in a while, just out of pure enjoyment.

No, this is not a good game. As a new player, you have two choices:
-Play PvE alone.
-Join a player corporation as a mining drone.
THAT'S IT!
There's a very interesting system of risk versus reward here. See, if you're in a solar system with security above 0.5, police forces will eventualy come to help you if somebody attacks you. It doesn't mean you will survive, just that the offender will get killed! But that is enough deterrent for most people not to shoot you in high sec. BUT the police does nothing if your corporation or alliance (which is a group with several corporations) is at war with the offender's corp (or alliance). Stuff you can get in those high sec systems is far less valuable than the one you can find on low or null sec. You take the risk and may get a far bigger reward and make up for any loses, which is OK.
What is not OK is that pirate groups declare war on EVERYBODY, on ALL the alliances and corporations they can find, so they can shoot them ANYWHERE without repercussions. They literally camp outside trade hubs 24/7 and shoot anything they can. All that elaborate security system, to the trash. All the guys who try to follow a PvE career have alts on NPC corps (like haulers, for example), so they can't get shoot that easily. Is moronic, really.
Also, if you kill an NPC, somebody steals the content and you shoot him... guess what? No police is going to help you! So, outside trade hubs, there are always guys marked as "suspect" (which happens when you steal something), waiting for people to shoot at them so they can blow you up.
So, you play alone (where you are in an NPC corporation and no war can be declared to you) or join a null security corp and go to a far place where you shoot anybody that is not in your corp and alliance and forget about PvE missions (Because, once in null space, it's VERY HARD to get to high sec going through other corps space). And, if you join a null corp... guess what is the first task you have to do for them? That's right, mining. You usually can sell the minerals to corporation itself, which use it or sell it at a HIGHER price (twice or more). You have become a mining drone. Congrats! I've met guys who doesn't even know how the game is outside null. They've played months and months, never doing missions or looking at a trade hub in their lives.
The designers want people to get together and make friends, so people can stay in the game. And then say: "Guys, go out there and loose a couple of ships! You will see it's not that terrible!". Of course, I guess for an old player, with a steady income, that can get very valuable stuff from null sec, with millions of points on skills, which does have a fair chance to stay alive after an encounter, it's not a big deal. For a new player, trying to sell the minerals it took him HOURS to get in high sec and being shot outside of a trading hub, just because he committed the sin of joining a corporation at war... it's bad. Very, very bad.
Those design inconsistencies between what they want and how they're (not) achieving it, are just awful. I guess they don't understand new players. Or PvE.
Not recommended.

I have over 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #35 - Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION
I haven't really played very many modern shoot em up games.  My history is more with the old school arcade shooters like Galaga and Galaxian.  Playing this is like seeing these old games on steroids.
Luckily for me, the game provides a choice of difficulty when starting a new game.  So novice players like myself can start with the Novice difficulty instead of Arcade difficulty.  You also get a choice of different modes to play in.  For the Novice difficulty I had the choice of Original or Boost mode.  They looked largely the same except Boost mode modifies the difficulty based on skill.  There is also an Unlimited and Time Attack mode, but these aren't available in the Novice difficulty.  I started with the Original mode.
You get an optional tutorial at the beginning to get a feel of the controls.  I liked that even as a modern shooter, the controls are still pretty simple to pick up.  You have the obvious controls of moving your ship around and firing your main gun.  You also get a secondary weapon where holding down the button will lock onto enemies.  Then when you let off the button you'll fire at everything that has been locked on to.
The third button I found pretty interesting as it does a couple of different things.  The game has a break mode gauge that fills as you kill enemies.  If you press the button, you'll drop a bomb which is basically an attack that hits the entire screen, but it also has the bonus of making you invulnerable for a short time.  But if the break mode gauge is full, then instead of dropping a bomb you go into "break mode"  In this mode your firepower increases big time for a short duration.  It's also possible to stack up 2 break mode gauges and get a double break mode, which will increase your firepower even more.
All of these weapons can be fired independently.  So for instance while you are firing your main gun at whatever is in front of you, you could be locking on to enemies to your side.  I found myself hitting the bomb at key times when it looked like I'd be unable to dodge the enemy bullets, so I'd get that bit of invulnerability.
The game starts out at a somewhat leisurely pace, but it doesn't take long for things to pick up, and the later levels really get crazy.  But I really appreciated the fact that the developers kept the game very accessible.  In the novice mode I played, I got all the continues I wanted after losing all of my lives.  In the latter stages that happened a lot.  But it seems the developers want you to be able to complete the game, and then focus on getting better at it.  So for the very casual player, you can still have fun blasting your way through the levels and dying a lot without any real penalty.
The 2D graphics are very nice.  There were some parts of the game it got so crazy it started looking like one of those visualizers you see in a music player or a screensaver.  I also really liked the soundtrack and thought it was perfect as the backdrop for an arcade shoot em up.
If you are already a shoot em up fan, then you probably already have this game or don't really need any convincing to pick it up.  But for the more casual players, I can still recommend this game, but you might want to catch it on sale.

I feel almost intimidated writing a review for this game, because it is - in my opinion - the best visual novel in existence, and my word stacking could hardly do it justice. That’s why I’m just going to write a simple summary first, before I make my attempt:
Complex and fulfilling story that draws out real emotions in the player
Realistic character development
Many, many plot-twists that tie in together perfectly
Beautiful art and mood-appropriate surroundings
Most likely the best soundtrack I have ever come across
Leaves an impact and a lot of thought in the reader
Struggles and dilemmas that are not presented cheaply, nor unrealistically
Auto-saving during choices and a lot of save spaces that can be locked so that you cannot overwrite them by accident
Extras
No “skip only read” option, although in this game that’s not really a problem
Now, let’s start at the beginning. When I first opened this game, the first thing I noticed was how the art and the original soundtrack worked perfectly to create an almost palpable atmosphere. That, together with the writing style, has set a mood so intense I could literally
all the emotions the characters were going through.
There was one thing I was disappointed with at first - the backgrounds. At the beginning of the game, it just didn’t seem to fit to me - everything had so much effort put into it, and so the background art looked simple and out of place in contrast. It even birthed a faint feeling of doubt in me. But as I delved deeper into the mansion and its story, somehow all of that transformed - the backgrounds were still done the same way, but I didn’t mind anymore, I actually loved it. That’s when I realized the choice to use those backgrounds was definitely the right one. They were perfect - didn’t show too much, just enough to hint on something deep within you and let your mind paint the picture.
Visual novel is a perfect fit for this story. I have read a lot of books that could be turned into visual novels, and a lot visual novels that could be turned into books. This one is unique - it works with everything it has, and uses every aspect of storytelling and each piece of what makes visual novels a genre, and ties them together. Words, pictures, sounds, emotions and assumptions all work in tandem to create an experience unlike any other, and really suck you into the lives and fates of the game’s characters.
Speaking of characters, I was surprised at how well they have been handled. Each and every one of them feels like a real person - one that you cannot just love or hate, but one that you can have conflicting feelings about or even change your mind about completely without forgetting their previous transgressions.
Without spoiling anything, I also have to praise the developer on how they handled gender and identity issues. It can be very tricky to tackle these things, especially in certain time-periods and settings, but they didn’t seem to struggle at all. I believe that players who have ever experienced gender dysphoria - or really any kind of dysphoria about their body - will really appreciate that.
I cannot but recommend this game to everyone. If you dislike reading, this game might be a bit too tedious for you, but if you enjoy books and/or visual novels, do not hesitate. I promise you that it will be a very rewarding experience.

What Remains of Edith Finch is as genius in its design as it is visually stunning. Grabbingly immersive and from the very first moment to its emotionally satisfying end, it was an experience unlike any other.
The haunting story is somber but somehow uplifting, its wonderfully crafted tableaus are each told in their own brilliantly unique style and tone that not only keeps the narrative fresh and surprising but brings deeper meaning to the stories by forging an emotional connection between the player and the subject.
The house itself is a facinating character and the phenominal level design turns it into a beatiful maze that somehow has no dead ends - because everywhere you go there's a rewarding surprise. I was constantly impressed with both its eerieness and its interconnectivity where I felt that my curiousity was always rewarded.
This game with strike you deep and keep you thinking long after the credits have rolled. A truly exceptional experience.

It truly matches up to the genre of visual *novel* in terms of sheer writing talent, and Mangagamer did a fantastic job localizing the title in all it's complexity. I don't want to speak too long about the game as I think it's something definitely best visited as blind as possible, but I can guarantee you this is a very powerful story that's worth your time and money. Grab it if you're looking for a beautiful, but heart-wrenching story to be completely wrapped up into.

My positive reviews largely consist of responses to criticism from the top negative reviews; simply piling on the positive adjectives seems hollow and tells the prospective customer next to nothing other than than the writer really liked it.
One review criticizes the prose as weak.  To the extent that prose refers to character dialogue, this is irrelevant: character dialogue should feel reasonably genuine, and this game's dialogue does.  This also seems like a remarkably empty complaint in a genre rife with awkward translations; all the writing is quite readable, which really ought to be enough.
There is criticism of the vocalized laughs and shouts.  Aside from "hehehe" being overused in the first chapter, this is really a non-issue.  I personally see no advantage whatsoever to "The Maid chuckled" over "'Hehehe'", especially when followed directly by more lines.
Some found the first few chapters boring, and quit before going further.  I can imagine this reaction, but I found them moderately pleasant on my own terms, myself.  That said, at around chapter 5 I was utterly engrossed, and reached the stage where I could not put it down, an experience I think is shared by many.
All in all, it's a very nice story, and the game is quite polished in that there are few if any noticeable flaws.  I heartily recommend this game.

There is an absence of challenge that most people will feel but being able to mess around with gels makes the level kind of enjoyable/fun.
