I played this game a lot on my phone, so I can say that for Yugioh fans, this game can be fun at times as long as you build your deck carefully. You get to play as a lot of characters from the anime, though some of them I question as they don't really fit the whole 'Legendary Dulist' catagoery. Kinda like Bandit Keith... He's only been shown in a few episodes and frankly... he's kinda underwhelming at best. Sure he uses machine type monsters, but he also cheats at times just to steal a victory. Not really something a 'Legendary dulist' would do. As for Weevil underwood, while having a few interesting cards of his own you can play around with, he's also not much of a 'Legendary Dulist' as bug brain also cheated a few times. Once by tossing all of Yugi Moto's exodia cards off a boat they were on, and for when he tried to fight against Joey Wheeler. I'm actually surprised that we don't get to play as Tristan Taylor in this game as he had the 5-headed dragon card as a boss monster and while some of his military themed cards weren't the best, he could be kinda fun to play around with. Other characters you won't be able to play as in the game I can think of off the bat, Chumley, Syrus&Zane Trusedale, Rubecca, Tyranno Hassleberry, Atticus Rhodes, and even if he was for an event, Jesse Anderson, and maybe just for fun, Duke Devlin.
This is also a good chance for the makers of the card game to look over some of the old archtypes in the game and give them some much needed updates. Like the neo spacians. We need to have NEX be more usable with the chaarcters shown on the card as it only affects a few of them. It would also be nice if the normal battles we have with the NPCs actually had some 'good' card rewards... as well as a list of cards we can look at when we battle them, It can also be said that we can use more characters to play as, even if some of them didn't do a whole lot in the anime or comics of which they are from. Overall, the game can be fun at times, just don't spend too much of your money on it unless it's for the special sales they have every now and then. All that's needed to make it better, new cards for the old archtypes that haven't been touched in a long time like the Neo Spacians I mentioned before, or any other archtype that could really use some new cards to give them a much needed boost and relavance in competitive play as well as letting us in the game be able to use the banned cards outside of the PVP when dueling competitively as well as possible lifting the ban on some of the cards that don't really need a ban on them as the newer cards of today outside of this digital game... well... they can absolutely destroy some of the banned cards without much effort. Take a look at Gaurdians for a moment and you can tell right away that they need some help, as well as a certian spell card un-banned so that we can use the monster it's supposed to let us use in the first place. The same can be said for a few other archtypes as well, other than that. I suggest checking it out and hope that in time we'll be able to get some of the cards we really needed for the archtypes that caught our eyes, but didn't have the tools needed to be useful. On another note... whatever you do, don't use the auto duel function. The A.I. for when you're set to auto duel can and will make so many mistakes. It will fail to play certain cards that are in your hand that could of and would of given you a victory if it had just played them, or at the very least gave you some breathing room in your duel against your opponent. Take any field spell card or Magical Mallet for example, you have a good monster out on your side of the field and your opponent has two monsters out, one of them being stronger than the other and yours unless you play the field spell, you have a field spell card in your hand that can help you out. The A.I. won't play it if you're in auto, instead it was attack whatever it can and end your turn, leaving you with a monster you could beaten if the A.I. was smart enough to play it first. Another example for Magical Mallet, let's say you got a bad hand, but have the spell card Magical Mallet to shuffle it all in your deck and get new cards, if you're in Auto duel, the A.I. won't play it and just end your turn, leaving you wide open for an attack that could very well lead to you losing before you even did anything.

There are some games where you need to trust that it's going to be good and just not care about the negative reviews, this is one of those games. Every negative review harps on about how the gunplay is bad or that the game only lasts 2-3 hours, the gunplay is really a matter of opinion (I personally like it, and that seems to be the popular opinion) but the playtime argument isn't really valid. replayability is very high, you can fail almost every quest, and you'll have to figure out a new way to get hints as to who the murderer is. Playing one questline will often make another group/faction's questline inaccessible. So you can't play through all of the content in one playthrough, no matter what. What that means is, the playtime may be 2-3 hours, but that's only for your first playthrough. after that you'll be able to explore all the questlines you didn't get to play, and on the way to those you'll probably find an entirely new storyline you had never even seen. The game is jam packed with content, most of which requires exploring to find.
You can beat the game only exploring around 25% of the map. Or in some cases, even finding the murderer by chance alone. The murderer is always walking around, so shooting random people is a legitimate strategy. You'll also unlock new characters to play as, allowing for challenge runs. The game also has a local co-op mode, though I never personally played it. The game is actually funny but doesn't go overboard on jokes, as to make it solely reliant on humor. You don't have to play through the same questlines over and over again for different playthroughs, the entire world is open from the start. So when you want to go back and find what other stuff you missed, you'll just be able to run to that location/look around for secrets.
The only complaint i can really issue is little, but towards the end game, so hover over if you don't mind spoiling some of the end game.
. Besides that, i really have no complaints. The game is very good and i would recommend it to anyone.

Okay, so I'm in my early forties and grew up playing...well, not strictly Dungeons & Dragons, but certainly a wide variety of tabletop roleplaying games, all of them undeniably owing their lineage to that great, wise ol' grandaddy of RPGs. While I don't roleplay too often these days, such tabletop games hog a HUGE sentimental spot inside my heart, and this is a documentary about another childish ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in his forties who refuses to grow up.
What's more, it's a very WELL-MADE documentary about a childish ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in his forties who refuses to grow up, which captures the youthful spirit of such dreamers very, very nicely indeed. It's perhaps not the BEST film about the subject in question - there's a recently-released fiction film called Zero Charisma which probably deserves that honour - but it is of indisputably good quality.
Two questions still remain, though: is it worth ten dollars to purchase, and should it be on Steam?
Hmmm...tricky questions, to be sure. To me, ten dollars? Absolutely. I didn't grow up in an entitled, selfish generation which believes it should get everything for free. Sure, I dubiously download plenty of stuff, but sometimes I'm willing to acknowledge that it took someone longer than 0.9 nanoseconds of their time to produce a product, and henceforth I'm happy to give them a small slice of what little money I have.
Trust me when I say that this documentary is unlikely to make anyone filthy rich, so this is clearly a labour of love. Henceforth, it doesn't deserve your vitriol as much as, say, I don't know...Bill Gates' recent pet virus, aka "Windows 10"? Whoever made this movie made it to share something with other human beings, not to buy more third-world, ten year-old sex slaves to fill the basements of their many mansions. Save your cynicism for the big guns.
Should it be on Steam? Hmmm...a harder question. Given that there seems to be no end of short and feature films with LITTLE TO NO RELATION TO GAMING on Steam of late, I'd say this one easily qualifies as "relevant" by comparison. Put it another way: without Dungeons & Dragons, there almost certainly wouldn't be ♥♥♥♥ing SKYRIM, or even Dark Souls for that matter. But for anyone who wants to make a lucid, mature argument that perhaps Steam isn't an appropriate platform for distributing videos, period, I'm not necessarily going to argue with you.
In all honesty, this product was an impulse buy, and partly because I had Steam dollars just sitting there waiting to be spent. Do I consider it ten dollars well spent? Absolutely. Could I have just downloaded it for free from somewhere else off the internet? Probably. But somebody, sometime, should perhaps pay for this♥♥♥♥♥♥ or else people will stop making movies altogether, and whoever made this isn't Michael ♥♥♥♥ing Bay. Ten bucks isn't a lot of money, and once Valve takes their cut, I sincerely doubt that anyone involved with this film will be buying their Mum a new mansion with the proceeds.
Short version: if you're looking for a Steam-distributed video to hate on, this really isn't the one. Start your battle elsewhere, and perhaps slowly make your way back to this if your vitriol carries you that far. As far as I'm concerned, any GAME-related (and not just VIDEO game-related) documentary has a place here. You don't agree, then don't buy it. Surely you have better things to do with your time than troll Store pages.
Cheers to anyone who bothered to read this far - I know this review has a few more words and far less pictures than your average Facebook post - and if you still think I deserve a big, fat thumb-down, go for it. I'll be the first to admit that I do enjoy a good rant. Cheers to Steam for giving me the space in which to do so (hey, whadya know, it IS still a "free" world after all...for another fortnight or so, at least)!!

While a very interesting topic, I found the documentary to be chaotic, kitchy and uninformative. After one and a half hours I would have hoped to know more about how the artist works, how he develops his products, how it compares to the competition, if there even is any, how the manufacturing process looks, how an average day might look, maybe get some details on artistic decisions, get to know some of his colleagues, hear some of their stories, see interviews with customers and hear their comments on the product, maybe get some commentary on his techniques, what sets him off against other artists etc. etc.
Instead the viewer gets a confusing mess of emotionally charged biographical tidbits, random direct quotes, redundant mundane scenes and philosophical platitudes. The documentary focusses a lot on the emotional bond the artist feels for his parents, yet fails to show how he coped with the realities of everyday life as an artist. How did he pay for his year in Italy, for instance? Who payed for college? How did he finance his company in the beginning? How did he cope in difficult times? Does he miss painting? Doesn´t he get tired of sculpting brick walls all the time? Why D&D? Why not some other pen and paper? I´m tired of documentaries about arts and music making it seem as though working in that field is merely some sort of dream state or long party. We see the artist laughing and drinking a lot, musing on the importance of doing what one loves without a thorough exploration of how exactly he made that work for himself. All the while a seriously untalented guitarist plays on a badly tuned guitar, covering the whole thing in sticky hipster sauce. This could have been sooooooo much better.

Deluxe Edition reviewed - 3rd party store that was £40.
FIRST IMPRESSIONS:-
Much improved iteration of the last 2 games, a lot of the models have been updated and better lighting effects, higher AA options, more creation content, replay editors, will update review once had more time to mess with it, but so far first impressions are better than 2k15 and 2k16 editions.
25 hours of gameplay later
---------------------------------------
Well a lot more time has passed and I have messed about with creation tools, played online matches, played solo career modes and have noticed subtle difference, which is easier to explain as Pros vs Cons against the 2k16 edition.
Pros:-
* More character ainmations
* Smoother animations between actions
* New taunting system is vastly improved, taunts can be performed in and around the ring, apron, and on the ropes etc. for the crowds or taunting wrestlers directly to get up etc... and the AI use it too, making it look and feel more like the TV show.
* Less input lag from controller - although some of the minigames are still so-so.
* Better lighting effect, noticebly more lights and smoke FXs
* 8xAA supported (4xAA cap last two versions) so better quality available.
* Performance of the game is still great, getting a solid 60fps in highest settings at 4k resolution, even with 8xAA it only drops by 2fps at most in a 30man Royal Rumble. (I7 3770k with gtx1080, 32gb RAM) and a lot of the cutcenes on intros are now running in 60fps (some parts are locked to 30fps still).
* Better CAW system
* New (text only) Promo mode added to career mode
* New batch of Superstars added to roster
* Simpler UI menus - stripped away all the fluff and literally just text menu system that shows everything you need to see all at once, saves a lot of time looking for sub-menus.
* New basic video editor tools for making match highlights into videos for your custom character's titantron videos, although the encode seems to be glitched is a very dark output.
* Loading times are vastly better, at least on my system, which helps a lot going between creator tools.
* Seems they have fixed the sound problems seen in 2k15 and 2k16 where I had lost crowd sounds in custom character matches occassionally.
Cons:-
* Still has the dumb as♥♥♥♥♥♥console upload/download system instead of Steam Workshop, as long as still having 100 slot cap, with 20 downloads per 24 hour period limit. (seriously???)
* Creation tools occasionally crash out when re-editing your characteers, causing a CTD device video driver crash - I've tried numerous drivers and nothing has fixed it, so will need dev patch.
* AI is still a bit wonky on the decision making in AI matches
* Some of the necklaces and gowns, cloaks etc. still suffer from clipping issues
* Commentary is still quite limited, hear a lot of things repeated
* Still no custom music importing
* Still no custom videos for Titanwall importing
* Paid DLC this time around - bit of a annoyance given it still had a 4-5 month delay in release, sorry but paid dlc should only happen if we get the game the same week as consoles, not midway into that season when 5-6 months to new build of the game.
*Still no roster updates mid-season, bit annoying if they are going to DLC things up and not have a roster update to reflect heel turns and changes to intros etc. EA / FIFA do this for free... just saying.
* Took out some of the old classic stars to fit in new characters, really this should ever happen, always add, never remove... I miss Honky Tonk Man etc.
* Online play while on the whole seems less laggy, the matchmaking service is a utter joke... seriously needs an overhaul, thankfully I mainly play solo and mess about with custom creations, but I'd guess this a big feature to be broken for the majority of buyers. When I have played online sessions it's strictly private matches with friends which was hassle free.
* Create a wrestler mode only borked one thing, they removed the ability to create fat / thin models entirely, despite having many skinny and oversized characters in the game.... that's a massive (pun intended) oversight to people that like to build freeks of nature, instead of buff medium bodied people.
Overall - I feel like this is a improved game and worth the price, hopefully once the bugs are ironed out it will become the defact wrestling game on PC (not thats it shard to be with no competition from EA UFC series).

Cons:

A point and click game based of a shooter franchise, what could go wrong? In this case, nothing, in fact it turned out better than everyone expected. A story in the Borderlands setting, matching the tone and expanding on the lore, this game is one that stands out for many, even those who aren't big fans of the point&click. A narrative like the one in Tales from the Borderlands is not one you could find in most games. It dares to be original, it dares to be humorous no matter what and it dares to change to a darker tone in key moments. Sometimes you'll laugh, sometimes you'll stare, most times you'll be relaxed. This game consists of 5 entertaining episodes, which tell a story in a fair pace.
Looking at the game-play mechanics, it follows the TellTale formula: lines of dialogue with limited time to choose, walking, pointing&clicking and the QTE's. Doesn't sound like anything special, but it's in those moments you realize how charming the game is. QTE's consist of awesome and often times humorous moments, dialogue choices are comprehensive and they can even extend to being choices of how you approach things, which garner different reaction for the rest of the game.
I'd like to say graphics are ageless due to their art-style, but while characters scale nicely with the resolution, there are some low texture environments, however their blended well with the rest(most of the time it's either rocky grounds or a wall with high quality posters). There are plenty of breathtaking views on the way, but personally I was too focused on the story to take my time. There are options to click for better views on certain things, which also come with one liners from the current protagonist.
Where the game truly shines is the story. 4 and a half of the episodes are narrated by the protagonists, which sometimes can lead to hyperbolous situations, quickly interrupted however. There are two protagonist, Rhys "The Salary Man" and Fiona "The Con Artist". The former works on Hyperion, dreaming day and night about owning the place and the latter is pulling a big score. The build up is quick, as halfway through the first episode, they cross paths and so does the story begin.  Having certain characters from past video games with the same old Borderlands end game of hunting for a vault and a narrative that was seriously worked on to not be serious, you have yourself a fine taste comedy that's blended in with a survival motif, obvious character development, that all leads to the sensation of completing a game you've enjoyed. The cast of characters is pretty extensive, from the young and "cutely" innocent to killers that looks like their inside rot is growing to the outside, just like you'd expect in Borderlands.  In direct proportionality with the character development, the tone gets darker, reaching the pinnacle in the last episode, where even the intro is different. However, in the second half, they get back to a more lighter tone since the gang is back together, however it's not the comedy it was before, as they face the grand threat, which as a substitute for the funny lines it had motivational ones and awesome moments, balancing the first half in order to maintain the more light-heartet tone of the series.  I won't give spoilers, but here are a few lines from the end which best describe the narrative:
Those lines are on point. Don't judge the writing though, it's just a casual moment.
One thing to add is that you don't need to have played any of the previous Borderlands games. While I imagine old fans would have their thrills seeing some of the NPCs and Vault Hunters in the story, new comers will have the right introductions to said characters, if not better ones.
If you want to have a good time, find out how loud you can laugh and expand your list of fictional characters you'll never forget, you can pick this game up. Full price, on sale that's up to you really. It's worth both and note, there won't be any future seasons, but it might be the game you'll replay once in a while, just out of pure enjoyment.

I honestly give this film a 10/10. This documentary follows Stefan Pokorny, an artist that creates gaming terrain for dungeons and dragons and other fantasy settings. It is a touching story that follows his journey through the years, with a focus on his most recent goals. Having been a dungeon master for many years, he always had a knack for making maps and designing worlds, so this documentary focuses on him making those dreams a reality. You see the struggle that he and his colleagues/coworkers face as they hope to raise the necessary funds for their project via Kickstarter. I believe that Stefan is a wonderful artist that shares his talent with the world, and I can appreciate that. There are moments that are very humanizing, and Stefan's perserverance is questioned. Regardless of anything, he pursues his artistic goals in hopes of being able to sustain himself through his work. I myself am a musician, writer and philosopher, I understand the struggle that one faces in attempting to pursue a profession that is fulfilling both financially and artistically. We all seek happiness, and I think Stefan Pokorny is very admirable for his pursuit of happiness. It is not solely for himself either, he wishes to share his happiness through his work that he gives to the world.
I have been a dungeon master for about 7 years now, starting around the age of 20. I always loved using my imagination, but that is unfortunately something that is stripped by the conventions of modern society. Adults are not encouraged to use their imaginations or engage in creative thinking often enough, and this contributes to many misunderstandings about d&d. Dungeons and Dragons is a social game where the dungeon master acts as a storyteller of sorts, and the players are the protagonists of these stories. I believe that far too many people give up on their dreams, and I applaud Stefan Pokorny's persistence and courage in pursuing his dream. I believe that the world would benefit greatly if people set their fears and inhibitions aside in search of their dreams. I only hope that I can hold onto my dreams as long as Stefan has, because regardless of the outcome, I would know that I had tried.
I found this film inspirational as a dungeons and dragons fan and as a human being. If you are any kind of artist, or if you care about following your dreams, then I think you will be able to appreciate this fine documentary. This is why I give it a 10/10!

This game is just phenomenal! The story is very good even though it is quite short. The characters and the dialouges are funny and entertaining as you can pretty much always choose between 1-3 answers. This makes the story a little less linear. The gameplay is something different than the usual games. You can leap around with your Hyper-Trousers by holding the left mouse button and releasing it. By scrolling up on the mouse wheel you enter the 'Crosslink-mode'. In this mode you can rewire certain things for example, instead of turning on/off the light you can rewire the light switch to open/close a door or even fire off a gun by a patroling enemy. But there are different circuits with different colours. You can wire a red light switch to a red door but you can't wire a red light switch to a bue door. Pretty obvious, right? You can also buy/upgrade your gear to make things a little bit easier but also more interesting. You can solve the levels in many different ways depending on the gear that you have bought with the money you get from completing a level. The levels all work the same way. Get in the building, hack one or more computers and leave without getting shot. You can do this stealthy and not kill anyone but you can also kill the guards and hack the computer without having to hope not to be seen. At least in the first few levels because as you advance in the story the buildings become bigger and the guards become more and stronger. But I don't want to spoil too much about the story as I think you should play it yourself. Another thing I really like about this game is the level editor and the Steam Workshop. The user-made levels can make you play the game even after finishing the story as there are so many and a lot are very good. Also the soundtrack of this game is just amazing but I suggest you listen to it yourself as it might not be the kind of music you like (opinions and stuff)!

It’s no secret that the presence of shmups has witnessed a decline over the past several years. While some might argue that such an occurrence is par for the course; given that the genre has always found its roots in arcades which have also become exceedingly rare; there are many who would nevertheless consider it a great shame to see a whole genre on the verge of disappearing altogether. Attempts have been made to breathe fresh life into the scrolling shooter, but the number that has been met with favourable commercial and critical results has always fallen shorter than what most shmup fans would have liked to have witnessed. It should be of great interest then to those invested in the fate of the genre to know that Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION is a shmup that comes of only the highest quality.
Crimzon Clover began as a Flash game developed by YOTSUBANE in 2011. After being re-released two years later in Japanese arcades the game was finally remade into what you have here: Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION – an international version of the surprise-hit arcade title. There doesn’t appear to be any overarching narrative to accompany the action of Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION and if there is, then it’s safe to say that it’s nowhere to be found in the game. Then again, games of this nature aren’t known for their need of any grand story in order to deliver the experience expected by their target audience.
The core gameplay of Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION revolves around the concept of the Break Gauge. After choosing from one of four different ships the player is presented with five stages of increasing difficulty, each of which is played in sequence. Defeating enemies using either the standard, forward-firing attack or the powerful homing attack releases scoring items and gradually fills the aforementioned gauge. When the gauge exceeds one of two thresholds the player is granted the ability to use a ‘bomb’ which could be useful should the bullet count start to pile up beyond what one might find manageable otherwise. Refraining from using a bomb enables the gauge to fill even further and upon exceeding a second threshold it becomes possible to enter Break Mode. Doing so dramatically increases the player’s firepower and includes the added benefit of raking in more points, though it should be noted that Break Mode only lasts a limited period of time, after which the player’s attack power and scoring capabilities both return to the default level.
It’s a great idea that employs the use of several short-term goals to encourage a very aggressive playstyle, one that sees the player always seeking to make the most of their time spent in Break Mode, and immediately looking to re-enter the mode as swiftly as possible following its closure. Enemy placement has been well thought out: weak but fast enemies appear in great numbers often to shield stronger opponents hiding further up the screen. This provides the player with a good opportunity to build up their score multiplier before going after the targets that are worth the most points. The fact that this formula pertaining to the arrangement of enemy formations persists throughout the entire game; and that it consistently yields itself to create a satisfying set of dynamics; is what makes Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION so impressive. It would be hard to find any obvious flaws in the game’s level designs, and for that YOTSUBANE and Adventure Planning Service are to be applauded.
The game includes four different modes of play, most of which can be played solo or with a second player through local co-op. The Original mode of play enables the player to extend their offensive capabilities even further upon breaching a third threshold in order to enter Double Break Mode, while the Boost mode of play automatically forces the player to enter Break Mode upon reaching the second threshold. As long as Break Mode remains active, one’s score increases, although this also comes at the expense of the enemies putting up more of a fight too. The Unlimited mode of play is a true test of how well one knows the game and it wouldn’t be inaccurate to describe it as being one of the most satisfying and rewarding aspects of the game. It puts players in the hot zone from the very beginning and doesn’t let up until all is said and done. Players who have the stomach for it will likely come back to this mode of play time and time again. Last but not least is the Time Attack mode of play, a short, single-player venture in which the player aims to earn as many points as possible within a limited period of time on a stage unique to that mode. Lives are unlimited but that doesn’t make Time Attack any less demanding; nor any less enjoyable; than the rest of the game.
Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION excels in the aesthetics department too. Each of the sprites has been made with meticulous detail, the bullets and various environments all sport a wide variety of different colours and overall the visual feedback provided to the player is excellent while soundtrack falls nothing short of being amazing. To some extent it looks like some degree of inspiration has been drawn from CAVE’s
series, particularly in regards to the appearance of the scoring items and some of the enemy designs. It might be nice to have a centralized element of the UI that displays the remaining amount of Break Mode time the player has left at their disposal, rather than having to take one’s eyes away from the action to check a panel positioned on the left side of the screen, and it wouldn’t hurt to have a boss health gauge display that becomes transparent when the player’s ship passes through it either, but both of these are minor issues and don’t do any great harm to the overall presentation.
In short it would be sufficient to say that Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION is everything a bullet hell game should be. Highly polished, highly refined and highly enjoyable, it’s exactly the type of game that arcades could have done with several years ago, and is certainly one that those in search of a worthwhile scrolling shooter could do with today. With developers like YOTSUBANE and Adventure Planning Service around, one can rest assured that the future of the genre lies in good hands.

As other reviewes have said, it was definitely interesting to use the gels instead of portals, but it just wasnt enough to compensate for the fact that the puzzles and story are so lacking.
The puzzles, while at first are easy enough to grasp and learn with, seem to taper off quality wise during the latter half of the game. They gain this 'fake' difficulty by using elements of precise timing, or in some cases, tricky level design. The timing bits wouldnt be as bad, but they are used in a manner where if not done correctly, you will have to repeat a long process (setting up gel or cubes, and getting into position) or even in one case, reload the level.  The 'tricky' level design is used in a way where parts of the level use mechanics that may not be apparent to the player, namely, Source engine trickery involving player movement and momentem.
While the level design wasn't bad, some of the puzzles placed obsticles in a way where the (what I believe to be correct) way of solving the puzzle involved 'cheaty' methods to actually solve the puzzle (coating cubes to bounce them closer to you, arcing gels to get them over emancipation grids, clipping parts of surfaces to get gel on them). There was also a reoccuring theme of using the deadly water in 99% of the chambers, making slight errors turn into bigger problems when you die and reset the level, potentially losing progress of gels or cubes. Some of the 'puzzles' werent even puzzles, and utilized a timed racing concept as the rooms' challenge (there was a skip level button, as a solution to a problem that shouldnt have been there in the first place). This broke immersion of the game and struck me as a complete afterthough of the game, most likely after the devs noticed an unintended side effect of the gels.
Gameplay wise, some gameplay elements seemed to not work well, and unfortunately, this included the gels. They were mostly fine on flat surfaces, but any other slightly rounded or sharp edges cause the gel to behave oddly. When you move over certain objects (buttons, cubes, rails) while under the effects of the gels, you sometimes fly off in random directions. This may be an unintended side effect of the Source engine not handling this mechanic well, but its infuriating nonetheless.

The House in Fata Morgana opens as you wake up in a gloomy mansion with a creepy maid standing by. She calls you her--and the mansion's--master, but what is this place and who is she? Is there really a witch haunting the mansion? Why does the maid insist on taking you through the house, opening doors that reveal tragic stories that seem ripped out of the pages of plays, fables, and cautionary tales? What connects the people in these stories that span hundreds of years? Most importantly, who are you, anyway?
Fata Morgana is a story about how grief, hatred, and vengeance create cages not just for your enemies, but also for you yourself. It's also a story about the ways in which ignorance and complacency can warp even the most well-meant and sefless acts into tragedy.  It's a story that gives you plenty of reasons to hate a large chunk of its cast, but then challenges you to think about their actions and motivations from other perspectives.  It's full of graphic depictions of violence, but it treats difficult subjects with a surprising degree of care and sensitivity. It's a bit of a hard sell for the first few hours if you're not interested in the first few doors' stories, but there's a reason why the maid is showing you them, and it's well worth sticking with the game and seeing in retrospect why it was important to watch them.
There are no "routes" in this game, though there are a few bad ends, mostly clustered around the final 5-6 hours, all of which are short and result from obviously bad choices.  It's easy to load your most recent auto-save, select the right answer, and move on; you don't explore alternative possibilities so much as watch as one long story unfolds. The game also telegraphs most of its big revelations well in advance, but the real pleasure of Fata Morgana (aside from its excellent soundtrack) lies in watching as the frame of reference for the game's events and characters gets bigger and bigger, and in seeing how the significance (and even sometimes the reality!) of its revelations changes in the process.
I have only two major pieces of criticism about FM. The first is that the art ranges from "gorgeous and perfectly fitting" to "so anatomically incorrect that it's distracting": some of its character portraits are noticeably worse than others. Regardless, the art is unique and stylish, so I can't fault it too much. The second bit of criticism is that this VN doesn't always do a great job of establishing its settings and character voices. There's a happy medium between having characters speak in "thee"s and "thou"s and going off on long tangents about medieval religion and politics, and having them speak like modern teens in casual conversation while only vaguely sketching out the background circumstances of their lives and beliefs. Most of the time, FM gets the balance right, but the times when it doesn't are immersion-breaking and they detract from the storytelling; luckily, I was too invested in the characters and their stories to care very much.
tl;dr: One of my favourite visual novels. Made me cry. Buy it now, then join me in waiting anxiously for the fandisc to be released.

This is a story of love that knows no time, no bounds, and that no matter how much you suffered, one day you are going to find someone or something that will make you wanna live with all of your heart.

Okay, here's my short review on my short playtime in the only Portal game I couldn't finish:
Pros:
Voice acting was fairly solid, despite occasional failings
Puzzle system is unique
It's a Portal game
Cons:
The game lacks serious polish, evident in a few of the nearly-copied levels from Portal 2
A gel gun is absolutely terrible to solve puzzles with
Some puzzles require downright perfection in execution, resulting in a jarring difference from Portal's typical acceptance of minor imperfections in movement or positioning
This game has a great idea, but executes it fairly poorly. The design of some of the surf-reliant sections is particularly bad, resulting in running into the side of a slope instead of sliding gently onto it from any point on the previous surface. If the developer softens the levels' expectations of perfection in every movement, it would definitely be worth paying for. However, as it is, I can't recommend paying for it as I can't possibly complete it. And this is coming from a lover of puzzle games (see my review on The Talos Principle for evidence).
So, no...I can't recommend this game until the developer repairs some of the glaring problems in it. It's definitely a game for you if you enjoy being known as a "try-hard", but if you're simply looking for more good Portal fun, this is not the place to do so. I couldn't even complete it. It would be recommendable if it were free, but as a sold title, it lacks the necessary quality assurance.

Even people who are put off by anime tropes and character designs should be able to enjoy this, since the style is very unique and the characters don't fit into any sort of trope. They are just people with complexity and flaws.
I would highly recommend this to anyone who wants a complex story with romance, drama, mystery, and a good touch of horror.

Sooo...  Minecraft: Story Mode - Season Two.

The Artwork and the Animations are mostly the old ones with alot of new ones, every Scene looks really well made, as you can see, in my 13 Hours of playtime, i uploaded over 100 Screenshots.
Music is pin'point Amazing, like allways. espacially the **** Ninja OST.
Everything just feels like home (Season 1) just even better!
So to answer my Question if its any good as Season 1?
It's even better!
Truely worth every Cent i spend on it. I would really like to see more, like in the first Season!

I'll start by saying I'm a huge fan of the series. I own every HoMM and every expansion and DLC 1-7.
That being said, I do not recommend the HD version of the game. My wife bought 2 copies so we could play together. Without a LAN feature (which was removed for this version) we were forced to play using the steam online mode, and after disconnecting a few seconds ino the game several times, even after forwarding all relevant ports, we swapped back to the Heroes 3 Complete from
($10 and includes all the expansion with no DRM).
The HD graphics upgrades are nice, and are undeniably better then the original graphics, however, the new set of problems (crashes) and lack of several features present in the cheaper non-HD version do not allow me to give a pass for this game.
If Ubisoft releases the expansions in HD, or heck, even just fixes the disconnecting issues then I may be able to change my recommendation.
I do appreciate the effort to modernize such a great classic as Heroes of Might and Magic 3, it truly is a masterpiece of a game. Playing through the single player campaign in updated HD will surely be a treat when I get around to it, but don't expect the multiplayer feature to work well in this mode. At least not as of this writing. The hotseat feature still worked fine, however.

A wonderful game to get into the Warhammer 40K universe.  Take your Force Commander and assemble your team to undertake missions that require either strategy, brute force, or a combination of both.  The game to me, seems to be true to the WH40K lore.

For me, Prototype 2 is far superior than the original.
Unlike the original, the unfair game mechanics and busywork of side missions are removed. Instead, the //BLACKNET side missions tell a seperate story that ties into the events of the second outbreak of the Mercer Virus; that is, if you care to know it. This time around, the story is actually interesting, and the main character is very likeable. He's a soldier with nothing to lose and everything to gain. Being a veteran myself, I like how the game lets you use combat tactics with the Hunt ability. It lets you assess a situation, plan, and execute - that is - if you choose to always use stealth like I do.
Additionally, the final boss battle is actually fun and satisfying. Unlike the final boss battle of the last game, you're not this biological super-weapon running around to avoid a boss that can one-hit-kill you. Instead, the final boss battle is evenly matched, and is purely a test of skill. You have to know your powers and use them accordingly to the situation.
Besides that, my only negative issue with this game is that it's still short just like the previous game. However, if this game were still $60, I'd definately say that I got my monies worth. I don't know why people have negative reviews of this game outside of their personal technical issues, but to each is own.

Crimzon Clover is the Quentin Tarantino of shmups. It is very up front and honest about its influences but manages to take the tropes of a given genre and make it into something fresh and new, which may be the wankiest thing ever said about this game.
Long story short, it's an excellent shooter. Various elements recall the best games from Cave, Raizing, and even Triangle Service without feeling derivative of any of them. Except Cave. The DoDonPachi vibe is strong with this one but the play system is different enough that it's more like a knowing nod to one of the greats than a pure ripoff.
Graphically the game is a bit hit and miss. Some sprites and backgrounds seem a tad too scaled up and as a result are more pixelated than you'd expect. The background variety is quite good though. Weapon and bullet graphics are excellent. Colorful enough that you never feel cheated, unlike every single game ever made by Raizing/8ing.
If you like shooters, you need this game. There's nothing here that's groundbreaking but not everything needs to be. This is a game made by a competent developer with an obvious love for the genre in general, and I can not wait to see what Yotsubane will come up with next.

Aperture Tag replaces your Portal gun with a new Paint gun. Now you must shoot blue and orange goo in order to solve puzzles. Portals still play a role in the puzzle solutions, but you don't get to control their placement.
This game consists of four chapters that ramp up nicely in difficulty from an introduction to jumping to some quite challenging combinations of switches, portals, blocks, and goo. Long time EVE player here. I thought I should probably leave a review to offset all the negative reviews recently.
Putting this game on steam for free was a mistake.
This is definitely not a "game" you just download and try out for a bit. Playing EVE has to be a conscious decision and requires a huge amount of upfront time investment and willingness to learn before it will start giving back. But
this game gives back, it will do so with some of the greatest experiences you can have in a game.
Saying that this game isn't for most people would be an understatement. Saying this game isn't for casual players, people incabable of handling stress and confrontation, people who expect things to be fair or even people who think you can play this game as a game would be an understatement as well.
EVE Online is for people who want to play EVE Online. There is no other game that even comes close to it in this particular niche. The day EVE started trying to be a popular game, it would cease to be EVE Online.
What I'm saying is that if you're on the edge about giving EVE a try, you should ignore popular opinion, as this game isn't a popular game, but a niche game. A very specific niche which will only appeal to a select few.
If you're not one of those select few, who happened to be looking for an unforgiving multiplayer space simulation with massive depth, that's cool. There's less taxing space games out there.
Just please stop critizing EVE for not trying to be World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 2, or any other casual MMO out there.
It can't and shouldn't be a popular game.

- The voice acting is just horrible.
- The monologue is horribly unfunny.

The Verdict:
Conditionally recommended. Get it if you love the paint gun, don't mind the mentioned bugs and it's on sale.

"It was like a bomb had gone off, killing everyone but sparing the furniture."
What a wonderfully melancholic game about family, memories, surrealism, child-like imagination, weird tales, unfortunate accidents, misfortune, and the drudgery of life. By the end, it made me appreciate my family a lot more, and made me tear up. What Remains Of Edith Finch feels like the culmination of what Gone Home, Vanishing Of Ethan Carter, and That Dragon Cancer were leading towards, but has enough of its own identity, perspective shifts, and gameplay differences, that it comes out as something all its own. It's quite coincidental that Blackwood Crossing came out earlier this month which also has a female protagonist, full body awareness, is surreal, and also about family and memories. Both work quite well as complimentary pieces, although they're emotionally hard-hitting so be ready for that.
We know the deal with firstperson narrative adventure games (or walking simulators if you want to call them that) now. It's going to have a short length, fitting for a short story. There's going to be lots of narration, lots of walking, quite pretty scenery, a sombre tone, and not particularly that much interactions. Except in the past year or so, that's changing especially on the gameplay verbs front. With games like That Dragon Cancer, Firewatch, and Blackwood Crossing, you're doing lots more actions with the controls. In the case of this game with the episodes pertaining to different family members, not only are you doing various actions with the same controls like flying a kite, making a toy frog jump in the bath, or taking photos of your daughter on a hunting trip, but also having whole perspective and gameplay shifts. Not only gameplay shifts, but even the tonal shifts match the age of the character, like those of Molly and Gregory being the youngest kids having the most playful sections in the game. One episode has you straight up playing a melee horror game with an amazing nod to Halloween that made me shout out loud in disbelief how they were able to secure the music. Another has you hopping between animals such as a cat, owl, shark, and tentacle. Last but not least, is the mind-bending multi-tasking Lewis episode where you're using your mouse for the drudgery of cutting up fish but also using the direction buttons to move a 3D king avatar in a top-down fantasy world at the same time which then transforms into a full-blown 3rd person perspective. This constant variety gives a real sense of adventure and memorability to these short stories about a family, while giving satisfaction that you've been through a lot in the 2-3 hour playthrough much like metaphorically the family has been.
What ties all these short stories and family members together is the tall and oddly-shaped Finch house. The attention to detail is incredible, even surpassing Gone Home, in what you can glean just from the environmental storytelling of mise en scene. Just even down to when you inhabit the bodies of the family members, looking down at your bodies thanks to the full body awareness to notice details like Edith's fingerless gloves and feather-ring necklace or Lewis as the king tells a story in of itself. Quite a few of the family members' rooms have specific books pertaining to their hobbies and interests, like Dawn's travel and english books for teaching abroad in India, Edie's conspiracy material, Odin's folktales, and Calvin's science books for his love of astronomy. Textually, the game never makes a point of it, but you can figure out why Edith and Lewis are darker skinned and mixed race compared to the skin tone of the other family members, which gives a nice sense of diversity and reality to how varied a family can be ethnically. All of the elements of the short stories are related to that family member's belongings such as animal toys for Molly or videogames for Lewis. The house is labyrinthine, which is a testament to how great the level design is that is tied directly to the visual storytelling. This is all backed by a beautiful music score thanks to Jeff Russo. Despite the game at the outset detailing that everyone in your family has died, there were still constant surprises and a couple of late game plot twists that I wasn't expecting that left me heartbroken.
After the game finished, I had to talk to my mom and sister immediately afterwards about appreciating them and being grateful for still having them around and for most of my immediate family still being alive. Giant Sparrow earns my congratulations for delivering one of my favourite games of the year in an already very strong year for videogames.

The House in Fata Morgana is a masterful piece of storytelling.
The game demands a lot from its reader, but rewards perseverance tenfold with an incredibly compelling and rich narrative. To say the story 'has layers' is a vast understatement, and yet to get much more specific would risk spoiling the effect for first time players. Suffice it to say that the game revels in challenging your perceptions and turning assumptions upside down as events unfold.
What begins as a seemingly straightforward and clichéd setup is soon unravelled and spun out into a kaleidoscopic exploration of themes and characters across various time periods and settings, framed by the oppressive Mansion that your character finds themselves in. As I mentioned, the tale is not always an easy read and takes some extremely dark, intense and uncomfortable turns, but the characters are so well fleshed-out that you come to feel truly invested in their trials and triumphs. So yeah; perseverance required, and moments of levity are well-earned.
I do have some minor reservations about the writing - the decision to represent laughter phonetically (such as 'Hehehe') detracts from the atmosphere on occasion by invoking more a feeling of online messenger chat than character dialogue, but I got used to it. Most of my other complaints turned out to be the game messing with me.
Finally, the music and overall sound design is fantastic and adds a lot to the atmosphere. So if you enjoy dark, character-driven story-based games, The House in Fata Morgana delivers in spades and I cannot recommend it highly enough. It will haunt me for a long time.

Ostensibly "open world," but this is perhaps the best example of what I call a "stealth linear" game--or a game whose linearity is enforced by difficulty rather than arbitrary barriers or quest order. This can become a bit absurd at times (for example, in instances where the difference between entering a new area by slaughtering a monster with little difficulty and beating it for hours with no damage is just one measly level up the world begins to seem considerably less "open"), but at least for the first chapter or so of this game (its most thrilling sections) this isn't as much of a problem just because basically everything will insta-kill you. So you have to make do with running and sneaking about. Once you choose a faction and the storylines kick in the game drags a bit (the Orc temple portions at the end are outright terrible grinds), but the early portions of the game are enough to earn it its status as a classic. A great game despite the weak landing.

I will list a few pros and cons I came across during my time with the game, to show what I observed and provide additional comments as I feel are necessary to explain.
Pros:
+ Horses you can use to fast travel
+ Extra "lives" (hats) from lining up shots just right, which helps balance out the deaths
+ There is a map, and a journal
+ Western-Style Murder Mystery (I'm not sure if the killer's identity is the same every time, or if it's like the Clue board game)
+ Quests
+ Go nuts murdering everyone in town; yes, almost everyone seems to have a gun, and killing them all is kinda relieving if you get frustrated with the game
+ Bank your money because if you run out of lives (hats), you lose half the money you have on you, which I think is pretty darn fair
+ Music was pretty nice
Cons (Adding spacing for clarity between each point):
- Tons of NPCs to talk to with repeating dialog, but you want/have to talk to every one or you might miss a clue or a quest
- No mouse support at all
- You have to press J to draw your weapon, then K to cLock it (can't say cLock without the L on Steam), then press K again to fire it, then press R to load each, singular bullet into your gun...that's right, emptying a gun with 6 bullets and refilling it takes 19 button presses, vs. the 7 or 8 it would take in almost any other game ever made
- Quest Overload (all at once), ala the original Mass Effect Citadel, the beginning of Morrowind, etc., where you have a large number of quests piled onto you in a very short time, rather than a small, controllable trickle of quests that keeps you wanting more; especially ugly and overwhelming when done early-game, as with Westerado
- Failing quests that cannot be repeated due to derpy AI: I was sent to find a man in a mine, and when I got there, I found out I needed a light, so I had to talk to an old miner in town (had to find him which took a couple of minutes to begin with), who then he tells me he wants a 25-year-old train ticket. Fine. So I go to the train station and get that, bring it back to him, he give's me a miner helmet, then I die while going through the mine, losing the helmet so I have to wing it in darkness. When I finally get the guy, some jerks start shooting at me, and while I'm shooting back at them, the guy I'm trying to guide out of the mine for my quest runs like a chicken with his head cut off, right into the line of my gunfire, getting himself killed, which basically means I wasted about 25 minutes of my time on a quest that failed in one instant of the AI suiciding
- Pop culture jokes: I used to love this stuff, but I don't need to see Game of Thrones jokes (yes, I saw one in this game) in my western game I'm trying to get into
- Non-human enemies such as wolves can be a pain to kill, simply because lining up shots the way this game's combat works is pretty challenging. I shot three guys' hats off in a row, getting an achievement for that, but could not manage to shoot a wolf despite emptying my gun on it at different angles, trying to score a hit
- 8-bit graphics are old hat by now, and this game's combat system suffers for it. Blaster Master has more angles you can shoot at, and that came out in 1988. They could do so much better without having to go too much higher on a technical level.
- Lack of a main quest/motivation: Sure, the game gives you an end goal, but the game is sort of like "Hey, just do everything, and you'll get clues about who the killer is whom you're trying to find." In other words, you're encouraged to do every quest, without being told which quest(s) are necessary to complete the game. You will be running around just doing crap hoping it gets you closer to the end of the game, without really knowing if it does or not. This isn't particularly compelling or exciting.
-----Conclusion-----
Although there are some nice positives to this game, the negatives outweighed it for me, with the weird gunplay/combat mechanics that predate games from the late 80s, and the heap of quests the game throws on you without any indication of what's important and what's just busywork for suckers. A few decent features unfortunately do not make the overall experience of this game an enjoyable one for me, so I cannot recommend it.

Be warned that the interface is difficult to grasp at first, but it is in my opinion one of the best of all time once you learned it (Hint: Use cursor keys while keeping the mouse button down). Beyond that, the game is hard. First thing you do is climb the social ladder, before you can even think of venturing outside and challenge wild animals - let alone more dangerous foes. But once you get into it, Gothic rises to true greatness.

Before I start, I’ll just say that I remember playing this game on the Adult Swim website. It was a Flash-based game then but it was well made. As far as I understand, this is just an expanded version of that, so assuming it’s still available, you can go and enjoy it for a while before making a purchase.
I got
from
, aptly named because it is exactly that ― a sweet little gem. It’s by no means huge, don’t take the talk about its open world to mean that this is one of those games where you can spend a hundred hours just wandering around and still not discover everything. Its size is instead rather fitting the 8-bit esthetics it carries. But still, there is plenty to discover, beautiful pixel graphics to enjoy, secrets and easter eggs to find ― and the game is partly randomized and possesses different paths you can take so that it really is a somewhat different experience every time. Overall, it took me 5 and ½ hours, according to the in-game timer, to complete it for the first time, discovering all of the map in the process (though not finishing all the quests). But you can also complete it in less than 30 minutes if you try to speedrun it.
I think that the relative, and apparent, simplicity of
is one of its greatest pluses. You know how sometimes video games draw you in with promises of an epic adventure or a deep story, and then it turns out that this gets completely compromised by the “gamey” mechanics? All of the big concepts get squished into the narrow constraints of a typical video game: a compass marker tells you where to go to complete your task, a named character means a quest giver, you’re presented with a “good” and an “evil” response during a conversation…
Well, what
does is kind of the opposite. You come in expecting a simple game where you shoot bad guys and collect bags marked “$$$”. You have hats which are tongue-in-cheek stand-ins for lives. You can also buy better weapons in the shop but don’t have to worry about ammunition, it’s infinite. Everything about the game, up to and including its graphics, tells you that it’s an arcade title, one that tests your dexterity for a while and then maybe assigns you a points score.
Only that it isn’t. What you will discover is a world full of characters whose fates you can indirectly decide. There’s never an obvious indication of the magnitude of your actions, you just do whatever feels right, and the consequences arise later. Don’t take me wrong, this game isn’t very serious and there aren’t huge moral quandaries. But what impressed me is complexity that arises organically from simplicity, rather than being forced from above and ultimately constrained. There is a kind of honesty that
has in comparison to most RPGs and the like.
There are, of course, bad sides to this game. The music is not terrible at all but there’s not a lot of it either ― I think only one track per area ― so you’re going to be listening to the same tune on repeat most of the time. Also, combat can be frustrating sometimes, weapons are not very well balanced, and there will be a new bug every couple of minutes. But overall, it’s hard not to recommend this delightful title, especially if you find it on a sale or something.

"It was like a bomb had gone off, killing everyone but sparing the furniture."
What a wonderfully melancholic game about family, memories, surrealism, child-like imagination, weird tales, unfortunate accidents, misfortune, and the drudgery of life. By the end, it made me appreciate my family a lot more, and made me tear up. What Remains Of Edith Finch feels like the culmination of what Gone Home, Vanishing Of Ethan Carter, and That Dragon Cancer were leading towards, but has enough of its own identity, perspective shifts, and gameplay differences, that it comes out as something all its own. It's quite coincidental that Blackwood Crossing came out earlier this month which also has a female protagonist, full body awareness, is surreal, and also about family and memories. Both work quite well as complimentary pieces, although they're emotionally hard-hitting so be ready for that.
We know the deal with firstperson narrative adventure games (or walking simulators if you want to call them that) now. It's going to have a short length, fitting for a short story. There's going to be lots of narration, lots of walking, quite pretty scenery, a sombre tone, and not particularly that much interactions. Except in the past year or so, that's changing especially on the gameplay verbs front. With games like That Dragon Cancer, Firewatch, and Blackwood Crossing, you're doing lots more actions with the controls. In the case of this game with the episodes pertaining to different family members, not only are you doing various actions with the same controls like flying a kite, making a toy frog jump in the bath, or taking photos of your daughter on a hunting trip, but also having whole perspective and gameplay shifts. Not only gameplay shifts, but even the tonal shifts match the age of the character, like those of Molly and Gregory being the youngest kids having the most playful sections in the game. One episode has you straight up playing a melee horror game with an amazing nod to Halloween that made me shout out loud in disbelief how they were able to secure the music. Another has you hopping between animals such as a cat, owl, shark, and tentacle. Last but not least, is the mind-bending multi-tasking Lewis episode where you're using your mouse for the drudgery of cutting up fish but also using the direction buttons to move a 3D king avatar in a top-down fantasy world at the same time which then transforms into a full-blown 3rd person perspective. This constant variety gives a real sense of adventure and memorability to these short stories about a family, while giving satisfaction that you've been through a lot in the 2-3 hour playthrough much like metaphorically the family has been.
What ties all these short stories and family members together is the tall and oddly-shaped Finch house. The attention to detail is incredible, even surpassing Gone Home, in what you can glean just from the environmental storytelling of mise en scene. Just even down to when you inhabit the bodies of the family members, looking down at your bodies thanks to the full body awareness to notice details like Edith's fingerless gloves and feather-ring necklace or Lewis as the king tells a story in of itself. Quite a few of the family members' rooms have specific books pertaining to their hobbies and interests, like Dawn's travel and english books for teaching abroad in India, Edie's conspiracy material, Odin's folktales, and Calvin's science books for his love of astronomy. Textually, the game never makes a point of it, but you can figure out why Edith and Lewis are darker skinned and mixed race compared to the skin tone of the other family members, which gives a nice sense of diversity and reality to how varied a family can be ethnically. All of the elements of the short stories are related to that family member's belongings such as animal toys for Molly or videogames for Lewis. The house is labyrinthine, which is a testament to how great the level design is that is tied directly to the visual storytelling. This is all backed by a beautiful music score thanks to Jeff Russo. Despite the game at the outset detailing that everyone in your family has died, there were still constant surprises and a couple of late game plot twists that I wasn't expecting that left me heartbroken.
After the game finished, I had to talk to my mom and sister immediately afterwards about appreciating them and being grateful for still having them around and for most of my immediate family still being alive. Giant Sparrow earns my congratulations for delivering one of my favourite games of the year in an already very strong year for videogames.

Yu gi Oh duel links is a battle card game where you can duel with or aganist characters of the Yu gi oh anime show like Yami Yugi, Kabia, Joey and even Jaden from Yu gi oh GX. You can use monster cards, monster abilities, trap cards and spell cards to defeat your oppenent. However, some cons to the game is that there are gambling elements like using gems to get card packs and you may or may not get the card you want. You will also have to do some grinding to get gems which are required to get more cards and key which you need to duel other characters in the game not the pvp. You can use real world money to buy card packs so you can say that the game is sort of pay to win especially on pvp. Though the game does give you enough gems and keys as gifts when dueling enough or just for login in to the game without having to pay any real world money. You can earn gold to puchace special cards but you won't use gold that much because you can't use gold to buy card packs. Early in the game the NPCs are far too easy to duel and take a little too long to become more challenging. Also right now the game is not full screen and you can't make the screen any bigger. If you are a fan of yu gi oh I recommend you give this game a try.

This game is beautiful.  It is beautiful in both the graphics and the different stories you experience.  I also enjoyed how the different stories have some variation in gameplay mechancis as well. It isn't the most active game (meaning you're not going to see hundreds of matches online at one time), but there's still plenty of players to keep up your enjoyment.
So if you want Halo on Steam, pick this up, you won't be disappointed.

Some of the levels are even recycled to use with the paint gun instead of the portal guns. The campaign is pretty fun, but when I was playing, I felt like I just wanted to get the game over with do to the monotone dialogue.
The multiplayer only has community made levels which you can download off of the Steam workshop. The gameplay (atleast with the paint gun) seems kind of broken. The House in Fata Morgana is a brilliant work of fiction in which an unnamed protagonist has to endure several painful tales told to him by a mysterious maid, guiding him through a mansion in the woods.
The basic premise is simple enough, but as it turns out, the game offers much more on it's plate.
Having just beat it, I consider this "game" a magnificent work of literature, as well as a masterful craft of sound design and pacing. It just engulfes the reader into a world of twirling despair, suffering, pain and emotional distress.
While the gist of the story revolves around the concept of "love", it is uncontrovertibly packaged with themes for every taste: physical abuse, schizophrenia, deconstruciton of character through psychological torture, carnage, suicide, homosexuality, revenge and forgiveness... the list could go on and on for quite a while.
The central subject in Fata Morgana, however you look at it, is Pain. Wether physical or mental, detailed in its own description or subtly hinted at, it's the motive that sets every action in motion.
So if you think you're getting into a regular novel, think twice, and be prepared to suffer. No character has a complete right to his\her own action, and the whole ordeal is filled with grey morality and black-stained paths which you'll necessarily have to cross at some point.
I have deeply enjoyed the narration, it managed to capture my interest until the last chapter, and successfully immersed me, also thanks to the amazing musical score. Graphics are really simple, with raw backgrounds taken from photos, the resulution is very low, but it didnt diminish the overall value of this product.
As it stands, I will give this novel a satisfactory 8.5 \ 10, very solid constructoin, fantastic use of plot twists and turns, however, if I had to address one big complaint, during the last quarter of the novel the narration dragged way too much, and the ending was very anime-like, something many may have appreciated, but given the quality up until that point, I was personally a bit disappointed. All in all, great read.

The House in Fata Morgana, as other reviews have said, is a work of art. Not just the sprites, or the music, or the writing. It is the combination of those three things that brings you to cusp of your emotions. The characters that you come to love, hate, or forgive are forged in front of you. The experience you receive while you play this game is something very few things can give to you. This is a herald of what the Visual novel genre can be; not porn, or a dating simulator. But a visceral experience that is multi-sensory. It allows you to empathize and fall in love with the people, understanding their motivations.
This is a story about what it means to be human, what our personal experiences and emotions can drive us to do. It will teach you that there is always a chance at redemtion, you just have to seek it. Remember, never let go of her hand.

also a recipe for banana bread
No need for a mixer for this recipe! Clean-up is easy too, if you want, you can mix everything in one bowl.
The best bananas to use for banana bread are those that are over-ripe. The yellow peels should be at least half browned, and the bananas inside  squishy and browning.
Ingredients
2-3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 cup of sugar (can easily use 3/4 cup, or drop it down to 1/2 cup if you want it less sweet)
1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
Method
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 10 minutes (check at 50 minutes) at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

Crimzon Clover didn't even take an hour for me to finish, but it's probably one of the best games I've played all summer.
TL:DR If you like bullet hells, challenging video games, and something with lots of replayability, look no further, you found the perfect game!
Pros:
-It isn't frustratingly difficult but it still is a hard game.
-It's super short, but that works out thanks to it's difficulty and tons of extra modes to play.
-The Boost mode is so cool: You basically are handicapping yourself by using the power-ups. The game's difficulty becomes crazy and goes at a exciting pace.
-Great visuals.
-A super energetic soundtrack that pumps out the adrendaline these kind of games have.
Nitpicks:
-Too much flair and numbers around the screen may make it a bit difficult to see what's going on but the bullets are colored specifically so they are much easier to see.
Cons:
-I don't have any
Discussion:
Bullet Hells aren't something I really play a lot. The closest I got to one was Galaga Legions DX, and that was in some form way too easy to even match the challenge of Crimzon Clover. Crimzon Clover is freaking awesome. It has so much stuff cluttered (Which is kind of something I'm a bit ehh at) but the bullets and enemy fire are much easier to see. You have to focus less on shooting enemies and more about dodging the fire, since your bullet spread is pretty much 1/3rds of the entire screen. It's a full embodiment of the Bullet Hell genre.
It almost seems bizzare that the Japanese indie scene isn't that large here. Like seriously, if indie games were the face of powerful innovation and fun, the japanese market is a great example of that.
If you are looking for a Bullet Hell, say no further to Crimzon Clover: WORLD IGNITION. This is the defining example of Bullet Hells, and is just straight up fun. Stop reading this review and buy it now.

There's a built in system where doing more damage and chaining builds up your limit break meter, which can be used for bombs, temporary invincibility or Saiyan mode - it's dynamic and doesn't rely on drops from enemies. You can also get lives more frequently than other SHMUPs.

Gunpoint is a game where you don't actually hold anyone at gunpoint until the final level unless you're playing it wrong. It's also instantly great because it gives you
when you complete it, and you can customize it and stuff. Fun!
Gunpoint is a short game. As in,
if you know what you're doing. When I played it again to write this review, I completed it in
and I didn't use any of the extras that weren't mandatory. Speaking of extras, there are many. To help you be a better spy, you can buy a thing that lets you mute the sound of breaking glass when you jump through it, a thing to silence your falls from great heights, and another thing to set traps to incapacitate people from another room. Also, you can rewire everything, including the guns of your enemies. You could go so far as to set one gun to set off another gun on a different floor, which would trigger a sound detector which would open a door and hit a guy in the face, which would cause another guy to run through a motion detector and shoot at you and open the trapdoor beneath your feet in the process while also incapacitating himself with an electrical socket.
The story, while well done, isn't anything special. Man talk to woman. Other man kill woman. Man swear revenge for woman he never met. Things happen. Mean other man is villain. It's not hard to predict, but who cares? The dialogue is great! Everything is presented as a sort of instant messaging thing, and it's written as such. It even made me laugh.
The graphics are wonderfully done, (I love me some pixels,) but everything is pretty small when you're playing, which takes a bit of getting used to. The soundtrack is absolutely wonderful and truly adds to the experience. If you play this game without its music,
Anyway, the main appeal lies in the gameplay. You play as a freelance spy who has some
BULLFROG brand hypertrousers, which let you jump around like a madman and break glass with your face like a clumsy butt, which alerts guards unless you buy one of the things I mentioned earlier. Speaking of the guards, you can punch them once, twice, three times, or even any other number of times, but they may die if you go past three. You also have the option of just
Or you could kill everyone with the gun you can buy. It's up to you, but you will be graded based on your actions, speed, and other things.
Now here's the best part:
Yes, you can make your own levels in any way you like. Make something easy, make something impossible, make something smart, make something stupid, or make
just use the level editor. Every game needs a level editor! Custom levels are so cool sometimes! Because of that, it's pretty cool that this game has Steam Workshop integration as well, so you can download hundreds upon hundreds of other peoples custom levels, share your own, etc.
Basically the only reason not to buy this game is if you're afraid of coats and hats.
Buy this game, jump over buildings, and punch people in the face repeatedly.

First of all this may seem like a simplified version of what we're used to expect from a YGO game BUT Duel Link's charm and appeal comes exactly from that. The duels are fast and fun without sacrificing depth and strategical thinking, I've been playing the game on my mobile for months now and I can guarantee that this is not pay to win game, if you plan your decks carefully you can have exactly what you need without spending a dime, infact with all the events and giveaways it's almost impossible not to gain the deck you want!
Now for the downside... The graphics look bad on PC... On mobile I could say that everything looked spectacular, however in this version some of the text is blurry, some parts of the background is pixelized and overall visual quality is worse than the mobile version by far. The other problem the game has, and this is shared with the mobile version, is the fact that you can't store more than 9999 gems which unfortunately forces you to spend them as soon as you reach the cap in order to receive more gems, now this may seem like a trivial problem but for those that want to save up for future card additions this is troublesome, it's been several times now that I'm forced to buy packs I don't need just so I can spend gems...
All and all this is, hands down, the best YGO video game I've played so far and I've tried most on all possible platforms.
Oh and if you think the game is too easy take it to the PvP and test your deck, I'm sure you'll have a blast!

I bought this game a long time ago, but I finally got around to playing after sifting through my library to try out games that I bought but haven't played yet. I have to say, I'm thoroughly impressed with various aspects of Gunpoint, the theme and story paid homage to older noir films (Trenchcoats, slow jazz, a gritty main character), whilst adding new twists through dialog choices, which generally consist of a response that would be expected of a noir film character, a questionable answer, or an outright silly one. The gameplay has various uniques aspects as main mechanics, such as super jumping, and rewiring electricals remotely. These mechanics allow for various unique methods of getting through levels, for example; sure, you could switch off a light and ambush the guard as he goes to inspect the switch, or you could also rewire that same switch to shock the guard through the electrical socket next to him, or maybe you want to give him a facefull of door as he walks next to it. I'd certainly recommend this game for people who enjoy puzzle games. The Steam Greenlight also adds a vast amount of new possibilities as players create and share their own levels.
