This mod does an amazing job at expanding on the Propulsion/Repulsion Gel from Portal 2. As a standalone, the Gels wouldn't function, and implementing more puzzles with them in Portal 2 itself would have been a bad idea. Yet, this mod allows you to use the Gels in a way unseen in Portal 2. The ambience fits the game perfectly, which seems to take place inside Aperture, like some division that's testing Gels instead of Portals.
Pros:
-Amazing music
-A handful of new puzzle elements
-Puzzles with unexpected solutions
-Humorous monologue
Cons:
-Puzzles sometimes feel a little sloppy (Too much accidental swimming)
-Monologue is sometimes a bit weak
-The price is a bit on the high side, for the amount of playtime you get
In short, a great game for those who seek the thrill of more Gel-based testing!
Play it while you listen to And So I Watch You From Afar and you will enjoy it at least 10x.

=HEADS UP=
This review is about my point of view. If you disagree: That is fine. If you want to discuss it with me: Go for it. You want to be♥♥♥♥♥♥about it and/or cant be reasoned with while using arguments that make no sense? Enjoy your block.
I accept everyones opinion but dont try to force your thoughts onto me. These are my thoughts on the game. If you dont like it, then go ahead and give my review a downvote.
=INFO ABOUT THE REVIEW=
1. This review is about the game being OK. Not more not less.
=REVIEW=
So the game starts off like the other games. You are in Aperture. Nothing new here except this time you face a new character to guide you through the facility. And the idea is most certainly not bad. The whole story is more than just ok. Its rather good, enjoyable and easy to follow.
The Audio of the game is as good as its original and the voiceacting is done by people that know how to do it, which is always good to see especially if it is made by fans.
Now what is the problem with this game? Overall the game plays just like Portal and Portal 2. But the problem with it is that it doesnt use the Portal Gun. And yes, before anyone says it, thats the point of the "Paint Gun Testing Initiative". To me however it seems like the Test has failed utterly. And here is why?

For starters, I've been playing Borderlands on the console since it's intial release day. I've put countless hours into this franchise and just recently got the collection on Steam. Interested in Borderlands? Check out my review below.
THE STORY SO FAR... (SPOILER FREE)
The first game in the franchise, Borderlands gives the player control over 1 of 4 Vault Hunters. The story starts on a bus traveling through a hostile and unforgiving planet known as Pandora. You've come to this planet in search of an ancient alien treasure known as the "Vault". Most people on Pandora don't believe the Vault is a real thing, but some believe it holds wealth and power beyond imagination. Your goal here on Pandora is to find the Vault and unlock its power for yourself. Throughout your quest you will make allies, meet some of the nastiest creatures and bandits on Pandora and make a profit along the way. Its a massive world out there, prepare yourself.
PROS:
Weapons. Weapons in Borderlands are like no game before it. The game offers a vast selection in the form of generated weapons. Rarely you will find the same gun twice. The weapons have tiers ranging from White-Green-Blue-Purple-Orange (When Grandma Burps Patrick Obeys). They also come with different elements! Fire, Shock, Corrosive and Explosive. If you're lucky, you may even stumble upon the Alien class weapons.
Replay value. The replay value in any Borderlands game is INSANE. They ability to beat the main story and all and then do it all again against enemies that scale to your level is amazing. The loot is better, the missions are harder and the game is far more intense!
Downloadable content: Borderlands is known for its amazing base game, but the addition of DLC is quiet nice as they unlock new areas for our Vault hunters to explore. Enjoy new stories, missions, people and weapons. Despite what some may say, the DLC in ANY Borderlands game is always well crafted and deserves a try, especially for a die hard fan of the franchise!
Gameplay. Borderlands gameplay allows you to be in control of your situation. Enemies are smart and for the most part will try to flank you, overwhelm you and even take cover. Does an enemy have alot of armor? Use a corrosive weapon to widdle him down. Maybe a bandit with an axe is coming right for you? Light him a blaze with a fire elemental weapon! Taking cover and playing smart in your environment is huge in Borderlands. Always assess the situation before engaging, it could mean life or death.
Comedy. The game is full of things that will catch you off guard. You will laugh. Alot. No, really. Alot.
CO-OP. You and three other Vault hunters can take on the world of Pandora! Or if you prefer to play alone, dive on in!
CONS:
The pricing. Now, hold on there big guy. I know it's only $19.99 at my current writing of this. But adding DLC and so on can tend to get a bit high in price. I would recommend buying the series during a sale to save that extra cash or buy a bundle! I recently bought the Humble Bundle for $10.30! Which included the entire series. Borderlands 1 came with all DLC, while the other two games came with certain items, no real gameplay DLC. Either way, if you want a game you can play for awhile, this game works!
The start. Borderlands doesn't go crazy in-depth about your weapons. It'll tell you what elements work best for what enemies, what specific weapons do and so on. But they never really talk about ammo capacity, accuracy and fire rate. I've seen new players not enjoy the first few moments because their initial weapon was insanely inaccurate. Have no fear! It will get better. As you progress and gain new skills and perks, along with weapons, your aim will be true. Just remember to look at the specs of the weapon, otherwise you may be suprised.
All in all, Borderlands is a fantastic game to own and the series is a blast. Looking for a comedic yet fun adventure, with a dash of gore and horror? Borderlands is for you!

This game deceives you at so many levels, that you begin to question wether anyhting you see is actually real in this game. even the characters sprites seem to be an unreliable source. Some concepts that we normally take for granted in vn's (like being able to read the last few lines again by scrolling up) are used here as  means of subtle foreshadowing. It's probably also worth it to read it a second time (haven't done that myself yet), because the foreshadowing is just that good. At first I thought it was a little expensive (since this story doesn't have branching plotlines), but I read through it only once, and look at my playtime. Definitely worth your money, even at full price. If you're looking for a mystery and drama vn (and a little bit of horror and gore), this is the one to go to.

Nothing i say could possibly do this masterpiece justice. From the stunning visuals to the extensive and beautiful soundtrack to the emotional twists and turns the story takes you on.

I had a few moments when i thought i was near the end and there couldnt possible be more reveals and every time i was shocked and delighted about what came next.
The music is easily the best ive heard for a VN, and some tracks will probably make it to the top of my all time gaming OST favourites. Each track fits the elements of the stories they are used for, blending prose and visuals together perfectly. My personal favourites are the tracks used in the later half of the game, which are just so haunting and emotional.
Overall, please buy this game! It deserves more attention then it has, and i would love to see more VNs like this availible to a western audience.

The House in Fata Morgana tells a beautiful story. A story about people who help and hurt, laugh and cry, love and hate, live and die. One life is ephemeral. But what about the soul? Do our memories persist upon death? The warmth of it? The sins we carry? It is these questions that Fata Morgana intends to explore in its ambitious story that spans a millennium and sweeps through an ensemble cast of characters.
The art is gorgeous and stands out from the traditional anime aesthetic; the music similarly evokes an ethereal, but gorgeous feeling. It has a fairly standard length of ~20 - 35 hours, depending on one's reading speed and whether one wishes to unlock all achievements and endings (there are 8).
Highly recommended.

If I could rate this game as neutral I would as the game itself is OK but the implementation, in my view, has a few unforgivable flaws which die hard enthusiasts will see through but I think is inexcusable. I got a refund because nearly half of the steam achievements are broken and unachievable, there are bugs in both the base game and DLC and there are broken promises from years ago with regards to text translations. A serious developer for a board game port would fix the issues: in a board game the rules are pretty important! I dont see enough evidence of support for this game let alone long term fixes. When a games most popular guide is a guide about how to get around bugs you know there's a issue somewhere.
As for the game itself, yes it is popular on boardgamegeek but does that make for a great game? I'm not convinced. It is a OK game for sure but the basis is playing cards and seeing for each country whether a number is higher or lower than the opponent. The game has a lot of not obvious or sensible restrictions in which countries can revolt etc. The whole World is a goal, with objectives specifically focusing on achieving control of Battleground Countries. The game can be quite drawn out and after a while on PC becomes a little dull. The AI spins round cards at lightning pace after a timer has counted thethdownm down making it hard to read let alone comprehend what is going on. The AI has mixed reports on its ability. I think this game is best left bug free and on the tabletop. There are better card based games available, better war games available. I have yet to find a good Cold War game.
If the game had no bugs and all achievements worked I would have kept it, but as it is I got a refund and my game rating is no more than 5/10. 50%: give it a try if you feel like it and you will know after 2 hours of tutorial if you like it. If you miss it, it's not a huge loss. The physical board game is probably better than this PC/Android copy. GMT should not have given their excellent reputation via licence to such shoddy developers.

I like it a lot! It has some problems stemming from basic design issues, but they're not impossible to look past. The idea is you're hunting down a criminal, but you don't know what he looks like and have to get hints from people to narrow down who it could be so you can confront and accuse them. This in practice boils down to doing sidequests and piecing together a picture of your culprit. Combat can be a little frustrating at first; you have to line up your shot, pull out your gun (without your gun you can only walk, not run),♥♥♥♥♥♥it, and shoot, each of which is a different button on your controller. In practice, combat boils down to getting right in your opponents line of fire and shooting them faster than they can shoot you. Shooting can only happen in two directions, so there's a lot of running around from all parties when a gunfight breaks out, and it feels like The Magnificent Seven (the new one, I haven't seen the old one), when all the cowboys are running and ducking about for cover before actually firing back.
A few of the quests are a little bit frustratingly ambiguous, but the world is small enough and your map is serviceable enough to help you find what you need to even when you're not given some sort of quest marker.
My biggest gripe with the game has to be how much things break down a little when you've gained a reputation. TL;DR - An immersive, but clunky, pixellated top-down shooter in an Old Western setting, worthy of at least one playthrough lasting 1-3 hours. Recommend purchase during sale/discount.

Received the game via Humble Bundle purchase. Heard about the game and how it's a one-time playthrough kind of game.
Starting the game, the visuals of the game are pixellated but with coloring to give you the sense of a western, desert environment. The music immerses you in an environment with various scenery and music to give a sense of cowboys and indians, ragtime in a saloon, and exploring mines. It very much feels as if you're involved in a time of the Old Wild West.
With immersion aside, the gameplay mechanics did feel clunky and frustrating. Navigating the map was often as simple as following the notches on the edge of the squares on your map to new areas. Combat involved lining your character along a plane so that your weapon fires at the enemy. This plane of firing is only horizontal, meaning it's more beneficial to wait for your enemy to walk into your plane versus walking into your enemy's. Quest mechanics felt very frustrating as your "objective" in your quest log wasn't always specific and left you talking to vairous NPCs/roaming the map looking for a distinguished character that may have some new information.
Both positive and negative considered, the game is defintely worth a pickup lasting 1-3 hours minimum for an initial playthrough, with further hours added for replayability in alternate endings, achievements, and easter eggs. I do not believe it is worth the current pricing of $14.99, but there are levels of polish with the music/visuals/side-quests that definitely make it worth the pick-up on a sale.

Before we get started just a note about this game:
You will get the best experience if you actually use it to learn how to cook. That means going out and buying the ingredients listed. This will probably mean getting accquanited with new parts of your local grocery store, searching for an asian grocery store, or making intelligent substitutions where appropriate. If you live in a rural area you may have to order a few things off the internet.
When you play the game actually cook along with it. The story isn't that great and probably won't hold up on its own. The game encourages you to repeat recipes.
The recipes are fairly basic but as you begin to understand them you can try to change them to suit your own tastes and style. Alternatively, equiped with a broader pallete you may see something that you might like to change in something you already know how to cook.
Gochi-show consists of 32 episodes divided into 4 categories:
- Introduction
- Washoku ( Japanese food ) Satomi
- Yoshoku ( Western food ) Momoko
- Chuuka ( Chinese food ) Mariko
The first half of each episode is like most visual novels: the plot advances and you periodically make choices that impact the girls' opinion of you. In the second half one of the girls will teach you how to cook that episode's dish.
* Story * 2/5
The story isn't the best that I've seen in a visual novel. I wouldn't consider them to be my favorite genre but I have played several amateur, fan translated, and thanks to steam official releases. Gochi-show struggles with a sub-par translation, cultural differences, and mistakes that can have disaterous consequences in the kitchen.
As the game progresses the quality of the translation gets sloppier and sloppier with frequent typos and patches of missing text. I'm typically not very picky about these sorts of things but sometimes it shows up in the cooking lessons which could obviously cause problems. Error on the side of caution and try to use some common sense.
I was actually shocked at how old fashioned and sexist the storyline seemed to me. I've been a closeted weeb most my life and by U.S. standards I'm hardly progressive when it comes to gender issues so this was a bit of a surprise. I'm not sure if this is due to the writers, the original audiance they were writing for, cultural differences, or if the tone was just lost in translation.
I was hoping that the story would immerse me in Japanese food culture and give me some context for the meals I've seen in anime and had in Japanese restaurants. All this dull romance had to say about food is that 'it's about friends and family'. This is probably a cultural universal so it really doesn't provide any insight at all.
It actually just left me with more questions. Why are these recipes so salty? Why does it taste like Hamburger Helper? Will I get lead poison from this?
* Art * 3/5
Backgrounds are decent and the character designs are servicable. The actual character sprites are not especially expressive and there is no lip-synching in this game which was more distracting than I would have expected.
Unlike a typical visual novel half of the artwork consists of diagrams and photographs of food preparation. These are not great but they do the job. I think I like the diagrams best though. They are useful, cute, and don't talk too much. The diagrams are my waifus.
The game is low-res by modern standards and seems to be natively rendered at ~ 1137 X 640. I am guessing that it may be a few years old and that it was intended for laptops and older mobile devices. For the most part this isn't that big of a deal but the character sprites suffer when upscaled to 1080p. I hope none of you were planning to play this in 4K.
* Sound * 4/5
Maybe I have a tin ear or something but it sounds pretty good to me. The voice acting isn't top notch, the sound effects are sparse, and the background music is a little repetitive. Really I have no complaints here.
It may say more about my priorities than anything else but I think they did a good job given the scope of the project here.
* Recipies/ Cooking Instruction * 3/5
I noticed on the store page that the developers say that the in-game recipes came from 'Shufu no Tomo' ( Housewife's Friend ) which according to Wikipedia was a Tokyo women's magazine that ran from 1917 to 2008. I would imagine it must have been something like 'Good Housekeeping' or 'Redbook'.
There are a lot of tips and instructionals on general kitchen skills in the cooking segments and I really enjoyed these. Some of them were new to me like steaming my eggs or rolling cabbage to make it nice and easy to cut into thin strips ( chiffonade ). Some of them I had heard of but just never bothered with like straining scum off the top of soup to clarify it. Others were things I already knew. I really think these short instructional segments have been the most interesting and most useful parts of the game for me.
The recipes themselves aren't bad but they are definately not my style. They remind me of recipes my mom would make from her betty crooker cook book or the back of a duncan hines box. I realize that they may be designed for housewifes trying to throw something together with common pantry items at the last minute. They just seem too salty and kind of bland. Like trying to cover up fewer and lower quality ingredients with low quality seasonings.
* Developers * Nice.
Active in comments answering questions and trying to resolve problems. Very important these days!

Some comments about the quality of the singleplayer ('offline') AI :
The AI fairly is tough, so much so that my record against the AI is actually worse than my record against human players. In real life I win about 85% of my games, against the AI here I win about 70%.
I suspect that the reason for why the AI is pretty good is that it calculates moves based on what action will give them the highest possible gain in potential victory points from scoring regions. This works in a superficial way, so long as the AIs scoring cards come up in a timely order, and especially if the AI posseses them.
However, once you figure this out, it becomes very, very easy to outsmart the AI. I've identified a number of major issues:
1) The AI focuses far too much on preparing for upcoming scoring cards, and doesn't seem to mind even conceding Control of regions once that scoring card has been played. Since most regions are played 2-3 times per game, this sets them up for a world of hurt.
2) The AI doesn't use events enough. The AI will, about 80-90% of the time, prefer to use operations points rather than using the events. For instance, I've yet to see the AI actually use 'Containment' in the Headline Phase, even though it's a truly marvellous card from the mid-game onwards, especially if you have a weak hand.
3) The AI isn't sufficiently afraid of its opponent's events. For instance, a common AI move as the USA is to play Suez Crisis for operations points. In many situations, this is a fantastic boon to the Soviets, as they often get to remove influence from controlled Battleground states, which is effectively worth double influence, plus a sizeable points gain. There are very few situations in which any US player should ever want to play that card. Wherever possible, they should Space Race it, hold onto it, nullify it with UN Intervention, or play it at a moment when it is least effective. Yet, they almost never do this. Over the course of a whole game, the AI loses out dramatically from situations such as these.
4) The AI is obsessed with coups (in fairness, so are many human players) and will launch them at every opportunity against battleground states. The problem is, the AI doesn't seem to possess any wider understanding of how the DEFCON track affects their prospects. For instance, it often makes more strategic to try and keep the DEFCON high when you are weak, to give you more opportunities to weedle your way into non-battleground areas and eventually level the playing field. Conversely, when you are strong, it makes sense to keep the DEFCON low so the odds of a lucky coup derailing your points haul are minimal. The AI has no understanding of this. Often they will launch a long-odds coup against a battleground state in one region, and thus give themselves no hope of even getting a presence in, say, South America. The advantage to this style of play arises only when the coup-happy player gets very, very lucky from the get-go, and rolls mostly 5s and 6s for their rolls. This puts the opposing player in a bind whereby they can't counter-coup much because of the low DEFCON, and the good results limit how much of a difference they can make. Ultimately, an emphasis on coups is a low-odds strategy, not unlike playing long-ball in football. You're gonna win out spectacularly sometimes, but the majority of the time, it's going to hurt you more than it helps.
5) The AI also doesn't seem to appreciate that, over the long term, the total anount of influence you can place will often outweigh disrupting the opponent in a minor way. For instance, it makes little sense to put 2 influence into making West Germany go from 0/4 to 1/4, when you could put that 2 into Spain/Portugal, Greece, or Turkey and potentially starve the opponent of domination through sheer number of states. Worse, it can easily get trapped in a loop of performing this inefficient action, whereby every time they place enough influence to disrupt your state, you put just enough to re-secure it; meaning that the next time, they will once again have to blow an extra influence. Ultimately, the instigating player will almost always lose out in this situation. It may not matter in the short term, but in the long one, the AI will lose out on a lot of influence. In fairness, I've seen many human players fall prey to this particular vice.
6) The AI doesn't seem to understand how to wrest control of a State over the course of more than one turn. For instance, while as USA it is happy to disrupt Soviet control of, say, Italy with a spoiler play, or else seize control of it by placing a few more influence, it would *never* make the move to go from 2/4 in East Germany to 5/4, and then 7/4 the next turn. It simply can't seem to conceive of these two-step actions.
7) This leads on to by far the AIs biggest weakness: it doesn't seem to know how to claw back a region that has been locked down. When human players lose control of a region, they will usually assess whether it's worth going toe to toe for that region, or whether they can afford to lose it and make up for that loss with a more widely spread investment in other regions. e.g. it's not neccessarily such a big deal to be losing the Middle East if you can make up for it with Africa and Central America. However, the AI often concedes Control entirely in key regions such as Asia, the Middle East, and even Europe, which can appear up to 4 times a game, and are generally worth more points. Indeed...
8) The AI seems to have no idea that losing Europe is so important, and seems to only devote resources to it proportional to the points it grants. However, of course, losing Europe will lose you the game. This is made worse by the fact that the AI tends to lower the DEFCON so rapidly that realignment and coups are out of the question. When I'm the Soviets, I always play NATO every time without any fear because I know it will never even be relevant because it would be a miracle if the AI let the DEFCON stays at 5 for more than 2 seconds. This is counter to what happens when you play human players in Europe. Human players are acutely aware that losing Europe is game over, and so, barring a lucky set of Europe-centric cards, Europe typically becomes a stalemate wherein any event or influence play in Europe is met with immediate suspiscion and disproportionate sensativity. Hell, I've gotten mileage out of placing a lone influence in Europe, and spooking my opponent in order to distract them from the wider picture
As an amusing aside, the combination of low-stability battleground states and high point-scoring volatility means that the AI is obsessed with Africa, and will often spend much of the early war lovingly setting up Domination there, whilst I take France, Italy, and West Germany without it even seeming to notice.

Review re-written on August 3rd 2015 due to two people's comments alongside that of my husband's commentary regarding my "quick test to see if it is what they say it is or not" turned into a half hour session.  Turns out (as far as I can tell) that the game doesn't like it if you haven't rebooted Windows 7 in over a month (I use my computer for various other things that require it to be on 24/7, such as Folding@Home and/or BOINC), in combination with running in windowed mode.  I'm leaving the original review up at the tail end.
Interestingly enough, this is the first time someone's gotten me to actually revisit a game through commentary, and definitely the first time I've gone from a "could be great but UI needs a lot of work and optimisation, therefore I'm definitely not a fan" to "I actually like it".
----- ----- -----
Having acquired the game through the Humble Game Creators Bundle, I figured I would give it a shot based upon the fact I used to absolutely LOVE playing Tyrian in the mid-90's, and also rather enjoyed playing Tyrian 2000.  After dealing with some initial lack of key response (or even recognition) issues alongside some gameplay fluidity problems that turned out to apparently be caused by not having rebooted for some time (despite having no such issues whatsoever with any other games), I found myself rather enjoying the game.
While it doesn't have a lot of the various gameplay additions other games have such as modification of ship's weaponry, additional/changing special weapons, XP system, or the like, such things would wind up making this game a lot less enjoyable.  You're given a choice of gameplay type, and then the choice of three types of ships, each with different playstyles.  That's it.  No arduous grind to be able to use the top tier gear, no idiotic levelling system, just plain run and gun while dodging a rather large amount of projectiles the enemies send your way.
And that's what makes it so much fun, even my two main issues are that the controls aren't easy to find in game (in fact, I had no choice but to randomly push buttons on the keyboard just to get in the first time, and then it wouldn't let player 1 sign in, just player 2), and that it's rather difficult to know whether a particular space is safe or not.  While the controls make sense once you've found them, it's kind of odd that unlike most other games you can't just hit the enter (or depending on your keyboard, the return) key to get into the main menu as a great deal of games let you do this, then you can look up the actual controls in the menus.
As for my complaint about what essentially boils down to hit boxes, it really is difficult to tell at a glance whether a place is safe or not.  Sometimes it's okay to have an enemy under you, other times your ship explodes rather unceremoneously.  Sometimes it's okay to barely graze an enemy projectile, and other times if it gets within three pixels your ship goes poof.
With all that said though, the main question that comes to mind is do I actually recommend it to others?  It depends.  If you want a semi-relaxed experience like Tyrian is in the initial levels, this isn't the game for you.  If you want a game where you're rewarded (or punished) for split second decisions and need to constantly be on the move, and don't mind a potentially aggravating learning curve (but nowhere near EVE's learning chasm of death, at least for basic gameplay) then by all means, give it a shot.
-----Original review (now outdated)-----

Well designed bullet hell shmup that takes simple mechanics and drives them up to insane levels.
Low learning curve makes this a good choice for newcomers to the genre, but does ramp up to provide a challenge for experienced players.
Unlike some other bullet hells, this game doesn't require as much pattern memorisation (unless you're trying to 1CC it), some parts did catch me off guard in the first playthough however.
Has pretty much everything you'd want from a bullet hell, 2-player coop, training, local/online leaderboards, replays, different modes, etc.
The graphics and sound effects are reminiscent of arcade shooters, though everything has a huge amount of detail put into it. Bosses are beautifully animated and very well scripted. I didn't really care for the soundtrack, but it fits in well with this kind of game.
Overall, if you're looking for a good bullet hell shmup to start with, or you're a veteran who's looking for another game to 1CC, I'd say full price ($10USD) is well worth it. If you're the least bit interested and it goes on sale definitely pick it up.

The learning curve is very steep, though, and it can get very boring drifting through space alone if you're not in a guild or have no friends to play with you. That being said, there are plenty of new player friendly guilds and plenty of information available online for anything from manufacturing guides to combat guides.

Hello Everyone!
My name is Ignacio Daimon, I have flown in Eve for 4 years now. Thousands of hours, countless months spent studying and learning how to truly understand this game. It is not for the feint of heart, It is not for the casual. It will feel like a job, Like a lot of games do. However with dedication, time, and persistance you can do things such as I have like, become one of the worlds best solo pvp pilots (Once upon a time), Write articles that thousands read and learn from the experience you have gained. Take down 500+ person alliances as a spy, Steal money, Lie, Cheat, Anything to get ahead.
PVP is the lifeblood of Eve, If you played and quit, you likely never got in a ship and went to blow up another. Its a rush, there's nothing like it. All your 'gear' on your ship if you will, on the line to be destroyed forever. Solo PVP is an amazing rush of skill and timing, where it goes from good to gone in around 60seconds. Small gang pvp, get a group with ships to cover all beneficial mods and go take on something large, Long range or short, take your fancy. Fleet PVP , this is where things get serious. Hundreds of people locked in a system for 1,2,3-10 hours of battle, risking $100,000+ more at times on the field.
Sure you can settle for a less then perfect game, we all can. Eve is no different. However it offers a unique atmosphere where people attach real life value to the ships and structures they own. Where everything you do is built on an empire of trust.  You have options from Faction grinding, Fleet Incursions (Raids for lack of a better word, Very trusted/skilled public groups). PVE content from level 1-5 where you can make millions, to billions depending on what you are willing to risk.
You can mine ore, You can mine moons, You can hunt ships that cost Hundreds if not a thousand dollars in real world value. Dive into wormholes, Hunt poor Truckers hauling goods in high security Systems where most of the population live in what they believe to be safe space. Study the Market tickers, Learn to gain some of the best income in the game which is just sitting in station buying and selling to becoming an Isk empire.
It takes months to get decent skills, I will not argue the difficulty of becoming higher quality. However with Ambitions and a Strong Alliance or Milita behind you, people will flock to your aid, help you become better. In Eve we all know one very important survival tactic, Teach others, and they will protect you.
You will either love it or you will hate it, However you must first, study, research, learn. Eve is a lifestyle, it's meant to be, In as close of an aspect of what universal warfare would be like, its a struggle, Every day is a struggle, Everytime you undock believe that your ship is dead, and you must fly to reclaim its life.
In Eve, when it dies, Its gone for good.

From the first moment Edith Finch delivers a mesmerizing story about a family that defies any reasonable explanation, and only the player can decide for themselves what the truth really is. It feels as if listening to the tall tales of a family member, skeptical of their information, but it is far more personal and deeply thoughtful in its structure.
More powerful than any walking simulator, and much more interactive than your average visual novel, Edith Finch seems to walk the line that ties several genres, and while doing so enrapturing the player in the dark with a glimmer of light that almost seems too good to be true.
Every now and then a game comes along that shows all of us why this medium exists; an example of art in motion that no film, book or painting can encapsulate. What Remains of Edith Finch is a new golden standard and a lesson in what video games can do to tell a macabre, but lighthearted narrative that will stay with you well after the credits roll.

I originally got this game because of the rich player based history, the epic space battles and all sorts of other good stuff you see on youtube when it comes to this game. The problem is that game is not the game you download and play. The game had a lot of good potential, but there are many flaws that a new player comes into the game have to jump in order to enjoy the game.
First the game is overly complex and relies on pop-up menus too much. This game is to MMORPG what ARMA series is too FPS. A game is suppose to be fun to play, detatch you from reality. Unfortunately like ARMA this game tries to make space exploration too much like reality. Which means HOURS wasted just getting from point A to point B. Extended periods of time working on controls. And dear go the amount of pop-up screens you have at any time to play the game effectivly is insane. I have 2 monitors, and the game on both of them, and I STILL feel like I do not have enough screen space to play. Yet of all the complex controls, huge amount of details, and 'sand box' feel the game is lacking in some very basic concepts.
Like why is there STILL not an option to have camera follow enable on your ship so you are always away and above your ship? If there is I do not see it online and it is not easy to find in the 8 control menus under options. Why do heat sinks and mining lasers look the same in my inventory? Are you telling me you cannot create different icons for the two? These sorts of details can really irritate you and pull you out of the world the developers try to make for the gamer.
The game is presented to us as a 'sand box' space game where the developers just maintain the box. In reality the game is more of a 'desert'. I mean that for 90% of the new players just coming in with no idea what the game is, like myself, you are lost. Sure I get a tutorial type missions, which waste about 10-15 hour of the basic 'go here and drop off x' 'mine y' 'kill z'. The missions are useful, they provide the player with the basics on what to do and how to do it, but they are way overkill. After about 2 hours in I found myself putting the ship on auto pilot and watching netflix (more on this later). But the worst part if after the missions a player has no direction. I get this is suppose to be part of the lure of the game, being full sandbox. But I found myself running through my options of what to do afterward and the answer was very limited.
Why was I limited on what I can do, it is because of how the skills are earned in Eve. Most games skills are learned from 'Do X 100 times' or 'Kill Y 100 times' and you earn xp. It is a very proactive approach. But in Eve it is 'spend Z time'. Not spend time in game, not spend time doing something, just...spend...time. So as I speak right now my character is leveling up. Even though I am not doing anything or playing the game. The main draw back from this is I cannot accelerate my character (without spending real life money) to get to my goals. And seeing how every little detail in eve, from the ship you fly, to the weapon you use, has a skill point that needs to be leveled in order to use, I have to waste real life money or a ton of time to get to any sort of enjoyable content.
Example you look at youtube videos on exploring, combat, hacking anything and you want to try one of those paths. Well in order to get to, for instance, (entry level ship) combat in low security space (more open to PVP and harder PVE) it takes 15 days. 2 weeks of having an account to do almost anything in game. Now this isn't new, WoW use to require a month of play time to get to end game content. But WoW gave you stuff to do in the mean time, leveling proactivly. Eve doesn't give you direction. So here I am, waiting for skills to level up, to go do something fun, using the entry level ship.
Now to be fair there are things to do while we wait. Explore, Mine, and combat. But all of these have to be done in high security space, which means almost no threat and little reward. I hear people saying 'Do you expect to step into a game and do end game content? You have to start somewhere.' In most games no I do not expect that, but in Eve I do. And the reason is again the true 'sand box' environment that is promoted and the lack of direction the developers give gamers. Litteral make New Eden what you want it to be. How do you claim you give gamers full independence, yet put in a horrible XP mechanic that limits them, not by skill, not by time played, not by money earned, but by how long they have their account? And this brings me to my last point.
The game is more of an AFK simulator and has almost no skill profieciency when it comes to PvE. You want to know how to get to point A -> B that is 15 jumps away? Set destination and put on auto pilot, watch netflix. How do you mine? Point to rock, hit 1 button, watch netflix and wait. I know what you are thinking, 'Most games are like that, you are being to harsh on Eve'. No, no I am not. I can excuse mining and auto pilot travel for being boring, it is a game mechanic that is hard to keep someone interested in. But when it requires 0 interation from me for hours on end, that is boring. I watched 10+ hours of netflix while my character did something in game with no interaction from me. Except for me point him in another direction to do the same automated action. And the worst part is PvE isn't much better!
Space combat in this game is HORRIBLE. It takes no skill at all. Now I cannot speak to PvP since I cannot do that for another 2 weeks due to the XP mechanic. But PvE combat is horrible. Target X, push auto laser button, profit. This is the extent of the skill you need. True story, I went into low security last night with a ship you get from the starting quest. I found a Battleship (4-5 levels in ship class above me). My experience 'fighting' it. Target, orbit, auto fire, afk. For 25 minutes my entry level ship, flew circles around a battleship hitting it with lasers. I did NOTHING, I was watching TV while I waited for it to kill the battleship. No resource management, no tactical manuevers, no worries. I didn't have to work to get an angle, didn't have to manage what lasers fired in what order, I didn't even have to worry about my shields recharging. When I can take on an NPC, that is at least 4 tiers higher than me while I am on the toliet, the game is broken/borning.
And for being such a complicated game, I would say overly complicated, yet having the core concept of Space Combat/Exploration/Mining being able to be done on 95% auto pilot. That is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ made game, and a poor gaming experience.

For starters, I've been playing Borderlands on the console since it's intial release day. I've put countless hours into this franchise and just recently got the collection on Steam. Interested in Borderlands? Check out my review below.
THE STORY SO FAR... (SPOILER FREE)
The first game in the franchise, Borderlands gives the player control over 1 of 4 Vault Hunters. The story starts on a bus traveling through a hostile and unforgiving planet known as Pandora. You've come to this planet in search of an ancient alien treasure known as the "Vault". Most people on Pandora don't believe the Vault is a real thing, but some believe it holds wealth and power beyond imagination. Your goal here on Pandora is to find the Vault and unlock its power for yourself. Throughout your quest you will make allies, meet some of the nastiest creatures and bandits on Pandora and make a profit along the way. Its a massive world out there, prepare yourself.
PROS:
Weapons. Weapons in Borderlands are like no game before it. The game offers a vast selection in the form of generated weapons. Rarely you will find the same gun twice. The weapons have tiers ranging from White-Green-Blue-Purple-Orange (When Grandma Burps Patrick Obeys). They also come with different elements! Fire, Shock, Corrosive and Explosive. If you're lucky, you may even stumble upon the Alien class weapons.
Replay value. The replay value in any Borderlands game is INSANE. They ability to beat the main story and all and then do it all again against enemies that scale to your level is amazing. The loot is better, the missions are harder and the game is far more intense!
Downloadable content: Borderlands is known for its amazing base game, but the addition of DLC is quiet nice as they unlock new areas for our Vault hunters to explore. Enjoy new stories, missions, people and weapons. Despite what some may say, the DLC in ANY Borderlands game is always well crafted and deserves a try, especially for a die hard fan of the franchise!
Gameplay. Borderlands gameplay allows you to be in control of your situation. Enemies are smart and for the most part will try to flank you, overwhelm you and even take cover. Does an enemy have alot of armor? Use a corrosive weapon to widdle him down. Maybe a bandit with an axe is coming right for you? Light him a blaze with a fire elemental weapon! Taking cover and playing smart in your environment is huge in Borderlands. Always assess the situation before engaging, it could mean life or death.
Comedy. The game is full of things that will catch you off guard. You will laugh. Alot. No, really. Alot.
CO-OP. You and three other Vault hunters can take on the world of Pandora! Or if you prefer to play alone, dive on in!
CONS:
The pricing. Now, hold on there big guy. I know it's only $19.99 at my current writing of this. But adding DLC and so on can tend to get a bit high in price. I would recommend buying the series during a sale to save that extra cash or buy a bundle! I recently bought the Humble Bundle for $10.30! Which included the entire series. Borderlands 1 came with all DLC, while the other two games came with certain items, no real gameplay DLC. Either way, if you want a game you can play for awhile, this game works!
The start. Borderlands doesn't go crazy in-depth about your weapons. It'll tell you what elements work best for what enemies, what specific weapons do and so on. But they never really talk about ammo capacity, accuracy and fire rate. I've seen new players not enjoy the first few moments because their initial weapon was insanely inaccurate. Have no fear! It will get better. As you progress and gain new skills and perks, along with weapons, your aim will be true. Just remember to look at the specs of the weapon, otherwise you may be suprised.
All in all, Borderlands is a fantastic game to own and the series is a blast. Looking for a comedic yet fun adventure, with a dash of gore and horror? Borderlands is for you!

What can I say about this game... it's not the be-all, end-all of Anime games, or even just Dragon Ball Z games. As a fighter, it's all been done before... This game offers no unique mechanics or new-to-dragonball-game features, in gameplay. But that's not to say it's BAD. The game is somewhat simple, sure. but all it's gameplay has been tested and loved in previous Dragonball games, and THIS one is avalible on the PC.
As for it's role-playing ascepts... ON-POINT! The ability to freely create a character from one of the 5 races (with gender differences on humans, Majins, and Saiyans) with a decent array of apperance options is great, combined with a veriety of outfits and hundreds of equipable skills, both normal and super, pulling from nearly every attack in the series, allowing you to make characters how you WANT instead of selecting, say, a somewhat different goku-clone like the last time this idea was tried.
There are strong flaws, there's going to be. Some of the role-playing elements leave room for improvement - you can't review clothes before you buy, you can't costume so good-lloking stuff might not help you because of it's built-in stats, and some poorly chosen combos and skills make the game unfair (Super Saiyan Spam >.>) But if you're honestly expecting the first time a fantastic game like this is made to be 100% complete and bugproof on the first go, you're asking too much.
As I write this, the Sequel is not yet out but WILL BE soon and thanks to betas we know several things have been fixed. Costume slots for clothes, Balences to certian OP skills, removal of ALL old Z-Souls for a new system (hopefully more balenced) and EVERY race has a transform skill, no longer JUST the Saiyans, So if you're choosing between 1 and 2, Get 2. However, if you buy BOTH and play this game first, you can transfer a chaacter from this game into the 2nd as an NPC (Mild spoilers as to their role) , making their equipment and skills avalible RIGHT away in the sequel. If you've got $100 to spend and no copy of Xenoverse yet, I persoanlly reccomend picking them both up; Xenoverse 1 is no perfect dream but it's still a REALLY fun game and worth playing.

Dragon ball Xenoverse is an rpg fighting game. You can mix a light attack, heavy attack, quick speed to get behind an opponent. There are different stat categories that you can increase by leveling up. The best part is that you can increase the categories the way you want to so the character is in your control. There are also certain ki attacks that you can use. These are all attacks from the series that are available in parallel quests, which involve completing side distortions which help the timeline i guess. In any case they are a way to grind for moves and levels if you get stuck. The best part of the game is that all of the parallel quests are cooperative, so you can do it with friends or strangers. Though the moves and items are completely random drops so you may get the item you want the first time or after dozens of tries. Each race has a different fighting style. This game interested me so much that i completed it.
Overall: 9/10 with the rating of finish or complete it

Now for the downside... The graphics look bad on PC... On mobile I could say that everything looked spectacular, however in this version some of the text is blurry, some parts of the background is pixelized and overall visual quality is worse than the mobile version by far. The digital implementation of Twilight Struggle is faithful to the award winning board game.  If you have the analog version and cannot find opponents, this is the game for you.
Set during the cold war, the game is a card driven battle for ideological world supremacy.  The goal is to gain victory points by dominating the various regions in the world by having the most influence there.
There are 3 ways to win:
1) have the edge in Victory Points at the end of 10 turns;
2) achieve an automatic victory by gaining 20 Victory Points
3) if the other player goes to DEFCON 1.
The key to playing this game well is the cards.  Playing your hand to your best advantage, or often, to the least detriment.  If you canget rid of the opposing players cards with the least amount of damage to your position you will do well.  In order to do that, you have to play, and learn.  The most dangerous cards to you are often the weakest in your opponents hand.
Play early, play often and enjoy every game.

Old review (First three great lads who marked this helpful were referring to this):
I've just finished the Satomi route for this game; I consider my playthrough done at this point.
srsly, this review is too long for almost literally everyone who will notice this
These guys put mirin in everything. I know it's minor and makes things taste better, but they've turned most dishes into an alcoholic one.
I don't think I have ever seen Mariko chill. Full time troll. She's like a child at times with her excitement.
Momoko is dangerous. I know she's not yandere; stay away anyways.
Why is the protagonist the only decent young man in the whole visual novel?
There are some rather cringe moments. Fortunately, it's not the kind of thing that I feel completely disconnected from; they're like... the cringe you encounter in daily life. They aren't unusually cringey, at least for me.
First, let's address some unsavory parts. This game has quite a collection of translation weaknesses and spelling errors. In my playthrough (Main storyline + Satomi route), I've only gotten one confusing translation, which made me pick the wrong option; the myriad of others were merely mildly distracting, and shouldn't be hard to correct for a native speaker.
There's a subtitles button where you can see the subtitles for the other language (English subtitles if you're playing in Japanese, vice versa), but it kinda blocks the middle of the screen. If you're sensitive to keeping an absolutely clear view of what's behind, it might be a bit shoddy of a placement for your tastes. It is still a useful feature, however.
Plus, although it's mostly sane, sometimes you have a confusing inconsistency in the length of the English text and the Japanese text. The worst offender is the
, where the text box shows a quick English sentence, but Satomi says 2 or 3 entire Japanese sentences. This wouldn't be too bad of a problem, if not for the fact that sometimes you have a Point dialog that comes after all dialogue is complete, which can be easily skipped if you get impatient and click the 'Next slide' button (This is a much bigger problem for me as a YouTuber instead of you guys, though).
Adding to the inconsistency is the difference in volume and tone between the episode and the recipe inside of it, as well as the occaisonal seeming voice actor substitution (I might be wrong). And speaking of inconsistency, it's not that the translator is bad. They seem like a native speaker in their presentation and words, but it drops sometimes.
Furthermore, there is a rather poor selection of options. You can't change your resolution, nor can you change the volume. This is a bit of a train wreck for recording the game because you get hit by a copyright dispute (monetisation claim) every single episode, unless you mute the entire game, because the music in this game is entirely from the NASH Music Library.
Sometimes you find that the sprites for the characters get unsafely scaled up, and they don't have enough resolution, so they look a bit pixelated. Furthermore, the selection of background scenes and characters is literally worse than a free Indie visual novel. It's rather embarassing.
Plus, a tiny issue; There's a rounded black bar at the top and bottom of the screen when you're in an episode or recipe, for seemingly no reason.
The game introduces two unique features in all the visual novels I've played. To finish an episode, you have to pass the Clear marker. You can progress by picking good choices that favour affinity with the Cooking Club members, recipe included. You can easily afford saying one or two neutral or bad options. However, if you be completely yourself and have the bad luck of picking all bad choices, you'll fail the episode after the recipe and lose all the Gochi Points you used to unlock that episode... which means you have to go repeat recipes to get them again. If you're ever panicking, just say your food is perfect after the recipe; that usually gives a massive boost.
And Gochi Points are the other mechanic. They're great for encouraging players to go check out unlocked recipes instead of just spamming the plot and running off, but it's a bit optimistic to expect players to read all of them through, let alone follow through in the cooking.
Now that we have all those silly negatives out of the way, let's get into what's good about this game.
I like how you aren't block from skipping anything, and this is useful for collecting Gochi Points for unlocking episodes. Many preparation lessons also won't begin unless you say "Show me how", so you can easily spare yourself from the repetition. However, it's nice how the different characters occasionally have different ways of doing things, or at least to different recipes. Hearing two different characters recite the same lesson is nice.
The subtitles button is a boon for English players if you want to keep track of what they're saying, and/or learn Japanese. Of course, it's the more advanced kind meant for native Japanese speakers, but if you're at that level, give it a shot.
But what kept me going in this game is the plot. It's not magnificent, but you do get to see each character have different personalities. You recognise their voices and their signature interjections. You do genuinely feel like you're a part of the plot (although you might have to intentionally remove yourself and see it in third person if you disagree with the protagonist's choice, like eavesdropping in the bath scene). I felt engaged enough to react to what's going on. I laughed at the jokes and occasional roast.
And although you couldn't favour anyone in the first storyline, I liked how you could choose your own route towards which club member you like, in complete violation of the club's rule, and it was something I looked forward to when I spotted those routes, locked, while doing the first storyline.

And of course, the VN is rather good if you're a complete noob in cooking. It has the flaw of not expecting you to screw up massively, but past that, it teaches some new things. I didn't know about buckling and drop lids before playing this (though drop lids are a Japanese thing).
Protip if you find the VN too static: Try to imagine the scenes yourself in your mind, like you're reading a book. Let the visual novel just initialise the environment for you. It helped me past the post-cooking conversations that usually were uncomfortable.
I got this on a sale. It was worth the money.
Out of sale? It's up to you and your wallet. I'm giving a sort of neutral review, considering that it can only closely compete with top tier free VNs. This VN isn't at the level of quality of Nekopara or Hatoful Boyfriend.
But if you're warm to the idea, play this. It deserves more players and coverage, and I'd support the developers for their next project. They've already finished the Shoujo version of Gochi-Show.
For my standards? 7.5/10, would play again.
For everyone's standards? 6/10.

This isn't a bad game. It's not a great game either, but I found it surprisingly enjoyable, even though I didn't really like the first game. -Much better story and characters than in the first game
-Plenty of side-missions and collectibles
Cons:

I'v been playing AVA back when it was in a alpha state with ijji and I decided after around 2000+ hours put into this game I would share my Pros and Cons about this game and some insight on my experience with playing AVA.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Pros:
-Easy to pickup FPS.
-Not being a Pay 2 Win game.
(Now I know a lot of people say AVA is a Pay 2 Win game when that's not true at all. I'v seen people who have not spent a single penny on this game and just destroy players who have AP weapons.)
-The ability to buy guns for permanent with "euros" (In game currency)
(Just a note, while back Aeria games took out the ability to buy normal guns with EUROS permanently but has recently reinstated the ability to purchase all euro guns permanently.)
-Huge arsenal of weapons to choose from.
-Tons of Gamemodes to play.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Cons:
-Hackers are starting to become a problem since most of them you can't kick out due to anti-kick hacks.
-Not a hugely populated game as it use to be.
-The servers are kinda lacking in quality so lag and the ability to login to the game becomes a issue.
-There are some bugs and exploits that can ruin the experience for someone but not a huge problem most of the time
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion:
-AVA is a fun F2P FPS I would recommend to anyone looking for something else to play that is free
-Hackers are present as they are in all F2P games but aren't normally a issue.
-The "Spyware" people keep talking about isn't harmful to your computer and its a False positive reading from your Anti-Virus. Most F2P games out there have something like this and its because of there Anti-Cheat System.
-The game is starting to get better as Aeria gets there act together and are now realizing there mistakes and are trying there best to fix up the game back to a good state and by showing that they did indeed re-add Permanent Euro Weapons back to the in-game shop

I originally got this game because of the rich player based history, the epic space battles and all sorts of other good stuff you see on youtube when it comes to this game. The problem is that game is not the game you download and play. The game had a lot of good potential, but there are many flaws that a new player comes into the game have to jump in order to enjoy the game.
First the game is overly complex and relies on pop-up menus too much. This game is to MMORPG what ARMA series is too FPS. A game is suppose to be fun to play, detatch you from reality. Unfortunately like ARMA this game tries to make space exploration too much like reality. Which means HOURS wasted just getting from point A to point B. Extended periods of time working on controls. And dear go the amount of pop-up screens you have at any time to play the game effectivly is insane. I have 2 monitors, and the game on both of them, and I STILL feel like I do not have enough screen space to play. Yet of all the complex controls, huge amount of details, and 'sand box' feel the game is lacking in some very basic concepts.
Like why is there STILL not an option to have camera follow enable on your ship so you are always away and above your ship? If there is I do not see it online and it is not easy to find in the 8 control menus under options. Why do heat sinks and mining lasers look the same in my inventory? Are you telling me you cannot create different icons for the two? These sorts of details can really irritate you and pull you out of the world the developers try to make for the gamer.
The game is presented to us as a 'sand box' space game where the developers just maintain the box. In reality the game is more of a 'desert'. I mean that for 90% of the new players just coming in with no idea what the game is, like myself, you are lost. Sure I get a tutorial type missions, which waste about 10-15 hour of the basic 'go here and drop off x' 'mine y' 'kill z'. The missions are useful, they provide the player with the basics on what to do and how to do it, but they are way overkill. After about 2 hours in I found myself putting the ship on auto pilot and watching netflix (more on this later). But the worst part if after the missions a player has no direction. I get this is suppose to be part of the lure of the game, being full sandbox. But I found myself running through my options of what to do afterward and the answer was very limited.
Why was I limited on what I can do, it is because of how the skills are earned in Eve. Most games skills are learned from 'Do X 100 times' or 'Kill Y 100 times' and you earn xp. It is a very proactive approach. But in Eve it is 'spend Z time'. Not spend time in game, not spend time doing something, just...spend...time. So as I speak right now my character is leveling up. Even though I am not doing anything or playing the game. The main draw back from this is I cannot accelerate my character (without spending real life money) to get to my goals. And seeing how every little detail in eve, from the ship you fly, to the weapon you use, has a skill point that needs to be leveled in order to use, I have to waste real life money or a ton of time to get to any sort of enjoyable content.
Example you look at youtube videos on exploring, combat, hacking anything and you want to try one of those paths. Well in order to get to, for instance, (entry level ship) combat in low security space (more open to PVP and harder PVE) it takes 15 days. 2 weeks of having an account to do almost anything in game. Now this isn't new, WoW use to require a month of play time to get to end game content. But WoW gave you stuff to do in the mean time, leveling proactivly. Eve doesn't give you direction. So here I am, waiting for skills to level up, to go do something fun, using the entry level ship.
Now to be fair there are things to do while we wait. Explore, Mine, and combat. But all of these have to be done in high security space, which means almost no threat and little reward. I hear people saying 'Do you expect to step into a game and do end game content? You have to start somewhere.' In most games no I do not expect that, but in Eve I do. And the reason is again the true 'sand box' environment that is promoted and the lack of direction the developers give gamers. Litteral make New Eden what you want it to be. How do you claim you give gamers full independence, yet put in a horrible XP mechanic that limits them, not by skill, not by time played, not by money earned, but by how long they have their account? And this brings me to my last point.
The game is more of an AFK simulator and has almost no skill profieciency when it comes to PvE. You want to know how to get to point A -> B that is 15 jumps away? Set destination and put on auto pilot, watch netflix. How do you mine? Point to rock, hit 1 button, watch netflix and wait. I know what you are thinking, 'Most games are like that, you are being to harsh on Eve'. No, no I am not. I can excuse mining and auto pilot travel for being boring, it is a game mechanic that is hard to keep someone interested in. But when it requires 0 interation from me for hours on end, that is boring. I watched 10+ hours of netflix while my character did something in game with no interaction from me. Except for me point him in another direction to do the same automated action. And the worst part is PvE isn't much better!
Space combat in this game is HORRIBLE. It takes no skill at all. Now I cannot speak to PvP since I cannot do that for another 2 weeks due to the XP mechanic. But PvE combat is horrible. Target X, push auto laser button, profit. This is the extent of the skill you need. True story, I went into low security last night with a ship you get from the starting quest. I found a Battleship (4-5 levels in ship class above me). My experience 'fighting' it. Target, orbit, auto fire, afk. For 25 minutes my entry level ship, flew circles around a battleship hitting it with lasers. I did NOTHING, I was watching TV while I waited for it to kill the battleship. No resource management, no tactical manuevers, no worries. I didn't have to work to get an angle, didn't have to manage what lasers fired in what order, I didn't even have to worry about my shields recharging. When I can take on an NPC, that is at least 4 tiers higher than me while I am on the toliet, the game is broken/borning.
And for being such a complicated game, I would say overly complicated, yet having the core concept of Space Combat/Exploration/Mining being able to be done on 95% auto pilot. That is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ made game, and a poor gaming experience.

After playing a match up with the dev, and feeling a bit bad for the previous review i wrote, here's a more updated, and more accurate one.
This game, is fun. I won't lie, I enjoyed it. Playing with the dev also made it a lot more interesting since we were doing different gamemode, different play styles, and all around just dicking around. It was fun, their play dates are pretty enjoyable. The gameplay, is also interesting. I can see a rather competitive side to this game that would be kind of halo-esc.
My only issue is, there is too much spotlight i feel on the zombies mode. This game has a -great- multiplayer that I feel should be on an ever expanding community. Each weapon feels like it's actually useful, from the miner gun all the way to the hookshot. There is a use for every weapon, and a certain usage for every weapon. Sure hit reg at times can feel a little funky due to it being players hosting the servers, but i feel if there were a few dedicated servers or something it'd be a little more even playing ground.

It'd be interesting to see a few suits available if possible, to represent rankings or maybe a level system to display who has more experience in the game than others.
Overall, this game is entertaining, and rather interesting, but it suffers from lack of players at times of the day. There -is- a plausable competitive league in the game, that should be promoted -far- more than the zombie mode should be. It's cool to see though, that there are different game modes out there, and so many interesting maps, that i believe are user created? I could be wrong. But there are a lot of maps and different gamemodes that if you can host the server, or find the players, would be very well to get together and enjoy the time with.

First of all this may seem like a simplified version of what we're used to expect from a YGO game BUT Duel Link's charm and appeal comes exactly from that. The duels are fast and fun without sacrificing depth and strategical thinking, I've been playing the game on my mobile for months now and I can guarantee that this is not pay to win game, if you plan your decks carefully you can have exactly what you need without spending a dime, infact with all the events and giveaways it's almost impossible not to gain the deck you want!
Now for the downside... The graphics look bad on PC... On mobile I could say that everything looked spectacular, however in this version some of the text is blurry, some parts of the background is pixelized and overall visual quality is worse than the mobile version by far. The other problem the game has, and this is shared with the mobile version, is the fact that you can't store more than 9999 gems which unfortunately forces you to spend them as soon as you reach the cap in order to receive more gems, now this may seem like a trivial problem but for those that want to save up for future card additions this is troublesome, it's been several times now that I'm forced to buy packs I don't need just so I can spend gems...
All and all this is, hands down, the best YGO video game I've played so far and I've tried most on all possible platforms.
Oh and if you think the game is too easy take it to the PvP and test your deck, I'm sure you'll have a blast!

I got this in the latest Humble Bundle, so I don't regret spending money to play it. In fact, the game does a lot of things right. It has a great art style, a bold and fitting soundtrack and what I liked most is it gives you a lot of freedom. Every character in the game as far as I can tell can be killed, which changes the game.
However, the most glaring issue is the combat. I'm not really sure why people are praising the gunplay in this game. It is simple but not in a good way. Overly simple to the point where aiming is just a chore. To fire your gun, you press J to unholster it, K to♥♥♥♥♥♥it and K again to fire. This is fine, but when you are given basically no idicator or reticle to where your shot will land it just ends up frustrating when you are certain you will hit someone and it misses. This could easily be fixed by simply adding a reticle to where your shot will land.
Omitting such an indicator isn't good design. It doesn't make the game harder in a way that is challenging yet fair. It's just annoying.
That said, if you can get past this, I would look at checking this game out for the aspects and mechanics it gets right. As I said, visually and audibly the game is fantasic. Both contribute to creating a world truly reminiscent of the wild west and to do so within the confines of a retro style is very impressive.
Character dialogue is also natural and written to match the theme well. No voice acting is present in the game, yet the dialect the characters speak in aid the western feel the game goes for, even if the "ah" in replacement for "I" can get tedious after a while.
I have only played under an hour, but I can only assume the hint system is in fact a system created to enchance the uniqueness of the game instead of just a way to advance the story. Furthermore the story is solid, albiet not wholly original. You play as a gunslinging rancher whos family are killed by bandit(s?) and you are set on your path of redemption.
Overall, this game just solidifies why the Steam thumbs up and down system isn't suitable. I'm in the middle. If you find the game on sale, try it, if not just to experience the world the game establishes. At just over £10 though I'm not sure the actual "game" part of Westerado is strong enough for a full price purchace.

American Conquest. Back when it first showed up around 2003; I was quite young and I didn't understand "strategy" games but somehow this game kept me playing it, if It was the campaign or fighting against the A.i and even on the editor mode. I never made maps, I just spawned Units and played for hours and hours on end
Skip to a few years later(this year) I've came back to love this little game again after all this time.
Playing the Campagin is all fun and it helps you get used to the controls and different units. Options are there for you to change your mouse and scroll speeds and the Game/Music volume sliders are serviceable but has no options for re-binding keys.
But! the real bread and butter is playing against the A.I, every faction has it's own strategy and tactics will keep you thinking and on harder difficulties can really overwhelm you, games can also last upto a few hours if you play slowly and or with many A.I, but this is what was fun, having to fight large armies and protecting your city/villiage. Sad that the multiplayer doesn't work, I would've loved to play PvP games. Every unit in American conquest filled a role and having large columns of soldiers marching on to the battlefield, or mass amounts of Archers and spearmen surrounding groups of enemies. Naval landing were also stressful knowing that your transport ship could be killed, losing all those supplies and manpower really kept me thinking and Improving.
If you have Some extra dosh lying about and you're a fan of older strategy games, I'd say pick it up and give it a try; both when it came out and today it's still an enjoyable game.

I would leave it a neutral review, but as steam doesn't allow it, I'll have to leave a negative one.
The problem with Fata Morgana is that it is not a bad VN as such but it is a very boring one, like I'd say unbearably so, considering its length, and as it isn't really bad, you might think that you just need to man up and finish it, but... it never really gets interesting and here is why:
1. Repetition, the worst crime a writer can commit, repetition is not good and it should be minimized, if it's required (different perspective from different characters), it should be done in such a different way as not to look like repetition.
2. Screaming, moaning, and other random sounds doesn't transition well to the written form, instead of doing AAAAAAAAAAAs, author is way better of telling what a certain character feels, that's what literature is for.
3. Characters are so one dimensional and shallow that they look like dolls with horrible stories for the most part. I don't need my literature to be realistic, no, but some depth to characters would have been nice. To be fair, it is a tad rectified at the end, but that's too little too late.
4. Interminable fussing over every little detail, on and on and on.
5. There is not enough going on for it being as long as it is.
6. Some nitpicking: art is odd, static characters look nice, but sometimes when they change position or show emotion they look nothing like themselves. Backgrounds leave much to be desired.
7. Final word, assuming that it is a mystery VN, it makes you wait for some suspense, and it is simply not there.

At the intersection of great storytelling and flawless production resides The House in Fata Morgana.
If you've read this game's description and are wondering if it can present a story without melodrama, cliche, and/or pretension, don't worry because they're all left at the door. What you will find here are genuinely well-written characters involved in a serious and heavy plot - but one that strikes a balance between maturity and light-heartedness. It's well-paced and interesting throughout.
Besides the story, other aspects of the game are just as good. The music in particular is top-notch - songs played during important moments often use minutes-long "continuous crescendos" that have incredible impact on the scenes they're used in. Character art, backgrounds, animations and other aspects of visual design are all excellent, and the translation is virtually error-free. This is seriously a high-quality production.
This is a story worth telling and worth reading. If you're a fan of visual novels, you need to play this game right now.

DOD:S is a first-person game set in World War 2. It's a class-based shooter I should say much the same as the older GoldScr game. You can choose between the following classes:
-Rifler:
Both the German and US soldiers possess a different rifle which is good for long and mid range combat. The German rifles kill in one shot, but are bolt-action, the US kill in two but are faster. Both also have rifle grenades,
-Assault:
Has an smg - good for close range combat, apart from the usual explosive grenade also has a smoke one.
-Support:
Has automatic rifles good for close and mid range combat, but still useful in long range, has a massive recoil you need to compensate for, but its pretty simple since it only goes up. Has a grenade.
-Sniper:
Self-explanatory, good for long range, doesn't have x-rair when unscoped but can still be used in close range like a rifler would.
-Machine Gunner:
Has a machine gun which can deployed with a bipod and used to defend flags and other objectives. If not deployed the MG has a GIGANTIC recoil.
-Rocket:
Has a Rocket Launcher that mostly kills in 1 shot. Needs to be deployed to shoot, good for eliminating snipers.
Some classes are better all around than others but each have their uses. There are numerous official and custom maps and its a fun game. The problems is there aren't many players. Furthermore, quite a bit of servers have dumb rules and you may as well be kicked or banned.
I would recommend this game if it's on sale.
