The level editor adds a lot of longetivity after the short campaign's credits roll, and is extremely simple to use. It also includes the funniest ability ever; making guards unsuspectingly knock themselves out with a door. It never gets old! The music is utterly fantastic, and the graphics are of no less of a caliber. The dialogue is pretty humorous as well and sometimes even a bit meta. For example, in one of the dialogues you have the option to say this: "Well, to be honest, I haven't really been paying attention to the plot since Level 2." Stuff like that.
TLDR; Must buy, no matter what. Unless you are against indie for no apparent reason, play this game!

Sonic Lost World is a bit of a mixed bag; on one hand the gamepaly itself is actually pretty fun and graphically it is really pleasing to look at. Of course, this game does have it's faults.
The biggest issue I had was one of conveyance; this game raises a lot of questions from controls to story. The game doesn't really do a very good job of telling you how certain controls work (I honestly had no idea how to activiate the in-game hints until AFTER I beat the game to look things up) and there are some situations where trying to figure the controls out can lead to some very aggrivating incidents. However, once you've figured out the ins and outs of the controls, navigating levels whether you want to explore thoroughly or just speed through is a pretty enjyoable time.
Now, I'm not going to sugar coat it, the story is a mess. Story cutscenes in Lost World tend to raise more questions than answer them, with a lot of scenes just being completely unnecessary. To be completely honest, I still have no idea what the names of the individual members of the Deadly Six even are after having played through the game and completed all the challenges. While I do enjoy a lot of the character interaction between Sonic, Tails, Eggman, and even Orbot and Cubot; a lot of things are nice to look at an raise a laugh every now and then; but for the most part this story is pretty basic yet somehow has a lot of missing details.
Frankly, aside from the weak story, control quirks you need to learn on your own, and a few levels with sudden difficulty jumps, I did still enjoy my time with Lost World, and will probably still find myself humming the theme every now and then. I'd recommend trying the game out sometime, but don't expect any epic storytelling or fancy sequences out of it.

I'm happy I tried Sonic Lost World and am happy it exists as a sign of Sonic Team's always interesting experiments (And almost always disappointing failed experiments.).
There are some great levels. There are a lot of really bad ones.
There are three main movement systems and none of them follow genre conventions. They are all clever new takes on the formula, but none are implemented well. The biggest new novelty it gives is that Sonic can now at long last do precision platforming in tight spaces where with boost physics it was better to just close your eyes and hit the jump+direction and pray.
Sonic Lost World, as always gives you a lengthy tutorial pop-up about pressing A to jump and you won't die if you have rings, but then doesn't explain any of this stuff at all, so you end up having to learn by doing. The parkour then feels like it interrupts your progress rather than speeds it up until you get a hang on it and even then it's still something that doesn't flow. It somehow translates to mantling walls, running along roofs, and wall-running but does it in a way worse than every other game in the genre has ever done these things, even the always terrible Assassin's Creed.
And this would all be forgiveable were it not for the levels. Quite a few are great; multiple paths, lots of speed, good variety. There are very few "on rails" segments in most of these, excluding of course a DKC-ish mine cart level, but then you get to the lame stuff. You're a giant snowball, you have to hop across a bunch of platforms to collect things, you have to guide a bunch of rolling things to a goal, you have to stop and kill every enemy to make a warp appear and the combat isn't any better than as boost game, it's just slower.
It got to be too much. I quit.
I loved the spark of creativity in it. Some of the dialogue really made me chuckle. But in too many ways it is a typical Sonic game: Ambitious, but unpolished and poorly explained. Too full of terrible spots and the good spots aren't good enough.
On the bright side, for all the usual Sonic Team errors they commit, at least you don't have five furries all yelling at you every boss fight.
This is one game that all gamer's must try to beat with out looking up a guide. It's a blast!

I've been playing the game actively for about a week, so here's my new player perspective:
There are a few types of reviews out there. I came to the game because a friend (a member of the infamous Goonswarm Corporation) tells me about how much fun it is, how good the graphics are, the opportunities in marketing, etc. I went in knowing that there are people, like my friend, who will blow your ship up if you don't watch your back after taking a single step. So for the reviews, the Recommend ones usually say "yes, but..." and the Not Recommended ones usually talk about the gameplay.
The "yes, but..." is because of people like the members of Goon. There are griefers on this game. Imagine anarchy, and anyone can do anything, and that's this game. There are very few places that are safe, and those are all docked inside stations where you aren't even playing the game. Go into the game expecting to lose hard work. So many missions have people telling you only to fly ships you're willing and able to lose, and it's absolutely correct.
The people who don't recommend the game usually don't like the UI, the griefers, the pay-to-win theme, or something along those lines. Addressing those,
(People who know what you're doing go ahead and skip down)
The UI is pretty much how you play the game. You can, but usually don't, fly your ship manually. The key to the game is a good Overview, which is your biggest tool. I spent forever trying to click on enemy ships before they moved away from my mouse, only to find out that was incredibly pointless. My overview has a General tab, a Mining tab, and a WarpTo tab. General has stuff like space stations, enemies, and overall most things. Mining has asteroid belts and asteroids and things of that caliber, and WarpTo is a menu to pull up when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, of basically anything to warp to as a last-ditch effort to get away from people. Again, the overview is your biggest tool. Everything you can do (radial menu etc) by clicking and holding on a ship, you can do to their name in the Overview. It just makes everything so much easier.
I won't go into the weapon types or anything that specific, but the general rules are your weapons are high slots, then everything else is fair game. Mid-low slots can be anything from modules that give your armor passive resistance against damage types to something that recovers your shield, and even high slots can be random things to help in different ways like launch scanning probes. I don't really get how overheating works except that it causes heat damage to your modules which is bad, but it makes them work better which is good. To move, you usually will find yourself orbiting an enemy or an object. Locking on is explained in-game, but my biggest problem is forgetting to either lock onto a new enemy or to fire my weapon before looking away from the screen. When you're not orbiting someone/thing, chances are you're warping somewhere. There isn't too much normal movement you do aside from combat and warping. On that note, using autopilot won't warp you right to your destination, so if you AFK then you're setting yourself up to be caught. There are modules that prevent warping, target locking, moving, and all other sorts of things, so the general rule I go with is if you walk away you're probably going to lose it, even if it doesn't seem like it.
As for the Alpha and Omega clones. I really enjoy the game and I know that there is a lot I'm missing out on. I'm not having as much fun as if I had slightly more open reach, if I could study every skill, etc, but I'm not paying for the game right now. The phrase I hear a lot is that it's free to try, not free to play. You get some small ships, even a few big ones, and you get one miner you can man. I'd say it's a 50/50 split in what you're missing out on; while you're still missing most of the ships and skills and big fancy things, you can have most of the fun with the smaller things. Another review said the ships just get bigger and have bigger pricetags, they're not necessarily more fun.
I had to leave in the middle of writing this so I'm not sure how coherent I'm being, but my general point is that I would recommend this game to a lot of people. It is a great business simulator style game, with a hint of anarchy because you're screwed if you don't watch your own back. If someone messes with you, get them back. Join a big corporation. You can't run an entire business by yourself, and as much as I'd like to say the game is just pvp, it's really not. You can make your money by fighting, but there is a lot of grinding and "business" as I would call it, just to get to a fun point in the game. After that, the game is what you make of it. You win some and you lose some. Every ship you destroy and every capsule you blow up is another player getting frustrated about so many manhours of game time grinding up to that point, so expect to be on that end of the screen a few times.

Being a free-to-play game, I entered this game not expecting much but a few cheap dialogs and meaningless character development for the sake of it only being the first of the series. Surprisingly, the game delivered more than what it offered, such as an enticing tale of a man's struggle to help those who he encoutered and also kicking a few butts along the way.
The game abruptly ends though, leaving the want for Act 2 to come fairly soon. I was honestly suprised by all of the elements in this game, as well as most of the visuals being such great quality. If you do try this game, I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did.

Borderlands was a cool concept, but there are a few things that hold it down, especially when compared to the sequel.  Firstly, the walk speed is pretty slow, which is annoying.  I played as the siren, so I had bursts of superspeed.  That helped a bit.  Secondly, there is quite a lack of dialogue, which leaves the game feeling quite lonely.  Lastly, the story is quite weak too.  Besides those things, I actually like the game, it can be fun to play from time to time, and the randomly generated weapons are nice; though after playing for a while, you realise that there aren't "millions" of guns.  Technically there are "infinite" guns, but they are procedurely generated from different parts and stats.  This isn't really such a bad thing, and it would be impossible for the devs to actually design hundreds of guns, but it's just something I noticed.  Overall, I like the game, but highly recommend that you get the sequel instead.

text:
Pretty fun JRPG-like game.   Never played Earthbound, so I cannot deploy the comparison everyone else is, but enjoyed my time with the game regardless.
Combat seems simple at first, but the battle system becomes a little more complex as the game progresses and party members are added (never getting too complicated or difficult, though).
Characters are rather bland, never moving beyond the initial stereotyping of their names, but that may be by design.  With 40 party members to recruit and use, though, the game encourages you to try new things and experiment with different party combinations, which helps keep things fresh.
Found the story rather bland as well, nothing beyond your typical "mysterious-evil-slowly-destroying-the-land" with a couple curveballs thrown in.  The setting was a nice change of pace from the typical RPG locales, given a bit of a modern, American flair to JRPGs.  Dialogue, however, is sharp, with excellent voice acting on a 15 dollar indie rpg.  The little easter egg jokes you find by exploring the world are good for a chuckle or two, as well.
Replay-wise, they do offer an option for a New Game + when finished, though I didn't feel compelled enough to run it a second time.  All of the achievements can be unlocked in one playthrough as well, defeating the completionist's need to run through it again.  However, you may find it enjoyable enough to revisit it at a later date.
Performance-wise, runs relatively smoothly, with a couple hiccups coming in larger areas late in the game, mostly when opening the map/menu.  Apart from that, the game does feature some nasty bugs which will often crash your game for you, but the solid Autosave system should prevent any serious data loss when it hits you.  And it will hit you. (Note, Devs are inquiring about bugs/glitches on the discussion boards, so they seem like they intend on fixing their game up at least. Bonus points, as always).
Overall I'd give it a 7/10.  For 14.99 you get a light-hearted JRPG romp with about 30 hours of gameplay.  Definitely worth a glance if you're already a fan of the genre, but not exciting/different enough to win over anyone that doesn't like JRPG's to begin with.

So I am gonna start this off by saying that I've been a watcher and an admirer of all things Dragon Ball for 15 years. Dragon Ball Z is my favorite show of all time and it's very sentimental to me since I watched it with my uncles a lot as kid and I still do to this day with Super and Kai. So you can rest well knowing this review is written by an almost lifelong fan of the series, or you can view it as biased, each to their own.
This is probably the Dragon Ball game that is most true to it's source material since the Budokai games. It nails the art style, moves, fighting and characters down to a tee. The only thing I was disappointed with is no blast struggles. I would have loved to reenact the Kamehameha vs Galick Gun or struggle with a player online or a friend.
The fighting is flawed but still fun in parts. The tracking can really suck resulting in wasted hits and special/ultimate attacks, you will experience a lot of missed attacks in this game. If you can cope with that like I do, that's great but there's no denying that it can be annoying.
The story mode has you going through parts of all the indivisual arcs of the Z series (Saiyan, Namek, Frieza, Cell Game, Buu and unlockable Bardock and Broly stages). It's pretty enjoyable overall if you know what's going on, no severe grinding is required to match the skill of a certain opponent and it's all pretty quick compared to the parallel quests.
The parallel quests serve as side missions where you can unlock attacks, z-souls, outfits and zeni (currency). These are just battle stages with some dialogue potentially pushed in. The difficulties of the quests are seperated. Completing these can be a task considering that you may have to grind due to the difficulty and time restrictions of some of the higher quests. It's not primary to play through these but it's there nonetheless.
I personally found trainers to be a promising concept but it was executed in a pretty lack luster way. Trainers are there to teach you moves that they use in the actual story. For example, Vegeta will teach you the Galick Gun and Final Flash amongst others. The only way to progress in the training once you learn a move is grind in the campaign or parallel quests and get good grades. You could also use the most recent move they taught you in missions but I've found this to be optional. It can be a grind to make it through training and it's kind of disappointing how once they teach you that last ultimate, you kind of just move on to the next trainer.
The leveling system is straight forward and what you'd expect a modern leveling system to be, gain EXP to level up. Once you reach level 80, this can begin to be a grindfest since you will rarely get above 60,000 EXP. So if you're planning to play this for a long time, keep that in mind.
The online overall is really fun, if you can find someone who's playing it. You will more commonly find people playing online parallel quests than online battles, but in my experience online battle are a ton of fun, especially when you and your opponent are neck and neck and don't use items.
Performance is not a problem, this game isn't costly to run which is good for a modern gen game. Although if you're playing on a casual laptop, don't be expecting to be playing at HD resolutions or high graphics.
In conclusion, Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a must play for gamer DB fans even for casual play. You will hit a few grinds and later on you will have more difficulty as you play, but overall the game is worth the £40 price tag and definitely worth the £10 price tag on♥♥♥♥♥

There's very little to say wrong about Aperture Tag beyond that I wish there was more. As an effective total conversion atop Portal 2, the 3-4 hrs you'll get from this tickles the Portal-sense of puzzle solving, as well as using the lore of Portal 2 well.
It's based on what the gel mechanics were in Portal 2, from "Tag : The Power of Paint", where in that game you actually shot paint to get the effects, as opposed to Portal 2 where you could only manipulate the flow of paint. Aperture Tag replaces the portal gun with a paint gun, while still keeping other Portal mechanics in play (including the use of portals at times, though you don't have the ability to set them).  In addition, it adds a mechanic where the gun is fully or partially disabled passing through certain fields, which adds to the puzzle elements. Most of the puzzles become thinking more vertically in nature, an aspect of using the blue gel for jumping.
Most of the puzzles are generally straight forward in the game's first 3 chapters out of four - the last chapter gets much more "free form" in nature although the puzzles still typically only have one solution. The paint mechanics are used well, both for moving your character around, as well as how it impacts other objects.  There is one puzzle that is very much time and reflexes-based - but wisely the game offers a short circuit if you cannot get the hang of this section as to not make it a stumbling block.
And of course, all this atop the fact it is a free mod.  There's very little to really complain about at that price. This is very good production value, and would like to see more, whether from this team or the community, to expand on it.

Tight controls, beautiful graphics, a colorful palate that makes the shots easy to distinguish, a dozen ways to play between the different ships and modes, and a host of unlockables and extras. Crimzon Clover WORLD IGNITION is probably one, if not THE best shmup to come to Steam so far. I’m sure some would make arguments for some other games that have tried new things (like Ikaruga) but for me this one is king. Clean lines and smooth gameplay just win me over any novelty factor others have had.
This is a game you play for hours on end trying to slowly get better, not just something fun for a laugh or two. Beyond the graphical clarity there’s also an excellent soundtrack, and the systems while very traditional shooter concepts are executed almost perfectly.  Wrack of combos, shoot everything that moves, use your bomb or save it and use multiple bomb charges to activate a mode called Boost which functions as a supercharge to the weapons as the meter slowly builds up to get the best combo, and try your best to 1cc it. It’s all very standard fare (save for Boost mode, where the goal is to stay in the Boosted state as long as possible, being hit taking you out) but it’s just done so well that you’ll keep coming back.
I find it hard to make a long review with a deep explanation because in truth it’s something every shmup fan knows well, all the usual mechanics are in place. But at the same time I want to say it’s a special form of that, expertly crafted, that’s going to be a highlight in any STG fans library.

This is an awesome board game, especially if you happen to be a big history fan. As the description says, this is a board game that goes over several incidents that occured over the 45 years of cold war. Some of the events include the Cuban Missle Crisis, the formation of NATO, and the "We Will Bury You" speech. They also include a few events based off of a few movies such as "How I Learned To Stop Worrying" from "Dr. Strangelove" and "War Games" from the movie of the same name.
The main trick to the game is to spread as much influence of your superpower to other nations, especially battleground nations. As the game moves on, certain regional scoring cards will enter player's hands that must be played by the end of the turn or that player will "accidentally" start a nuclear war, thus ending the game.
There are several ways to spread influence in the game. Some cards have events that allow players to place influence on certain countries. They can either do what the card states or use its operation's value to place influence on or agacent to countries that have their influence. They also could use the cards to attempt realignments in other countries or coups. Coups are the most ideal way of removing opponent's influence while possibly placing your own afterwards. This is also a great way of performing necessary military operations to prevent loss of points at the end of a turn. But whenever a coup is performed in a battleground country, the defcon level will be decreased by one, adding limitations to both players as well as bringing the world closer to a potential nuclear war.
Although I do have some dislikes with the A.I. at some times, this is still a very great adaptation of the board game, especially since there are almost always people to play with online. I'd strongly suggest this to any big fans of board games or any big cold war historians.

Westerado Double Barreled is a rare game that somehow introduces its own genre to the gaming world. The game isn't long, but there are loads of ways to play it and loads of ways to get what you want. You can choose to help out anyone who needs it, but of course if you want to be the tough guy, you could just murder everyone. It won't get you any clues but it will get you loot, so you have to choose between loot and clues.
The combat is great - easy to learn but hard to master - and every kill feels satisfying no matter what weapon you use. The gunfights tend to be rather short, most taking place under 20 seconds, but it feels frantic and tense through the whole fight.
The missions are mostly minigames or fetch quests, but don't let that put you off - the minigames are good fun and there's sure to be a good gunfight or two during the fetch quests. On top of that, some quests require that you don't shoot up a place in order to start, so much of the time you're gonna have to think twice before you start spraying and praying, as the people you kill might be significant to that quest you're currently on.
(Spoilers-ish) The only thing I don't really like about the game is the end sequence, mainly because it's the same every playthrough apart from a possibly varying plot twist once you defeat the murderer.

Boy... this game i was sure it was going to be some sort of 06 disaster but it's far from that.
As far as i'm concerned it's mainly lambasted for not being really a sonic game as it takes a lot of inspiration from Mario games (mostly mario galaxy) and as such its pace is slower than what you'd expect from a sonic title (especially after the boost became a defacto staple of the series).
This apparently lit up the fanbase evenly divided between those who stopped worrying and learned to love the boost, adventure fans, and purists who stick only for the 2d momentum based games.
And to lost worlds bad luck it didn't particularly please any of those groups.
Gameplay wise the game is split into 3 kinds of levels.
Cylindrical 3d "exploratory" levels (Exploratory only if you collect red rings otherwise you just race to the other end of the tube)
Autorun levels (self explanatory, the only real innovation here is that you run down the outside of a tubelike structure).
2d levels (Which are not at all like the old sonic games and play nothing like modern sonic 2d sections from other sonic titles, Overall those reminds me more of Rayman Origins/Legends than Mario at least.
So long story short. This is a decent platformer but outside of the characters it has almost nothing to do with the rest of the Sonic series.
The addition of parkour is a nice idea that fits sonic as a character but the execution could be better and more fluid.
tl;dr
Good game as long as you think of it more along the lines of spinoff like tails adventure or All-Stars and less of it being a sequel to generations.

Ok, before I start, THIS IS NOT A MINECRAFT CLONE. Secondly, I have been playing this game since 2 weeks after it's debut on the Xbox Live Indie Games section. After all my experience with it after its beta stage up until the newest update, I can say it still is an amazing game. In fact, this game is what got me interested in Halo, I had never played Halo properly before then.
So what is Murder Miners? It's essentially FPS inspired by the gameplay of Halo with the graphics of Minecraft. In fact, that's all it has to do with Minecraft. Now onto the gameplay. The weapons included (the main ones being the Pistol, Machinegun, Shotgun, Sniper and Battle Rifle) play pretty much the same as their Halo counterparts, particularly Halo: CE because of the 3-headshot-kill Pistol. This will appeal to Halo fans but also most FPS fans as a whole because they are just so balanced. However, movement I find is quite unique. Yes there is Halo jumping, but there are also pretty nice mechanics including wall-jumping, multi-directional dashing and unlimited sprint, which I feel pretty much allow you to be a ninja.
While what I have metioned so far describe this as a competitive shooter (which it is), it also has a great casual side. The main part of this being infection mode. This is my favourite mode in MM, as I feel it is the best infection mode out of any FPS game I played, as the zombies are not underpowered as they have a grappling tounge to move across the map quickly, and are able to devour corpses to level up.
Another great thing about murder miners is the map creation. Now I'm not too into map-making myself, but the game's Minergun allows you to place and destroy blocks with different modes. These options allow you to make maps pretty much any way you want. It's also really easy to use so map-making won't be too complicated, although it can take a while depending on what sort of map you want to make.
Are there any bad points about Murder Miners? Well, not too much. The only real thing I have a problem with is that when playing with a lot of people (particularly 18+ people) the game can tend to lag a bit. However, I have an i3, so it could just be me, but I have also seen this problem on the Xbox version. But thankfully this doesn't happen too much. Another thing to mention is that JForce are really involved with their community and respond to any suggestions or complaints they may have. Also updates used to be very frequent last year (pretty much every month), but are kind of slow at the moment, but this is due to the big vehicle update late last year and with porting the game to PC. I'm sure updates are likely to be frequent again, which is a good thing.
All-in-all I fully recommend this game, as it is really good and fairly cheap (£1.59). I would also highly reccomend getting a 4-pack, as it is not too much more expensive and this game is awesome with friends. I have been playing this game for a long time and will continue to play it.

A few years ago, I picked this game up on my wii u, I disliked it and sold it after world 1. I picked it up recently do to it being on sale and being interested in it. And just let me tell you, I had to literally FORCE myself to finish this game.
The first 1-3 worlds are honestly, amazing. I was convinced this would actually be the best 3d sonic game ever. World 4 was not as good as the first 3 for one reason I will talk about later, world 5 was a huge drop in quality, by world 6 I was hating the game, and by world 7 I was considering never touching this again.
First, id like to talk about the positives:
Looks fantastic
Good soundtrack
First 3 worlds are some of the best in 3d sonic history
Replaying old levels to get an S rank is fun and challenging
Now, the negatives, oh boy:
Story is bland and boring
Deadly Six are bad villians and have very bland personalities
Last 2 worlds are some of the most infuriating, poorly designed levels I have seen in recent years
Achievements can only be obtained 3 at a time by finding Omachao on the map randomly
Sonic feels extremely sluggish and hard to control
Parkour wall climbing system doesnt work half of the time
Game does an awful job at explaining its mechanics
Bosses are either way to easy or way to obscure on how to win
Cheap deaths and infuriating level gimmicks everywhere. Let me mention most below:
World 4-2. where you become a hard to control snowball and have to roll around
There are a few levels where you have to fly around with awkward controls
World 5-2, which has a random and unessecary stealth section at the end
World 5-4, which really highlights the games awful physics in the 2d levels
World 6-2, which has an annoying boss where your chain of homing attacks randomly will stop
World 6-4, which has a boss that doesnt tell you how to hurt it, and thats the only reason its hard
World 7-1, a boss rush level that after killing the second boss, a random piece of the floor turns into instant kill lava without warning
World 7-2, which is boderline impossible without memorizing the stage and knowing  when to do some VERY presice jumps
World 7-3. which the boss at the end doesnt tell you what you are supposed to do to hit it, and caused me to die 5 times because I had no idea what to do
And did I mention this game has a live system? Not only do you have to deal with stuff like I mentioned above, you also have to deal with a very unessecary live system where dying at the end and getting a game over will force you to start that ENTIRE level over. The game is also VERY stingy on lives and has MANY instant death traps
At its best, Sonic Lost world is one of my favorite sonic games ever, and at its worst, Sonic Lost World is a game I never want to touch again. If you want a good 3d sonic game, get generations. Not only is it $10 cheaper, it is an massivley more fun and enjoyable game.
Two-player coop campaign is the best vs. AI RTS/RPG co-op experience I've had so far (and I've played many RTS games). It's action-packed, strategic, "to the IP", and overall a hell lot of fun!

I had fun with Sonic Lost World. However, I would only recommend this game to the hardcore Sonic Fans. It plays very similar to a Mario game which might turn off some people. It is not a beginner friendly game and only the players who are looking for a completely new experience and are willing to look past the frustration the game throws at you will get the most enjoyment out of it.
Sonic Lost World story is mediocre at best. Eggman, Cubot, and Orbot are the best characters in the game when they interact with each other especially when teaming up with sonic. Amy, Knuckles, Tails, and the Deadly Six (with the exception of maybe Zavok) are stereotypical characters and one dimensional. Especially Amy and Knuckles as there no point for them to be in the story. The Lost Hex is devoid of any world building as the game doesn't bother giving you lore throughout your experience. This is definitely one of the weaker stories in the series and I recommend just skipping the cutscenes.
The game presentation is good. Sonic Lost world runs at a smooth 60 fps at 1080p. Levels are colorful and detailed though, aesthetically basic (not a fan of the tubular level design graphically and gameplay wise). Music is catchy but personally not memorable. It is not the best looking or sounding Sonic game but it does it job well.
Overall I would give this game a 6 out of 10 just above average. If your just starting to get in to the series I would recommend staying away from this game. I personally had fun with it more than what others have said about the game. It is definitely not a game for everyone.

The Dig. A legend.
Back in the golden age of adventure gaming, The Dig was The Thing - something we talked about and which, when completed, brought us pride.
Then, I forgot The Dig for some years. I played different games. And, for a while, didn't play at all. After realizing that work with no play made me a dull boy, I one day went through Steam - and bumped into The Dig.
Now, older, I appreciate the flawless writing and a grand Sci/Fi epic even more. I'd love to see this as a movie - with early 80's effects, no less. Hell, maybe even the new style. This is now, regardless of media, one of my favourite Sci/Fi epics ever. The one from the age of Space Exploration. From the times when future still was an utopia.
Fully recommended. And the graphics still are perfect.

Been playing for a little over a month now ( ~160 hours or so ) and I don't believe I will continue playing going forward.
Reason 1:
Your ability to do much in this game is tied directly to how well trained your character is with the bazillion skill traits that are available to you.  Unlike other MMO's, these skills do not improve with use.  Rather, they are added to a skill queue where they are constantly training in the background ( even while logged off ).  There are five levels to any given skill and each level takes longer to train than the previous one.  Initial levels of the skill can take maybe half an hour to train, whereas the level V variants of a single skill can take upwards of a MONTH.   You can only train a single skill at any given time.  So if you want to train three level five skills, ( after you've trained the pre-requisite skills and skill levels I-IV ) you can be looking at three months timewise.
There are two account types.  Alpha and Omega.  Alphas are free to play, but are limited in what skills they can train and what ships they can fly.  Omegas are the subscription accounts and can train and use all skills and ships.  They even train skills at 2x the rate of Alphas ( but still can take up to a Month to train a Level V skill, which means an Alpha would need TWO months to train it ) but it's still a long wait.  In order to fly some ships at an Expert Level ( Level V Mastery ) or even some of the larger ships ( Capitol ships and the like ), it can easily take YEARS of 24/7 training time in order to do so.
There are some implants you can buy / outfit to boost your training times a bit, but the good ones are horrendously expensive and come with a risk that I will talk about next.
Reason 2:
Eve is open PVP.  The 'world space' is broken into various security ratings.  High-Sec, Low-Sec, Null-Sec and Wormhole Space.  There is some protection from PvP in High-Sec space, but not 100%.  Very little or none in the others.  This basically means that you can be attacked and destroyed pretty much anywhere in game for any reason.  The lower the security rating for a system, the greater the liklihood of you having a bad day.
The problem, from my perspective anyway, is new players are trying to come into the game to learn it ( Eve has the steepest learning curve of any game I've ever played in twenty years of online gaming ) but are pretty much cannon fodder for the existing veteran players who have no qualms about killing you just because they enjoy doing so.
As a new player in a new ship with very few skills trained, you'll come through a JumpGate ( the mechanism utilized to warp you from one Solar System to another ) into what's known as a GateCamp.  Where members will sit and wait for ships to come through, then destroy them.  No reason, just because.
These folks are usually veterans flying high level ships, outfitted with the best equipment and backed up with years worth of skill training.  Not to mention, you're likely going to run into a group of anywhere from three to a dozen ships.
Basically, you're walking into a trap with zero warning and absolutely no means to survive it.  Any work, ISK ( money ) and / or effort you have put into the ship you're flying or the cargo you're carrying will be lost.  Additionally, recall the implants I mentioned above that reduce your skill training time ?   The best ones are stupidly expensive ( half a billion ISK or more for the set ) and if you die ( most gate campers will kill your pod after they destroy your ship just because ) you not only have lost your ship, any cargo you were carrying, but those very expensive implants get destroyed as well.
You'll basically need to join a Corporation ( Eve's version of a guild ) in order to survive, though doing so has it's own issues as well if your Corp is at war with one or more other Corps.
It's a very frustrating experience overall.  Maybe later on once you have enough skills trained to fly better ships and outfit them with better equipment it changes.  There are those who say skill makes the pilot and I will acknowledge that to a degree.  It is, in my opinion, only part of the equation as a highly skilled pilot in a starter ship using starter equipment still has zero chance of survival when warping into a gate camp comprised of overwhelming numbers, ships and equipment.
For the existing folks, it's probably a fun game.
For any who are just now thinking about playing, it's just a whole lot of frustration.

Get it if you love:
- Turn-based RPGs
- Political satires
- Earthbound/Mother and/or Suikoden

- Humor
Don't get it if:
- You wanted something more hardcore (Unless you adjust difficulty via a citizen)
- You want something serious
- You want a long game
- You hate everything politics related.
- You lack a sense of humor
Though graphically outdated, this is still a very fun game.

In The Bug Butcher you take on a role of Harry, a intergalactical mercenary bug exterminator who has been given a task on planet Zoit to deal with an bug infestation in a research compound. You must clear the research lab of bugs in order to keep the scientists working there safe.
Graphic design and visuals could be defined as grose and cute at the same time. All enemies you encounter are unique in terms of how they look and what they do, wrapped up in a cartoonish colorful look.
Before long you are freezing, bursting, frying and lasering hordes of strange-looking alien bug-beasts, and it feels so damn satisfying. Gameplay evolves around a static and unchanging environment where enemies dodge, crawl, fly, smash, bounce and even give birth to smaller versions of themselves.
As you progress through the levels you will acquire more powerful weapons, upgrades and power-ups. You will also collect coins from bugs you slaughtered in order to upgrade your stats and equipment.
Soundtrack is absolutely amazing and I wouldn’t be surprised if one day we get a soundtrack edition of the game.
The Bug Butcher is a fine example of a old-school style of gameplay with a lot of fun-factor involved. Although it lacks some verticality The Bug Butcher will make you spend hours on end progressing through the well designed and easy to look at lab slaughtering relentless hords of interesting and unique bug-like aliens.

Yotsubane single-handedly (and single-personedly, this game was made by one guy) out-Caves Cave.

I've bin holding off on reviewing this mod for a long time, mostly cause someone bought it for me and said they wanted a positive review on it because of that. I told him I'd give an honest one, what I truly think of the game, but let me tell you right now, even though I don't recommend the game, doesn't mean its utter garbage.
The creator of this mod had a great idea, the gel gun, completely new testing element, never bin used with this game before. Although on the outset, I thought I was going to have control of not only a gel gun, but a portal gun as well which would have bin awesome, when I found out I wasn't, it was a huge bummer. None the less the idea of gels as the core testing element and virtually having full control of it (with the exception of having to account for gravity as the gel does come out in a straight line, but rather an arc) is a great idea and they should be commended for that. And although it could still use a little work, the idea is there, so for that it gets a 9/10.
It has some pretty good puzzles, but only like 5 in the entire game that I really think are great, the rest are kind of meh, they lack the fullness that the Portal and Portal 2 levels have. Now I'll admit it's not easy creating a puzzle where the main and sometimes only testing element is gel; none the less, most of them just weren't that great. They included auto portals in some tests that you controlled in various ways, but they only contributed slightly to the tests. I will say that some of the ways that they made some areas "non-gelable" were interesting, but it doesn't make up for what the puzzles are lacking in. Overall for puzzles, left much to be desired. 3.5/10 (Oh yeah, and generally, this game can be spedran in about 24 minutes, and exploits and unintended solutions abound, even if you aren't a speedrunner..boooo!)
One word, shoddy. It's like the ppl that made it knew some stuff in hammer, but not that much, and certainly not enough to make a full mod out of (especially that they charge for). One of my friends (who did NOT work on this mod, but should have cause he's a hammer god) even said "We do not talk about the poor mapping practices of Aperture Tag." Of course I laughed, but because its true; if the ppl that made this mod knew half of what they should have bin doing, it might actually look good. The way it is now, very basic and like they wanted to give off the appearance of being hammer guru's, without actually putting the necessary work into it; well guess what guys, you failed. Now I'm not saying none of them knew what they were doing, I know Mevious worked on it (and most of his stuff is really good), as well as at least 2 others, but the rest of them need to go to hammer school, BAD. Overall, the aesthetics probably leave more to be desired than the puzzles, though they are a start, they should not be in a full mod, especially one that isn't free. There is also quite a bit of nodraw (a type of invisible wall) that you can see without too much effort, and its something that shouldn't ever be seen. Exhibit A of what i give it a 2/10 for aesthetics.
Absolutely the best part of this mod! I've listened to the soundtrack on YouTube probably twice as long in hours and minutes then I've played the mod itself (if not more), honestly, I'd pay 7 or maybe even 10 dollars for the music by itself. The game? That's another story. I didn't love all the songs at first, but as I've listened to them they grew on me and now I love them all, so the music alone gets a 10/10. (In-game it's actually not really all that great cause you don't hear it everywhere like in portal, and it's kind of stuck in the background as a result, so use of music gets a 6/10)
It didn't do too well for me, whether i payed for it myself or not, it wasn't worth $7, I wouldn't even say it's worth $5 actually, 2-3 dollars is an ok price to pay for this one. So my suggestion to you after reading this if you are still interested in this mod (you're amazing for reading this far btw :p), wait for a sale that its less than $3, that way you wont feel like you've wasted your money.
It has workshop support, but the coop is the most irritating (it could be good, but its hit and miss to make the gel appear, even when its enabled; also, the person holding the gel gun is placing portals, and the one with the gels is holding nothing; that's just terrible, it also doesn't have a coop story mode), and the sp, well its pretty much the same story as the Portal 2 workshop, but there's not really much they can do about that.
The average of the 4 places i reviewed here is about 7/10, although I'd probably just give it a 4/10 for little details and nitpicks that aren't worth mentioning here that are also lacking in this mod. If you still think you're interested in it after all of this, you either don't know much about those little details, or you don't care, which is completely your deal. But now you know why I don't recommend buying this game, at full price at least.

Nice and quaint little 2D game. The story is pretty generic, but the attention to detail is great. Lots of secrets hidden all over the place (Also, did I mention, "more secrets?" because there are MORE than lots of secrets hidden away that are great to discover). The music sounds nice, but I personally wouldn't listen to it very long, as it goes from nice to being slightly annoying after hearing it for over two hours straight. The graphics, though extremely simplistic, look great, and remind me of the GBA versions of Pokemans. I like the way the social interactions work in-game, and how so many of the characters are interconnected in different ways to each other. The gameplay mechanics (and controls), though slightly unorthodox, are great to use with a little practice. My only real complaint is the multiplayer (co-op if you're wondering, though friendly fire is possible). Apart from being able to help out in firefights, "Player 2" has a lot less ability to do stuff than player one. Player 2 can't open dialogues, and nor can he/she go very far from player one (They need to be in the same region, and only player one can move the camera to different places). Besides Player 2's inability to do anything of great use, however, this is a great play for anybody who's even remotely human. If you're the sort of person who'd spend ten dollars on a game like goat simulator for two hours of fun, $15 is well worth paying for for a few playthroughs of Westerado: DB.

Everything about this game is terribly inconsistent. From the dialogue and cutscenes to the gameplay elements, everything finds a way to make you wonder "why?". One moment Tails is convincing Sonic that they need to work together with Eggman. The next, Tails is complaining that Sonic agreed to work with Eggman. One moment water is an instant death pit, and the next it will only cause you to lose your rings, but then later it's required for progressing through the stage. Inconsistent. Plus, the controls and physics are very unintuitive.
Positives: There were a few lines of dialogue that actually got me to laugh. Most of them came from Eggman.
Negatives: I had about fifteen minutes of total fun through my approximately 6 hour first playthrough.
I rate this game a 4/10, but the WiiU version would get a 6/10 because it has the Hyrule and Yoshi Story DLC stages in it, which are actually more fun than the "real" game. +3 for adding fun to the game, -1 for making it DLC.
This is a game which is completely lacking in fun but somehow manages to avoid being boring or terrible. This is not a bad game, it is not a boring game, it definitely isn't what most people would consider a Sonic game: it's just a game.

Sonic Lost World is... a very confused game. I can absolutely see how it would be divisive and I can't say I think it's great, but there's still a lot to like.
The core mechanics are pretty cool, the parkour elements by themselves can lead to interesting platforming... when the game decides to take advantage of them, which is rare. There's only one really extensive parkour segment in the entire game, in Silent Forest Zone 3, and only if you want a red ring. Beyond that the most intense thing you ever do with the parkour is a few basic wall run things which doesn't amount to a lot in the end. And the mechanics can be a touch buggy anyways, so maybe that's why they didn't do more, but yeah. A bit of wasted potential there. But I mean, the stuff we do get is cool.
The homing attack is... a bit less cool, it's a bit weird in this game, allowing multiple lock-ons to multiple enemies or even a single enemy, the former of which is rarely taken advantage of, the later of which demolishes any and all boss fights with ease. The spindash in this game is great though, you can just dash infinitely. It's kind of like the boost of other modern sonic games, except no meter, and not as fast (this is a GOOD thing by the way, the speed in this game is far more playable and allows for actual, y'know, platforming). I don't really know why the game decided to have a run button since aside from a few ice levels there's literally no reason to ever let go of it but eh whatever.
But then the rest of the game... fails to take advantage of its mechanics a lot. A lot of the level design is not designed with any kind of flow in mind, speedruns of this game often look weird and clunky just because of poor enemy placement or awkward level terrain with no good way of traversing it, at least in the 2D sections. The 3D sections are generally a lot better but there are moments where they don't feel particularly good either. And then you have to deal with somewhere around 30-40% of the levels being weird diversions from platforming. The first world is pretty good about keeping focused but it starts falling apart in the second world; there's an auto-runner level (which is, okay enough) and an AUTOSCROLLER of all possible things. World 3 has a level where you mostly spend all your time guiding fruits around (not quite as bad as that one Gelato Beach mission in SMS but still) and another level where you're just grinding rails the whole time (again, okay enough, and with a great soundtrack). World 4 really crashes and burns hard, with the infamous snowball level and an out-of-place and clunky casino level. World 5 mostly gets back on track again with straight platforming, then World 6 comes and kills that momentum again with the blandest possible sky chase level. World 7 has two whole stages dedicated entirely to boss fights and another stage that's another rail grinding stage (and a much more poorly designed one, let's be honest). And the hidden world is just dumb unused gimmick concepts as far as I can tell, none of them are interesting or fun at all.
I actually am pretty alright with the story in this game. It's full of cliches but the stakes are solid, the humor is there, it's a bit cheesy but I'd expect that from a Sonic game, and it's ultimately inconsequential and a small part of the game as a whole, so y'know whatever. The game looks pretty dang good too, a nice cartoony style where a lot of the environments just pop well, though at the same time some levels can look really blocky. It's... a weird style but I don't mind it, though yes, it is very Mario Galaxy-esque. I definitely prefer the visual style of other sonic games where the worlds feel like actual -places- but I don't mind this style either.
The game itself is decently challenging for a Sonic game, though far from the hardest, and the game feels like it showers you with lives, I never game overed once. There's 28 main stages, 2 bonus stages, 1 free DLC stage, and 4 hidden stages, so there's an okay amount of content for the price, plus 5 red rings to collect in every main stage, time trials for each stage (which I did not fully complete; Frozen Factory 2 can screw off and I just didn't feel like tackling the monolithic time trial on Lava Mountain 3), and 100 missions to complete... which are mostly dumb checking-off-bullet-point style things, they don't add a ton to the game and the items you get as a reward are mostly useless if you ask me, but whatever.
I'd say get this if you're really craving more Sonic, or something a bit different for the series, though absolutely flawed. Not for full price mind you, $15 at most is what I'd recommend, it's not even a $30 game if you ask me, but what do I know. It's alright. A high kind of meh game, one that could've been so much better with a better sense of direction and less arbitrary/unfun gimmick stuff.

A nice Lucasfilm adventure game from the golden ages of point-n-click. Somehow I missed this one and when I picked it up in a pack I thought I'd give it a try.
While not as polished and slick as the Monkey Island series, this game still has a lot going for it. The humor is snarky, the pixel art is on-point, and the voice actors are pretty decent as well. The game is a pretty decent length for an old-school adventure game too, which is nice for those folks who want to get their money's worth in play time.
The only problem I had was with the puzzles. Some felt intuative and satisfying, but too many were either obscure  guessing-games, irritating pixel hunts, or chore-like grocery lists. There were too many times that I was left trekking accross multiple environments aimlessly hoping to find the key to progressing, only to resort to a guide because I can't be bothered to click over every inch of ground. By the end of the game I was flipping over to the guide regularly because I just wanted to get through the puzzles to find out what happens in the story.
TL;DR: I found the story enjoyable, but the puzzles less-so. Worth a buy though if you love classic point-n-click.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I've over 400 hours of playing this game so decided it's about time to write this review. You'll see that I never recommended this game, but why?
Once you start playing the game, you're instantly bombarded with icons all over the place. It's quite an overwhelming experience. Thankfully that eventually subsides the more you start to play. It's a beautiful game to play and you don't really need a high tech machine to be able to play the game. However, what you do need is time and ALOT of time at that.
There are two kinds of player the alpha clone and the omega clone. This resorts to those who don't pay to play the game and those who do. The alpha clone is vatly and I mean vastly restricted to the number of ships he or she can use, the number of skills and equipment. Skill training is all about time and omega clones train their skills twice as fast.
In order to pay to play you need to purchase PLEX. You can buy it online for around £16 a month for 500 PLEX. You will be given a discount if you buy more than one month at a time.
You can however buy PLEX with the ingame currency of ISK (Inter Stellar Kredits) and 1 PLEX roughly goes for around 3million ISK. Therefore you'll need to accumulate 1.5billion ISK to pay for a month. This, can, be done through salvaging and hacking data and relic sites, of course with much more risk involved.
So why don't I recommend the game? Well, simply because it's another life inside the computer. You need to spend a long time, just to do simple storyline missions which get incredibly tedious and boring after a while. There's also the added factor that outside of high security space you're dead meat, more so if you're an Alpha. And this is where you have to go to make your ISK to pay for PLEX. Plexing your account is really the only way to play this game. Even in a cruiser, as an ALPHA clone you'll be easily destroyed by an OMEGA frigate (the lowest class of ship in the game), due to them having far superior weaponry to you.
But probably the main reason I stopped is I got bored. Yup. The game still runs when it's off, meaning you can train all skills offline, but really, I've no desire to go back to playing it. I've got about 350k ISK saved up but not really any desire to play it. The thought of going into Nul Sec (no security space) and getting blasted to pieces by a gang of Omegas just doesn't appeal. The want to go into wormhole space (again Null Sec) and have to do long, boring scans of the area to find relic and data sites to hack, simply has lost it's appeal as well, even more so when there's a high chance you'll fly into a site to find it guarded by awakened sleepers who'll kill you in 2 hits and thus, you losing everything that you've collected before hand, which in one instance, for me, was about 150million worth of saleable goods. And then there's getting out of wormhole space and making it to a station without being killed and looted by another player.
I just think that there are far better, far more rewarding MMO's to play out there that have a far better community and more fun in the missions available. Lord of the Rings Online, Guild Wars 2, Black Desert Online, DOTA, Conan Unchained even are far more rewarding in my opinion than Eve.
It's just an opinion and everyone has them, but I don't recommend it. I may go back to it, that's for sure, but only for a glimpse. Would rather play other MMO's really.

Undenialbly one of the best games I have played in the past few years after its release.
GunPoint is a 2D stealth action and puzzle game, which forces you to adapt to each induvidual level that it throws at you, you can also say it is hardcore in a way, as it only takes one hit for you to get killed by a security guard. The story, from my perspective anyway is cool. You play as Richard Conway, a freelance spy who is equipped with a special pair of trousers which allow him to jump at great lengths and to places where no person without them can go. Thats all i'll go for at the moment but some of the major plot points are seen in the early stages of the game. But here are some of the good things about the game.
- Allows you to do any level the way you want to.
- The soundtrack is really good, giving you that sense that you are playing a Noire-type of game
- The Sneaky sections of the game are well done for a 2D oriented game.
- It is also hardcore, meaning that you die in one hit from a gunshot, similar to the system in hotline miami.
- The crosslink upgrade allows you to become a true hacker.
- And finally the game has a lot of strategy behind the game, meaning that ou have to use your brain to figure out the best possible way to complete your objective.
There are some Hicups i the game though that I would address;
-The game is locked at 60 frames per second, meaning that your beast of a PC won't be able to boost out over 9000 frames per second on this game.
-Some of the deaths of this game are kinda cheap, but thats probably just me.
-And a few game setup issues (for me anyways) prevented the game from starting up.
Overall score = 9.0/10 - Even though the game has a few negatives surrounding it, the positives far outweigh them, and its only for £6.00. for a far complete game that has a good chance of a sequel coming out in the future.

So here are my thoughts on Citizens of Earth so far. Destructoid was right, but I don't agree with their final score. You level up fairly quickly and with the exception of certain optional boss fights, the game never really feels like it throws you any major challenges unless you increase the difficulty.  However, I chalk this up to wanting to target a more casual audience, so that's not necessarily a bad thing
It also means you can fly through the game quickly if you want to or increase the difficulty for a tougher, more oldschool challenge. There really doesn't seem to be much of a penalty for death either.  They don't allow people outside the party to level up unless you enroll them in school, which costs money. Still an interesting option as I don't really use the money for much of anything else so far (you get a fairly steady amount of items through battle alone).
However, this goes back to does a game have to be hard in order to be fun? No. No it doesn't. CoE is funny, cheesy, and silly all in one. There are a lot of groanable one liners, but ultimately it hits the mark in terms of weird and comedic values.  At the end of the day, if you liked Earthbound, you will like this title. Just don't expect it to actually BE Earthbound.

OK, listen up: Gunpoint. It's a fantastic ♥♥♥♥ing game.
The style (8bit) and music are both very IN right now, 'specially with the Hipster crowd, and that kinda puts me off, but the concept and genre (cyberpunk/noir) very much caught my attention.
Well, the outcome of this impulse purchase was a very excellent gaming experience in a funny, film noir, cyberpunk setting.
The story is really very good, a nice little mystery that keeps you wanting to move forward. It was very fitting for both the Cyberpunk and Film Noir aspects the game had adopted.
The levelling system found in many games is represented here by physical Cybernetic Augmentations and Equipment, allowing you access to new abilities.
The game has a massive hard-on for stealth, which is definitely a point in it's favour, and the designers are loathe to force you into a "shoot your way through the level" kind of scenario, especially when you're as squishy as you are.
The characters are kinda cool, though there's not much scope to get to know them as they're sort of remote, contacting you through a messaging service, which is fine and is actually a trope of these sorts of novels/films/RPGs.
The game also includes a Map Editor, for those of us who like to tinker around, and it's class to see the Dev's include these kinds of facilities to us. The Editor is VERY easy to use.
Play this game, when you're sick of shooting non-descript middle easterns or russians in your Yank Flag Wank Simulators, and see the awesomeness that can be achieved for a fraction of the cost and time used to make AAA games.

Gonna keep this short-ish since Xenoverse 2 is coming soon, so this game is gonna be somewhat irrelevant after that I imagine.
But let's just put it this way: I have 180 hours in this game. I love it. I also hate it, but I mostly love it.
The fighting is fun. In one way, all the characters are very samey. You have fast attacks and heavy attacks, but it hardly matters which ones you use, and you have basic ki blasts which are only kinda useful and don't do much damage. However, it's the supers and ultimates which define your play style.
Depending on the skills equipped to a character, you can make some fairly unique and differing play styles.
So, to boil this down, I'm just going to say that I really like this game, and that if you're a fan of Dragon Ball Z you'll probably enjoy it. I'll list some negatives and then let you decide if you should buy it or not after that:
1. Grinding and RNG. You can create your own character (which is awesome) but you must go through things called Parallel QUests in order to gain experience to level up (boost your stats) and to earn a majority of the clothing and skill options. Often, a single mission can have THREE layers of RNG (random number generation) to get through to see if you'll get the skill or item you want. Some of these missions are also kinda long, but never longer than 15 minutes (if it passes 15 minutes you lose due to running out of time anyway...) Replaying these missions until I got everything is about 70% of the reason I have nearly 200 hours in this game. (I suppose it says something either about me or about how fun the game is that I was willing to put in all that time... I think it's mostly me unfortunately...)
2. Multiplayer is dead. Few to no people left playing the PvP stuff, and not too many doing coop either. Also, multiplayer has some nasty lag. More so than a lot of other mutliplayer games in my experience. Sometimes it's bareable or even not too noticeable, oethr times it actually breaks the game entirely.
3. Horrible lip syncing. I think the characters were only animated for the japanese voice acting. It's a little funny actually... but a bit annoying as well.
4. Voice acting is inconsistent. Some people, like the main villain, have great voice acting (really good, honestly in my opinion). Unfortunately others, Goku for example, have some pretty... average at best voice acting. Just seems really awkward at times. Your personal character only has a few voice lines, and that's only for certain attack names in battle. You can hear your character shout "KAMEHAMEHAA!" but they don't speak (audibly) in cutscenes. The few times they "talk" it's totally silent with some hand gestures... which is a little weird. Understandable I suppose, but weird since everyone else has a voice.
5. Some pointless customization limits. 99% of clothing will bost/lower certain stats. THis means that if you REALLY want goku's clothes, but are using the stats it lowers, you're either out of luck or will have to make some sacrifices to your power. Also, only a few original clothing items can be recolored. All the character outfits (Goku's, Vegeta's, Buu's, etc.) have one set color pallete... which means mixing and matching can have some really awful color coordination that can't be fixed.
6. The AI is god awful. Just absolute trash. I've seen my allies square off against an enemy, and they'd jsut sort of hover in a circle staring each other down instead of fighting. Your allies are often a distraction at best, but can actually make your job harder at the worst. THe only good thing is that your allies highest priority (as long as they're ones that you picked to help you on a PQ) is to revive you if you get KO'd. They're very reliable for that... and nothing else. Only on some missions will the enemy be a challenge, but that difficulty is usually artificial in one of two ways. 1: They have "super armor" which makes them immune to flinching upon being hit, or, 2: they outnumber you and will just gang up on you and keep you from fighting back until you find some breathing room... and then your only real option is to fire back with as many big blasts as you can muster.
Once you get some skill with the game and/or a powerful character, a normal 1v1 will probably be child's play.
I just wish my allies would stop shooting ki blasts at the enemy and making my skills miss due to some annoying invincibility frames...
7. A few characters are missing that would have been nice to see. Also SSJ4 Vegeta is unobtainable as he was a pre-order exclusive...
So, in conclusion, why is this game fun? Because it's some f***ing fantastic fan-service. It's pretty, it mostly plays well, and you feel like you're IN Dragon Ball Z and GT. Seeing your character be thanked by Goku and stand beside the Z Warriors is really something special. Having someone say "With then, I think we really stand a chance" and knowing that they're talking about YOU is really cool.
The story is refreshing, the comedy is there, and it's just a fun ride. Growing your first character from a weakling just barely on par with Raditz to then challenging Majin Buu and other godlike beings is a great experience the first time around... and probably a second or third time so you can watch your character in the cutscenes with all the cool gear you've collected through later PQs.
. . . and if you're still transformed when a cut-scene starts, you'll appear transformed during most cutscenes. . . it's a nice touch.
It might not be the best DBZ "fighting" game, but it's certainly one of the best "DBZ" games in general if you know what I mean.

I think it's fair to say that Sonic reviews have a problem.  It's not completely unearned, with outings like '06 and Boom, but it seems like there are wildly inconsistent expectations cited as explanation of disappointment. The boost games? " Boost to win. Too easy."  Mania and Generations?  "Good, but relies too much on nostalgia" Pretty much every 3D Sonic? "Scripted spectacle."  Nostalgia is dismissed, innovation is derided. Lost World never had a chance.
Duke Ellington famously said  “If it sounds good, it IS good.” I'd adapt this for games to read "if it's fun. it's good".  So is Lost World fun?  My answer is yes.
Will it play like any other Sonic game? Nope.  It lacks the boost of recent games, but the payoff is greater control, which is necessary with the planetoids format. It introduces the challenging to learn but so rewarding parkour mechanic. It takes some learning, but is fantastic once you get it.  It relies more on precision than running through countless enemies which in many ways makes it one of the 3D games that comes closer to the original outings than most others. Really.
The villains, like the rest of the world, are beautifully designed, colorful, and cartoony. Many will complain that they’re too one dimensional. I’d counter that they lack the misplaced pretension of other outings. . Others will say that the story is too much of nothing. I’d counter that simplicity is a virtue and what it lacks in over the top ‘06 nonsense is made up for excellent character work. I can’t think of any other Sonic that explores the dynamics between characters better. Tails, rather than being the starry eyed fanboy we usually see, becomes irritated with Sonic.  Sonic, likewise, shows impatience with Tails until in one moment he’s jolted from taking his sidekick for granted. Eggbotnik shows more sides than ‘cackling villain’, with Orbot and Cubebot adding deflating hilarity. Sonic sassing the enemies gives some genuinely delightful humor, making it perhaps the first Sonic game that makes me eager for interstage cutscenes.  I think when people say the story is lacking in this game, they're referring to the plot. The plot is indeed a wee bit generic. But "plot" and "story" have different meanings, and the story here is in the interacrtions between characters. These interactions are far more fully developed than I've seen in other games. Granted, that's a low bar to clear, but I found it welcome.
The worlds are gorgeous, the gameplay is, yes, fun, and the presentation is delightful. This game is a gem that will be ultimately be rediscovered and appreciated in the future once the fog of Sonic Cycle madness clears.  Give it a chance, and you might just adore it too.

This is a game about inflicting horrible situations on yourself, and using the meager resources from those crises to balance out the damage. It's a game where nucular armageddon is a viable winning strategy, as long as you trick your opponent into burning the world first. It embodies Cold War fears and all the best propaganda has to offer.
Some people resent how much luck has to do with winning this game, but that's ultimately only a small part of the strategy. Rolling for coups and realignments requires careful planning and well-placed risks, and luck can be overcome by persistence and hand management.
Edit (9/25/2017): While I still recommend the game, I want to write in again to express my confusion over how the AI handles DEFCON and European Control. Simply put, the AI can't respond to these strategies very well. About a third of my wins against the AI are to these strategies, almost all unforced errors and bizzare, suicidal plays by the AI.

Westerado: Double Barreled is a top down, open world shooter where you play as a man who (light spoiler)
in this western world. The thing I love about this game is its open world nature, and your ability to kill anyone at any point. This ads a lot of variety to an already varied world with lots of things to do. You can do bounty quests, kill random people for money, and even play a few(or many) hands of poker. The world is so varied, and has a vast array of side quests. It reminds me of something like Morrowind, where you can kill any character at any time and it can impact your story. To show an example of some variety, I'm going to tell part of my adventure in the next paragraph. It will contain some spoilers, jump ahead to the next paragraph if you wish to avoid them
I was doing some side quests to try and find more information about my killer. Your killer is randomized, which is one of the cool things about this game. You can't just memorize the details of the killer and do it every time, it will be different each time. Anyway, I'm told by the banker to find the ranchers and get the money he needs to pay off the Oil Tycoon man. So I go to each of them, and I end up slaughtering all of the ranchers. I had no idea what this would do. There are several quests that ask you to get help from the ranchers, or even recruit them. I had to skip these parts, or simply fail the quest because they were already dead. I decided that this was all the Oil Tycoon mans fault, so I decided to pay him a visit after acquiring a rifle. which is in my opinion the best weapon in the game(that I've found). I slaughter his men and him as well, and steal his stash of money. Feeling well rewarded, I return to the bank to find the Bank owner now wants nothing to do with me, I think because I killed the ranchers. This would have went very differently depending on my choices.
Based on that story, you can see how many different paths you can take. If you skipped it based on spoilers, just trust me, it is a world were your choice matters. Another great element is the ability to pull out your gun in the middle of any conversation, making dialogue very interesting. Westerado is a great game for those on a budget looking for an open world that rivals any AAA game.
Pros:
-Strongly woven together open world
-Multiple side quests and other things to do
-Choices with NPC's matter
-Several different hats with different functions
-Optional fast travel(works similar to Morrowind)
-Guns for different situations
-Variety in the environment
-Randomized bounty hunter missions
Cons:
-Main story is very short if you find your killer quickly enough
-Some bugs, One of them required me to quit and restart from an earlier autosave
-Pixel graphics can occasionally(not often) make it hard to see your bounty target.

To me, Sonic Lost World has the feel of a Mario game more than a Sonic game at times. Those that are used to the Sonic controls will have to get used to Sonic having a run button. There’s also the fact that each world is broken up into four stages, just like SMB1. However, Sonic has his classic speed and many of the moves he’s rocked in previous games, and that’s in addition to him having parkour in his skill set, which actually fits Sonic’s character. There is a little bit of a learning curve regarding the game’s control scheme and interacting with the levels themselves, but it’s not a difficult game overall once overcoming that. Most of the bosses are fairly easy to defeat, with the exception of one later in the game that relies on fake difficulty, one of my pet peeves, and frustrated to try and defeat it.
While the story overall isn’t as great as Colors and Generations before it, there’s still the great one liners from the characters that made me laugh, even as I kept losing over and over.
There's also a small glitch you might encounter at first where the framerate goes really slow, but there's an easy fix you can find on the forums if it occurs.
Overall, the game is decent, but I wouldn’t get it at full price.

The Dig is one of Lucasarts' less known and less succesful point and click adventure games. Unlike most of their comedic fare, this one's played entirely straight; a sci-fi story of exploration and solving puzzles. The interface is very simple, no "use, look, pick up, etc" commands, just a simple choice between interacting or examining. Despite that, it can be pretty challenging at times and even have you stumped for a good while.
Good: fantastic music, seasoned voice actors (Robert Patrick, Steven Blum), nicely painted backgrounds, challenging puzzles, good gameplay length and some lovely animated cutscenes.
Bad: at times frustrating, dialogue can be kind of stilted and will endlessly repeat as you try to solve puzzles, simple interface makes for less creative adventure gaming, low res sprites, and two or three puzzles that will really send you runing for gamefaqs.
Overall: still a great classic. Avoid a walkthrough as much as you can and you'll definitely enjoy the experience!
