Sonic Lost World scraps the formula we've had for the past few games. No more fast-paced boosting and a new take on level design.
Not necessarily a bad thing, but unfortunately this game is a heavily mixed bag. There are times when its a ton of fun.. and other times when its a huge disappointment. Sonic Lost World lacks any form of consistency and even polish. I'll still give it a positive rating because there is SOME good in it that I did enjoy, but take it with a grain of salt.
Sonic Lost World slows down the speed a bit. I actually like this change. Sonic can still get fast times, but he can no longer boost and there's even a run button. As much as I love the boost gameplay, its fun going back to an older style that is more focused on platforming. The physics, however, are pretty bad. Turning causes you to lose so much speed and it just feels bad. The spindash has hardly no power to it and the platforming can be clunky. The 2d sections have a very sluggish feel to them, as if Sonic doesn't have quite enough speed for his jumps. The 3d portions of the game are pretty fun nonetheless and the new parkour system is rather enjoyable, but not without its flaws. Grinding does make a return, but only in two stages and both of those stages only consist of grinding.
The only real problem with Sonic Lost World is its level design. There are some fun levels in this game.. there really are, but they aren't the majority. There's a handful of 3d stages with solid level design. Slopes, hills, some automation, and even multiple paths. I really enjoy playing these levels and if every level in the game was like this, this could have been one of my favorite Sonic games. Unfortunately these levels are only the first act of each zone and even then - they often have a tedious cloud jumping section or a part where you have to fight a set number of enemies. Forced gimmicks to make the levels longer.. Speaking of gimmicks, that's something Sonic Lost World relies on. There are other 3d levels and sections, but they're usually much more linear and don't have very good level design or rely on an obnoxious gimmick. A lot of the levels will be 2d and as mentioned above, the 2d gameplay just isn't fun at all this time around plus the level design isn't very good either. In one level you control a giant snowball the entire time. In another, all you do is push fruit around into holes. There's a couple others where you're floating through the sky. The list goes on much longer, but I'll stop there.
Basically, Sonic Lost World has a few awesome levels and a ton of truly terrible ones. The only levels worth replaying in this game are the first acts of every zone (minus the last) and a few 3rd acts can be fun. Playing the 2nd and 4th levels is also a bit of a pain because you always have to fight the boss at the end, no matter how many times you clear it. Its really too bad. If this game consisted of nothing but levels like the ones mentioned then it would be really good.
Another thing to note is Sonic Lost world does have a gravity gimmick. It was often compared to Super Mario Galaxy, though this gravity mechanic was used back in SA2 long before that game. It actually didn't feel anything like Mario Galaxy and reminded me more of Sonic Xtreme. While I wouldn't say it was necessary, I did kind of enjoy it at times. The wisps also return and are completely unnecessary. They just slow the game down and felt kind of forced.
All in all, Sonic Lost World has some really fun moments but the forced gimmicks and simply bad level deisgn make the rest of the game a total drag. Don't even get me started on the bonus world stages.
Sonic games have always had incredible soundtracks. Sonic Lost World.. completely fails there. This game might have the worst music of any Sonic game so far. Its not to say the compositions are truly terrible. They just are very cheesy and forgettable. There's only one musical composition that I enjoyed in this game. Its also the only one I can remember other than the main theme.
The visuals are a massive step back from Generations and Unleashed. It looks decent I guess and the grass is okay, but its a huge graphical downgrade from what we were used to. I'm guessing this is purely because it was originally a Wii U release and Nintendo consoles are usually weak.
I will say the few CGI cutscenes looked amazing though.
The story is terrible. Sonic 3&K had a better story. Not joking. Its just bad.
This port is okay. I remember having some FPS drops on my old graphics card so it may not be as optimized as Generations, but for the most part it runs without any problems. No crashes or major glitches.
There are some mods for PCs. Some levels, characters, the usual stuff. Nothing too essential or game-changing though.
As said before, Sonic Lost World is really a mixed bag.
I love playing through some of the first acts, but the majority of levels are terribly designed. The music and physics don't help the presentation either.
All in all, I still enjoyed playing through it and liked the unique style it had. However, I don't really recommend this game to anyone but hardcore Sonic fans.
If you're a new to the series, try Sonic Generations instead. That game is incredible.
If you really love Sonic though, you can probably get a little fun out of it so give it a go in that case. Just wait for a sale.

Gunpoint is a really good game.  The premise is that you happen to be present in a building after-hours when a murder occurs, but are not guilty.  Nonetheless, you are likely to be framed for it due to security camera footage.  Initially, you are to erase that footage, but that in turn makes others more suspect, and this leads to a serious of choices, sometimes morally ambiguous, about what to do next.  All the way through, you are able to make use of an increasing amount of spy gear to break into and escape from buildings.
The gameplay itself is solid.  I don't consider myself a fan of puzzle games (one of the top tags for this game), but while I can see how it is classified as such, it isn't frustrating games like many older puzzle games with just one solution can be.  There are multiple ways through each level, and they're challenging enough to make you think, but not so much that you quit in frustration or have to look up guides online to keep going.
The writing, though in small quantities, is also good.  The way people behave and interact seems plausible, and incomplete knowledge of others' motives is used well to keep decisions interesting.
From a technical standpoint, I happened to be playing the game on Linux (Mint), and the game itself worked very well.  There were some Steam-integration issues (particularly, the Steam overlay froze my system when I tried to close it, and achivements didn't fire), but the game itself ran without issue.  I would assume it would run as well on Windows, but have thus far only played the demo on Windows.  You should give the demo a try yourself; if you like it, you'll like the full game, too.

Prototype 2 has a completely different playstyle as compared to 1 In terms of the ability tree. Unlike 1, P2 is much less confusing with less item on the power wheel and more focused on one-butten skills rather than P1's massive array of combo. However there's still cons when you actually spends time on this game. One such con would be equipping two ability for both mouse buttons. Prototype 2 does not have much of a combo and is more on the charged 1-hit to take out non-human targets. So having a second mouse button is next to useless if you're a power mixer. Right, even if you DO managed to fork out a combo, you've probably fail 3 in a 4 chance because the evolved were too fast or brawlers cannot be stunned during their onslaught. Last but not the least, removal of human disguise ability. Why!? D: the air strike was so fun, I know Heller wasn't as sly as Mercer so why did the air strike have to go with Patsy? T_T
Gone with the con, it's getting long but the pro arrives! Heller's whipfist is an automatic field sweeping tool that is easy to use as compared to P1, although range is not as long. His's hammerfist doesn't have the rocket launch but makes up for it by having the stun ability to stun almost everything. Controls were much better whe gliding is much easier and vehicles were much better than before. There's much more pros but it's best to find them yourself as you enjoy the game.
Additional details of the recommendation: I've recommended the game not only because of the story, but other features such as tearing off vehicle's secondary weapons and the side stories from those trucks. If you so happen to also consider getting the radnet pack, those are also a fun add-on to play with as it offers additional abilities that can assist you in the story further, or to let you screw up the game entirely once you're done.

Gamers know whether a game has good replay value within the first 10 minutes of playing, by that time if the mechanics of a game don't capture your imagination, you can forget replay value. I'm a very positive person and I'd like to start by saying that if there ever was a Prototype 3, I would play it and give the series another chance to redeem itself, so dear develompent team working on Prototype 3 and development team who produced Prototype 2; please review some notes below in regards to why Prototype 2 sucked, and what was good about it.
-The reason Prototype 2 sucked:
The mechanics and controls were nowhere near as fluid as the first installment of the game(starting out), nor did they emulate the controls of the first game very well. The game does not feel as 'quick paced' as the first. What I mean by this is that even turning around is too slow, running up buildings I feel like some fat guy with a corn cob shoved up his butt, trying to race to the nearest toilet, casually. Gamers need that 'parkour' feel that the first game had without the fat guy running to the toilet feel the second game has. Your gamers want to feel like ninjas, Super Hero Ninja Samurai Monks(title in development) running through the city, thumping into people and body checking them just to see them slowly stand up and act like nothing happened.
The camera controls felt a little laggy for default, and sometimes did't work at all when trying to get an outward view while running up a building, it was very frustrating trying to fight the first 'Pink Hulk guy'when you changed the dodging mechanics that the first game had. I mean, are you guys even gamers? You do realize that you DON'T need to change essential game functions like that to create a great sequel? Anyway, besides the controls there were several other problems with the game that was basically annoying to sit through and act like I care:
The story was way too linear, and the intro/tutorial was too long, and should have had an obvious 'skip' option for the experienced Prototype One players, and if there was an option to skip the nearly hour to two hour long intro tutorial garbage, I couldn't find it. Thats one thing top gaming companies have a problem with, turning videogames into an interactive movie that you have to sit through, thats one thing that destroyed my joy for the Assasins Creed titles. I'm sorry I'm the type of gamer that needs to hear my objectives and story while I move around and goof off, its more emmersive (its one gameplay feature that Doom 3 and half-life did very well, and I am hoping to play the latest iteration of these games also.)
Character didn't feel as powerful when landing, climbing and picking up objects. There were much bigger and more pronounced textures and effects in the first Prototype when landing and running up buildings(the cracks on the walls and holes in the ground left from contact with his powerful limbs.) This was a particularly satisfying touch to the first game, makes you feel like you can break through anything(without leaving the destruction around for too long.)
The way levelling your character worked: I prefer the Evolution Points method, seeing that you have hundreds of thousands of 'something' on the HUD when your playing as a super hero, and then spending it all, has its appeal. It has a certain appeal in a lot of games actually, makes you feel more accomplished.
Did I mention that the intro tutorial was TOO long, limited, and drawn out??
What Prototype 2 did right: Explosions worked pretty well, but thats one feature that is easy to make look good.
The boost wave effect when you hold down the run button was a nice touch, but somehow wasn't the right kind of emphasis on his actual speed in the intro.
The overall textural appearance of the wolverine ability was much nicer and cleaner, and the fighting style for that super power wasn't bad either.
The new enemy types were a great and welcome addition, namely birds and other land creatures. Its nice when game sequals give you a fresh variety of enemy types to combat.
I liked the effect of the hunting ability, the radar sense was pretty cool, but I think it would have been better if the minimap was involved in the hunting ability, then you wouldn't have to be required to get to a really high building just to seek out targets. Gamers like the freedom of choosing how they execute a search, as long as the enemy/target general location is easily determined.
Like I said, I really hope for a Prototype 3, And don't give me this 'theres too many super hero games out there' crap, the super hero genre is alive and you have a whole class of gamers waiting to play the newest original title. By original I mean, NOT a Disney/Marvel mashup,but a game like Prototype with its unique querks and storyline.

A love letter in many ways to classic Western movies and classic games, Westerado: Double Barreled starts with a familiar premise: your family has (spoilers for the first 30 seconds of the game) been murdered. Your ranch has been burned down. With nothing but the hat on your head, the shirt on your back, and the revolver in your holster, you set out on a quest for vengeance.
And then the game basically turns you loose on a sandbox Western action-RPG and lets you do whatever the hell you want.  Sure, you're supposed to find your family's killer and enact your revenge, but let's be honest: there's a lot more to do in Westerado, and you'd be foolish to simply skip through the main storyline and be done. Most people will probably do the same quests first: helping a concerned wife bring her drunk husband home, clearing out a graveyard of bandits, etc.
The quest design at first seems pretty straightforward, but there's actually a great deal of freedom here. As far as I can tell, literally every single NPC in the game can be killed, which can be a boon during certain quests whose other option for completion is a hefty amount of money. In one notable mid-game quest, a local Indian chief tasks you with freeing buffalo from ranches. I did so with a blend of violence and not-giving-a-damn and wound up finishing with the blood of a few ranchers on my hands but the satisfaction of herds of bison now roaming free.
Upon attempting to finish another quest, however, I learned that this quest was now failed because the woman who gave it to me was angry at me for killing one of the ranchers. It's this inter-connectivity that makes the quests interesting, and as the game goes on the quests get bigger and more important.
In my favorite questline, you're tasked with trying to bring peace between said Indian chief's tribe and a local militia. I don't know how much else I could've done, but let's just say it didn't go well. In my story,

The main questline is unique in one feature, however: for most of the bigger quests, completing them gives you a detail about the murderer. As far as I can tell, the murderer's identity is randomized fully, so it's not the same game for anyone. In mine, I learned that he had a medium-brimmed hat, then learned it was a ten gallon, then that he wore blue, etc. until I had a reasonable picture of him. It's a satisfying way of tying sidequests to main storyline, but it's important to note that you can confront ALMOST ANYONE in the game through dialogue. I think if you got lucky you could confront the murderer right away if you happened to find him.

With all this talk of systems and RPG mechanics, I want to make one thing clear: this package wouldn't work if the core gameplay wasn't top notch. Fortunately for everyone, it is. To fire a shot you have to unholster your gun with a button, then press a button to prime it and the same button again to fire. This methodical, three-step process every time you want to shoot something feels good, and it can lead to stressful moments in firefights with more than one enemy. Reloading is a similar process of hitting the reload button once per bullet, so to fully reload you have to mash R like a madman to put your six shots back in your revolver.
That said, is the combat itself any good? The answer is yes. Westerado's health system boils down to you having up to three hats: each hat is an extra life point. Get shot with no hat, and you die and are returned to a respawn point, half your money gone. The upside of this is that each enemy is the same; shoot an enemy and his hat flies off. At this point, sometimes he'll surrender, but other times he'll keep on firing. Shoot him again to put him in the ground.
Occasionally, one shot will kill an enemy who's wearing a hat, but I couldn't figure out consistency on this: whether it was where I aimed, some sort of critical hit system, or what. Sometimes the hats from dead enemies fall on the ground, and you can quickly pick them up to restore hat-health (to your maximum of three). It's a fun and lethal system that feels close to the likes of Hotline Miami or other fast-paced, everyone-has-low-health games.
Though you start off with only one revolver, eventually you can buy other guns, including a shotgun, dual revolvers, or a rifle. I only purchased the rifle, and it was a great upgrade; though slower-firing, it could pierce through enemies and offered a wider view of areas.
I'm running rapidly out of room, but I'll spare a few sentences for aesthetic and aural notes. The artstyle of the game is a beautiful mix of spritework that doesn't adhere specifically to any sort of artificial old-school hardware limitation; because of this, color abounds and there's a lot of variety. The characters all sport a lo-fi charm, and the animals are both cute and occasionally deadly.
Bodies remain where they've fallen, so it can be fun to walk through a location you've cleared of enemies and look upon their fallen remains as vultures fly in to scavenge their corpses. It sounds morbid, but the cheerful cartoon artstyle doesn't make you feel bad for your enemies as their bones are picked clean.
On the sound front, the music in this game is sublime. Harmonicas carry the main weight here, evoking a Western feel that makes you want to strap on some spurs and spit into a jar. (Editor's Note: Cade does not support spitoon usage and urges people to find other pastimes less harmful) The music changes crazily when it's fighting time, pumping you up to pump lead.
Once the last enemy is killed, a triumphant trill lets you know you've lived one more battle. It's well-done and exciting each time.
Westerado is a fantastic game that blends action and player choice, and I've tried to keep spoilers to a minimum. At one point, I wandered off the map through a tiny, not-really-visible path, and found a crazy area that made me at once intrigued and amused.
The writing in the game, while sparse, is charming and interesting, and keeps you wanting to solve mysteries, get in gunfights, and help out townsfolk. While the normal price and even the sale price is a bit steep, there's nothing like Westerado out there and there appears to be considerable replay value (the randomized murderer, extra player characters with their own motivations, hidden boss fights, etc.).
Though the lo-fi aesthetic may initially appear to be just one of many, the unique touches and captivating gameplay elevates Westerado above the rest in the indie scene. Though the game's length is short (I finished the main story with the first character in roughly two hours), it's well-paced and I didn't do anywhere near everything.
Highly recommended, though perhaps waiting for a sale is the best option; for non-completionists and speedier gamers, you may come away disappointed at the relatively short length.

text:
Sonic Lost World is the definition of a mixed bag. There are some truly great ideas in this game, but there are just as many awful ones, and almost none of these ideas are executed to their full potential. The game feels like a middle-school rehearsal: sure, some of these kids have talent, but can you even hear it over the cacophony? There is simply no focus in Sonic Lost World. One level will take place on a large cylinder with plenty of room to run fast, the next will be all 2D and focus on slow platforming, and the next might be a one-off gimmick that will never be seen again. The rail-grinding mechanic, for example, is introduced for one level and then abandoned for several worlds before being suddenly brought back with an expectation that the player has now mastered the mechanic and can navigate a difficult obstacle course full of instakill hazards using it.
The game attempts to mirror the impressive variety of Mario Galaxy, but fails to realize that variety is worthless if there is no solid foundation from which to build new ideas off of. Sonic Lost World is so scattered that it’s difficult to even determine what the core gameplay even is, and all this variety comes off as a futile attempt to try and hide this fact. The game is so inconsistent that even the speed at which Sonic moves varies depending on the direction he is moving in, or if the game is in the 2D or 3D perspective. Speaking of control, it feels incredibly unnatural. There is no momentum or weight to Sonic: you just push a button and off he goes. Even in Mario games you had to run for a couple seconds before reaching top speed, but not here. It's incredibly awkward, and it sucks out most of the fun that could have been had with the few well-designed levels in this game.
The level design overall leaves something to be desired. Most sections of this game are designed in ways that don’t compliment the control scheme, forcing you to fight the game in order to progress. Many levels in this game are extremely cheap, with unfair deaths caused by poorly-placed hazards and awkward jumps. Many other sections, meanwhile, feel too empty, with a scattered mess of collectibles and obstacles that try and disguise how little substance these levels have. Many other levels rely on a gimmick, like rolling a snowball or free-falling, and these are the worst of all, due to their poor control and bland design. The overall layout of these levels and how the player interacts with it was very poorly thought out, and clearly needed more playtesting. Also, if you value your sanity, never try to get a red star ring. It’s not worth it.
The story is hardly worth talking about. Story in Sonic games is rarely good, but even by Sonic standards this story is putrid. Every character except Eggman is unlikable and the plot introduces and abandons seemingly random elements at will, with no coherency whatsoever. The game gives us a new setting and new characters, but never explains what these things are or where they came from or why they exist: we are simply supposed to go along with it. Speaking of the new characters, the Deadly Six are some of the worst even written for this series. All of them are insulting one-dimensional stereotypes with no depth at all. They were clearly nothing more than a marketing gimmick, with only the bare minimum amount of effort put into their actual personality. The worst part is that they talk to you in several of the game’s levels, meaning that even skipping the cutscenes won’t free you from having to endure their awfully written dialogue.
The presentation, while good overall, is severely lacking compared to most other Sonic games. The game looks nice, but compared to the stunning beauty of Unleashed and Generations, it fails to impress. The art design is also extremely bland, calling to mind the same lack of detail and strict adherence to tropes found in the New Super Mario Bros games. Most other Sonic games, good or bad, at least had some unique and creative environments, but this one feels like it wasn’t even trying. Despite the lack of creativity, the game does look good overall, with smooth animations, clean models and bright colors. The music, thankfully, is great as always. There are some tracks that do just feel like B-List Mario music, but for every uninspired track there is a fantastic one. It’s still one of the weaker soundtracks in the series, but a weak soundtrack by Sonic standards is still superb by any other. The amount of technical polish, like other recent Sonic Team games, is also on-point. I encountered no glitches, visual or mechanical, and the game ran at a smooth 60 FPS for the entire experience. It’s encouraging to see that, along with Unleashed, Colors and Generations, Sonic Team seems to have finally mastered the art of technical polish that eluded them for so long in the past.
Sonic Lost World is a classic case of too many cooks spoiling the broth. There is no one element in Sonic Lost World that is irredeemably awful or offensive, but the fact that all these different elements are shoved into one product with no thought given to how they would work together ruins almost any fun that could be had with the experience. Playing Sonic Lost World was not torturous, but it wasn’t pleasant either, and the overall experience leaves me with the same emptiness and indifference that games like New Super Mario Bros did, except that game at least had good controls and level design. If the game had narrowed its laundry list of ideas down to the few that worked best and focused on polishing them to perfection, it might have been a great game. Instead, it wallows in mediocrity, existing as living proof that if you try to please everyone, you end up pleasing no one.
Score: 5/10

Not the best Sonic game, but far from the worst. But quality trumps quantity here, the wisps are much more user friendly, and while you might miss the tutorials for some mechanics (you have to hit select when the colourful question makr pops up on screen), it does mean that you boot up the game, watch a short cinematic and go. No tutorials, no hand-holding, you watch a movie and run along the totally tubular levels.
Weird complaint, the direction buttons don't actually make Sonic move. It only really affects the 2D sections where D-Pad input is prefereable to Analogue Stick input, but it's a nit to pick and if one is looking for that, there it is.
Otherwise, plenty of mods, plenty of fun to be had, the bosses are pushovers and whether to homing attack or kick enemies isn't very well telegraphed but Lost World is for the most part fun. The infinite spindash trick let's you speed through levels stupidly fast, the parkour is actually a pretty welcome addition even if it is hard to figure out how it works in some places and Sonic moves well and responds to input.
Worth a play if you're a fan, but I'd still recommend playing Generations before this if you've never played a Sonic game.

Sonic Lost world is the exparamental title pushed out after Generations as an answer to the now creativly stale boost mechanic of yore. You can tell they had their hands full with this one, as they try a number of things trying to strike a chord with the ever picky fanbase. It's probably the backlash to this game that lead to Sonic Mania and Sonic Forces.
Lets call a peach by it's name. This game is just a few ticks shy of being a good game. There are so many issues, oversights, and peeves that the game houses that can bog down those of lesser interest. Towering above all that is a mismatch of character and level. Sonic doesn't feel like he should be in these kinds of levels. These are mario levels layed straight so Sonic can run on em. How Sonic handles and plays doesn't quite pair with the wanky levels. The only time that I feel like they lined up was during some of the 2d Sections set in vertical shafts, and that's only because I loved using the parkour system. The game suffers as a whole since your skills are only kind of useful outside of off the road paths that end at the same place.
Sonic handles well, having good speed and reliable offense once you ajust. His Double jump makes horizontal jumps easy to control, if a little stiff since you don't have momentum contorl after you jump without it. It's quite rewarding to make a long jump off a running start.
One of the major problems is how sonic handles. When you make a turn, there's no weight or curve to it. You will make an angle turn and forfit some speed, making wide open areas less enjoyable to snake through. Sonic feels like he has no weight to him, which is a bit sad because they nailed it in Sonic adventure.
This game had loads of potential. Sonic himself is a joy to control, but the levels dampen the experience over all. If you want a taste of what this game should have been, I recomend playing it on its native console the WiiU For the Zelda and Yoshi DLC levels they have. Those are much better made and hallmark what should have been.
TLDR: Sonic is good. Shame the levels aren't.

After playing through several of Telltale's adventure games, as well as the latest Broken Sword, I had worked up a powerful appetite for some old-school point-and-click. I think I had played a demo for Dig waaaaaay back in my youth, and seeing it available on Steam, decided to give it a shot. I'm glad I did.
As far as adventure games go, this is a very solid offering. The graphics do a good job holding up, and most of the visuals are still beautiful. The puzzles can be a bit complex (using alien technology isn't always straightforward), but almost always proceed logically (for a point-and-click). The sci-fi elements aren't particularly deep, but do a good job keeping the story (originally by Steven Spielberg) going. Finally, the dialogue, co-written by Ender's Game author Orson Scott Card, is a bit hokey but has a sort of charm to it.
Overall, people looking for a fun throwback with high production values need look no further.

TWILIGHT STRUGGLE was the number-one-rated board game on boardgamegeek for something like eight years until it was dethroned by Pandemic: Legacy last year. Now it is number 2.
It is a game of Cold War brinksmanship and high strategy for two players or one player vs a pretty decent AI. You take the role of either the United States or the Soviet Union and the game begins in 1945, with the battle lines drawn between the liberal capitalist Western Europe and the Communist Eastern Europe and Asia. The goal is to use world events, coups, and political realignments to shift the governments of a region toward one bloc or the other. Controlling a region nets victory points; earning 20 victory points at any time, or having the most VPs at the end, wins you the game.
If you start Global Thermonuclear War, you lose. But sometimes there are immense temptations to walk right up to the razor's edge. It's a one-of-a-kind experience that puts you right into the ♥♥♥♥ed-up brain of a Cold War strategist, making choices that are completely logical and rational from a game theory point of view but are horrific when you stop to think about what they mean in the real world.
Will you change history? Or will you be buried by it? That's up to you.
The gameplay of the original boardgame is imported basically seamlessly into this adaptation. Like the Sentinels of the Multiverse adaptation, there are a few areas where you can kind of tell this was developed to work on touchscreen devices as well as PC - lots of big buttons and dragging things into highlighted areas - but Twilight Struggle's support for the PC interface feels a little bit more robust. You CAN play cards by dragging them around the screen or you can just click them and then click the menu option for what to do with them.
The interface is polished enough for a small-scale game. It's not bare-bones. There are fun little aesthetic touches, like the tap-tap-tap of Morse code when it comes time to confirm your turn, or audio clips made from famous speeches by Stalin, Truman etc when new turns begin. Eveyrthing seems to work so far.
I haven't tried the multiplayer yet, but the single-player works well. The AI isn't stupid; it's not like playing some kind of cosmic genius expert at the game, but it doesn't do obviously stupid things and it's a great way for beginners to learn the ropes. Also, the developers have apparently committed to constantly refining the AI based on the outcomes of games played out in the real world, so we can expect it to get harder and better as time goes on.

A legendary game, yet one of LucasArts' lesser known pieces due to its somewhat-awkward presentation.  The DIG started as an idea by Steven Spielbeg that he soon abandoned with nowhere to take it, handing it over to his friend George Lucas' studio to make something out of it.
What they created was something magical.  An odyssey into space and the man's determination to survive and explore.
Playing as the aging astronaut Commander Boston Low, you must traverse a strange and marvellously deadened world beyond our reach, of a planet long abandoned by most of its former inhabitants.  Joined by his two crewmates being the severe reporter Maggie Robbins and the cool-minded geologist Ludger Brink, Boston must use his natural survival instincts and quick-witted skills of human engineering to try and formulate a way to escape, explore, and uncover the origins of this mysterious planet, and how they must find their way back home.
While the DIG may not be LucasArts' best work by far, it is certainly not one you should miss if you love their library.  The graphics are not the best, being that while the LucasArts style works well for more cartoony games such as Sam & Max or Monkey Island, it's a little more uncertain to do so with actual human characters and as a result they can look rather off during cutscenes.  Like "monkeys wearing human masks" off.
Nevertheless the rest of the game shines through with its pure atmosphere.  The graphics for its weird alien backgrounds are gorgeous, the sound design is just absolutely at the top of its game more than ever from LucasArts with roaring waves, howling winds, deep resonance within space and the most oddest of creatures wallowing and shrieking from all around you.
The dialogue is rather snarky in about 80% of its places but that only makes it more fun with the likes of Steve Blum and Robert Patrick delivering the most deadpan of deliveries.  The puzzles are...infamous to say the least and in truth one or two of them could have been much better designed.  I'll give you a hint for free, the head of the skeleton is not meant to be on the top left, but bottom right.
Regardless, I say go ahead if you love LucasArts' work, and try out this gem from the past that, while is a little rough around the edges and is perhaps at the lower end of their library, is nevertheless one worthy of playing if you are a fan of such games.

Firstly game enviroments feels very much like Cube world more than minecraft in my opinion. The terrain has some great effects when travelling from biome to biome (much better than Cube world in my opinion). Towns seem to be in the game but other than the  starting town (with walls around it) the other towns just seem barren by comparrison (just a few  buildings scattered quite far from one another  and  no road going  through them in most cases.  I hope the developers plan to tweak and add  more to the current towns on roads and make them unique in each biome (eg different looking buildings - e.g. in forrest roofs made out of leaves, plains roofs made out of hay etc......). Gameplay is interesting. It is somewhat basic at this time (although being an Alpha I expect that will hopefully change for the better). Finding items out in the wild is very limited at this time (the best thing I found randomly was a Magnificent Key). Most of the time you will find chests with no keys or barrels filled with fruit (very useful). Keys in particular seem very hard to find (too hard in my opinion). You can level up as you explore/fight although the effects do not seem to do much at this time (im my opinion). And yes I know it does raise my health  as I level up. Also have not found any major weapon upgrades other that armor shoulder pads at this time. one time found a spellbook (from a dead friendly AI) and could not figure how to use it, and  also a glowing green staff.  (most of my time was exploring anyway so not important). I feel this game has alot of potential like Cube world. I hope they are able to continue to work on this jem. The graphics look great although this game seems to struggle on my system (i5- 3550,  8gb ram and a 295 GTX graphics card). Make sure you turn down AA expecially. I was having a slide show when trying to run on Ultra with 4x AA enabled. Much better with Medium with 2x AA enabled although I does still seem to chug at times (obviously being an Alpha I also understand that tuning with come later - maybe at the  beta stage). Basically at the end of  the  day I do not regret purchasing this game at all and really looking forward to what they do next. I have already read on the work on the terrain generation (great) and I hope they can flesh the game out (more weapons,armors etc..) and would like to see some variations on  monsters for specific biomes (e.g. monsters in the snow biome will not be seen in the jungle biome for instance). Great job to the developers. I do not regreat investing my $14.95 purchase price towards supporting this game into a bright future. Thank you four your hard work.

So here it is - my review for 'Prototype 2' on Steam.
If you are interested in my opinion of the Original 'Prototype' game you can find the review here:

So this time it's yet again your turn to stop "Blackwatch" and the infection going on in "NYZ" but this time you are playing the role of the ex-military 'James Heller'. His team had an operation in ''NYZ'' but got killed when they encountered the main antagonist of the game: 'Alex Mercer'. -
Unlike his goal in Prototype 1 he now wants to take over the City and kind of re-populate with evolved made by him with similar abilities . As the only survivor of his attack.. he infectes you with the "Mercer Virus" and now the game begins.
We discover that it was Mercer killing his wife and daughter with his "second outbreak" of the mercer virus (first outbreak would be the one of 'Prototype 1') and now crave for revenge and make him suffer as we did.
During all this yet again alot of twists will come up and in the end you find yourself chasing after something way more important than 'Alex Mercer' himself..
Thats it from me about the story since I dont like revealing too much for potential buyers.
The gameplay stays more or less the same as in one with further improvements and a combat system to die for.
Its too much fun running, flying, slashing ,beating or body surfing your way through the City with an endless amout of ways to kill people, new monsters and tons of side missions that can keep you busy for a good while. I even recommend buying the DLC "RADNET Access Pack" if it's on sale since it adds new activities and a ranking system for you and your friends that unlocks rewards and Skins for 'Heller' if you complete them.
The achievments are again just fun to attempt with good challenges and references to movies or other games.
The graphics though are a mixed bag to me...some of the textures just look like they are from 2002 while animations and especially 'Hellers' different forms look very detailed and cool. But overall they are perfect fitting for a game like that and I am sure it won't stand in your way.
Again I was using an Nvidia Graphics Card and haven't encountered any technical issues with that game on highest settings but I am aware that 'AMD' cards are horribly optimized in this game so I'd recommend to get it on console ('AMD' users) if you have one.
On sale both (Game + DLC) cost me ~ 10 bucks and I dare to say that its a good invenstment since you can spend a good amount of hours in this game trying to complete it 100%. If you just care about the Story (wich may not be the most interesting for everyone) you can leave the DLC behind and finish the main Story in about 10 hours then quit and have another game on your "Story-Completed-List".
Overall I can say that if you loved the first one you will cheat on it with PROTOTYPE 2.
Gameplay feels more satisfying than in any other third person game (with hack 'n slay elements ofc) and the over the top gore is just great.
I highly recommend yet another game of my list that I used to love back in 2012 / 2013 and now got it again on steam.
As always I hope that my review was good / helpful and you might have found something interesting for yourself.
Have a good day! :D

Rewriting my review to ensure everyone would know how awesome the game is. Been playing with the Matrix Store version of the game prior to its steam release. I believe the game has been around for quite awhile now but it is only known to a few number of people. I was browsing the Matrix store a few years ago after hearing about Distant Worlds and I stumbled upon this gem.
The game is a wargame with a lot of mechanics like entrenchement, morale, supplies, etc. The game may not be the prettiest but it is appropriate for a game of its kind. The game looks like a hex-based boardgame with the unit counters on the tiles. The default units look like the actual units but for those who want something realistic then I would suggest getting the NATO counters mod for the game.
Advanced Tactics gold is made by the same person who made the Decisive Campaigns series for the PC. Advanced Tactics is a traditional wargame that sits in the sweet spot between beer and pretzel Panzer Generals to the complex mind-boggling simulation that is War in the East/Pacific. The game is easy to learn but hard to master. The game could be played like many traditional wargames where there are scenarios (I think it includes a WW2 scenario and some scenarios could be downloaded from the ATG site). The best feature of the game is the random map generator where you can tweak some options like expensive research or starting with only the most basic military tech and researching improved units. The randomly generated map could be tweaked from presets if you want more oceans (if you want more naval combat/invasions) or more land (simulate the eastern front)  and a whole lot more. Playing random map generator sorts of lets you play the game as something like most 4x games where you have to uncover the maps and capture resource sites and build some fortifications, ports, factories, etc. The cities serve as important hexes that gives victory points. Capturing victory points would let you win the game.
The best part of this game is that you can't win by brute force. You have to put a lot of things in to consideration. So lets say you got the tech for the biggest tanks but these tanks uses a lot of fuel. A low fuel reserve might turn your tanks in to useless piece of scrap metal. So you are not protecting your supply lines? A well-placed paratrooper unit behind your lines would cut your supplies and weaken your forces. You got 100 rifle units and the enemy has only 50 SMG units well entrenched in a city? They will cut you to shreds! Oh you are laughing at that unit with only 15 rifles and 3 machineguns and you think your 50 rifle units could roflstomp them? Well I don't think so! Your oil reserves are dwindling and you want to move your artilleries around fast? Then you better get the horses to drag them!
Its things like this that make this game close to infinitely replayable as every game can turn out differently and you can choose whether to use air superiority, drop tons of troops more that what was paradropped during market garden or do an amphibious invasion that would put overlord to shame, then you have the option in this game! I paid around $50 for a digital copy of this game and I must say that I have no regrets! It is really worth it. It makes you think and does not ensure that you would just start to steamroll over your opponents once you get your advanced units. I will be bold to say that IMHO this is the best wargame ever!

Story: Two years after the events at Maple Creek our intrepid and stubborn female detective has heard rumors of mysterious disappearances in Northern California's Redwood National Park.  Believing the elusive Maple Creek Preacher is involved, she goes there.  While driving through a remote part of the redwood forest overlooking the coast she is nearly hit by a black cloudy flying "thing" before encountering what appears to be an accident scene involving a family camper.  No accident, as it turns out when the black cloudy raven with red glowing eyes attacks again to retrieve the girl child who escaped the first time.  Drawn both willingly and cautiously into the dark sinister world of Ravenwood Park, (most probably an unregistered and unheard of tourist stop about the past lumber industry), she once again encounters dark and evil forces at work as she thrives to rescue the captured family.  Old friends, new friends and a lethal enemy.  Be warned, friends are only enemies with mutual goals.
Gameplay: Hmmm....I must digress slightly here.  I will compare this to Enigmatis: Maple Creek first, since generally fans of a particular company will play the sequel (or more) even if they hated the previous game if they like the company that made it.  (Or there was spectacular advertising,)
First of all Enigmatis: Ravenwood plays so much easier then Maple Creek.  Artifex Mundi turned the volume down on the horror and suspense but upped the creepy and supernatural elements, yet left all the mystery, anxiety and urgency.  Like that or not, this game is PG, not PG17, and I for one thank Artifex Mundi for doing this.  Even the few jump scares (mostly at the beginning) were not that bad.  Though I must say there were some truly terrifying and horrifying scenes in this game.
The second thing Artifex Mundi did was stop being "jerks" in the hidden object scenes.  ("Jerks" by my definition make find clues in hidden object scenes so hard or so obscure the find clue is nearly impossible to locate.) Thank you for that too.  Ravenwood plays like a dream compared Maple Creek in that aspect.
Third thing:  There is a no-penalty fast travel map.  Thank you so much.
Now just about Ravenwood, well almost, since it retains the same investigation "evidence board" as the first game.  The "evidence board" is where our detective places all the clues she finds and groups them together in circles concerning a certain subject like identity, location, crime, suspects, etc.  This is a clever mechanism for storytelling and informing the player what has been and still needs to be accomplished, as well as subtly reminding the player this woman is a resourceful detective.  (In my opinion she is just as resourceful as Macgyver.)  If this series continues, I do hope they continue using this play strategy, it is very different from other games.   One even gets an achievement for finding all the evidence, and another for conditionally placing it correctly.  Now that is clever.
The Hidden Object scenes vary from straight find lists with the added extra twist of locating the object first such as in a drawer or pouring a glass of wine from a bottle, to what I call shape picture puzzles.  (Those are the puzzles that show a shape that must be found first then used, such as the shape of a key which once found opens something.)  Not so easy to be simple (They did not overcompensate from Maple Creek.) but not so hard the gamer rage-quits either.  Just good even average on the difficulty level.
The actual puzzles are easy to understand and relatively challenging.  I do believe I noticed that as the game progressed the puzzle challenges slowly increased in difficulty as did actually finding all the pieces of the puzzle.  By the end of the game as the game scope narrows the player frequently has an empty or near empty inventory.  For me it increased the "felt" urgency as if I could actually be late and "not save day".
This game (probably due to the age) introduces the alternate hidden object play I have come to think of as one of Artifex Mundi's signatures.   Instead of doing the hidden object scene, one can play a matching game instead.  (This is Mahjong in the Nightmares from Deep series).  Unfortunately this also requires a second playthrough if achievement hunting.  I really wish Artifex Mundi (or any game developer for that matter that forces a second playthrough) allowed the other set of achievements (play all hidden object games or play all alternate games) to be gotten by the playing all the hidden object scenes in the extras as one or the other.
There are two sets of extra find objects.  One the "Illusion" objects that even though they fade in and out, do so rapidly and are quite large.  It is very hard to miss these.   The Illlusion changes from well maintained to decrepit abandonment, which is in keeping with the Ravenwood game theme.  These are kept track of in the notebook at the back, which is a very nice touch.  The second set are the "Ethereal Butterflies"  These are easier to miss 1) because they are smaller and 2) the gamer gets distracted.  Make sure to get them before moving on, there are one or two the gamer can not go back for.  These are not conveniently kept track of either.
Overall, a good game and I hope the series continues since the ending was left open.

If you like Dragonball at all, you should probably skip reading reviews and snag this game-- it pretty perfectly encapsulates the action and aesthetic in a fun gameworld with tons of stuff to do and customize.
Even if you don't, this game may bear a look.  Deep character customization and colorful, over the top anime battles make the game tailorable to a variety of playstyles and senses of cool-- though the campy DBZ elements will be ever-present, and in some cases made fun of by the game.  It's a very self-aware narrative, here and there, which generally serves it well IMO, but sense of humor will always vary.
Gameplay-wise it's fast and frenetic, complex button inputs from most fighters replaced with three sets of command inputs for your controller's face buttons (or keyboard bindings, I presume), each corresponding to a different tier of options (basic commands, super moves, and ultimate moves).  The special abilities aren't all attacks-- there are many poses, escape techniques, and counter moves for various other types of moves to toy with in tweaking your fighter(s).
Battles play out in a relatively expansive 3D arena, most if not all from various show and manga settings, and as mentioned the action is over the top with massive explosions and dizzying series of strikes, some of which may seriously injure a fighter if they're caught in them-- depending on their investment in the health and stamina statistics, at any rate.
As I alluded to, the game is highly customizable and you can fight from afar or up close in a myriad of different ways, faciliated by hundreds and hundreds of unlocks that skew builds this way and that, or provide unique activations and passive mechanics.  It's imba in all the right ways, full of options to own and gleefully rain havoc on your enemies, fill a ridiculously goofy fighting niche, or hit a sweet spot in between.  Can't remember the last time I had more fun unlocking a game.

OK, played some more after comments from dev.
The game reminds me of Cube 2 Sauerbraten (FPS + ability to co-op edit maps) but not as pretty and with slower pace. However it has vehicules, ability to destroy maps, and zombies for some modes.
The main differentiator is the Infestation mode where you turn into a zombie once dead. Zombies cannot pick-up guns but come with their own weapons (claws and tongue). Overall, this is a fun mode.
Main problem for me with the game is that the maps, while fun, are not well balanced. A lot of them are very open, which means that a sniper or someone flying high above with a vehicule can spam the map. You often see zombies coming from far away. There is an option to remove some weapon (e.g. sniper) so could potentially help, but it feels like a cheap trick.
The +
--- Co-op editing

This is my first impression after playing for 20 minutes.  I have a KVM setup so I can switch between the old version on a Windows XP machine, and the new version on Windows 7, viewing both on the same monitor.
My first impression was positive.  The initial screens looked better and more crisp.  The color palette is the same, bright colors that made the original artwork charming. This is an interesting 1v1 game with a pretty steep learning curve. The rules and cards aren't hard to comprehend - it's just that there are lots of them to memorize, and games are pretty long with lots to keep track of.
The games are decided by 3 things: skill (most of which is experience/memorization), card-drawing luck, and dice-rolling luck.
This game is less about strategy/simulation and more about probability-based calculation that relies on memorizing lots of events. The computer does help you see the probability distributions and visualize moves before committing to them so that finding good moves is easier. The interface is better as a result, but the actual game is still held back by being a board game.
The optimal move has little to do with analyzing the situation and making a decision based on strategy - it's about minimizing your vulnerability to predetermined events that will happen in the future based on fixed event cards.
For example, you have to avoid spending your moves building up a presence in Romania because there's a card that removes all your influence in Romania and gives it to your opponent. What makes Romania different from Bulgaria or Hungary? Nothing that actually matters in the gameplay rules or the map geography, and nothing that has to do with strategy or what the game is trying to simulate.
The basic problem is that the event cards are completely predetermined (seemingly inspired by actual historical events). When you make moves that seem like they should exploit a weakness or create different opportunities, the game doesn't generate new or different event cards. The game doesn't recognize that the situations which allowed those historical events to happen might not exist in your game. It's just a digital version of a board game that has hard-coded events.
Once you have memorized all those events, you can plan better and the game becomes more interesting. But there's still a huge luck component that will make the experience less rewarding and unnecessarily slow down the process of learning/improving.
I'm not sure how balanced the two sides are. There are some options to handicap one of the sides, so there's probably a workaround for potential imbalance.
It was a few hours of fun, so I'll "recommend" it assuming the multiplayer works well, but the AI doesn't seem to understand how to play for victory. I might play it more if the AI gets better, but I'm not convinced that multiplayer is worth the time to really learn.
The computer version could have fixed the luck-based aspect and the hard-coded events with something better, but for matches that are as long as the ones in this game, I'd rather play something that's more skill-based. Maybe they did the best they could for a board game, but it's not the best option for a PC game that claims to be about strategy.

HYBRID BABY! What do you get when Halo and Minecraft do the nasty and make a baby? You get this bad boy, Murder Miners.
Though some may call it a Halo-inspired Minecraft shooter, don't expect to see much building in this game because of the title "Minecraft". In fact, this game does some great fan service to the Halo kids who happen to enjoy that touch of Minecraft.
Halo players will feel right at home in this game, using some of the weapons such as the battle rifle, sniper, shotgun, machine gun (assault rifle), frag grenades and plasma (sticky) grenades, energy sword, etc. You get to customize your own character (spartan) and play in game modes such as  Murder Match (free-for-all), Team Murdermatch (team deathmatch), Murder the Flag (Capture the Flag), and the games own modes like Map Making Mode and Zombie Survival. Even more fan service to the Halo kids, there are future game modes planned to come such as Murderball (Hot Potato / Odd Ball) and Murdernaught (Juggernaut ), some familiar playgrounds. It's pretty much Halo, retextured Minecraft.
Along with the Halo fan service, there are also some game modes for those who enjoy building. I guess this is where the building part comes in. I mentioned Map Making Mode earlier and I've seen some awesome maps made by the community. Custom maps for any and every game mode. You can create solo or host a server and have public or private friends join and build whatever your heart desires. I've even seen remade CoD maps like Nuketown from Black Ops and maps from the Halo game itself. There's a little something of everything for everyone. Heck, there are even vehicles you can ride and fly around in on some maps. (*NOTE* that the game does have its own original maps, it isn't completely a Halo game)
Most multiplayer games these days have a leveling system where you have to grind it out and spend hours reaching levels to unlock decent equipment to be right there with every other player; this game, however, has no leveling system. Your skill grows with the time you spend playing, and you don't need to grind out hours to unlock anything. You have everything given to you from the start and it feels great.
My only complaint about the game is the community falls short. My time playing, I didn't see much activity going on. Every server I joined didn't  have that many players, there weren't that many servers up, and if there were, if was from players who hosted game modes and set the rules so they could win. It just felt unfair at times, it was really cheap; however, I did find some moments to host my own deathmatch servers and have a nice amount of players join. Occasionally, some decent death match and CTF servers were up, and I was able to record some awesome gameplay footage for my YouTube channel.
This is a game I will be playing for a while. As a fan of Halo, I feel right at home and I've been addicted and recording. Some gameplay footage can be seen here-
I wish all of my friends had this game, and I wish more people played the game. This is a game I would highly recommend.

TL;DR: You are getting one of the best strategy games of all time for $15 or less, when the normal board game version costs $40, and takes much longer to play than the digital version. If you like history even a little bit, or strategy games at all, I would highly recommend this game.
Twilight Struggle is an incredible game where every move feels like it could be your last, every mistake is paid for dearly, and every minor victory feels so, so rewarding. This game features a 1v1 tactical deathmatch between the US and USSR during the Cold War, and each side tries to best the other by spreading their influence throughout the world. Play is mostly card based, and each player must decide which cards to play each turn to destroy their opponent: but not all cards are helpful to you, and the threat of global nuclear warfare constantly looms over you. This is probably the most intense and fun strategy game I have played, and seeing it finally brought to Steam is a blessing.
PROS:
- One of the best startegy games ever
- I find the interface to be fairly good, save for a few hiccups
- There is a pretty good tutorial for any newcomers
- You can play online multiplayer or offline against an AI
- The game gives you several options for modifying the base game, if that's your style
- Atmoshpere, music, etc. is the best I could possibly imagine it to be for a Cold War strategy game like this
- Tons of historical references for any history nerds out there
- Considering the physical board game version of this is usually more than $40, and THAT price is worth it, $15 is pretty damn cheap
- Taking over the world and nuclear warfare are ALWAYS fun
CONS:
- This game has a pretty big learning curve, in my opinion. The tutorial is good, but you may have to play several games before you get the hang of things
- I have noticed several minor glitches, usually when trying to get past a certain screen or when trying to click something, but I have found none of these to be game-ruining
- May have to nag your friends to buy a copy if you want to play with someone you actually know
- The AI takes a bit of time to make moves
NEUTRAL:
- Not sure if I just suck, but the AI seems to be pretty brutally difficult. Some people may like this, others not
- This game does involve chance: picking up cards and rolling dice. Some people may like this in strategy games, other people might not
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game. 10/10 board game, 10/10 strategy game, 7/10 video game. You will have a lot of fun spreading freedom as Murica, and a lot of fun killing capitalist pig-dogs as the commies. I think the asking price isn't bad, and I would definitiely pick this game up on sale.

Gunpoint, one of my favorite games as of late. Let's go over some of the main parts of the game. First off, let me say that while I have low hours, that is because this is a game that most people can complete in one sitting, but it is a very satisfying one sitting.
__
Alright, so here's the rundown of the very absolute basics of Gunpoint.
Gunpoint is a fairly unique game. You play as a noir-style freelance spy named Richard Conway that can leap very far, cling and climb on walls and ceilings, and can survive long falls thanks to what the game explains simply as advanced equipment your character possesses. In every level, you must infiltrate a building to get to the goal (which is almost always a computer you must hack) and get back out without the guards shooting you. Guards can see you and you will not lose, unlike some other stealth games.
__
Now, for some of the more clever mechanics in the game.
A big part of getting in and out of the buildings in Gunpoint is the Crosslink. Once you have the Crosslink after the first few tutorial levels, you can switch into Crosslink mode quickly and smoothy by rolling your mousewheel down a click. Every device in Gunpoint uses wiring systems, and in Crosslink mode you can rewire any device to any other device. Wire a lightswitch to a hand scanner that wires to a door, and when you hit the switch the end result is the door opening. Wire a guard's weapon into a power socket he's standing near, and when he tries to fire it the socket will overload and shock him.
You can't wire a guard's gun right at the start of the game, however. There are upgrades you can to get from the ingame store (all of the upgrades become available fairly quickly), one of which being the ability to wire guns. Other abilities are things like being able to go through a window without making a loud noise, and there are more unique purchases, such as the Resolver, the only gun you can use in the game.
Guards can be snuck past (my personal favorite way is to cling to the ceiling above them as they patrol), taken down by leaping at them and knocking them out with a punch, or killed by tackling them out a window (or punching them several times, if you're excessive like that). As said before, you can use more creative ways of knocking out a guard, like with power sockets. There are multiple types of guards, some are the standard that can be easly tackled to remove, some a more advanced kind that can only be taken out through more robust methods. All guards shoot on sight, which can be a bit finnicky at times (specifically after you get the upgrade that makes them sometimes miss) but overall works very well. A single bullet will kill you instantly, but the game has a very good checkpoint system, autosaving your position every few seconds. This allows you to jump back a little ways if you make a mistake without restarting the whole level, or allows you to restart the whole thing if you decide on a different approach.
__
The Experience
A general level goes like this: You start off the left of a building. First you must find a way in, either through diving into a window or finding a way to open a door (or entering into an already-open door). You need to open the doors to the computer you want to hack on the third floor, but it runs on blue wiring, and you only start with red. You must sneak hijack the blue wirebox on the first floor in order to manipulate the blue wires on the third. After a quick look over the building, you decide the best way to get in is by leaping through a window on the second floor. However, doing so would alert the guard, who will shoot you on sight. There happens to be a camera outside the building, and a light in the room the guard is in. You wire the camera to the light, then go under the camera. The light turns off, and the guard wanders into the next room over, looking for the lightswitch. You quickly leap into the window while his back is turned and dash down to the first floor, right as the lights come on. In the first floor, you quickly leap into the guard before he turns around and knock him out. After that, you can get to the blue wirebox, allowing you to manipulate the doors on the third floor. You sneak back up past the guard on the second floor, up to floor three, where you open the doors by wiring the blue lightswitch to the blue door. After that, you dash through the window on the third floor and make your escape off stage right.
__
The Story
When you accept a mission, there is a brief dialogue between Conway and whoever is giving you the mission. You can choose many dialogue options for different paths in the game (the paths, however, do not really change level layouts and mostly affect dialogue options). There is also a dialogue scene like this after you complete a mission. The story is a murder-mystery noir-styled tale that will quickly grab your interest and keep you begging for a resolve. For this reason, I cannot go into specific depth on the story, but I will say this is one of the strongest points of the game. You could make a movie out of it, and it would be awesome.

The Dig was released in the closing days of the point-and-click adventure genre, back in 1995. Unfortunately, due to a number of delays which beset the development team during its production, it was released years later than intended. By this point it was considered 'dated', despite its fantastic story dreamt up by none other than Steven Speilburg himself, and was poorly reviewed.
The Dig is an underappreciated gem of a game that I believe any adventure fan would find worth in revisiting. Its graphics, though outdated even at the time of its release, are still beautiful in their own way. The bright environments of the alien world Cocytus look as though they were drawn with colour wheels and charts always at hand!
Pros:
- An intriguing and well-written story which will keep you guessing, easily its best quality
- Beautiful, colourful environments
- Well composed; its score is moody and atmosperic
- Features the voices of a number of celebrity voice actors, including Steve Blum and Robert Patrick; also, most of the voice acting is extremely well done
- Quirky 2D animated cutscenes, like MS Paint Disney!
Cons:
- Frustrating and extremely time-consuming puzzles which require a lot of trial and error. Trust me, you'll end up looking for hints more than once
- It is a very old game, so it displays in a tiny box in the middle of the screen and can't be resized
- While I said above most of the voice acting is good, Robert Patrick occasionally voices his lines with a little less emotion than he should
- The game is very short if played with a guide, so the difficulty of the puzzles was probably intended to pad out the game's length.
TL;DR: This is an old game, and of a genre that's lost its popularity. Still, it's a forgotten masterpiece that's well worth experiencing. If you enjoy adventure games or just games that are story and character driven, I can't recommend this one enough. It deserves more praise.

If you played the first Prototype and liked the story, Prototype 2 will be a letdown. The story has all the major underlying plotlines - which were left hanging in the last game - are all but completelly ignored, in favor of some easier to understand "angry soldier kills tough guy". The final battle with Mercer feels too cheap and easy even in the higher difficulty settings, and the ending itself is one big meh.
Prototype 2 also simplifies the power and upgrading system, the new one feeling so much shallower than the original; we also see that many of the interesting powers from the first game didn't make a return on this one.
If you need a game in which you slice people up at will, go ahead and buy this; if you expected a true sequel and an ending to the many cliffhangers of the original Prototype, well, you'll be left hanging.
Edit: I see a lot of people complaining about the port, which was, in my experience, one of the greatest parts of this game, with the controls being extremelly fluid, no noticeable lag or technical problems (running on a GTX960 at max settings).

I like these games for the puzzles (mini games), I would be happy with just them and no Hidden Objects and no story. Often enough the rest is fun too though.
First (as I had to scroll through endless reviews to find that information): There's fast travel. Though a bit compressed, you get to jump to one place from where you can reach a few other locations. I prefer a spot on the map for every location.
The story here is interesting, though the twist is a bit obvious. I kept saying to the game,
but would it listen? Also, the background rubbed me the wrong way. I don't mind obvious myths put into games, I do mind myths put into games that far too many people world-wide think are real. Makes it look like the game claims it's real.
The hidden object games are just right for my taste (medium difficulty), no endless searching for the last invisible object. I also like that you return to previous spots to find more objects from the same clutter. I think for once that part was the most fun (what with all the other things I complain about).
The puzzles are ok. Got a bit used to ever the same kind by now, though, the novelty has worn off a bit.
The pair matching as alternative to the hidden object games is a bit weird. Other alternatives I've seen were more fun. I hope they don't put this one into other games. (Playing through again for that was no fun, just a chore.)
I don't like the achievements at all. Especially "find n of whatever for an achievement". That just distracts from the story and hampers immersion. At least in the second play through I only had to find the ones I missed the first time round. Trying to get all the butterflies in one play-through in-game, even with guide, still failed. Must have been distracted by the game at some point and missed one.
And I'd much prefer the achievements for all hidden object/all alternate games could be done via the extras, not needing a 2nd play through (which, due to achievements, is still more concerned with them than the story and scenery, never mind that all the cut scenes just get skipped).
I also don't really need cut scenes. I'd rather play than watch something doing its own thing. Plus, the butterfly on the teddybear goes missing within one scene early on. There in one position, gone in another.
For once I didn't turn the music off first thing, and apart from a few times where it became a bit repetitive, it didn't bother me.
It's a nice game, but would have been a lot more fun without those stupid achievements. I was hoping for something mystery when it turned up on sale on my wishlist. Starting it eagerly with enjoyment, that was quickly ruined by achievements. (I'm getting ever more annoyed with achievements across all sorts of games.  Recently added Terraria achievements interfered with what I actually wanted to do in the game. A while ago Hexcells achievements about perfection were just plain waste of time due to having to copy a state from screenshot after a misclick, every damn time... They just never add anything, only interfere with actually playing the game.)
I guess there's no hope that Steam gives me a button to simply turn them all off.
On the bottom line, if they don't bug you, this game is recommendable.

A truly original western epic that still feels like the classic movies. I normally don't review games, but I feel like this one deserves it.
The story may start out as the over-used revenge story, but by the time you finish it feels completely fresh. The tutorial introduces the plot right away (a mysterious bandit burns down your ranch), and the rest of the game is dedicated to your personal vendetta. The mechanic here is interesting, because every playthrough the outfit of said bandit changes, and you are tasked with asking around to learn what he looks like. This is achieved through a multitude of ways, from rumors, to quests, to even blaming everyone until you find him. Seriously, this game takes free-roam to the next level. Even in conversations, you're not only given dialogue different options, you can pull out your gun,♥♥♥♥♥♥it, then fire it if you want. You can also just walk away. These are legitamate options, and the characters will respond appropriately, some will just hand you money when you threaten them or get annoyed if you walk away. Personally, I find this incredibly satisfying.
This open endedness extends to everything too. To earn money you can do jobs for people, mug strangers, or even rob the bank. And you don't need a quest or specific button to rob the bank, you just go in, shoot everyone, grab the money, run, and pray to god that the sheriff doesn't find you. The map is pretty massive for such a short story, and there's a ton to do. Every quest has several different ways to go about it, and quite a few of the quests will depend on you not doing another one. For example, you can help free the buffalo for the Indian Camp, but if you do that, you can't help the army fight them.
Customization is there, if you're wondering. They have different outfits and hats to buy or pick up all over the map. There's no RPGish skills or anything, but it's not needed. The game depends on the player skill.
The music and sound are not only authentic, but match the mood and fit the game perfectly. I would say the same about the art style. It's simple and pixelated, but get's the job done well. Even though the characters are basic and abstract, some of the backgrounds are detailed and gorgeous. The art and sound design fit Westerado well.
Now you might be asking if there's anything wrong with this game. I have only one small complaint, so
The combat is weak. It's a 2D shooter, and while it fits the game well, it can be a bit clunky and difficult to aim. The depth is unfortunately hard to judge, and several times I found myself shooting right behind enemies. And in a game like this, a few misses will cost you. It's such a small issue though, and the rest of the combat system is quick and satisfying. Also, here's a ton of different guns which brings variety to the mid-game, and improves the combat system.
Replayability is also high, with 4 different characters and tons of different options each playthrough.
TL;DR: Buy this game, especially while it's on sale.

This is a great game, and I'm not just saying that because of my name!
First, if you prefer to skip the essay and just watch some gameplay, you can check out my playthrough here:
Westerado is a simple looking game, yet with so much detail it's impressive. The graphics are similar to 8-bit style, yet look great when playing. The lighting and mood change as you transition between sections, and as you move between dark and light areas. There are multiple different NPCs which all have varying appearances to keep from repeating too much. There are also plenty of animals and aggressive enemies in this game that you must keep an eye out for, so don't just go running through the desert expecting it to be uneventful!
The premise of the game is to find your family's murderer, which involves getting clues about how the murderer looks, which help finalize an overall picture of who you're looking for. Your job is to then search the impressively large map to find this man/woman, which can seem daunting considering how far you have to travel. There is the ability to ride a horse between cities though to cut down on time.
In orer to do this take, you must perform jobs, many of which involve escorting wagons, buffalo, etc. from one place to another while a group of bandits try to steal/kill your cargo. These minigames are actually very challenging, and I died many times attempting, as you can see in the video! The shooting mechanics in this game require you to♥♥♥♥♥♥and fire your gun, including reloading bullet by bullet, which make maneuvering and fighting that much more difficult. I'd recommend constantly strafing up and down the screen to avoid getting shot and to help you line up yours better.
Attaining money can be a challenge aside from finding bags on the floor. Most missions involve having to defend something, while others require you to simply pull your gun out. Either way, buying things required for missions takes away from being able to purchase new guns and clothing, so I typically stayed away from those missions. There are plenty of side missions to choose from though, so you will have plenty to do in this game.
Overall, this game is tons of fun, and well worth the money. It's meant to be replayable, and I can see myself replaying this game multiple times, each with a new murderer to search for. I'd highly recommend trying this game if you have the time/money.
