Gunpoint is short, fun, funny and challenging.
You play as a spy who can hack into electronic devices and rewire them to achieve various effects. Initially you start off simple... rewire a light switch to open a door, and so-on.
Then you start to get more ambitious... Rewire a motion detecting camera to turn off a light, then the guard will try the lightswitch, which you've rewired to open the security vault door...
By the end of the game, you're cross-wiring so many systems to achieve things that make you feel like a genius;
A lightswitch could send an elevator down a floor, the 'ping' of the elevator's arrival triggers a noise sensor which opens a skylight for you to jump out, the elevator is rewired to go back to the top floor on arrival, and in turn switch off a light as it arrives, making the guard turn and move to the lightswitch, just as you land silently behind him. The switch the guard presses now opens a door, which in turn triggers an alarm drawing the guards away from the door... Anyway, you get the picture.
It's entertaining, it doesn't overstay its welcome, it has a great sense of humour, doesn't take itself too seriously, and there's a level editor and Steam Workshop support for hours and hours of extra fun. Highly recommended.
It's an amazing thing, and I will continue to believe in it. Until it's finished, or I die. Whatever comes first.

I tend to have a mixed relationship with stealh gameplay. If it's pure stealth it can get frustrating to me a lot of the times because it just ends up being a puzzle game with trial-and-error gameplay, whereas good stealth games give you options to solve a problem in case one of your strategies doesn't work and indeed give you multiple ways to solve puzzles from the get go. Gunpoint doesn't quite manage to give multiple ways to solve puzzles, but this is remedied by the fact that the player can easily assess the situation of the entire level from the start, so obviously you have an advantage here that makes up for the linearity of the puzzles.
As a result, I had a lot of fun playing the game because of the interesting mechanics it offers, be it jumping ludicrous heights, wiring switches to doors, trap doors, guns, etc. to incapacitate or otherwise distract enemies, etc. And the story is actually quite interesting. It's a nice little pastiche of noir stereotypes where the main character gets tangled up in the story as it unfolds and it's up to the player to decide which direction it takes in the end. The dialogue between the characters is also very amusingly written. The only real complaint I have against the game is that it's too short. Again, I'm not the brightest guy so I managed to beat the entire game in less than 3.5 hours and I assume most people will do it faster. Admittedly, I only paid half of what they're actually asking for it since I bought it during a sale, but still I would've liked it even more if it were longer.
Overall I'd definitely recommend the game since it's just a lot of fun and the world it's set in is nicely realized with well-rounded characters (though like the visuals much of the story is reduced to the bare essentials).

Originally, I wasn't going to buy this, but it grew on me.
Toadled has the addictiveness of clicker games, but without that "just one more click and then I'm done" twitch. It has plenty of charm through its art and music with simple premise: an innocent frog grows and mutates as he eats everything thrown at him. The whole experience definitely has a "Katamari Demacy"/"Tales From Space: Mutant Blobs Attack" feel to it. The gameplay therefore, is straight-forward: You collect coins, you upgrade stats, and maybe try to rule the world in the process - You can even slow time in the process if everything flying at you just feels too overwhelming!
It may be short, as I nearly 100% it in a few hours, but I don't consider that a bad thing, since I expected it to be short. In fact, despite its length, it's the best dollar I've ever spent on Steam (and believe me, I've spent a ton of dollars on wicked-cheap Steam games over the years). It's challenging without the frustration too.
Add in trading cards, achievements, and even a little backstory in comic form, and overall, you've got the best bang for your buck in a casual Steam game.

Prototype 2 is fun to play. Prototype 2's story and characters are fun to ignore.
The comparisons to the Infamous series are apt - both are games about genetic mutants being hunted down by insidious government organisations, and fighting back for their freedom and the truth. Both also contain protagonists that are pretty unlikable, although Prototype makes no attempt to try and morally pigeonhole your character.
While the first Prototype is rather clunky and dated both technically and graphically, Prototype 2 is a significant improvement on both fronts. However, like the first game, Prototype 2 is still full of trite dialogue, repetitious gameplay and a plot that tries for complex and dramatic but comes off as convoluted and melodramatic. The player character is a vicious, angry piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥who is supposedly motivated by the death of his wife and child, but is (and I suspect always was) a callous psychopath. Your character is told about 6 hours in to be careful of losing his humanity. I then continued to slaughter innocent and guilty alike, just I had for the entire 6 hours up until that point. The good news is that the game makes few attempts to cover up the fact that it's basically a playground for the player to commit innumerable brutal, violent atrocities against anyone standing in their way. The game doesn't hold back when it comes to gore, and the player is given a large range of powers almost straight away, so you can expect to be running, jumping, gliding, and tearing opponents (or civilians, if you feel so inclined) limb-from-limb from the moment you set foot in the world.
In reality there is only one type of mission in the game - you consume a person, gain information from them that leads you to another person, place or thing, and then you destroy that person, place, or thing and escape the area by disguising yourself. Bar some minor collecting, everything else that happens is some variation on this, which would be a bad thing if you weren't given the freedom to wreak havoc with impunity. The enemies are basically blind, and all you have to do is turn a corner and disguise yourself and you're a free man, not to mention the fact that you can consume people who are standing right next to someone else as if peripheral vision doesn't exist in this world. But this just serves to lighten the restrictions on the player.
I wouldn't recommend the first game, but I would recommend this as a guilty pleasure. Be aware that it does get repetitive, so get it cheap.

I was really excited for this game to be released as I have bought a game from the same company before, The Men of Yoshiwara. So when I saw that the company wanted to release another otome game, I was like 'I HAD TO GET IT!' I got it at 40% off, thinking to myself, 'Wow! This will be such a great deal!'.
So this game starts off with you and your boyfriend (ex..?) breaking off, you became really sad and went home and suddenly your 4 out of 5 pets became human. (Yeah, I wish that happens in real.) I really liked how Lize looked, so I went into his route first. AND HOLY SH**. Ok.. *Heavy sigh* Lemme lemme lemme explain first.. why I gave this game a thumbs down.
1) First of all, the MC (you) was not even curious as to know why they became humans. She did ask once but that's all. As a normal human being, or a normal hot-blooded female, you would question EVERYTHING. She just went 'Oh, you guys are still humans? Meh. No big deal. I'm not even going to ask.' like it was part of her everyday lives where pets become human. No girl, you should be SUPER curious about it.
2) This line bothers me a lot 'Whenever Lize cooks food, the food always looks as amazing as it taste' Wasn't he a rabbit yesterday? Since when did he ever cook for you before today? Don't you find it really weird?
3) When Lize went missing because of a fight, you called Ramin, he picked up the phone. Since when did he knows how to pick up a phone or even have a cellphone?!
4) When they revealed how they became human and what is their contract (about you loving them within a week so they can continue to be a human to stay next to you), the MC(you) suddenly proclaims your love for Lize... HELLO GIRL, YOU JUST BROKE UP WITH YOUR BOYFRIEND 3 DAYS AGO. I know you love your pets a lot but don't you think that loving them as a human is a bit too sudden? I mean, if there was more development plot in between the 3 days, (I honestly don't mind the 3 days being dragged across the chapters like in Voltage's 10 days with my Devil just for the character development)
5) Honestly the game ends too fast, the whole story was going on so fast that I feel like I was just reading and not passionate about the story like how I was in 'The Men of Yoshiwara'. I am a very emotional person, I cry easily during touching scenes where the men of yoshiwara do anything he takes to be with you, but THERE WAS NO TEARS SHED IN THIS GAME. I was just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off like how the story ended so abruptly and there was no development!
6) I finished one route in less than 1.5 hours while in other otome games, I finish the route in 3 hours.
7) I don't know where this story plot is going. The human-pet guy confesses his love to you and you two did not even do much, your heart suddenly beats faster? I don't get it.
You may say that otome games are not based on logic. Totally wrong, This is a dating sims, it should make me feel like I'm dating the guy and going through the relationship with the guy properly instead of dumping the character who is head over heels over loving in front of you and expect the relationship to work. I don't even feel like I'm dating Lize in the whole process, I just feel like he is dating another girl, not me. And that girl is just high on something to suddenly love him. I will continue supporting 'The Men of Yoshiwara' but not this game. So sorry about this bad review, I hope to see better otome games from this company though. Thank you.

- the skin (most of the routes have a bit of fan service, with a hint of smutiness in them. It is neither too much nor too little, and it adds up quite nicely to the story of each character)
- the overwhelming pink flowerish romance feeling (for me it was a breath of fresh air after all the angst, tragedy, unfulfilled wishes the otomes i lately played were filled with. Seriously, sometimes you just want to pay for something that doesn`t resemble real life, and this game provides exactly that, a little nice piece of a fairy tale)
- the extra stories (epilogue and side story) are a nice addition, bringing you closure for each character
Cons:
- no "auto" button, which means you need to endlessly click through all the "...." and the "umm" replies
- the music is not so great and it quickly gets repetitive and annoying
- no voicing (yes i`m spoiled, i know)
- the story is very short. too short in fact
- after you complete all the routes, you notice that at some point the whole story doesn`t add up anymore
- this can also be a plus, depending on personal preference: there is no truly bad ending (you know, the everyone-dies-end-of-the-world-broken-heart-forever type of ending)
Overall probably 8/10.

I watched the Let’s Plays of Chapter 1 and 2 of this series on YouTube and it looked like so much fun that I decided to buy Chapter 3 myself so that I could have the pleasure of finishing the story at my own pace. As you know, adventure games are all about story, and you won't be disappointed with this installment in the series. It has that same pulp mystery movie feel to it that Chapter 1 and 2 has!
I have to say that I was surprised with the ending! Even though a lot of it gets explained very quickly at the grand finale I was pretty satisfied overall, that is until they had the cliffhanger after the credits!
The overall feel and gameplay was very similar to Chapters 1 and 2, so if you liked those then this title will definitely not disappoint. Now it is longer than Chapter 1 but is shorter than Chapter 2. I’d say it has more “content” in terms of following the main story arc, but has far less open world and has no big maps like Chapter 2 had. It’s a lot more linear but still has a few tricky puzzles and collection quests just like the previous two titles.
Because of the intrigue behind the new cliffhanger I went ahead and listened to the director’s commentary (comes free with the game and is under your music page on steam). It was interesting, spontaneous and often hilarious, I definitely recommend it to anyone who has become a huge fan of “Silver Creek Falls” (like I have) and wants to know a bit more behind it’s creation! Anyway, as I was saying, I gave it a listen and the director did say that they were thinking of doing a spinoff with Mark/Phil as the protagonist and that more of the mystery would be solved there. So I’m looking forward to that and for any of you that have more questions I really recommend you give it a listen.

Gunpoint is short, fun, funny and challenging.
You play as a spy who can hack into electronic devices and rewire them to achieve various effects. Initially you start off simple... rewire a light switch to open a door, and so-on.
Then you start to get more ambitious... Rewire a motion detecting camera to turn off a light, then the guard will try the lightswitch, which you've rewired to open the security vault door...
By the end of the game, you're cross-wiring so many systems to achieve things that make you feel like a genius;
A lightswitch could send an elevator down a floor, the 'ping' of the elevator's arrival triggers a noise sensor which opens a skylight for you to jump out, the elevator is rewired to go back to the top floor on arrival, and in turn switch off a light as it arrives, making the guard turn and move to the lightswitch, just as you land silently behind him. The switch the guard presses now opens a door, which in turn triggers an alarm drawing the guards away from the door... Anyway, you get the picture.
It's entertaining, it doesn't overstay its welcome, it has a great sense of humour, doesn't take itself too seriously, and there's a level editor and Steam Workshop support for hours and hours of extra fun. Highly recommended.

I tend to have a mixed relationship with stealh gameplay. If it's pure stealth it can get frustrating to me a lot of the times because it just ends up being a puzzle game with trial-and-error gameplay, whereas good stealth games give you options to solve a problem in case one of your strategies doesn't work and indeed give you multiple ways to solve puzzles from the get go. Gunpoint doesn't quite manage to give multiple ways to solve puzzles, but this is remedied by the fact that the player can easily assess the situation of the entire level from the start, so obviously you have an advantage here that makes up for the linearity of the puzzles.
As a result, I had a lot of fun playing the game because of the interesting mechanics it offers, be it jumping ludicrous heights, wiring switches to doors, trap doors, guns, etc. to incapacitate or otherwise distract enemies, etc. And the story is actually quite interesting. It's a nice little pastiche of noir stereotypes where the main character gets tangled up in the story as it unfolds and it's up to the player to decide which direction it takes in the end. The dialogue between the characters is also very amusingly written. The only real complaint I have against the game is that it's too short. Again, I'm not the brightest guy so I managed to beat the entire game in less than 3.5 hours and I assume most people will do it faster. Admittedly, I only paid half of what they're actually asking for it since I bought it during a sale, but still I would've liked it even more if it were longer.
Overall I'd definitely recommend the game since it's just a lot of fun and the world it's set in is nicely realized with well-rounded characters (though like the visuals much of the story is reduced to the bare essentials).

I remember this game since i was younger.
I remember seeing people in the CafeNet i used to visit often play this game and i would just look the people play the game for hours.
EvE is the game that got me Hooked to Space Games.
Yet i always dreamed of it going free to play.
After years of waiting and waiting to the point i forgot i was waiting for it, i still would visit the EvE page to check if its free or not once every 4-5 months.
Years of patience and i find out from a friend that the game i love and adore has gone Free to Play.
I kid you not. I rushed to my steam account typed as fast as possible on the steam search engine "EvE Online" and i saw it... Finally it had gone Free to Play!
I left everything i was doing and downloaded the game.
I finally had the chance to try out EvE Online with my own two hands! Yes!
I knew the game was very hard to get your head around everything.
Learning the crafting systems.
Trading routes.
Fighting positions and tactics.
The Economy of the gamme.
I was ready for all this.
I was ready to sink hours and hourss into this game knowing i would no regret and instead i would enjoy!
But... it was to good to be true.
After a few hours of playing i got stuck.
The game was asking me continuasly to go Premium ..to pay.
I kept trying to skip and find another way around this in my every single move,quest,trade,craft and buying.
But i couldnt.
I could not get the items i wanted or do quests i dreamed of for many years because those i loved needed me to pay.
I Googled solutions how to get around this whole situation yet... all i saw was "You have to go Premium"
Sadly after 3.5 Hours i realized i had to give up on the game because thats how little it takes for you to realize there is no way around it.
I had to Log off and delete the game from my computer.
The game i was waiting for so many years to go Free.
I felt dissapointment but ...sometimes you have to let go even from the best.
I know now that the game will never go fully free to play.
So i say this to you EvE ...Good Bye.

The Bad
For a free game, there was nothing that I encountered that I’d feel good about putting into this category.
The Meh
I’m going to stick to my guns as to the above statement in the “Bad” section. I’ve got nothing bad to say about Port of Call.
Verdict: Yea
You’ve got virtually nothing to lose by getting PoC from the Steam Store and taking it for a playthrough. Two playthroughs will get you all seven achievements and my first play through was just shy of thirty minutes. The game itself is a fun game and it is completely free. If you’re looking for a lightly spooky game, look no further. As always, thanks for reading.

UPDATED: After going through several routes, I really wished each story was LONGER so we could get to know each character better. I feel that each story is TOO SHORT to buy at full price...so I recommend getting it at a discount price. Each story is good but they could be great if each story was given more depth and made quite a bit longer.
This is another great game from the creators of Men of Yoshiwara (both Kikuya and Ohgiya) and Pub Encounter. I feel that each character route is a bit shorter than their other visual novels mentioned previously. Although this is a bit shorter, there are a lot more choices to decide in the story. However each choice may not give likeability. Meaning you could pick from two choices, but neither will give likeability it will just give a slight variation on dialogue or scene. For example when the pets turned human help out the protagonist cleaning, there are three choices that dont affect likeability but give different scenes or a slight variation on dialogue.
I do WISH there were more CGs as there are not enough (at least in my opinion). I also HOPE in the future that the creators add story routes for both Georgie and Fumiya, because I would love to get to know each of their characters a bit more intimately ;)
***I definitely recommend this at the sale price as I am a bit hesitant to recommend to buy it at full price since it is shorter than Men of Yoshiwara. I do want to point out that it has a somewhat similar plot to Dandelion-Wishes Brought to You just without the skill grinding. But like Men of Yoshiwara the artwork is great as expected and is a story that pulls you in from the moment you start reading. ***

One of the best Artifex Mundi titles, Enigmatis 2 offers a thrilling story, good voice acting, excellent level design, wonderful graphics and nice puzzle variety.
Enigmatis 2: The Mists of Ravenwood could be one of the best games to showcase what the hidden object puzzle genre is capable of.
The story does a great job of keeping up the interest with adding new layers to the already complex mystery. Although it ties perfectly to the previous episode with a good amount of returning characters and expanding upon the events we saw in Maple Creek, it’s still unique enough to stand on its own. The voice acting is nice, and the amount and distribution of the cut scenes is ideal for the pace.
Whereas Enigmatis 1 put a large focus on the hidden object scenes, Mists of Ravenwood tries to create an ideal balance between those, the point ‘n’ click parts, and the conventional puzzles. This also means that none of them are particularly difficult, nor too easy. They are what they are meant to be: an immensely fun enjoyment for a lazy afternoon.

I bought this way back when it wasn't free; and am replaying it now. I consider it worth the original selling price of ~$15 base, it being free makes it absolutly worth your time, so long as you have any taste at all for tower defense.
Let's get the cons out of the way 1st:
1. voice acting is horrible. Think Tony Wiseau monologue / old kung fu movie dub bad. You can kind of enjoy it for it's corniness, but it is very noticeable
2. game is short. I had 4 hours on my 1st aborted playthru, and I was around 1/2 way in. Others seem to have beaten the game with both characters in 16 hours... so yeah 8 hour playthru
It's a tower defense game, but with some rather unorthodox gameplay & features.
Rather than moving map to map, you play on the same map over and over, with different enemy waves & pathing. Playing on the same map might sound boring, but the map is very large, and they continue to add new sections to it as play progresses.
Another unusual feature is that you will NEED to move your character around and actually fight things. The traps are an unusual mix of pure utility effects, one shot damage, and requiring manual activation thru the use key or shooting with the rifle. There is no aspect to play where you pick build the perfect meat grinder and then watch it go.
The final unusual aspect is that some of the traps/structures cost money, and are permanent (until you activate them); this basically adds a long term base building element. Right now I have a centralized transport system set up with watchtowers, established over the course of 3 matches.
The story & setting are very nice; if you have a taste for history & historical fiction especially. It's set around the 1850s in Canada, and plays on themes of Native American vs. Christian myth & folklore. The game mechanics nicely back up the setting & aesthetic, the traps all act & feel as you would expect a wolftrap, a bonfire, etc. to act, rather some game-ified infinite ammo turret, reskinned to be in the Canadian frontier.
It isn't the best TD ever, but it is unique and satisfying, worth your time. Especially now that it's free.

Out-and-out Pay-To-Win cancer. I only played this because a friend already plays it (and is far too invested in it to give it up).
Unlike fairer games, payments don't merely get you items with a small statistical advantage, and you cannot grind to reach the same level as a rich player through virtue of effort. Some 90% or more of the game's content is gated by monthly payments, including most importantly,
.
This means that 'alpha clones' can be easily ganked while mining or questing by some rich kid with every shiny fitting attached to their ship, which, provided they are not completely incompetent, will then blast you out of the sky as fast as you can say "target lock".
What makes this extra disappointing is that they also have cosmetic add-ons available in their store, so they could switch to a fairer business model and open up that gameplay-crucial content, but they have so far chosen not to do so.
There is an opportunity to get a brief taste at the wider game should you grind for long enough to buy 'PLEX' on the in-game market, but then after a month you are once again locked out of any higher-tier stuff as if you had spent nothing. Don't go thinking that's something you can easily work for though, as my friend who has played this for about 10 years
is only now looking at being able to become self-sufficient through selling capital ships in order to make the billions of in-game credits needed to upkeep monthly extensions.
Somehow after nearly 15 years this game still has an awful unwieldy UI, where there are keyboard shortcuts missing for simple crucial actions such as launching drones, there is no in-game encyclopaedia listing details of ores, crafting, etc, but you must look at item details one-by-one, and the presets for sorted lists of nearby objects are quite impractical, so that you must rely upon wikis and hacks shared by existing players merely to have a decent sense of what threats are around you.
This is not a skill learning curve. These are fixable UI problems that waste every new player's time. The game actually has a far too shallow learning curve and holds your hand continually through its tutorial of extremely simple combat mechanics, before dumping you into the wild wide world of cutthroat nonsense.

If you forgive the dated graphics, CCP may have inadvertently created a masterpiece of dystopian horror with this game, as its structure projects some of the worst elements of contemporary human society into this galaxy. As a result this means that people who already have a real-world advantage also get one here and can exploit the hard work of the rest of the player base in order to buy the best ships and wreck those same newbs for a laugh. Like the real world, you may still encounter a few good caring people in this game banding together in spite of the competitive structure that encourages being selfish, but the remaining toxic player-base can easily wear you down.

Aperture Tag: Introducing a wonderful game mechanic
The backstory here seems to be set at some indeterminate time (presumably between the two games). You've been awoken from stasis by 'Nigel', who is going to test your use of the paint gun. The story is pretty ok, given that this is a mod. It does a good enough job of setting things up. However, personally, I don't think the story is too important here.
The concept of the paint gun is well thought out, based on one of the original concepts behind the portal 2 game. As far as its implementation, the paint doesn't actually come out of the gun, but just in front of it. A minor note, as once you get used to using it you stop looking at the paint coming out anyway.
I'm still not entirely sure I get the right concept behind the "paint enabling/disabling" fizzlers, but through trial and error I figured it out well enough to play properly.
The levels are well designed, offering a good range of puzzles. There is a very nice mix of old, modern and 'outside' style puzzles. A minor annoyance is the extended time it takes to travel between some of the test chambers through long pipes. The developers probably could have cut that out and not lost any value.
I played using  the keyboard/mouse. It looks like it supports controllers, but it is first person, so I wouldn't bother trying a controller.
The graphics are mostly good. The new assets look very nice in this mod. The gun looks very nice. However, for some reason when I play assets involving 'glass' do not seem to render correctly all the time. Occasionally switching between tinted and fully transparent. This doesn't really give much cause for concern though.
The soundtrack to this is great. Partly done by Harry Callaghan, it captures the style of portal really well, while avoiding being too samey. Voice acting for Nigel was good too.
I completed the game in about 4 hours, so it's fairly short, but there are a lot of community-made maps, and a level creator, similar to the original portal 2 game, so there's a lot more levels to try after completion.
I found no game-breaking bugs in this mod, and there were only a few minor annoyances [like the glass rendering bug], and something seemed a bit off when I was modifying the key bindings in the menu, but that didn't affect gameplay.
This mod is great, and any fan of portal should definitely try it. The paint gun is a great addition. My only request with the mod is it could have done with a lot more of the fast-running parkour style levels.

The Dig is a classic LucasArts adventure game. ...What, you're still here? Geez, you're a tough crowd. Okay, well it's your standard full-talkie puzzle-and-story-driven adventure fare running on everyone's favorite SCUMM engine seen in such games as The Secret of Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle. Unlike those games, however, it uses a much more simplified interface which more closely resembles a typical Telltale adventure. One click fits all, and there aren't a vast many things you can click on in any one screen. Not that there's a lack of things to look at, however. Be prepared for some truly gorgeous alien scenery. And don't forget it - it may help calm you down when you inevitably get stuck. Don't get me wrong, The Dig isn't supermassively hard. But there always seems to be that one thing that just doesn't enter your mind, or something you never think to pick up, or the turtle skeleton puzzle. It doesn't help that you probably only have access to - and the materials to work on - one or two puzzles at any given time. So once you're stumped, there's nothing really to do but walk around as you become increasingly frustrated. This does, however, come hand-in-hand with an immense feeling of satisfaction whenever you complete a challenging puzzle without consulting the Internet, so it's not entirely a bad thing. Overall, The Dig is a little more serious than the LucasArts adventures you may already know and love, but in the long run it's a beautiful game with a strong atmosphere, a decent story, and several interesting and occasionally brain-racking puzzles. If you've played the other classics, The Dig deserves the next spot in your collection.

If a significant portion of your gaming life was not once dominated by the venerable point-and-click adventure genre, it might be hard to understand its appeal.  Because there haven't been a great many modern takes (with some exceptions, like the marvelous Gemini Rue) on the genre, it's easy to miss out on these games or overrule them as 'dated.'
In a way I understand; clicking a character through a set of static screens, searching for clickable or interactable objects, and having an inventory full of objects whose purpose is often unclear could be seen shallow.
But it is not!  This is some of the greatest interactive storytelling of all time.  The Dig is one of LucasArts' crowning achievements.  WIth a concept penned by Steven Spielberg, full orchestral soundtrack and voice acting, rich dialogues and an imaginative premise, this game is in my Top 20 of all time.
In the first 10 seconds of the introduction, it was apparent to me already that this game was trying to be something special.  Michael Land's rich, mysterious soundtrack along with a fairly convincing dialogue (written by Orson Scott Card) go a long way in giving flesh and legitimacy to this science fiction concept originally created by Steven Spielberg.
If you grew up with Sierra's "Quest" titles, or LucasArts SCUMM games like Monkey Island, it's unforgivable to miss this.

I only sampled the Steam version briefly. I have the Pre-order Deadly Six Edition for Wii U, and as an avid Sonic fan, I enjoyed this game well enough to buy it twice. However, your expectations going into this one need to be managed.
Sonic Lost World is another Sonic title that falls into that weird niche that the franchise tends to have with games like Sonic Adventure 1 and Sonic Heroes. However, unlike those two titles, Lost World isn't a broken mess or glitchy as sin to certain players (Egoraptor). I'm not the biggest fan of Adventure 1, or a fan of Heroes at all. But those games have a weird niche and Lost World will fit in there.
The level design, while some say it's like Mario Galaxy even if it's nothing like Galaxy at all, functions as expected. It's fun, well layed out, and allows you to show off your skill like any other Sonic game. The natural signs, such as flowers, to show you where to go are a really nice touch. The level design is some of my favorite in Sonic's history aside from two levels; one in Frozen Factory, I think it's Act 3, and Lava Mountain Act 2.
The soundtrack, while great, is a large step down from previous Sonic games. While it gave me some of my favorite Sonic songs like; Sea-Bottom Segue, Frozen Factory Act 1, Desert Ruins Act 1, Eggman Showdown, and Dragon Dance, overall it's a much weaker OST than Sonic fans will be used to.
The new mechanics of Parkour is something I'm mindblown wasn't incorporated sooner. While it's explained poorly and in a clunky manner, they give you ample room to practice. It's also NEVER required to finish the game. There's no ranking system for default play in this game, but if you master your returning Spin Dash, Parkour, and Double-Jump, you'll be S-Ranking in no time. It's a pretty fast paced game if you're good at it. I'm not, but I've seen skillful gameplay and it's incredible.
Overall, I can recommend this game purely to hardcore Sonic fans, and casual gamers lightly. If you're expecting a fast-paced Sonic speedrun game, look elsewhere. I love this game, but I understand some of the people who dislike it. This is one of Sonic's hardest adventures in a while in an unpleasant manner sometimes, but it's a good game. It's just safe, and not the Generations 2 we wanted. I hope to see Parkour and Precision Platforming incorporated into a new Boost-Style gameplay format in the future.
I'd also like to add that this game wins my award for best aesthetics. If I were to make a game, I'd want it to look this great.

I started playing EVE Online back in 2010 long before it was free. I have played on and off since then.
~ Subscription versus Free to Play:
The game is now "Free to Play" (debatable to some).  And you can continue to play for free.. forever if you wish. You will experience much of the core gameplay within the limitations of the Alpha Clone state. While under the Alpha Clone status you will be restricted to basic access of spaceships, ship equipment, and ship upgrades.
However, if you want to train up and/or access skills beyond the free Alpha Clone limitations then you will be required to upgrade your account to the premium Omega Clone status. Activation is done in monthly installments as per your classic paid MMO subscription services. You can upgrade with real life money or in-game currency (ISK & PLEX). But, grinding in-game currency for premium Omega status can be a whole other job. If your subscription ever expires your Omega Clone skills will remain intact but you will be locked back to Alpha Clone skills limitations and restrictions. So you can resubscribe later and still access your Omega Clone skills and continue building up premium grade skills at a later date.
~ Gameplay:
The game truly shines when you have a group of people to play with. If you have no one to play with then you might eventually find the game feeling stagnate and frustrating. There is large chunks of content and gameplay that can require large groups of players. And due to the "fleet" based mechanics of EVE there is only so much a solo player can achieve. This is much akin to any other MMO with bosses and end game content. This can be a good or bad thing depending on your own social skills and personel gameplay preferences.
On the other hand, if you enjoy market spreadsheets and calculators you could have fun being a solo merchant player and make a virtual fortune. EVE Online is renowned for having one of the most strict and consistent game economies if not the single best iteration of a virtual economy of any game ever made.
Or if enjoy taking screenshots of neat looking space vistas or playing hacking mini games you could have fun being a solo explorer / treasure hunter. If the scanning and probing feature of EVE is something you get into then you could work with others sharing and selling location markers and information.
There is lots to do in EVE Online. But, many players would do well to study and research EVE Online out of game to get a bigger picture of the mechanics of gameplay.

Tales from the Borderlands is a successful adaptation of the Borderlands IP into another epic from TellTale Games. The game is, as always from TellTale, a story-driven, episodic, point & click, adventure game, featuring two playable main protagonists: Rhys, a suave but cowardly businessman from the Hyperion Corporation; and Fiona, a hardened and beautiful con artist born and raised on the Planet Pandora. After things go south for Rhys when his rival steals his chance at the big leagues, and a job for Fiona goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ the two reluctantly team up for one extraordinary adventure that eventually leads them to the spoils of a Vault.
I have a fairly recent computer, still lacking a GPU I’m afraid, and I was able to easily play this game with 720p and high settings. For the unique art style of Borderlands, the game looks great and I can’t recall any times I had lag because of hardware issues.
Thanks to this game being episodic, we get more awesome intro and outro pieces for each episode. However only the finale gets individual songs for its intro and outro, for the rest each respective song plays at the beginning and end of their episode. Other musical pieces featured in the game will perfectly set you into the mood and place on Pandora.
Despite that I had a lot of fun with the main story, I’m a little disappointed we didn’t spend some more time world building. Granted, I’m thankful we got to see more from Hyperion and learn they’re not completely filled with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Learning that there are some genuinely “normal” people on Pandora is great to lighten up the mood for the planet. Before we meet Fiona and her peers, our idea of the common Pandorans were Psychos and Bandits, this game makes that seem like less of the case. Getting back on topic, what I would have wanted to learn more is stuff outside of Pandora. Not counting this, we’ve spent two games on Pandora and one on its moon, Elpis. I would’ve loved to learn more outside of these two. Over all a diaspointment, coming off of the exceedingly well recived Sonic Generations, Sonic Team decided to ignore the cheers of fans screaming they finaly had sonic right again. Instead they gutted almost all of sonics mechanics in place of some poorly implemented Mario Galaxy clone. This game speed is your enemy. Thats right, the main defining aspect of Sonic is now to your detriment. most areas its much better to walk and carefully guage your moves.  Why? well the hex worlds have wonky and inconsistant gravety, sonic floats around with slightly better then ice physics (the ice lvl is actualy somewhat easy due to this) Homeing attack lock ons are unpredictable and now there are TWO kinds of homing attacks, the normal and a kick and you have to figure out what kind you have to use on what. As far as i can tell there are no overt indicators. Wisps are back in force for better or worse with no explination as to how they got there. also wisps control terribly too aside from the rythem and some what drill ones.
Some good points? I love that *spoiler* Robotnik (sorry im an american who grew up in the early 90's thats his name to me)  ISN"T the major bad of the game, he is for the first half then the new group kicks him aside. These guys are actualy a delight and very funny. I do like the LOOK of the new worlds, very pretty and colorfull, and a nice return to badnik robots from the bland eggpods that have infested the series. Music is soild as can usealy be expected form a sonic title though thus far no real stand out tracks. The chalanges to get items you can use at any point in any lvl are also very appreciated.
Honestly rather then trying to chase on the coat tails of Mario Galaxy, Sonic Team should have focused on improving what they already got so right in generations. Refine the formula, give a few slight new mechanics to keep it fresh, and give us a longer more substansial game (love Generations but it was painfully short). It was Sonic Teams chance to regroup and rebuild the franchise. Hopefully they remember this with the next anivercery game coming out which looks to be a generations 2.

A good game, but one that feels more Mario-like, rather than a Sonic game.
The parkour mechanics are neat, although a little tricky to get used to. Certain tasks are only possible while holding the right trigger on controller, which is also the "run" button. This run button isn't a bad concept, but it's definitely one that needs work in Lost World. The game has a sluggish feel to it and, well, even while holding down the run button, you'll be asking yourself, "is this it?"
This easygoing gameplay style calls back to early Mario titles, but even compared to games like that, Lost World feels horribly slow-paced. Some folks have made mods that place Mario levels inside the game, and unsurprisingly, they feel right at home!
The graphics are pretty nice, which is great, because the game runs really well too! However, the art style is a little...weird. Sonic and co. almost feel out of place here, but at the same time the art style doesn't really feel fitting for...anything I've played.
The writing isn't a main focus of the game, but BOY OH BOY is it unbearable. Characters have inconsistent personalities that conflict with how they acted in past games, and the plot feels basic, not very well thought out... I wasn't a huge fan of Sonic Colors' writing, but looking back, it's somehow nicer in comparison to Lost World's.
Sadly, I noticed SEGA took out one of the big features of the Wii U release, and that feature was the multiplayer. A two-player race mode which, from looking at gameplay videos, actually seems pretty fun! But it's completely absent in the PC release. I guess it's understandable why it wouldn't be available from launch, but after over a year, I'd expect them to have made it work by now. Oh well. All I can hope is that modders bring it somewhat back.
Sonic Lost World is a decent game, but feels awfully slow for a Sonic title. If you're not too worried about that, I recommend this game. But to most long-time Sonic fans wanting a true speed boost, you might need to skip past this one.

NOTE: THIS IS A VOICE BASED DEBATE GAME, A MIC IS REQUIRED TO PLAY IT! (obviously)
So this an online version of a popular table top party game. Just like in the card game you play in real life with your friends you get a character card and a set of conditions for that character, then argue with another player over why your character would win the fight.
Much like similar games (IE Cards Against Humanity) it's best played with an audience (and prob while drinking) Which is why this game includes Twitch login and stream support. Once logged into your Twitch account while streaming your viewers can actually participate in the game by casting a vote on who they think would win by using hashtags in the chat. While being a streamer or even having one in your game is not required to play, it does make for a better experience I think when an audience is deciding the winner instead of one of your friends in the game.
Also supports a webcam but this is not required (although does make for a much better experience when you can see the faces of everyone in game and their reactions to the arguments presented)
--Pros--
-Online play true to the source material
-twitch streaming friendly with viewer participation
-lots of card for a variety of super fight match ups
--Cons--
-Only supports twitch streaming participation, no youtube gaming or beam or any other service (yet)
-At first many of the low level matches are the same. As many of the cards are locked behind a level system for some reason. Meaning you don't seeing much variety in the fights and conditions until a few hours into the game
-No filtering option or host controls for online matches. It would be great to blacklist cards that seem to pop up too often and never lead to an interesting argument. I saw Helen Keller way too often and no one ever had a good argument for why she would win. Also be nice to filter the card to have themed matches (only super heroes or pop icons for instance)
-Could use a rule screen or tutorial to help new players learn the ropes, some cards are vauge and could use a better description on how they should effect the match. For instance everytime I got in the match with the "opposite day" modifer card, everyone had a different thought on what that card meant and how it should effect the match.
All in all this game is CRAZY fun and leads to new friendships and hilarious moments! The twitch engagment only adds to the game by making the game fill full of players beyond the 4 on screen, even for the players in the match who arent streaming. If one guy and he has viewers, the outcome of the match just became wildly unpridictable and makes players want to step up their argument cause they know they are being watched.
It's hard to recreate the feeling of being a room full of live people playing an game based on what if arguments, but SUPERFIGHTS pulls it off rather well. The mic requirement forces the same level of person to person interaction you would get in real life with the card game, and the twitch viewer wildcard is a bonus. If you love Cards against humanity or the actual SUPERFIGHTS card game. Or just arguing with your friends about who would win a fight. This is the game for you! If you're just looking for a good drinking game this is the game for you! It's price is set at 10 dollars and its well worth more and the Devs have promised DLC card packs to come (many are set to be free)

Aperture Tag is an interesting mod, lacking some polish and quality. Still, the mod was enjoyable and worth playing. I picked the game up just short of $5US and felt satisfied. The later sections felt weaker, but I wanted more by the finale.
The major criticism is, the game is not "there", not polished and ideal. Voice acting left a lot to be desired. Honestly, I picked it up as a fan of Harry Callahan's music, and a fan of Portal. The music is pretty great, but attaching it to in-level speakers means the volume is very inconsistent. Having your ears blown out by standing near the speakers is realistic, but the difference between max volume and minimum is too much. Maybe it's tied to Source, but I'd like to see the volume rebalanced.
Gameplay has some neat elements, but I think being gel-focused makes puzzles too limited. There were some times I thought "Was that the solution?" as the technique I used didn't seem intentional. Gameplay is less thoughtful than Portal, with more platforming puzzles. Gel is easy to apply everywhere, compared to limited portal surfaces in Portal. The ability to coat most levels in gel allowed several boundary glitches and shortcuts. I was hoping for more interesting levels, as many were very flat in layout, where vertical challenges would've been nice. Workshop support does help to add more content, but that still doesn't add to the story. I feel like there must be more to the storyline, and I'd like more story content added.
As some new Portal mods are coming out, this mod is facing some stronger competition.
is interesting, but still lacks elements to justify a price. Considering the control scheme is a stickied post in their forums, they failed to ease players into the new mechanics.
and
have yet to release, but could be the mods to rival Valve's quality. Aperture Tag approaches Valve's style and still works on its own.
A bit better story, stronger voice acting, and some level fixes would go a long way to make this game greatly appealing. Although the middle-section of the game approached boring, the ending left me begging for more. It's probably 4 hours long for most, with a good price-per-hour and enjoyment value. I'd like to see Valve show some stronger support for the mod, maybe connecting it to an ARG to show some information for Portal 3, but that's just a dream and a wish. But THAT would get me excited. For what is available here, it's decently enjoyable. Understand that it's not Valve's level of polish and quality.

What would portal be like without portals? What would aperture science be like if you weren't the chosen one? The answer to both of these questions is: still pretty awesome. I enjoyed myself the entire way through this game, even with the frustrating bits, and the puzzles were a wonderful mix of fun, challenging, frustrating, and head-scratching.
Even if I thought the audio for Nigel sounded a little low-budget,I love the character. He's just a humble personality core whiling away his time in a tomb-like research facility-come-rube-goldberg contraption, and he's trying to keep himself occupied. So he decides to make use of all the odds and ends left lying around after GLaDOS blew up, so he decides to do what he was programmed to do: test. Only he hasn't quite gotten everything up and running 100% and you have to use the vacuum tubes, and not all the tests are connected to each other. . . Still. It stops him from getting lonely. He's got this endearing incompetence to him that reminds you of Wheatley only nowhere near as dumb, and he's got to follow the rules, sorry about that, but he's not as malicious as GLaDOS.
So the flavour of this is PERFECT, it hits every right note in the Aperture symphony. The psychotic disregard for safety, common sense, reality, scale, scope, proportion, practicality. . . The list goes on and on. The completely nonsensical nature of why it is you're doing what you're doing. I mean, you're pursuing a career in death defiance to test WHAT exactly? bouncy and speedy paint?
The ending is a surprise, but not in a bad way, just a subversion of expectations. Which is NICE once in a while, and it still fits with the flavour of all things portal. . . Kinda tastes like citranium actually.

So all in all, it honestly is a beautiful game but there is no long term storyline, no greater goals, F2P is limited to 1/4 of the game items, and

As a mod developer myself, I'm reluctant to spend money on somebody else's mod since most are given out for free, but I'm glad that I took the time and a small amount of money to give this one a try. While it's not the best mod in the World, it is definitely very well made and a lot of hard work has clearly gone into it.
I don't understand why the mod has been getting as many negative reviews as of late, it isn't deserving of them, in my opinion at least. While I can agree that the mod is relatively easy to accomplish (most Portal veterans would agree) it is still somewhat challenging and brings quite a bit of fun to the table with some of the challenges that it sets out for you, particularly the "escaping" scene which was a lot of fun to do.
I agree that the voice acting isn't exactly the best but there is definitely much worse out there. The dialog is actually quite amusing and a lot of effort has clearly been put into it, so since the guy isn't exactly a professional actor, he should be cut some slack.
I recommend Aperture Tag to any Portal fans that are interested in trying it out. Don't expect it to be up to par with the Portal games themselves because it isn't, but it is still a fun experience and is worth the money.

Tales from the Borderlands is an entertaining adventure that follows a story from two different perspectives. Here you follow Rhys, a worker from Hyperion, and Fiona, a thief that lives on Pandora, as they travel around Pandora to look for a vault.
Those that are familiar with the Borderlands series will find themselves at home, with witty and hilarious writing throughout the game. With that being said, this is not a typical Borderlands game, meaning that you will not be running around as a vault hunter shooting people around Pandora to get loot. Instead this follows the Telltale point and click style of gameplay as the story unfolds.
Those that are new to the series will get a decent introduction to many of the characters and the world of Pandora. While there are some call backs and references that may be missed, there's enough content here for newcomers to enjoy.
As with most Telltale games, there are many choices that you may make that will affect the world of the game. While the story is linear
the choices here will affect the way people in Pandora sees you.
Overall, the presentation, writing, music, and choices are solid. If you are a fan of Telltale or if you are interesting in trying out Telltale games, this is definitely one to pick up.

So a few years ago- before I bought the game on Steam- I was bored one day and decided to play this game.  Originally it was a joke, I was a fan of Naruto and Ultimate Ninja as a kid but as an adult my interest in the show was pretty much nil and the games pretty much met the same fate after a disaster of a romp through the demo back when UNS first came out (to say nothing of what I think of the latter now).  So I booted up the game, watched the opening cutscene, and immediately remembered what it was that I loved about CyberConnect 2.
Ultimate Ninja STORM 3 is an Arena-style Fighting game that, for the most part, is pretty simplistic.  The main draw of this game, as odd as it might sound for a Fighting game, is its story.  Now, probably the biggest problem with Bandai porting UNS 3 specifically is that UNS3, despite originally starting before the events of the series, the game is mostly still a sequel to UNS2, and while the events are referenced and mentioned, it doesn't actually give any real form of a recap.  This in mind, the Ninja Timeline lets you replay fights that took place in the past with descriptions, so if you
find yourself wanting to brush up on the story a bit, the option's there.
One thing that's worth noting about the game's Story Mode is that it represents what, to me, is the biggest selling point for the Ultimate Ninja Storm series: the presentation.  I mentioned above that, before I played this game, I was basically pretty Naruto neutral.  The anime's quality varied too often and had too many episodes for me to want to get back into and I just couldn't motivate myself to read the manga.  I'd say my stance on the series had basically become that of the masses and it was just kind of...there.  Along comes Ninja Storm 3 to practically sweep me off my feet thanks to CyberConnect 2's amazing cinematic direction.  There aren't too many games I can think of that can present their anime titles in such a way that they really feel like their own, that they don't simply feel like a cash-in of a product that was more popular as an anime/manga/LN/VN/take your pick.
The Story Mode has a bit of exploration in between its cutscenes and fights, but for the most part, it's told in the latter two formats- after beating the story you can explore as you wish, so there's no real loss here.  Though, when compared to something like Ubisoft's Rise of a Ninja series, the exploration here definitely feels rather lackluster.  This is something of an unfair comparison, though, as that series was partially advertised for its exploration, but even when compared to the original Ultimate Ninja games (2 and 3 in particular), the exploration feels superficial during the campaign and unintuitive after all's said and done.  However, it rarely lasts for a long enough time that it's particularly boring.
When a fight does take place, you will be taken to a menu that will allow you to ready your ninja tools.  For the most part this is pretty arbitrary and it's unlikely that you'll actually use them, but it's an option.  From here the fight will begin, assuming you aren't given an Ultimate Decision.  Ultimate Decisions are points in the game where you need to make a choice and that choice will affect the fight.  In a very brass tacks sense, this is just choosing the difficulty of a fight and if you know how hard you want it to be, you'll know which one you want to pick, usually.  But this difficulty switch generally feels pretty tangible, and while the choice has no real affect on the story, it does affect the gameplay.
For example, at the beginning of the game you're presented with a choice between saving going to protect the currently-under-fire Leaf Village or investigating the strange masked man that was at the scene.  Should you choose the former, which is a Hero's Path option, you'll skip the first fight with the Masked Man and go straight to controlling the Third Hokage.  In the Legend Path, though, you do both.This decision isn't always as simple as just skipping parts of fights, however.  In later parts of the game, the decision can change the nature of a fight altogether or change it in smaller, more interesting ways.  It's a system that could've been a lot more superficial than it turned out to be but actually adds a bit of replay value to the story.
As for the fights themselves, these are, as stated above, pretty simple.  Combos are generally as simple as either attacking with the one attack button or attacking with the one attack button and also inputting a direction, and you also have a ranged attack and a justsu at your disposal, as well as a Secret Technique.  If you're expecting a complex fighting experience here, there's not really much to see.  Along with the combos being particularly simple, the jutsu (which basically just means technique), is merely a two button process, that's really all there is to the game.  And while this might not sound particularly exciting, the various parts of the gameplay blend together rather nicely.
For the most part, it's a game about maneuverability.  The various arenas in the game can be pretty large, but since you're ninjas you'll be jumping and dashing all over the place, and for the most part this feels pretty good.  Being able to close the distance between someone and create a similar distance between the two of you all while trying to predict who will strike when so as not to use up your substitutions is harrowing.  What are substitutions?  Basically the most important mechanic in the game.  Essentially, substitutions are a regenerating resource that lets you avoid damage by replacing yourself with an object (a log, usually).  Relying on substitutions too much, however, will generally leave you with a depleted resource and no way to defend yourself from your enemy's onslaught.  This isn't to say that substitutions make it impossible to maneuver effectively, as it's generally that type of thinking that leads to prophecies being self-fulfilled, but they certainly do play a major part in one's overall mobility.
Also QTEs.  In Story Mode, after certain events, the game will go into QTE mode and you'll have to enter actions in time as they appear.  Now, most people would generally groan at this, but those who have played the game will probably agree that QTEs rarely see better usage than how they work here.  Once the cutscenes start, it's all gratification the whole way through, and you know you're going to be in for some eye candy if you do everything right.
Now, the problem with this fighting system, and the reason I recommend this game for its Story more than anything else, is that the simplicity of the combat can make it a bit tedious.  Sure, online play (which works well but can be a bit wonky, especially when playing internationally) and local multiplayer is there to entertain you and there are a few small modes outside of the story to keep things fresh, as well as a bunch of unlockables, but all-in-all this is likely the type of game that (after completion) you'll be playing a lot in short bursts rather than for long periods of time.  This isn't necessarily a bad thing but it definitely does leave more to be desired.  I can't help but feel that more in the way of customization or just a little more depth to the battle system could really make the game a far more engaging experience, but after completing the game there really isn't all that much to do and it's basically best to just jump into Ultimate Ninja Storm 4 (because you really don't need to play Revolution.  Really.)

Superfight is an enjoyable and addicting cardgame with two colossal imperfections: a lack of players, and the incessant stream of downloadable content. I love the game. It was fun when I had the chance to play it during beta and early release. But now it's a ghost town.
While not game breaking, releasing five dollar packs - to what was an already strained community - damaged the game more than it did benefit. By actively swaying potential customers, you unintentially killed the game with the periodic release of paid content, which ultimately has culminated into a fifty dollar bundle. For a game that isn't even six months old, ridiculous.
As for the second, and the biggest fault, the active user install base. I would otherwise recommend this game if not for the sole reason that no one plays it. As of writing this review, I have been waiting in the single lobby, by myself, for a little under an hour. No one has joined, and I except no one will. If I were playing during peek hours, maybe there would be a few participating lobbies.
I sincerely hope that the game can make some sort of comeback. Either through going free to play, or by launching a large advertisement plan to entice unaware buyers, or both.
If you're willing to take the plung, I highly suggest you bring in with you friends. Else, you will find the game sorely lacking.

This is a great example of the casual adventure genre.  Yes, it is technically a hidden object type game, but there's variety in the types of puzzles.  You can do hidden object minigames or mix it up with a type of two of a kind card matching game.  There are standard point and click adventure elements, very nice graphics, decent sound and voice acting, and a story that's not too shabby.  The story was decent enough that I was a little bit disappointed that the first one in this series wasn't available on steam.  There were numerous references to events that happened in Enigmatis 1, which is not available on Steam at the time of this review.
This version of Enigmatis, which is actually the Engimatis 2 collector's edition, contains both the main story (about 4 hours long) and a side story that's maybe 1 hour long.  The side story adds a bit of back story to the main, so don't play it until after completing the main game, as it will spoil the few twists in the tale.
My personal opinion on this game, as with all games, is that fair pricing depends on the value you feel it brings.  This game has very little replayability as it is story based with little variation in puzzles between playthroughs.  The story is relatively short, but it is a great example of a short, casual adventure game.  I recommend it, but I wouldn't pay more than $6-7 for it.

There are several negative aspects about this game that often cause frustration and outright boredom throughout. Its glaring flaws include its RNG based system in which victory and reward conditions never guarantee you anything other than a chance at unlocking game content. Another I can mention right off the top of my head is the multiplayer lobby in which not all players appear in your search results for possible team mates; so, you have to rely heavily on finding help and friends   from other sources such as steam and third party sites. PvP was reportedly outright killed by cheaters who edit their save files to make their characters invulnerable to damage with infinite resources. And as for PVE, the AI provides no real challenge to players. It's as if developers decided it'd be easier to equip the AI with a variety of cheats such as extra defenses and damage rather than make an attempt at programming it to respond smartly to player actions. There are known bugs in the game that have gone ignored and will remain ignored what with the upcoming release of DBXV2.
Why would I recommend this game to anyone? Because, for all its flaws, it is a game me, my friends, and my family can play without taking too seriously. And that's all I really wanted and that's exactly what XV provided. It reminds me of why I enjoyed videogames. It contains a decent enough story for players to adventure through on their first go around. And all the side quests known as PQ's provide an opportunity for multiplayer PvE in which gamers can just have a nice, enjoyable, and relaxing time together.
For an RP-themed dragonball game, XV is not all that bad and the aspect I truly enjoy is the fact I am able to customize my own character and deploy it alongside characters of other players.
And, for hardcore grinders, there's plenty of content to unlock. Dozens of skills, several pieces of equipment including Z-Souls for empowering your character, and the big level 99 to achieve a stat total of 300.
So, if you can ignore some flaws here and there and you just want to play something a little more on the casual spectrum of gaming then give XV a go.

Watchers view your arguments and vote for the victor.

I believe this is the fourth time I've attempted to play Dead Island. I always end up losing interest and being irritated by the bugs before I even finish Act II.
I had hoped that the Definitive Edition would fix the things that were stupid--a list too long to go into here--but it didn't. I'm not really sure why the Definitive Edition even needs to exist. It seems to have no purpose other than to bait suckers like me into buying it in the hopes that the awesome game that Dead Island could have and SHOULD have been had finally been released.
I can't think of another game that seems like it could be awesome, and would be awesome if not for stupid bugs and dumb design choices--NEVER auto-equip items to a player's hotbar--holding it back from you actually enjoying the game.
I think people love to hate Dead Island because we see that it could be awesome, but the game-breaking design flaws and completely-ignored bugs show a group of developers who rushed a great idea and didn't care to go back and correct their mistakes.
Not only do I not recommend this game if you've played the original--because it's the same damn game--I don't recommend it if you've never played it. I got it on sale for about $3, if I recall correctly, and I guess if you want to pay that much just to see what everyone hates about it, I can understand.
Dead Island is infamous, and for bad reason. It deserves that infamy, but don't hold it against Dying Light (the spiritual sequel to it). Dying Light is the sequel to what Dead Island could have been.

Got this in a Humble Bundle. I haven't spent very long on the PC version, but I played the WiiU version to the end, and I have spent enough time to say: this is a bad PC port of a bad game. It runs very badly, alternating between stuttering and slowdown everywhere that isn't just 2.5D, despite the fact that it isn't appreciably more beefy than Sonic Generations, which works just fine. The game pauses every time you use a Color Power, which was a concession to switching between the TV screen and the WiiU pad, which doesn't exist in the PC version. This all calls to mind the "well, it's
" mentality that plagued the series between 1998 and 2006, resulting in games which were buggy, unpolished messes at their
points.
And, y'know, it's still Sonic Lost World.
Sonic Lost World is a perfect storm of bad ideas. It is an example of what I've been saying for years, of a problem Sonic Team has which they've had since 1998, namely: they have absolutely no filter for ideas. When they get together to come up with a new game, there's no one on the team who says, "Should we really have a slow-moving cat with a fishing-minigame as one of the playable characters?", or "The 'werewolf' gimmick is kinda neat, but as written, it's not the kind of thing that belongs in a Sonic game", or ... everything about Sonic 2006.
And Sonic Lost World? Sonic Lost World tried to put cram this kind of terrible idea in at least half of the game. Sonic Lost World has a stupid plot in which, among other things, Sonic temporarily has to ally with Eggman, who then proceeds to get in the way of his friendship with Tails, and Sonic is dumb enough to fall for this. Sonic Lost World requires you to grind for collectibles before you can unlock the boss-levels. Sonic Lost World has a level where you roll around in a giant snowball with really awkward controls, and rings and other items stick to the snowball without actually getting collected until you reach a checkpoint. Sonic Lost World has not one, but
levels in which you spend the entire time grinding on rails, but unlike every other 3D Sonic game with rails except Sonic 2006 (funnily enough), the only way to transfer between two rails is to jump, try to maneuver Sonic in midair with something resembling precision, and hope
that you land on the other rail instead of falling between them to your death. Sonic Lost World has a sequence in which Sonic must slide down a half-pipe
the camera, so that you cannot see any obstacles and powerups in his path until there is very little to do about them. Sonic Lost World has a FREAKING STEALTH LEVEL.
One of the other elements which I thought was weird was that the different zones aren't thematically coherent across each act. (I'm referring to the collections-of-levels-under-one-name as "zones" and the individual stages within each collection as "acts" even though Sonic Lost World calls them "Desert Ruin, Zone 2" and so forth.) For example, the acts in the Desert Ruin zone are, in order: 1. a desert, 2. a bee-themed level where you're mostly falling and running downward through a honeycomb, 3. a food-themed level called Dessert Ruin, and 4. another desert. I mean, I'm not saying that all levels within a sequence MUST have the same theme, Mario also has that kind of variety, but in Mario's case the different worlds are numbered, not named; if they come together under a
, you'd expect the name to actually mean something.
But yeah. The bottom line is, don't pay money for Sonic Lost World.

The game starts out innocent enough with your toad eating simple insects to help him grow. Later on as you become larger, the toad will go on a genocidal rage and eat everything in sight. The entire premise is to eat whatever you can so you can grow…and that is it.
This is a basic setup, you eat the enemies that try to harm you and avoid the bombs that fly by because they will harm you, except for the missiles from jets…which is weird. Coins are always floating around that you collect by just putting the target near them. Collect enough and you can upgrade the frog to, among other things, help him grow faster and increase his health. You can also slow down time for a few seconds, if you feel overwhelmed, by hitting the spacebar.
Complete certain objectives in each level and you can unlock pages from the comic to help you understand why our cute but homicidal frog is the way he is.
Now, let’s talk about some pros and cons.
Pros:
-The game is simple to get hold of since it is just a ported phone game. Point and click.
-The style is bright, colorful and humorous. It is a bit comical watching this thing grow into the odd shapes he forms in each stage.
-After beating it in normal mode you can go back to any stage you want to complete certain tasks, or a survival mode to see how long you can last.
Cons:
-It is extremely short. In fact, I can safely say it took me longer to write this review than it took in beating the game.
-You might have a seizure. A lot of the windowed texts and settings shake like crazy for some unknown reason. I’m sure it will be fixed before it is realized, but it strained my eyes pretty bad while trying to read anything.
Overall? It was fun, I received a code on this, so I’m not sure on the cost. If you are into point-and-click games or something to bide your time this does the job pretty well.

I guess there's a lot to say about the game but I'll keep it short for ya'll. If you really want to read some in-depth critisism you can check out the lower part the review. If you just want to know if this game is good for you, just read the short COOL-list up here.
COOL:
+ Tales really captures the Borderlands' iconic mix of action and humour.
+ Dialogue is quite solid, be it in a serious or humorous scene. Has it's off-moments though, but that's to be expected when...
+ ...You have about 10 hours of story going on. Quite a long journey with lots of twists and turns.
+ Which means it's definately worth it's price, especially on sale.
+ It feels interesting to control two protagonists and how your choices on one can benefit/harm the other.
+ Exploring Pandora from a different perspective is exactly what I wanted from this game.
+ Strong female lead characters? Hell yeah, all over the place. Vallory is the BOMB and love Athena as well.
+ Compared to the main series, this game's ending(s?) actually feels more satisfying imo. All nicely wrapped up and makes you rush to the interwebs to see how other people dealt with it all.
+ Handsome Jack
+ Loader Bot
NOT-SO-COOL:
I don't have much to complain about with Tales. It might not be for all Borderlands fans because the experience is something completely different but it does what it wants to do nearly flawlessly. Normally I make a small list but there are only two big gripes that I have, mostly because I like the game so much, so I'm sorry if they take a bit longer to explain:
- Very little "game" going on here. I know that's what most people expect from games like these, but let me explain a little why that's sometimes a problem before you dismiss this review. There is a ton of action to see, and it's all REALLY cool but comes with some problems. It sometimes takes over 20 minutes of 'movie' before you have to do anything, and then it even comes completely without warning. (Making you spill your delicious whatever-you're-holding as you rush to the controls) With this it feels random when you can or can't control things, as you can sometimes go through a bunch of action scenes without pressing one button and suddenly you're in charge of a single dodge or whatever. And on top of that EVERY ACTION in the game is literally just "up-down-left-right and mash the mash button". Come on TellTale, your adventures are supposed to be more on the creative side. On top of that, the game-interface can sometimes really distract you from the cool action or vice versa.
- The thing about strong female characters I said before? I comes with a catch. The catch being that every single MALE lead in the story is either incompetent, evil, insane or a combination of these traits. You don't notice at first, but the more the story progresses the more you see the "Girls rule boys drool" theme that, as the story builds up and I was waiting for Rhys to get some redemption (that never came), the entire story started feeling less genuine and real and more written as a "take that" to some of the more generic opinions about women in games out there.
Two quick examples of how this started to feel weird
SPOILERS. SKIP THIS PART AT YOUR OWN DISCRETION.
- Argually the most badass bunch of scenes in the game; Vallory shows up to capture Athena, Fiona and Gordys. Through this ENTIRE sequence all we see Rhys and Vaughn do is be pathetic in several degrees. Granted, Vaughn is a badass just for surviving on Pandora being the Desk-Monkey that he is, but it still feels... off because while all the girls seem to get some character development and become more badass as the story goes along while the guys.... just kinda stay the same one-note characters they were at the start of the game. Vaughn, who became a 'rebel leader' of sorts, is still as incompetent at the final battle as he was all game. Which was a sad surprise.
- If the last bit didn't make you mad yet, then this might. Fiona... is a Mary-Sue. Yes, yes. I know many people use that argument incorrectly, but let's look at the evidence. No matter what decisions you make, unlike Rhys, NOBODY will start hating her outright, and even distrust is soon waved away. She excells at nearly everything and never messes up, even if she's improvising at something she's NEVER done before. Athena taking her under her wing to become a Vault Hunter feels like a mistake. She was a "Badass Normal" as TVTropes would describe, but then the game hypes her up to be the next Big Vault Hunter because... why exactly? That's never explained. Does Rhys ever get a similar type of treatment? No. He just stays gullible and idiotic all the way up till the finale so they could have Jack betray him again.
I don't know. Seems to me the writers had a definite favourite here. I loved Fiona at the start of the game. Her attitude, her 'lack of skill' similar to Rhys. The game itself made me slowly dislike her though, to the point where when she beat Rhys on the final sprint to the vault all I could say was "Off course she did, can't have Rhys take one little victory even at the end, eh game? Fiona is always on top of everything." When I said that, the feeling sunk in completely and kinda left a bad aftertaste in my mouth about the game in it's interity, and why half of this review is about this gripe of mine.
And that wraps it all up.
So Tales of the Borderlands is a definite recommendation for both Borderlands or TellTale fans, just be aware you might have to sit back for long bits so the game can play itself. If you think the things I mentioned sound good enough but are still unsure of playing this type of game, I really recommend checking it out when it's on sale.
If you have any questions or think I'm being unfair with my gripes let me know. I think I've done quite a bit of thinking and my critisism is fair, but more insight is never a bad thing.
Have a nice day and thank you for reading.
